The Graphersal Documentation

Introduction

Graphersal is an in-memory graph database and traversal engine written in Rust. You ask it questions in plain language or in Gremlin. In the AI chat you simply write what you want to know, and the model of your choice turns it into queries, runs them and answers. Gremlin is the query language of Apache TinkerPop™: start somewhere in a graph, walk along its edges, filter, group and count. Read queries may also be written in GQL, the ISO graph query language (Cypher-like patterns; experimental).

Try it now in the live playground: the real engine in your browser, nothing to install. The source code, releases and issues are on GitHub.

Why Graphersal

AI moves faster than the tools around it. We built Graphersal so you don't have to wait for them: a lightweight, embeddable graph engine you can turn into whatever your AI solution needs — a library inside your application, a tool for your agents, or a full server with your own features on top.

It works out of the box: a browser UI, an MCP endpoint for AI agents, an AI chat where you simply ask about your graph in plain language and it writes and runs the queries for you, durable storage and transactions, and the safety to run queries you did not write — permissions, read-only access, resource limits and timeouts. You start with a working system, not with a list of components to wire together.

A first look

// who created software together with marko?
g.v().has("name", "marko").as("me")
  .out("created").in("created")
  .where(P.neq("me"))
  .path().by("name")

What you get

  • Gremlin, two ways. Build traversals in Rust (g.v(None).has_label("person").out("knows")) or write them as text in the Gremlin DSL, TinkerPop's steps in snake_case or in Gremlin's own camelCase (hasLabel, outE). The text runs the same everywhere: in the browser, in the command line, from Python and through an AI agent.
  • GQL patterns (experimental). g.gql(..) runs ISO GQL queries (MATCH (p:person)-[:knows]->(f) RETURN f.name, INSERT, SET, DELETE, Cypher spellings as aliases) on the same engine, and Gremlin steps may follow. Its subset and answers may still change between versions.
  • A playground in the browser. The real engine, compiled to WebAssembly: write a query, see a table, the graph drawing, the schema and the optimized plan. Nothing to install.
  • A command line tool. One-shot queries for shell scripts, an interactive REPL with completion and help, and a local server that brings the playground UI to a graph on your disk.
  • AI agents on your graph. The server speaks the Model Context Protocol (MCP), so Claude Code or another MCP client can query the graph you are looking at. In the playground's AI Chat tab you ask about your graph in plain language, and the model of your choice writes and runs the queries (experimental).
  • Values with real types. Besides numbers, strings, UUIDs and nested JSON: five date and time types modelled on PostgreSQL (time zones from the IANA database, calendar-correct arithmetic, TinkerPop's date steps), and vectors for embeddings with exact similarity search and quantization (Embeddings and Vector Search is the hands-on tour).
  • Safe by construction. Every traversal is atomic: it commits completely or leaves nothing behind. Schemas (a subset of JSON Schema) are enforced on write and fill create-time defaults. Limits, timeouts and permissions make it safe to run queries you did not write.
  • Durable when you need it. A graph lives in memory, and the Store keeps it on disk: every commit is in a write-ahead log, you can go back to any point in time, fork, roll back, back up and repair. The file format is a public specification.
  • Fast and observable. A rule-based optimizer rewrites each query and answers has() filters from declared property indexes; profile() shows the optimized plan with timings, traverser counts and memory per step.
  • Open for integration. Rust and Python APIs, saved (named, parameterized) queries stored in the graph, change capture with commit hooks, GraphSON and GraphML files, and a storage trait to run the whole engine on a storage of your own.

Graphersal is not a complete copy of TinkerPop. It follows the TinkerPop specification for every step it implements and checks that with TinkerPop's own test suite, but some steps are not implemented yet and a few behave differently on purpose. Each difference is documented where the feature is described and collected in TinkerPop Deviations; see Graphersal and TinkerPop.

Installation

The command-line tool graphersal (the one-shot query runner, the REPL, the dev server and the graphersal store commands) comes as a prebuilt binary for Linux, macOS and Windows, or builds from source with Cargo. The engine is also a Python package and a Rust crate. To only try it, nothing has to be installed: the playground runs in the browser.

Prebuilt binaries

Every release on the releases page has one archive per platform:

PlatformArchive
Linux x86_64 (any distribution, also Alpine and WSL2)graphersal-v<version>-linux-x86_64.tar.gz
Linux aarch64 (ARM64)graphersal-v<version>-linux-aarch64.tar.gz
macOS on Apple silicongraphersal-v<version>-macos-arm64.tar.gz
macOS on Intelgraphersal-v<version>-macos-x86_64.tar.gz
Windows x86_64graphersal-v<version>-windows-x86_64.zip

Each archive holds one directory of its own name with the graphersal binary (graphersal.exe on Windows), the licence files, the third-party licences and README.md. The Linux binaries are statically linked, so they run on every distribution; see Performance of the prebuilt Linux binaries before you benchmark with them.

On Linux and macOS (pick the archive of your platform):

VERSION=0.2.0
NAME=graphersal-v$VERSION-linux-x86_64
ARCHIVE=$NAME.tar.gz
curl -LO https://github.com/graphersal/graphersal/releases/download/v$VERSION/$ARCHIVE
tar -xzf $ARCHIVE                  # unpacks into the directory $NAME
mkdir -p ~/.local/bin && mv $NAME/graphersal ~/.local/bin/    # or: sudo mv $NAME/graphersal /usr/local/bin/

~/.local/bin must be on your PATH; if it is not, add export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" to your shell's start file (~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc).

On Windows, in PowerShell:

$Version = "0.2.0"
$Name = "graphersal-v$Version-windows-x86_64"
$Archive = "$Name.zip"
Invoke-WebRequest "https://github.com/graphersal/graphersal/releases/download/v$Version/$Archive" -OutFile $Archive
# the archive holds one directory $Name with graphersal.exe
Expand-Archive $Archive -DestinationPath "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\graphersal"
$Dir = "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\graphersal\$Name"
# put the directory on the PATH of your user (takes effect in a new terminal)
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("Path", [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "User") + ";$Dir", "User")

Check the download

Each release also has a file SHA256SUMS with the checksum of every archive. Download it next to the archive and check:

curl -LO https://github.com/graphersal/graphersal/releases/download/v$VERSION/SHA256SUMS
sha256sum -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS      # Linux
shasum -a 256 -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS  # macOS

In PowerShell, compare (Get-FileHash $Archive -Algorithm SHA256).Hash with the archive's line in SHA256SUMS (the case of the letters does not matter).

The archives are built on GitHub Actions and carry a GitHub build-provenance attestation, which proves that a file was built from this repository by its release workflow. With the GitHub CLI:

gh attestation verify $ARCHIVE --repo graphersal/graphersal

cargo binstall

With cargo-binstall, Cargo downloads the prebuilt archive of your platform instead of compiling:

cargo binstall graphersal-cli

From source

With a Rust toolchain (1.88 or newer, rustup):

cargo install graphersal-cli      # the binary is `graphersal`

On Linux this build uses the system's C library (glibc) and its allocator, so it is the one for benchmarks and heavy workloads (see the next section). From a clone of the repository, cargo build -p graphersal-cli --release writes target/release/graphersal.

Performance of the prebuilt Linux binaries

The prebuilt Linux binaries are statically linked with musl, which makes them run on any distribution, including Alpine and WSL2. musl's memory allocator is noticeably slower than glibc's on allocation-heavy queries (large group(), path() or to_list() results, imports): measured on the large sample graph, the same queries took 1.07 to 1.39 times as long as with a glibc build of the same source (the most for group() and write-heavy scripts). For benchmarks and heavy workloads, build from source with cargo install graphersal-cli, which uses the system's glibc. The figures in this book come from source builds. The macOS and Windows binaries have no such penalty.

Windows Subsystem for Linux

Under WSL, use the Linux binary: linux-x86_64, or linux-aarch64 on ARM Windows. WSL1 is not supported.

  • WSL2 forwards localhost to Windows, so a graphersal --server started in WSL is reachable from the Windows browser at http://localhost:<port>/ (port 8080 unless you give --port).
  • Keep a Store in the Linux file system (~/...), not under /mnt/c: the Windows drives are mounted over 9p, where fsync is slow, and the store's LOCK file does not protect against a native Windows graphersal.exe opening the same files. Never open one store from both at once.

macOS and Windows security prompts

The binaries are not code-signed.

  • macOS: Gatekeeper blocks a binary downloaded with a browser ("cannot be opened because the developer cannot be verified"). Remove the quarantine flag once: xattr -d com.apple.quarantine ./graphersal. A download with curl or cargo binstall is not quarantined.
  • Windows: SmartScreen may warn when you first start graphersal.exe; choose More info, then Run anyway.

Verify

graphersal --version                      # graphersal 0.2.0
graphersal -e 'g.v().count().next()'      # 6: the vertices of the TinkerPop "modern" sample

The Command Line goes on from here. The dev server (graphersal --server) is a demo and development mode, not for production: see Dev Server and MCP.

Python

The Python package (wheels for Python 3.10 and newer):

pip install graphersal

See the Python Quick Start.

Rust library

cargo add graphersal --features script,io,display

script is the Gremlin DSL as text, io GraphSON and GraphML files, display results as tables; add persist to keep a graph on disk. Library Features lists every feature, and the Rust Quick Start is the first program.

Try It in the Browser

The playground is the quickest way to see what Graphersal does. It is a web page that runs the real engine, compiled to WebAssembly, inside your browser: no server, no account, and your data never leaves the machine.

Start it

rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown                      # one-time
cargo install --locked wasm-bindgen-cli --version 0.2.129     # one-time
playground/build.sh                                           # builds playground/pkg/
python3 playground/serve.py 8000                              # open http://localhost:8000/

The start page offers sample graphs, or a GraphSON or GraphML file of your own:

Pick Modern (TinkerPop): four people, two pieces of software, and who knows and created what. Most examples in this book run on it.

Run a query

Type a traversal into the Query panel and press Ctrl/⌘+Enter. The results appear as a table (also as JSON and as the raw text the command line prints), and the Graph panel draws the graph. Typing . offers every step with its description and a runnable example.

A few queries to start with; Run in the playground under each one opens it there:

g.v().has_label("person").values("name")                       // all people

g.v().has("name", "marko").out("knows").values("name")         // whom marko knows

g.v().has_label("person").has("age", P.gt(30)).values("name")  // people older than 30

g.v().has_label("person").group().by("name").by(__.out("created").count())   // software per person

The Examples menu holds about thirty more, grouped by graph and topic.

See how it ran

With Profile on, every run also shows the plan the optimizer made of your query: each step with its calls, traversers in and out and its time, plus the optimizer rules that changed the plan. Here has_label("person") was folded into the start step (v(labels: ["person"])):

Look at the schema

The Schema panel infers the structure of the data: the labels, their properties and types, and which edges connect which labels. You can edit it, and Freeze as open or Freeze as closed turns it into a schema the engine enforces on every write.

Walk a bigger graph

The File tree sample is a small directory tree: good for recursive traversals with repeat().

What else is in there

  • several query tabs side by side, a history and saved scripts;
  • a graph editor (add, change and delete vertices and edges by clicking);
  • a fast WebGL drawing for large graphs, label graphs and neighbourhood views;
  • saved queries, compression rules and property indexes in the Catalog menu;
  • a Store in memory with commits, marks, point-in-time views, forks and rollback (the Store menu);
  • downloads of the graph (GraphSON, GraphML, snapshot), the schema and the catalog.
  • vector search over embeddings: the Examples group "Embeddings (vectors)" and Embeddings and Vector Search.
  • the green Share link button in the top bar: a link that opens your query together with a small graph, for example in a bug report (Share a query with its graph).

Every feature is described in Web Playground. The same UI also runs against a graph on your disk, served by the command line tool: Dev Server, MCP and AI Chat.

The Command Line

The graphersal binary runs Gremlin queries from a terminal. It has three modes: a one-shot query runner for shell scripts, an interactive REPL, and a local server (next chapter).

Install it from a prebuilt binary or with cargo install graphersal-cli (Installation), or build it in a clone of the repository:

cargo build -p graphersal-cli --release      # target/release/graphersal

One-shot queries

Pass a query with -e; the result goes to stdout and nothing else does:

$ graphersal -e 'g.v().has("name", "marko").out("knows").values("name")'
╭───────╮
│ value │
├───────┤
│ josh  │
│ vadas │
╰───────╯

Without --graph it runs on the TinkerPop "modern" sample. --graph also takes empty, large (about 110,000 elements), tree, a GraphSON or GraphML file, a snapshot or a Store directory:

graphersal --graph people.json -e 'g.v().count()'
echo 'g.v().values("age").max().next()' | graphersal --graph modern     # the query from stdin
graphersal -e 'g.v().has_label("person").values("name")' --format json  # also markdown, mermaid, ...

A query that fails prints its diagnostic on stderr and exits with 1, so a shell script or a CI job can check a graph:

# fails (exit 1) when a server has no owner
graphersal --graph export.json -e 'g.v().has_label("server").has_not("owner").fail("a server without an owner")'

The REPL

Without a query, graphersal starts an interactive shell with history, Tab completion of steps and tokens, and the documentation of every function:

$ graphersal
graphersal> g.v().has_label("person").values("name").limit(2);
╭───────╮
│ value │
├───────┤
│ marko │
│ vadas │
╰───────╯
graphersal> let n = g.v().count().next();
graphersal> n * 10;
60
graphersal> /help values
values  (step, terminal or source method of a traversal)
  values()
  values(arg1: any)
  ...
Yields the values of the given (or all) properties; a jpath() key reads a nested value.

Example: `g.v(1).values("name", "age").to_list()` returns `["marko", 29]`

Variables live across lines: a script is ordinary Rhai code around Gremlin traversals, so loops, functions and maps work as well.

See the plan

profile() prints the plan the optimizer made, with timings and traverser counts:

$ graphersal -e 'g.v().has_label("person").out("created").count().profile()'
Traversal Metrics
Step                                                         Call      In     Out       Time    % Dur
=====================================================================================================
v(labels: ["person"])                                           1       0       4    5.667µs     8.66
out("created")                                                  1       4       4    5.125µs     7.83
count()                                                         1       4       1      125ns     0.19
                                                      TOTAL:             execute:   65.417µs    16.69
=====================================================================================================
Optimizer rules applied: source_filter_pushdown

Keep a graph on disk

graphersal store creates and manages a Store, a graph on disk with a write-ahead log, and every mode opens one with --graph <dir>:

graphersal store create data --from people.json    # a new store from a graph file
graphersal --graph data -e 'g.add_v("person").property("name", "ann").iterate()'   # durable
graphersal store info data

More: The graphersal store Command.

Embedding models

embed() computes vectors from text with an embedder; built in is hash-ngram/1 (lexical only). graphersal embed-model download <repo> fetches a real Model2Vec model from Hugging Face once (the only network access of the tool), and --embedder NAME=REPO (or NAME=<directory>) loads it for any mode, --default-embedder NAME makes it the default:

graphersal embed-model download minishlab/potion-base-8M     # into ~/.cache/graphersal/embed-models
graphersal embed-model list                                  # repository, size, model identity
graphersal --embedder potion=minishlab/potion-base-8M \
  -e 'g.set_schema(g.infer_schema(), SchemaMode.open);
      g.embed_property(#{label: "person", from: "name", to: "emb", embedder: "potion"});
      g.v().has_label("person").nearest("emb", "Marco", 2).values("name").to_list()'

embedder: "potion" picks the embedder by the name given to --embedder (without it the default runs: --default-embedder, else hash-ngram/1); g.embedders() lists the names. The schema then records the model's full identity, model2vec/minishlab/potion-base-8M@fac4fa854e68, the one embed-model list shows: copy it from there when you declare a vector property by hand.

The models directory is $GRAPHERSAL_EMBED_MODELS (or --dir), else the user cache. A model that does not load stops the command with exit code 2 and the reason. More: Embeddings and Vector Search.

Every option of the tool is in graphersal --help and on the Command Cheat Sheet.

Dev Server, MCP and AI Chat

graphersal --server brings the playground UI to a graph on your disk. The browser talks to the native engine in this process instead of WebAssembly, and the same process can open the graph to AI agents.

DEV mode. The server is for local work: it listens on the loopback interface (inside a container on every interface, or where --host says), has no user accounts, and its HTTP API changes without notice. See Listening address and Docker.

The playground over your own graph

graphersal --graph people.json --server --port 8080      # open http://127.0.0.1:8080/

--graph takes everything the command line takes: a sample, a GraphSON or GraphML file (Save to file writes it back), a snapshot, or a Store directory, whose commits are durable and whose history (marks, points in time, forks, rollback, backups) is in the Store menu.

An AI agent on the same graph (MCP)

With --mcp the server also offers a Model Context Protocol endpoint. An agent such as Claude Code then works with the same graph you see in the browser: it runs queries, adds data and evolves the schema through MCP tools, and the page reloads by itself when the agent changed something.

graphersal --graph modern --server --port 9000 --mcp
claude mcp add --transport http graphersal http://127.0.0.1:9000/mcp   # then start a new `claude`

Ask the agent, for example:

  • "Use the graphersal tools: who does marko know?"
  • "Add a person ada, 36 years old, who knows marko." (the browser shows the new commit)
  • "Infer the schema, store it in mode open and add an optional string property email to person."

The agent gets the tools query, the schema tools (get_schema, infer_schema, set_schema, patch_schema, validate_schema, diff_schema, ...), statistics, graph_info, the saved queries, the compression rules and the property indexes, plus the DSL reference as a resource. --mcp-read-only lets it only read, --mcp-token requires a bearer token, and --mcp-query-tools offers every saved query as a tool of its own.

AI Chat in the playground

EXPERIMENTAL. The configuration and the tab change without notice.

With --ai FILE the agent loop runs inside the server itself: the Query panel's + opens an AI Chat tab where you ask questions in plain language. The server sends them to the LLM you configured (Anthropic, OpenAI or an OpenAI-compatible endpoint such as Ollama), runs the tool calls the model asks for on your graph and shows each step: the queries the agent ran, their results, and its answer with tables and runnable queries.

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...                  # the key stays in the server process
graphersal --graph modern --server --ai crates/graphersal-cli/examples/ai-anthropic.json

What the agent queries is sent to the provider you chose; the key never reaches the browser.

Every option, the configuration keys, the safety notes and what data leaves the machine are in Dev Server and MCP.

Embeddings and Vector Search

An embedding is a list of numbers that a machine-learning model computes for a piece of data: a sentence, a document, an image, a product. The model places similar things close together, so "how do I feed my cat?" and "Feeding your cat" get vectors that point in almost the same direction, while "Rust for beginners" points elsewhere. Searching by embedding finds what is meant, not only what is spelled the same. Graphersal stores embeddings as a vector value, searches them exactly with nearest() and similarity(), and combines the hits with everything a graph does well: filters, edges, paths.

Graphersal never calls a model on its own. A semantic model runs in your host program (Python, a server, an MCP tool), which writes the result as an ordinary property value, or registers the model as an embedder that the embed step calls. Built in is one small embedder, hash-ngram/1: no model, lexical similarity only (typos and word forms, not meaning), enough for fuzzy lookup and for trying the steps; the reference page has the details and the reasoning. The graphersal command line registers a real semantic model for you: a downloaded Model2Vec model, run locally.

This page is the practical tour. Every detail (element kinds, metrics, schema rules, formats) is on the reference page Vectors.

Try it in the playground, without a model

Real embeddings have hundreds of dimensions. To see how the steps behave you can make up toy embeddings with three dimensions whose meaning you pick yourself:

AxisMeaning
1animals
2food
3technology

"Training a puppy" is mostly animals: [0.8, 0.1, 0.2]. "Robot chefs" is food and technology: [0.1, 0.6, 0.8]. A question about pets becomes [1.0, 0.0, 0.0].

Every block below is a complete script that starts on the empty graph, so each one runs on its own: the button in the margin opens it in the playground and runs it. The first lines are the same in most blocks: a schema that declares emb as a 3-dimensional f32 vector, and seven documents.

The document graph and a first search

The schema declares the property emb with the format vector. In mode open a list of numbers written to it becomes a vector, so the host can send plain lists (or JSON arrays). nearest(key, q, k) then keeps the k documents closest to the query vector q, best first:

// Toy embeddings with three axes: [animals, food, technology].
g.set_schema(#{mode: "open", vertices: #{doc: #{schema: #{type: "object", properties: #{
  emb: #{type: "array", format: "vector", element: "f32", dimension: 3}}}}}});
for d in [
  ["Cats and dogs",        2024, [0.9, 0.1, 0.0]],
  ["Training a puppy",     2026, [0.8, 0.1, 0.2]],
  ["Feeding your cat",     2025, [0.6, 0.7, 0.0]],
  ["Pasta at home",        2025, [0.0, 0.9, 0.1]],
  ["Robot chefs",          2026, [0.1, 0.6, 0.8]],
  ["Rust for beginners",   2024, [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]],
  ["GPS collars for dogs", 2026, [0.7, 0.0, 0.6]],
] {
  g.add_v("doc").property("title", d[0]).property("year", d[1]).property("emb", d[2]).iterate();
}

// The list was stored as a vector: vector([0.9, 0.1, 0.0])
g.v().has("title", "Cats and dogs").values("emb").next();

// The three documents closest to "animals":
// ["Cats and dogs", "Training a puppy", "GPS collars for dogs"]
g.v().has_label("doc").nearest("emb", [1.0, 0.0, 0.0], 3).values("title").to_list()

nearest() is an exact search: it scores every document it receives (cosine similarity unless a metric is named or the schema declares one) and keeps the best k. The dimension is checked: a query with 2 or 4 numbers against these 3-dimensional vectors is an error, never truncated.

Ranking with scores

To see how close each document is, score it with similarity() and order by the score. project() builds one row per document; anonymous steps take the __. prefix and the order token is written out (Order.desc):

g.set_schema(#{mode: "open", vertices: #{doc: #{schema: #{type: "object", properties: #{
  emb: #{type: "array", format: "vector", element: "f32", dimension: 3}}}}}});
for d in [
  ["Cats and dogs",        [0.9, 0.1, 0.0]],
  ["Training a puppy",     [0.8, 0.1, 0.2]],
  ["Feeding your cat",     [0.6, 0.7, 0.0]],
  ["Pasta at home",        [0.0, 0.9, 0.1]],
  ["Robot chefs",          [0.1, 0.6, 0.8]],
  ["Rust for beginners",   [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]],
  ["GPS collars for dogs", [0.7, 0.0, 0.6]],
] {
  g.add_v("doc").property("title", d[0]).property("emb", d[1]).iterate();
}

// A question about "animals and technology":
let q = vector([0.5, 0.0, 0.5]);
g.v().has_label("doc")
 .project("title", "score")
   .by("title")
   .by(__.similarity("emb", q))
 .order().by(__.select("score"), Order.desc)
 .limit(4)
 .to_list()
// GPS collars for dogs 0.997, Training a puppy 0.851,
// Rust for beginners 0.707, Cats and dogs 0.703

nearest("emb", q, 4) gives the same four documents in the same order without the scores; to have both, search first and project after it: nearest("emb", q, 4).project("title", "score").by("title").by(__.similarity("emb", q)).

Filtered search

Put ordinary filters before nearest(): it then ranks only what passes them. Here only the documents from 2025 on:

g.set_schema(#{mode: "open", vertices: #{doc: #{schema: #{type: "object", properties: #{
  emb: #{type: "array", format: "vector", element: "f32", dimension: 3}}}}}});
for d in [
  ["Cats and dogs",        2024, [0.9, 0.1, 0.0]],
  ["Training a puppy",     2026, [0.8, 0.1, 0.2]],
  ["Feeding your cat",     2025, [0.6, 0.7, 0.0]],
  ["Pasta at home",        2025, [0.0, 0.9, 0.1]],
  ["Robot chefs",          2026, [0.1, 0.6, 0.8]],
  ["Rust for beginners",   2024, [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]],
  ["GPS collars for dogs", 2026, [0.7, 0.0, 0.6]],
] {
  g.add_v("doc").property("title", d[0]).property("year", d[1]).property("emb", d[2]).iterate();
}

// "Cats and dogs" (2024) is left out:
// ["Training a puppy", "GPS collars for dogs", "Feeding your cat"]
g.v().has_label("doc")
 .has("year", P.gte(2025))
 .nearest("emb", [1.0, 0.0, 0.0], 3)
 .values("title").to_list()

A filter is exact: unlike an approximate vector index, a filtered search never returns fewer than k hits when k documents pass the filter. A where(__.out(..)...) filters by the graph around each document the same way.

GraphRAG: a vector hit, then the graph

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) gives a language model the passages that answer a question. GraphRAG starts the same way, with the documents nearest to the question, and then follows the edges: who wrote them, what they are about, which other documents share the topic. Here each document has an author (wrote) and a topic (about). This block has no schema, so the lists are wrapped in vector(..):

// Documents with toy embeddings [animals, food, technology], their authors and topics.
for d in [
  ["Cats and dogs",      "Ada",  "pets",        [0.9, 0.1, 0.0]],
  ["Feeding your cat",   "Ada",  "pets",        [0.6, 0.7, 0.0]],
  ["Pasta at home",      "Ben",  "cooking",     [0.0, 0.9, 0.1]],
  ["Robot chefs",        "Cleo", "cooking",     [0.1, 0.6, 0.8]],
  ["Rust for beginners", "Cleo", "programming", [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]],
] {
  g.merge_v(#{"T.label": "person", name: d[1]}).as("a")
   .merge_v(#{"T.label": "topic", name: d[2]}).as("t")
   .add_v("doc").property("title", d[0]).property("emb", vector(d[3])).as("d")
   .add_e("about").to("t")
   .add_e("wrote").from("a").to("d")
   .iterate();
}

// "What should I cook for my cat?" ~ [0.5, 0.8, 0.0]: the two best hits with their context.
// [#{"author": "Ada", "title": "Feeding your cat", "topic": "pets"},
//  #{"author": "Ben", "title": "Pasta at home", "topic": "cooking"}]
g.v().has_label("doc").nearest("emb", [0.5, 0.8, 0.0], 2)
 .project("title", "author", "topic")
   .by("title")
   .by(__.in("wrote").values("name"))
   .by(__.out("about").values("name"))
 .to_list()

One more hop finds documents that a vector search alone would rank low, but that share the best hit's topic:

for d in [
  ["Cats and dogs",      "pets",        [0.9, 0.1, 0.0]],
  ["Feeding your cat",   "pets",        [0.6, 0.7, 0.0]],
  ["Pasta at home",      "cooking",     [0.0, 0.9, 0.1]],
  ["Rust for beginners", "programming", [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]],
] {
  g.merge_v(#{"T.label": "topic", name: d[1]}).as("t")
   .add_v("doc").property("title", d[0]).property("emb", vector(d[2]))
   .add_e("about").to("t")
   .iterate();
}

// The best hit for [0.5, 0.8, 0.0] is "Feeding your cat"; its topic "pets" brings in:
// ["Cats and dogs"]
g.v().has_label("doc").nearest("emb", [0.5, 0.8, 0.0], 1).as("hit")
 .out("about").in("about").where(P.neq("hit"))
 .values("title").to_list()

The host then turns the rows into the prompt for its language model. In Python this is a few lines (below).

GraphRAG with text: embed_property() and a text query

The same flow without making up any vector: embed_property() embeds every document's title with an embedder (here the built-in hash-ngram/1, which compares spelling, not meaning; a host registers a semantic model the same way) and records in the schema which model produced the vectors. A query then passes the question as text: nearest() embeds it once, with that same model, so the question and the documents are always comparable. Both need a schema attached (mode open or closed):

g.set_schema(#{mode: "open"});
for d in [
  ["Cats and dogs",      "Ada",  "pets"],
  ["Feeding your cat",   "Ada",  "pets"],
  ["Pasta at home",      "Ben",  "cooking"],
  ["Cooking for robots", "Cleo", "cooking"],
  ["Rust for beginners", "Cleo", "programming"],
] {
  g.merge_v(#{"T.label": "person", name: d[1]}).as("a")
   .merge_v(#{"T.label": "topic", name: d[2]}).as("t")
   .add_v("doc").property("title", d[0]).as("d")
   .add_e("about").to("t")
   .add_e("wrote").from("a").to("d")
   .iterate();
}
// Embeds the 5 titles into "emb" and declares {"format": "vector", "embedder": "hash-ngram/1", ..}.
g.embed_property(#{label: "doc", from: "title", to: "emb"});

// [#{"author": "Ada", "title": "Feeding your cat", "topic": "pets"},
//  #{"author": "Ada", "title": "Cats and dogs", "topic": "pets"}]
g.v().has_label("doc").nearest("emb", "feeding cats", 2)
 .project("title", "author", "topic")
   .by("title")
   .by(__.in("wrote").values("name"))
   .by(__.out("about").values("name"))
 .to_list()

The job works page by page and never holds the graph's lock while the embedder runs, so a slow model does not block other queries; a second run embeds only documents added since (Embedding a property). One more hop works as before:

g.set_schema(#{mode: "open"});
for d in [["Pasta at home", "cooking"], ["Cooking for robots", "cooking"], ["Cats and dogs", "pets"]] {
  g.merge_v(#{"T.label": "topic", name: d[1]}).as("t")
   .add_v("doc").property("title", d[0])
   .add_e("about").to("t")
   .iterate();
}
g.embed_property(#{label: "doc", from: "title", to: "emb"});
// The best hit for "cooking pasta" shares its topic with: ["Pasta at home"]
g.v().has_label("doc").nearest("emb", "cooking pasta", 1).as("hit")
 .out("about").in("about").where(P.neq("hit"))
 .values("title").to_list()

More like this

The query vector can come from the graph: take a document's own embedding, label it with as("q") and search with __.select("q"), leaving the document itself out:

g.set_schema(#{mode: "open", vertices: #{doc: #{schema: #{type: "object", properties: #{
  emb: #{type: "array", format: "vector", element: "f32", dimension: 3}}}}}});
for d in [
  ["Cats and dogs",        [0.9, 0.1, 0.0]],
  ["Training a puppy",     [0.8, 0.1, 0.2]],
  ["Feeding your cat",     [0.6, 0.7, 0.0]],
  ["Pasta at home",        [0.0, 0.9, 0.1]],
  ["Robot chefs",          [0.1, 0.6, 0.8]],
  ["Rust for beginners",   [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]],
  ["GPS collars for dogs", [0.7, 0.0, 0.6]],
] {
  g.add_v("doc").property("title", d[0]).property("emb", d[1]).iterate();
}

// Like "Feeding your cat" (animals and food): ["Pasta at home", "Cats and dogs"]
g.v().has("title", "Feeding your cat").as("me").values("emb").as("q")
 .v().has_label("doc").where(P.neq("me"))
 .nearest("emb", __.select("q"), 2)
 .values("title").to_list()

Recommendations with vector_mean()

vector_mean() averages vectors, component by component. The mean of the documents a user liked is a "taste" vector; search with it among the documents the user has not liked yet:

g.set_schema(#{mode: "open", vertices: #{doc: #{schema: #{type: "object", properties: #{
  emb: #{type: "array", format: "vector", element: "f32", dimension: 3}}}}}});
for d in [
  ["Cats and dogs",        [0.9, 0.1, 0.0]],
  ["Training a puppy",     [0.8, 0.1, 0.2]],
  ["Feeding your cat",     [0.6, 0.7, 0.0]],
  ["Pasta at home",        [0.0, 0.9, 0.1]],
  ["Robot chefs",          [0.1, 0.6, 0.8]],
  ["Rust for beginners",   [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]],
  ["GPS collars for dogs", [0.7, 0.0, 0.6]],
] {
  g.add_v("doc").property("title", d[0]).property("emb", d[1]).iterate();
}
g.add_v("user").property("name", "sam").iterate();
for title in ["Cats and dogs", "Training a puppy"] {
  g.v().has("user", "name", "sam").as("u")
   .v().has("doc", "title", title).add_e("liked").from("u").iterate();
}

// Sam's taste: vector([0.85, 0.1, 0.1])
g.v().has("name", "sam").out("liked").values("emb").vector_mean().next();

// Recommended: ["GPS collars for dogs", "Feeding your cat"]
g.v().has("name", "sam").out("liked").values("emb").vector_mean().as("taste")
 .v().has_label("doc")
 .where(__.in("liked").has("name", "sam").count().is(0))
 .nearest("emb", __.select("taste"), 2)
 .values("title").to_list()

Quantization: smaller vectors

An f32 vector takes 4 bytes per component: 1.5 KiB for a 384-dimensional embedding. Declared with element: "i8" it takes 1 byte per component (plus 4 bytes for a scale), with almost the same search results (measured on the reference page). The schema's element wins on write: a list or an f32 vector written to an i8 property is quantized as it is stored, so the host keeps sending what its model gives it:

g.set_schema(#{mode: "open", vertices: #{doc: #{schema: #{type: "object", properties: #{
  emb: #{type: "array", format: "vector", element: "i8", dimension: 3}}}}}});
for d in [
  ["Cats and dogs",      [0.9, 0.1, 0.0]],
  ["Pasta at home",      [0.0, 0.9, 0.1]],
  ["Rust for beginners", [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]],
] {
  g.add_v("doc").property("title", d[0]).property("emb", d[1]).iterate();
}

// Stored as i8: vector([0.9, 0.0992126, 0.0], "i8"); an f32 query searches it.
g.v().has("title", "Cats and dogs").values("emb").next();
g.v().has_label("doc").nearest("emb", [1.0, 0.2, 0.0], 1).values("title").next()   // "Cats and dogs"

The same rule works against you when you quantize a property that is already declared as f32: set_schema/patch_schema to element: "i8" is refused while the stored vectors are still f32 (the schema would not fit the data), and a rewrite with quantize("i8") under the f32 declaration is turned straight back into an f32 vector. Switch the checks off for the migration, rewrite the values, then declare the new element:

g.set_schema(#{mode: "open", vertices: #{doc: #{schema: #{type: "object", properties: #{
  emb: #{type: "array", format: "vector", element: "f32", dimension: 3}}}}}});
g.add_v("doc").property("title", "Cats and dogs").property("emb", [0.9, 0.1, 0.0]).iterate();
g.add_v("doc").property("title", "Pasta at home").property("emb", [0.0, 0.9, 0.1]).iterate();

// 1. Mode "none": no checks, no conversion on write.
g.patch_schema(#{mode: "none"});
// 2. Rewrite every vector quantized.
g.v().has_label("doc").property("emb", __.values("emb").quantize("i8")).iterate();
// 3. Declare i8 and switch the checks on again: the data fits now.
g.patch_schema(#{mode: "open", vertices: #{doc: #{schema: #{properties: #{emb: #{element: "i8"}}}}}});

g.v().has_label("doc").values("emb").to_list().map(|v| v.element)   // ["i8", "i8"]

The playground runs a whole script as one unit, so a failure on the way leaves the graph as it was; from Python pass atomic=True to execute() for the same.

Real models: Model2Vec

The graphersal command line (and the dev server it starts) can run a real, semantic text model itself: a Model2Vec static embedding model. Such a model keeps one vector per token and averages them for a text, so it needs no GPU and no neural network at run time: a small model like minishlab/potion-base-8M (256 dimensions, about 30 MB) embeds thousands of sentences per second on a laptop CPU, and it captures meaning, not only spelling ("car" and "automobile" come out close). It is less precise than a large transformer model, and much faster.

1. Download a model once. This is the only step that uses the network:

graphersal embed-model download minishlab/potion-base-8M

It fetches config.json, tokenizer.json and model.safetensors from Hugging Face into the models directory ($GRAPHERSAL_EMBED_MODELS, else ~/.cache/graphersal/embed-models, on Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\graphersal\embed-models; --dir overrides it), checks the SHA-256 Hugging Face states for the large file and the git blob id of the small ones, and writes a manifest graphersal-embed-model.json (repository, revision, the commit it resolved to, the files with their sizes and SHA-256). A failed or interrupted download leaves no model behind. --revision <branch|tag|commit> pins a version; HF_TOKEN is sent for gated or private repositories. graphersal embed-model list shows what is there:

REPO                           SIZE  LICENCE  IDENTITY
minishlab/potion-base-8M   29.5 MiB  mit      model2vec/minishlab/potion-base-8M@fac4fa854e68

2. Register it under a name. --embedder NAME=REPO (a downloaded repository) or --embedder NAME=PATH (any directory holding a Model2Vec model) works with every mode: a one-shot query, the REPL, --server and its MCP tools, a Store. --default-embedder NAME makes it the embedder embed() uses without #{embedder: ..}:

graphersal --embedder potion=minishlab/potion-base-8M \
  -e 'g.add_v("doc").property("text", "a graph database stores vertices and edges")
        .add_v("doc").property("text", "banana bread recipe with walnuts")
        .add_v("doc").property("text", "traversal queries over a network of nodes").iterate();
      g.set_schema(g.infer_schema(), SchemaMode.open);
      g.embed_property(#{label: "doc", from: "text", to: "emb", embedder: "potion"});
      g.v().has_label("doc").nearest("emb", "how do I query connected data?", 2)
        .values("text").to_list()'

embedder: "potion" names the embedder registered by --embedder potion=..; without it the default runs (--default-embedder NAME, else hash-ngram/1). The text query needs no embedder: it uses the model the schema recorded for doc.emb.

"traversal queries over a network of nodes"
"a graph database stores vertices and edges"

The model loads once when the command starts (a model that does not load stops it with exit code 2 and the reason); the built-in hash-ngram/1 stays registered beside it. g.embedders() lists both, GET /api/info of the dev server too.

What leaves the machine. Only the explicit embed-model download: it connects to https://huggingface.co (or the mirror in $GRAPHERSAL_HF_ENDPOINT). Loading and running a model is local: no text is sent anywhere.

Model identity. Each embedder reports a model identity (g.embedders(), field model): model2vec/<repo>@<12 hex digits>, the start of a SHA-256 over the model's three files (without a manifest model2vec@<12 hex digits>). It names the model, never a path: a copied or moved model directory keeps it, a changed file gets another one. Vectors are comparable only between embedders of the same identity, so embed documents and questions with the same model. embed_property() writes the identity into the schema itself. To declare a vector property by hand, copy the full identity, hash included, from graphersal embed-model list or g.embedders(): a schema naming a model without its hash matches no embedder (the error shows the full identity of the one you tried), so a changed model file can never quietly mix its vectors with the old ones.

Licences. A model's licence is the model's own, set by whoever published it (see its Hugging Face page); Graphersal downloads and runs it but does not license it. potion-base-8M is MIT licensed. A download keeps the model card (README.md), the repository's licence files and the licence id beside the model, and warns about an unknown or non-commercial licence or a gated repository; embed-model list shows the licences.

A model inside a store. graphersal embed-model download minishlab/potion-base-8M --into data/ puts the model into the Store data/ instead: whenever the store is opened, its models are loaded without --embedder, and every copy of the store carries them with their licences (see Embedding Models in a Store).

The Rust library has the same embedder as graphersal::vector::Model2Vec (feature model2vec, native targets; it loads from a local directory only), see Vectors.

With real embeddings (Python)

With a real model the steps stay the same; only the vectors get longer. This example uses sentence-transformers and the small model all-MiniLM-L6-v2, which gives 384 numbers per text and runs on a laptop CPU (pip install graphersal sentence-transformers):

import graphersal
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")      # 384 dimensions

graph = graphersal.Graph()
graph.set_schema({
    "mode": "open",
    "vertices": {
        "chunk": {"schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {
            "text": {"type": "string"},
            "emb": {"type": "array", "format": "vector", "element": "f32",
                    "dimension": 384, "metric": "cosine"},
        }}},
    },
})

# The host's data: documents cut into chunks, plus the topics each document mentions.
docs = [
    {"title": "Cat care", "topics": ["pets", "health"], "chunks": [
        "Cats need fresh water every day.",
        "Most adult cats do well on two meals a day.",
    ]},
    {"title": "Weeknight pasta", "topics": ["cooking"], "chunks": [
        "Salt the pasta water generously.",
    ]},
]

for doc in docs:
    graph.execute('g.add_v("doc").property("title", title).iterate()', params={"title": doc["title"]})
    for topic in doc["topics"]:
        graph.execute(
            'g.merge_v(#{"T.label": "topic", name: topic}).as("t")'
            '.v().has("doc", "title", title).add_e("mentions").to("t").iterate()',
            params={"title": doc["title"], "topic": topic},
        )
    embs = model.encode(doc["chunks"])               # numpy float32, shape (n, 384)
    for text, emb in zip(doc["chunks"], embs):
        graph.execute(
            'g.v().has("doc", "title", title).as("d")'
            '.add_v("chunk").property("text", text).property("emb", emb)'
            '.add_e("part_of").to("d").iterate()',
            params={"title": doc["title"], "text": text, "emb": emb},
        )

A one-dimensional float32 numpy array passed in params arrives in the script as an f32 vector (so does a graphersal.Vector(values), built from a list or a buffer); the extension reads it through memoryview and does not depend on numpy. A list in params is not supported: wrap it in graphersal.Vector(..).

The search embeds the question with the same model and passes it as a parameter:

question = "How often should I feed my cat?"
q = model.encode(question)

hits = graph.query("""
    g.v().has_label("chunk").nearest("emb", q, 3)
     .project("text", "score")
       .by("text")
       .by(__.similarity("emb", q))
     .to_list()
""", params={"q": q})
# a list of dicts, best first: [{'text': '...', 'score': ...}, ...]

GraphRAG from Python

The context for the language model is the hits plus what the graph knows about them, in one query:

rows = graph.query("""
    g.v().has_label("chunk").nearest("emb", q, 3)
     .project("text", "doc", "topics")
       .by("text")
       .by(__.out("part_of").values("title"))
       .by(__.out("part_of").out("mentions").values("name").fold())
     .to_list()
""", params={"q": q})

context = "\n".join(f"[{r['doc']}; topics: {', '.join(r['topics'])}] {r['text']}" for r in rows)
prompt = f"Answer from this context only.\n\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}"
# send `prompt` to the language model of your choice

To let an AI agent (an MCP client or the playground's AI Chat on the dev server) run the search itself, store it as a saved query whose parameter is the vector; the agent still needs the question's embedding from a tool of the host:

graph.define_query({
    "name": "semantic_search",
    "params": {
        "q": {"schema": {"type": "array", "format": "vector", "dimension": 384}},
        "k": {"schema": {"type": "integer"}, "default": 5},
    },
    "body": 'fn semantic_search(q, k) { g.v().has_label("chunk").nearest("emb", q, k).values("text") }',
})
graph.call_query("semantic_search", {"q": graphersal.Vector(q), "k": 2})

When the host registers its model as an embedder and the documents were embedded with embed_property(), the schema knows the model, and the parameter can be the question itself: nearest("emb", question, k) with params: {"question": "string"} embeds it with that model, so the agent needs no embedding tool at all. From Python that is graphersal.Embedder("minilm", model.encode, dimension=384, model="sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2") in Graph(embedders=[..]), then graph.embed_property(label="chunk", source="text", target="emb") (Python Quick Start: Embedders).

Any model works. OpenAI, Cohere, Ollama or a model of your own: an embedding is just a list of numbers. Keep the schema's dimension equal to the model's, embed documents and questions with the same model, and pick the metric the model is meant for (most text models: cosine).

Sizing and performance

nearest() scores every element it receives, with no index to build or keep up to date, so its time grows with the number of vectors times the dimension. The measured numbers (10 000 vectors of 384 dimensions) show that this is fast enough for most in-memory graphs; a filter before the search scores fewer, and an i8 property takes a quarter of the memory. There is no approximate (ANN) index yet (Current Limitations).
