Workload Statistics

A graph instance keeps statistics of what was done with it: which scheduled jobs ran and how long they took, how long writers held the graph's lock, which queries ran, and which properties they used and how. They describe the instance, not the data: they are not versioned with the graph, never written to the journal, and never part of a commit, so they do not move with a rollback and are not replicated.

Levels

LevelWhat is kept
offnothing
memoryin memory, gone with the process
persisted (default)in memory, and in the Store's sidecar file WORKLOAD, read back when the store opens

The level is set when a store is opened (StoreOptions::with_workload_level); it is not stored. Switching to off keeps what was collected; only clearing deletes it.

Time buckets

Every series keeps three tiers of buckets, like a round-robin database:

  • one bucket per minute for the last 60 minutes,
  • one per hour for the last 48 hours,
  • one per day for the last 90 days.

Each bucket counts the occurrences, the failed ones, the items they touched, their total and their longest duration. The sidecar keeps all three tiers, so a restart loses none of them; buckets that aged past their window while the process was stopped fall out at the next sample.

Channels

Every sample is counted under the channel of the work that produced it, so the report says who runs what (which queries the AI agents run, which ones the page):

ChannelWork
playgroundqueries run from the browser playground (in the page, or over the dev server)
mcpthe MCP endpoint's tools and the AI Chat's agent
clithe command line: one-shot scripts and the REPL
pythonthe Python binding
jobthe actions of scheduled jobs
hostanything else (an application embedding the library)

Only a user's queries count. The work a front end makes up itself (drawing the Graph panel, the inspector, schema inference, the panels' lists) is technical and not counted. A host declares its channel around the work it does for a request with graphersal::workload::scope(channel, technical, || ..), or once for a thread that serves one front end with set_thread_default(channel, technical); a front end that marks its own work technical runs a user's query in scope(current_channel(), false, ..). Scopes nest, and a job's run is always job.

The graph's lock

The graph has one writer lock: a writer excludes readers and other writers. To see whether it is a problem, three series measure it under the channel of the work that took the lock:

SeriesWhat it measures
write.waita writer asking for the lock until it holds it (contention)
write.holda writer holding the lock (what readers and other writers wait for)
read.waita reader waiting because a writer holds the lock (an uncontended read is not counted)

Each bucket has the count, the total and the longest time, so the mean and the worst wait are at hand. A Store attaches its statistics to its graph; a graph of your own counts after Graph::attach_workload_stats(stats). Work a front end marks as technical (its own drawing and panel queries) is not counted.

Queries

Every run of a traversal on a graph with statistics (GQL included: it runs the same pipeline) counts in the series of its fingerprint: the optimized plan, as .profile() names its steps, with every literal replaced by ?. g.v().has("name", "ann").values("age") and the same query for "bob" are one series, v().has(?, ?).values(?); a list of literals is one ?. Each run adds its result count (with bulk), its duration and whether it failed. A saved query call counts once more as saved:<name> (the call itself; the traversal it returns counts under its plan when it runs). At most 500 query series are kept: a new one beyond that replaces the one run least in the last 90 days. Like pg_stat_statements in PostgreSQL, this answers "which queries run, how often, how long", by channel (which ones the AI agents run).

Properties

The same run also counts, per property, how the plan used it: series (element, label, key, access), each counted once per run with the number of traversers that reached the step using it. The access is one of

AccessSteps
filter_scanhas(key, ..), has(key), has_not(key), has(key, __.to_lower()...), a has folded into v()/e()
filter_indexthe same filters when a property index serves them
readvalues, properties, value_map, element_map, a by(key) of project/select/path/tree
order_groupa by(key) of order, group, group_count, dedup
similaritysimilarity, nearest, embed
write / removeproperty, add_v/add_e properties / remove_property

The element kind and label are what the plan states before the step (v(labels), e(labels), has_label, out_e(labels), add_v(label)); a step that reads every property (value_map(), element_map()) names the key *, and a use inside a child traversal (where(__.out().has("lang"))) has no element, no label and no traverser count. A jpath key counts under its top-level property. These counts answer "which properties are filtered without an index, which are only written, which are read at all": the input of the planned storage advisor.

Memory

The statistics stay bounded (at most 500 query series, at most 60 + 48 + 90 buckets per series, only buckets in which something was counted). Their memory is shown as workload_bytes in g.memory_usage(), in the dev server's and the playground's statistics (Profile ▸ Statistics, Workload statistics), never added to the graph's total_bytes.

The sidecar

A writable store writes WORKLOAD once a minute (the system job stats_flush, see Scheduled Jobs) and when it closes. After an orderly stop nothing is lost; after a crash at most the last minute. The file is best effort: a missing or damaged file means the statistics start anew, never damage, and the store opens as usual. It is never copied into a backup, a fork or a repaired store: a restored store starts without statistics. Its byte layout is section 4.4 of the format specification.

A backup opened read-only, a read-only or maintenance-mode store keeps statistics in memory only.

Reading them

Front endHow
playgroundOptimize ▸ Workload: tables with a sparkline per row and a chart per series (Optimize)
REPL (--graph <store>)/workload: one line per series, last 90 days
dev serverGET /api/workload (the JSON below)
MCPtool workload_statistics {max_rows} (at most 50 rows per list by default)
Pythonstore.workload_report() (a dict)
Ruststore.workload_stats().report(now), WorkloadReport::to_property() / to_json() / Display

The JSON form (WorkloadReport::to_json) has the keys level, queries (query), properties (element, label, key, access), locks (lock) and jobs (name, last_run); every row has its channel and the windows last_hour, last_two_days and last_ninety_days, each with count, failed, items, total_micros and max_micros. Rows are sorted by total time over 90 days. A graph outside a store answers level off with empty lists.

History. Asked with a tier (?history=minutes|hours|days on the dev server, the MCP tool's history, Python's workload_report(history="hours"), Rust's report_with_history(now, HistoryTier::Hours)), the report adds history_tier and gives every row its history: the buckets of that tier within its window (the last 60 minutes, 48 hours or 90 days), oldest first, only those in which something was counted, each {start, count, failed, items, total_micros, max_micros} with start in microseconds since the Unix epoch. That is the data of a chart: how often a query ran and how long it took, minute by minute or day by day.

use graphersal::persist::{MemDir, Store, StoreOptions};
use graphersal::workload::{Channel, Sample, SeriesKey, SeriesKind};

let dir = MemDir::named("memory:stats");
let store = Store::create(&dir, StoreOptions::new()).unwrap();
let stats = store.workload_stats();
let now = 1_800_000_000_000_000; // microseconds since the Unix epoch
stats.record(
    SeriesKey::new(SeriesKind::Lock("write.hold".into()), Channel::Cli),
    now,
    Sample::new(10, 250),
);
let report = stats.report(now);
assert_eq!(report.series[0].last_hour.count, 1);
store.close().unwrap(); // writes WORKLOAD

Optimize

The storage advisor turns what the engine already measures into concrete advice: the memory report (what the graph holds), the workload statistics (how it is used) and the catalog. Every recommendation names the ordinary catalog command that applies it, a savings figure measured on the data where one can be measured, its cost, its impact and how sure the advisor is. Nothing is applied automatically, and every action of this version can be undone (drop the index or the rule again).

The recommendations

KindWhenEffect
create an indexa (label, key) filtered by a full scan at least 10 times in two days, on a label of at least 1,000 elements, with no index serving it and values an index holdsthe scans become index lookups; the index takes memory (estimated)
drop an indexno query used the index in the time observed, after at least 7 days of statisticsfrees the index's memory (measured)
compress or deduplicatea top-level string property of at least 256 KiB without a rule, not indexed, read fewer than 1,000 times in two days, whose best codec (lz4 or dedup) saves at least 64 KiB and 20 %frees memory, measured by estimate_compression with the rule's own code
stop compressinga compressed key read at least 1,000 times in two daysreads stop decompressing; memory grows back (measured)

Every recommendation has an impact, what applying it is worth, and a confidence, how much data its figures rest on: the two are separate, so a saving measured exactly on all the data (confidence high) can still be worth little (impact low).

KindImpact highImpact mediumImpact low
compress or deduplicate, drop an indexfrees 10 % of the graph's memory or morefrom 2 %below 2 %
create an indexits scans read 100 million elements or more in two daysfrom 10 millionbelow
stop compressingread 100,000 times or more in two daysfrom 10,000below

The graph's memory is its estimated total footprint (the memory report's totals). A saving of 6 MiB in a graph of 700 MiB (under 1 %) is advised with impact low.

The list is ordered by impact, the highest first; within one impact new indexes come first (by the elements their scans read), then compression by bytes saved, then unused indexes and hot compressed keys. The thresholds can be lowered: Every candidate in the playground, everything: true in the API, or each threshold on its own. Without workload statistics (a graph outside a store) only the data is looked at, so there is no index advice.

Dismissing, and what an applied one did

A recommendation can be snoozed for 7 days or dismissed for good; it is then listed under Dismissed (with Restore) until its time. Applying one records the memory before and what it promised: for 30 days the advice lists it under Applied with the memory freed (or taken) since, measured on the graph's property and property index memory (other changes of the data in the meantime count too), and for a new index the indexed lookups of its key. Dismissals and these records are settings of the instance, not data: they are kept in the store's workload statistics sidecar and need a store.

In the playground

The top bar's Optimize opens one panel with three tabs:

  • Recommendations: each with its impact, its evidence, cost, memory effect (with its share of the graph's memory), confidence and the exact command; Apply runs it (one commit, recorded in the change feed like any catalog change), Copy copies the command, Snooze 7 days and Dismiss hide it; below the list, Applied (the outcomes) and Dismissed (with Restore).
  • Workload: the workload statistics as tables (queries, properties, locks, jobs) for a window (the last hour, 2 days or 90 days) and a channel, with a sparkline of the runs per row; a row opens its chart: runs per minute, hour or day with the failed part, and the mean and the longest time.
  • Memory: the memory report: the totals, then the properties and the labels, the most bytes first, with what is compressed, indexed or a vector.

Other front ends

Front endHow
dev serverPOST /api/advise with the thresholds ({}: the defaults); POST /api/advise/apply {id, spec} applies one by its id; POST /api/advise/dismiss {id, days?} and POST /api/advise/restore {id}
MCPtool advise {everything} (reading, also in read-only mode); the agent applies a recommendation with create_index, drop_index, define_compression or drop_compression when the user asks
RustGraph::advise(&AdviceRequest), module graphersal::advisor
use std::sync::Arc;
use graphersal::advisor::AdviceRequest;
use graphersal::prelude::*;
use graphersal::workload::{WorkloadLevel, WorkloadStats};

let graph = GraphSource::tinkerpop_modern();
graph.attach_workload_stats(Arc::new(WorkloadStats::new(WorkloadLevel::Memory)));
for _ in 0..3 {
    let found = graph.read().traversal().v(None).has_label("person").has("name", "josh").to_list();
    assert_eq!(found.unwrap().len(), 1);
}
// The modern graph is tiny: every candidate.
let advice = graph.advise(&AdviceRequest::everything()).unwrap();
let index = advice
    .recommendations
    .iter()
    .find(|r| r.id == "create_index:vertex:person:name")
    .unwrap();
assert_eq!(index.action.command(), r#"g.create_index(#{label: "person", key: "name"})"#);

The JSON form (Advice::to_json, the answer of every front end) has workload_level, observed_since, commit_seq, property_bytes, graph_bytes (the memory impact is measured against), estimates and recommendations, each with id (stable: the kind and the target), kind, element, label, key, title, evidence, cost, memory_bytes (freed; negative when it takes memory), measured, impact and confidence (each low, medium or high), reversible, command and action (the catalog change as fields); then dismissed (id, title, until: null for good) and applied (id, kind, title, at, promised_bytes, measured_bytes, index_lookups), and memory_bytes, the figure the outcomes are measured on.

Scheduled Jobs

The engine runs background work on a schedule: jobs with a standard 5-field cron schedule (minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week, e.g. */5 * * * * for every five minutes, 0 3 * * * for 03:00 every day; ranges 1-5, steps */15, lists 1,15, names jan/mon). Times are wall-clock times in the instance's local time zone.

Who drives the clock

The engine owns no thread: the host calls the scheduler's tick periodically with the current time, and the scheduler runs the jobs that are due.

HostTicks
Dev server (graphersal --server)a thread, every 5 seconds, in the machine's time zone (TZ or /etc/localtime)
Browser playgrounda timer in the engine's worker, every 5 seconds, in the browser's time zone
Your own programcall Scheduler::tick(now) yourself

The CLI (a script or the REPL on a store) and the Python binding do not tick: a store opened there runs no jobs (its workload statistics are still written when it closes). Open the store with the dev server, or tick a Scheduler in your own program, to run them.

Daylight saving time. A schedule is read in the local wall clock. A time that does not exist on the day the clocks go forward (02:30 in most of Europe) runs right after the gap (03:00); a time that happens twice when they go back runs once, at its first occurrence.

A job never overlaps itself: due jobs run one after another. A time missed while nothing ticked (the process was stopped) is skipped: the job runs at its next scheduled time. A failing job (an error, a panic) is recorded and runs again at its next time.

Limits per run

A job may limit each of its runs: a timeout and a memory limit (JobLimits, both optional). The engine cannot interrupt arbitrary code, so the limits reach the checks every traversal already makes: while the job runs, its remaining time caps each traversal's evaluationTimeout and its memory limit caps memory.limit (a query's own stricter value stays). A breach fails the traversal as any timeout or memory limit does, its work is rolled back, and the run is recorded as failed with the reason. An action doing long work of its own checks limits.timeout itself; if it finishes past its timeout anyway, the run is recorded as over time.

System jobs

A Store brings its system jobs (Store::system_jobs()):

JobScheduleDefaultWhat it does
stats_flushevery minuteonwrites the workload statistics to the sidecar
compact03:00 dailyoffreleases spare capacity of the in-memory structure

System jobs cannot be removed; their schedule and switch can be changed (the playground's and the dev server's job list, POST /api/jobs/schedule and /api/jobs/enable, or WorkloadStats::set_job_override in your own program). The change is a setting of the instance, not of the graph: it is kept in the store's workload sidecar (at the level persisted, the default), so it survives a restart but is not carried by a backup or a fork. Every run (start, duration, error) is recorded in the workload statistics.

Jobs of users

A user's job is a catalog definition (kind job, beside saved queries, compression rules and property indexes): it is versioned with the graph, written to the journal, carried by checkpoints, backups and the catalog file. Its action is one of

ActionWhat a run does
querycalls a saved query with fixed arguments
checkpointwrites a checkpoint of the store
backupbacks the store up into a directory (the first run a full backup, the next ones increments)
g.define_query(#{name: "purge", params: #{label: "string"},
    body: "fn purge(label) { g.v().has_label(label).drop() }"});
g.define_job(#{name: "nightly_purge", schedule: "0 3 * * *", action: "query",
    query: "purge", args: #{label: "software"}, timeout_ms: 30000});
g.jobs().map(|j| [j.name, j.schedule, j.action])

g.define_job(#{name, schedule, action, query?, args?, path?, enabled?, timeout_ms?, memory_limit?, run_on?, description?}) defines or replaces a job, g.jobs() lists them, g.drop_job(name) removes one. The arguments are checked against the query's parameters when the job is defined.

Rights. A job runs with the rights of whoever defined it. When it is defined, the definer's authorizer is asked for everything the job will do: Execute on the saved query and every data write the query may make, Create on the backup directory; the allowed requests are stored with the job as its effects, and every run may do exactly them (and read). If the query is changed later to write more, its runs are refused until the job is defined again. Revoking the definer's rights later does not stop a job until it is redefined (the engine has no identities; an embedding server that has them re-checks on every run). A browser playground cannot define a backup job: its pages have no files.

A job of a newer version (an action this version does not know) is kept as it was written and never run; g.jobs() lists it with served: false and the reason.

Running. The jobs of a store's catalog run on the store's scheduler beside its system jobs: the dev server and the playground pick up a defined, changed or dropped job at their next tick. A query job's run is one transaction whose commit metadata carries job: <name> (the change feed and the history name the job), its queries count under the channel job of the workload statistics, and its limits per run apply. A run that fails (a write outside its effects, a timeout, an error of the query) changes nothing and is recorded with its error; the job runs again at its next time. A job on a graph outside a store is kept but not run (there is no scheduler). In your own program, give the scheduler the store's user jobs and sync them whenever the catalog's jobs changed. Store::user_jobs lists the job definitions it does not schedule beside them, each with the reason (an action or run_on this version does not know, run_on: "replica" on a single instance, a stored schedule that does not parse), so none is dropped silently:

let found = store.user_jobs()?;
for skipped in &found.not_scheduled {
    eprintln!("job {} is not scheduled: {}", skipped.name, skipped.reason);
}
scheduler.sync_user_jobs(found.jobs);

In the playground, Catalog ▸ Scheduled jobs lists every job (the system jobs first) with its schedule, the next and the last run (with its error), the runs of the last two days and a switch; a job of yours has Run now, Edit and Drop, a system job Run now and Schedule (empty: its built-in schedule again). New job opens the form: the name, what it does (a saved query with its arguments as JSON, a checkpoint, a backup directory), the schedule (5-field cron, with presets), on or off, a timeout and a description; a refused job shows the engine's message next to the field.

History. Every run (start, duration, error) is counted in the workload statistics as series job per minute, hour and day: the job list shows the runs of the last two days, Optimize ▸ Workload ▸ Jobs draws them over time, GET /api/jobs/history?name=..&tier=.. answers the buckets.

Front ends. The dev server and the playground share one job API (graphersal-session):

Dev serverWhat it does
GET /api/jobsevery job: the system jobs, then the jobs of users: schedule, on or off, next time, last run, the run counts of the last hour, two days and 90 days, whether it runs (and why not), a user job's action, arguments and effects
POST /api/jobs/definedefines or replaces a job from the keys of g.define_job; a refused job answers the wrong fields
POST /api/jobs/drop{name}: removes a job of a user
POST /api/jobs/enable{name, enabled}: switches a job on or off (a user job's definition keeps its effects)
POST /api/jobs/schedule{name, schedule}: a system job's schedule (null: the built-in one); a user job is defined again instead
POST /api/jobs/run{name}: runs a job now, whatever its schedule
GET /api/jobs/history?name=..&tier=minutes|hours|daysthe job's runs per minute, hour or day: count, failures, total and longest time

The dev server's user owns the machine's files, so a backup job defined there may name any directory; the browser playground has no files and refuses backup jobs.

In your own program

use graphersal::jobs::{Job, JobKind, JobLimits, Scheduler};
use graphersal::persist::{MemDir, Store, StoreOptions};

let dir = MemDir::named("memory:jobs");
let store = Store::create(&dir, StoreOptions::new()).unwrap();
let mut scheduler = Scheduler::new()
    .with_time_zone("Europe/Berlin")
    .unwrap()
    .with_stats(store.workload_stats());
for job in store.system_jobs() {
    scheduler.add(job).unwrap();
}
scheduler
    .add(
        Job::new("hello", JobKind::User, "0 * * * *".parse().unwrap(), |run| {
            let _started = run.started_at; // your work; traversals here get the limits below
            Ok(())
        })
        .with_limits(JobLimits::new().with_timeout(std::time::Duration::from_secs(30))),
    )
    .unwrap();
let now = 1_800_000_000_000_000; // microseconds since the Unix epoch
scheduler.tick(now); // plans the first runs; call it again every few seconds
assert_eq!(scheduler.jobs().len(), 3);

Embedding Models in a Store

Vectors made by a real embedding model are only useful with that model: a text query (nearest("emb", "a question", 5)) embeds its text with the model the schema recorded for the property (model2vec/<repo>@<12 hex digits>, see Which model produced a property). A Store can keep the models it needs inside it, beside the graph, so the store opens with its model wherever it goes: on another machine, from a backup, after a fork.

Putting a model into a store

A model enters a store only by an explicit command, never on its own:

graphersal store create data/
graphersal embed-model download minishlab/potion-base-8M --into data/
graphersal embed-model import ./my-model --into data/ --repo acme/my-model --license mit

download --into fetches the model from Hugging Face (as embed-model download does, plus its model card, its licence files and its metadata) and puts it into the store instead of the models directory. import puts a local Model2Vec directory (a download, or any directory with config.json, tokenizer.json and model.safetensors) into the store; --repo names its repository when the directory has no manifest (the repository is part of the model identity), --license its licence. Both load the model once as a check. The store must be closed (a server holding it open keeps its writer lock).

In a program: Store::add_model(NewModel::new().with_file(..).with_repo(..).with_license(..)) on an open store, Store::add_model_dir on a closed one.

Opening a store loads its models

When a store is opened (graphersal --graph data/, the dev server, Python Store.open), every model the store keeps is registered as an embedder (under its repository name, minishlab/potion-base-8M; a model the schema names under the identity the schema records), so text queries and embed_property() work without --embedder:

graphersal --graph data/ -e 'g.embed_property(#{label: "doc", from: "text", to: "emb", embedder: "minishlab/potion-base-8M"})'
graphersal --graph data/ -e 'g.v().has_label("doc").nearest("emb", "connected data", 3).values("text").to_list()'

An embedder you register yourself for the same model wins (--embedder potion=..., Python embedders=[...]): the stored copy is not loaded then. A model the schema names that neither you nor the store provides is a note on stderr (Python: a UserWarning) naming the command that adds it. The REPL and a one-shot run print one note per model, with its licence; the dev server lists the models (name, repository, licence, where each comes from) and these notes in the Embedding models section of its start banner instead (Dev Server):

note: loaded the embedding model model2vec/minishlab/potion-base-8M@fac4fa854e68 from the store data/ as minishlab/potion-base-8M (licence MIT)
note: the schema names the embedding model model2vec/acme/gone@0123456789ab (doc.emb), which is neither registered nor stored in data/: add it with `graphersal embed-model download acme/gone --into data/`, or pass it with --embedder NAME=<model_dir>

A program asks for the same with Store::stored_embedders(&registered) (features persist and model2vec), which returns the registry to use, what it loaded and the notes (a model that does not load is a note; a models/ directory that cannot be read is the call's error). Models of other kinds than Model2Vec are not kept in a store yet. The WebAssembly playground keeps the models of a store (in its copies and downloads) but cannot run them.

Listing and removing

graphersal store models data/
graphersal store models remove data/ model2vec/minishlab/potion-base-8M@fac4fa854e68

model2vec/minishlab/potion-base-8M@fac4fa854e68  29.5 MiB  licence mit (standard text, written by Graphersal)  used by the schema

graphersal store info data/ shows the same block; the Store menu of the playground lists them with their licences, and Python has store.models(). A removal is the only way a model leaves a store; the schema keeps its identity (a later open notes the missing model).

The licence travels with the model

A model's licence is the model's own. When a model enters a store, its licence comes with it:

  • the model card (README.md), which states the licence and the attribution;
  • the repository's licence and notice files (LICENSE*, NOTICE*) when it has them;
  • the licence id from the repository's metadata (cardData.license, an SPDX id such as mit), else unknown, the models it was made from (base_model) with their licences, and whether the repository is gated;
  • when the repository has no licence file (none of the Model2Vec models from MinishLab has one: their licence is only in the card), the standard text of an MIT or Apache-2.0 licence is written beside the model as LICENSE, marked as a template (license_text: template) and saying where it comes from;
  • when a base model has another licence than the model's own (a tokenizer may come from it: minishlab/M2V_multilingual_output is MIT, its tokenizer comes from the Apache-2.0 sentence-transformers/LaBSE), the standard text of that licence (MIT or Apache-2.0) as LICENSE-BASE-<licence>, e.g. LICENSE-BASE-apache-2.0, naming the base models it covers.

download and import warn when the licence is unknown or non-commercial, or the repository is gated: the terms you accepted may restrict passing the model on.

A store handed on redistributes its models. A backup, a ZIP backup, a .gsnap export, a fork or a copied store carries every model with its card and licence files, and whoever passes it on must follow the models' licences. The copies you hand on can leave the models out:

graphersal store export data/ graph.gsnap --without-models
graphersal store backup data/ data.zip --zip --without-models

The reports of store export, store backup and a fork list the models (and licences) a copy carries. The playground's Store menu offers each snapshot download with the models and without them. The receiver of a copy without models adds them again by the identities its schema records.

What carries the models

OperationModels
checkpoint, prune, compact, rollback, atticuntouched
store verifyevery file checked against its SHA-256; a damaged model is a problem (exit 1) but never makes an open store read-only
backup (full and incremental)carried, checked in the store and in the copy; a damaged model stops the backup
ZIP backupcarried unless --without-models
.gsnap exportcarried unless --without-models; store create --from x.gsnap (and loading it in the playground) puts them back into a store
fork, attic fork, convert, upgrade, restorecarried
repairthe intact models carried, damaged ones listed as not carried

Older Graphersal versions

Models do not change the store format version. Graphersal 0.3.0 opens a store with models and ignores (and keeps) them, loads a .gsnap with models and ignores them, but refuses a ZIP backup with models as written by a newer version: hand it one made with --without-models (details in format spec 4.5).

The graphersal store Command

graphersal store <COMMAND> ... manages a Store from the command line. The store itself is used with graphersal --graph <DIR> (the REPL, -e, --in, --server): every commit of a query is durable before the query returns.

graphersal store help                 # the overview (also: graphersal store, without a command)
graphersal store help rollback        # one command
graphersal store rollback --help      # the same (-h works too)

Conventions

  • DIR is a store: a directory, or a single-file store (an existing file, or a new path ending in .gstore). Every command works on both.
  • TARGET is one of --at-commit <N> (right after commit N), --at-time <TIME> (after the last commit at or before TIME) or --at-mark <NAME>. TIME is an RFC 3339 / ISO 8601 date-time with a zone (2026-10-08T02:43:00Z, 2026-10-08T02:43Z, 2026-10-08T04:43:00+02:00) or microseconds since the Unix epoch; it covers the whole second (minute) it names. A bare date (2026-10-08) is refused with the explicit forms to write instead (2026-10-08T23:59:59Z for the end of that day in UTC, 2026-10-08T00:00:00+02:00 with an offset). See Point in Time.
  • Options take their value as the next argument or after = (--up-to 5, --up-to=5). An option a command does not know is a usage error.
  • Exit codes: 0 ok; 1 the operation failed (the diagnostic with a Help: line is on stderr), verify found damage, or repair lost data; 2 invalid invocation (unknown command or option, a missing argument or option value, a bad time, graphersal store without a command). The same holds for graphersal --graph <DIR>: a store that cannot be opened (in use, damaged beyond a read-only open, an older format) exits 1; a <DIR> that is not a store (without --create-store) or a wrong option exits 2. A command whose stdout was closed before its output was written (graphersal store info x | head -1) completes, closes the store and exits 141 (unless it failed: then its own code).
  • Warnings of the store library (damage found, a read-only open, a failed write of GRAPH, a failed automatic checkpoint) are printed on stderr as WARN graphersal::persist::store: ..., never on stdout: by the store commands and by every mode of graphersal --graph <DIR> (-e, --in, a script file, the REPL, --server). GRAPHERSAL_LOG sets the level: off, error, warn (default), info, debug, trace.
  • A read-write open (--graph <DIR>, mark, prune, rollback, compact, attic restore|remove) that finds one GRAPH copy missing, damaged or stale rewrites it from the other and says so in one line: note: the store data/: GRAPH.copy is not usable (...); GRAPH is used; the other copy was rewritten from it.
  • Times are printed in UTC (2026-10-08T07:05:08Z), in the form --at-time accepts back.
  • While the store is open elsewhere (a dev server, a REPL): info, list, marks, verify, fork, backup, export, repair, compact-advice and attic (list, changes, fork) work; mark, checkpoint, prune, compact, rollback, attic restore|remove and convert fail with "in use" (exit 1): use the dev server's Store menu, or stop the writer.
  • On a backup directory the reading commands work, prune prunes the backup, restore makes it the live store, and the commands that write report that it is a backup.

Commands

CommandDoes
createcreate a store
infoidentity, position, snapshots, marks, WAL size
listthe snapshots
marksthe marks
markname the current position
checkpointmerge a snapshot now (closed store)
verifyscrub every checksum
forka past state as a new store
rollbacktake the store back in place
atticlist, inspect, restore, fork, remove rolled-back history
backupfull, incremental or ZIP backup
restorea backup (or ZIP) as the live store
exporta stored snapshot as a .gsnap
modelsthe embedding models the store keeps; remove one
pruneremove old history
compactprune to now; give a single file's free space back
compact-adviceis compact worth it?
converta directory into a single file, or back
upgradea store of an older Graphersal, converted to the current format
repaira damaged store, repaired into a new directory

create

graphersal store create <DIR> [--from <SOURCE>] [--chunk-size <BYTES>] [--single-file]
                        [--on-damage maintenance|continue]

Creates a store in the new (missing or empty) DIR, at commit 0 with one snapshot. The chunk size, the damage policy and the backend are fixed for the store's life.

Option
--from <SOURCE>the initial graph: the --graph sources modern, empty, large, tree, a GraphSON/GraphML file, or a packed snapshot (.gsnap, copied as is). Default: an empty graph
--chunk-size <BYTES>the snapshot chunk size (default 1 MiB), fixed for the store's life
--single-filea single-file store whatever the name (a DIR ending in .gstore is one anyway)
--on-damage <POLICY>what the store does when damage is found on disk while it is open: maintenance (default: it turns read-only) or continue (it keeps committing and reports the damage); fixed for the store's life
$ graphersal store create data/ --from modern
Created the store data/: graph 01a11a54-8209-7661-92e2-147ae6d8bbd3, commit 0, 1 snapshot(s); damage policy maintenance (fixed for its life).
Use it: graphersal --graph data/ (or --server)
$ graphersal store create graph.gstore --from modern --on-damage continue
Created the single-file store graph.gstore: graph 01a11a54-8ca5-7fd3-8ed5-fcd7729f0e80, commit 0, 1 snapshot(s); damage policy continue (fixed for its life).

Exit 2 when the source cannot be loaded or --on-damage names no policy; 1 when DIR is a directory that is not empty (cannot create a store in data/: the directory is not empty, with the help to choose an empty or new directory, or to look at it with graphersal store info data/ if it is a store) or a store already (it is a store already). graphersal --graph <DIR> --create-store [--on-damage <POLICY>] creates a store on first use instead (--on-damage without --create-store is a usage error; for an existing store with another policy it is refused: the policy never changes).

info

graphersal store info <DIR>

$ graphersal store info data/
store       data/
format      version 2
graph id    01a11a54-8209-7661-92e2-147ae6d8bbd3
state       closed cleanly
commit      3 (2026-10-08T07:05:08Z)
snapshots   2
  latest    commit 3 (8 vertices, 6 edges)
marks       1
definitions 2 (compression 1, query 1)
wal         2 segment(s), 462 bytes
file        a directory
fixed at creation (never changed):
  store id      01a11a54-820a-7c33-b1f0-5d2e9a7c4e10
  created       2026-10-08T07:05:08Z
  chunk size    1048576 bytes
  on damage     maintenance (damage found while open makes the store read-only)
  backend       directory (format version 3)

Also printed when they apply: parent and branched at (a fork, a rolled-back store), backup up to commit N, taken T (a backup), attic N entr(y/ies), the embedding models the store keeps (a models block: one line per model with its identity, size, licence and where the licence text comes from, used by the schema; a model the schema names but the store lacks as missing, see models), and for a single file file single file, 23.0 KiB (23.0 KiB live, 0 B free space inside: ...). state is open (in use, or not closed cleanly) while a writer has it (or after a crash).

A store written by a newer Graphersal (its GRAPH, a snapshot or WAL file, or the single file's container of a newer format version) is not read: info, like every store command (upgrade and repair included) and --graph, exits 1 with the refusal and changes nothing (no lock file either):

$ graphersal store info data/
Error: Unsupported format version 4 of the store data/ (store format version): written by a newer Graphersal (this build reads up to version 3)
Help: The store or file was written by a newer Graphersal; open it with that version (or a later one). ...

See Format Versions.

list

graphersal store list <DIR>

      commit  last commit             vertices       edges  name
           0  -                              6           6
           3  2026-10-08T07:05:08Z           8           6  nightly

The snapshots, oldest first: the commit, the time of that commit, the counts, the name. Reads only the manifests' first 4 KiB.

marks

graphersal store marks <DIR>

           1  2026-10-08T07:05:08Z  before-import

The marks: commit, time, name.

mark

graphersal store mark <DIR> <NAME>

Sets the mark NAME at the current position (Mark "before-import" at commit 1.). Names are unique along the store's whole history. "In use" while a server has the store open (its Store menu has Mark).

checkpoint

graphersal store checkpoint <DIR> [--name <NAME>]

Writes a snapshot of the current state of the CLOSED store, merged from the last snapshot and the WAL after it without loading the graph (how):

Snapshot at commit 3 (8 vertices, 6 edges).
Merged from the snapshot at commit 0 and 3 commits: 4 segment files reused, 0 copied, 1 written.

Nothing was committed after it: no new snapshot written. when the newest snapshot is current. "In use" while another process has the store open (a server's Store menu has Checkpoint, which merges the same way while commits go on). Damage in what it reads stops it with exit 1 and nothing written; run verify.

verify

graphersal store verify <DIR>

Reads every checksum (snapshots, WAL, GRAPH, marks). Exit 0 with ok: no damage found; exit 1 with every problem and the damage report (the donor of each damaged item). See Verify. Files of a newer format version are never listed as damage: verify exits 1 with the "written by a newer Graphersal" refusal shown under info (no DAMAGE lines, no repair advice), and store repair refuses such a store the same way.

fork

graphersal store fork <DIR> <NEW_DIR> [TARGET]

A new store in NEW_DIR (it must not exist, or be empty) from the state at TARGET (default: the latest), with a new lineage that records DIR as its parent. DIR is not changed.

$ graphersal store fork data/ branch/ --at-mark before-import
Forked into branch/ at commit 1: graph 01a11a54-87d2-7995-b2cb-e450e4319735 (parent 01a11a54-8209-7661-92e2-147ae6d8bbd3).
Marks not carried (1; they stay targets of data/ only):
  before-import @ commit 1
Open it: graphersal --graph branch/ --server (or the REPL: graphersal --graph branch/).
data/ is unchanged; to undo the fork, delete the directory branch/.

A fork starts without marks: the Marks not carried lines (printed only when there are any) name the source's marks at or before the fork's position. Exit 1 when the target is not reached (Recovery target mark "nosuch" not reached).

rollback

graphersal store rollback <DIR> TARGET [--delete]

Rolls the store back in place to TARGET: everything after it moves to the attic (with --delete: deleted, no undo), and the store continues as a new lineage. Prints the attic id and the commands that undo it. Exit 2 without a target; exit 1 when there is nothing after the target or the store is in use. See Rollback and the Attic.

$ graphersal store rollback data/ --at-commit 1 --delete
Rolled back from commit 4 to commit 1: new lineage 01a11a54-8b90-7dba-b74a-cadc851e226f.
The history after it (commits 2..=4, 1 snapshot(s), 2 WAL file(s)) was deleted: this cannot be undone.

attic

graphersal store attic <DIR>                       list the entries
graphersal store attic <DIR> changes <ID>          the commits of an entry
graphersal store attic <DIR> restore <ID>          undo its rollback
graphersal store attic <DIR> fork <ID> <NEW_DIR>   the entry as a new store
graphersal store attic <DIR> remove <ID>           delete the entry for good

$ graphersal store attic data/
20261008T070510Z-00000000000000000002  commits 2..=4 rolled back at 2026-10-08T07:05:10Z (rollback to mark "before-import"), 9.3 KiB, 1 snapshot(s)
$ graphersal store attic data/ restore 20261008T070510Z-00000000000000000002
Restored 20261008T070510Z-00000000000000000002: the store is at commit 4 again.

restore works only while nothing was committed or marked since that rollback; fork always does (and lists the marks of the entry's history it does not carry, like store fork). restore and remove are "in use" while a server has the store open.

backup

graphersal store backup <DIR> <BACKUP_DIR> [--full]
graphersal store backup <DIR> <FILE.zip> --zip [--without-models]

A consistent copy up to the last durable commit; works while a server has the store open. Into an empty or new BACKUP_DIR: a full backup. Into an existing backup of DIR: an incremental one. --full forces a full backup (the directory must be empty or new). --zip writes one ZIP archive (always full; the file must not exist; feature persist-zip, on in the CLI).

$ graphersal store backup data/ backup/
Full backup into backup/: snapshot 3, the WAL up to commit 3 (1 segment(s)); 8 file(s), 9605 bytes.
The backup is read-only (graphersal --graph backup/ opens it so); `graphersal store restore backup/` makes it the live store.
$ graphersal store backup data/ backup/
Incremental backup into backup/: nothing new since commit 4; the backup is current.
The backup is read-only (graphersal --graph backup/ opens it so); `graphersal store restore backup/` makes it the live store.
$ graphersal store backup data/ data.zip --zip
Full backup of snapshot 3 and the WAL up to commit 4: 8 file(s), 9688 bytes, in data.zip; every checksum read back.

The store's embedding models are copied too, with their cards and licence files, and the report lists them (It carries 1 embedding model(s) with their licences (handing it on redistributes them): and one line per model): who hands a backup on redistributes them. --without-models (with --zip only; a usage error otherwise) leaves them out: such an archive is also restored by Graphersal 0.3.0, which refuses one with models as written by a newer version.

Every checksum of what is copied is read in DIR first and again in the copy (a ZIP archive is read back). Damage stops the backup (exit 1): nothing of it is kept (a new directory or archive is removed, an increment rolled back), and the report names the damaged files and recommends repairing the STORE (store repair DIR --to NEW_DIR), never the backup. Damage of a redundant copy (one GRAPH copy, one manifest copy, the marks file) is a warning: on stderr; the backup is intact.

$ graphersal store backup data/ backup/
Error: The backup stopped: the store data/ is damaged: wal/00000000000000000001.wal at byte 64: record of commit 1: checksum mismatch; nothing of the backup into backup/ was kept
Help: Repair the MAIN store, never the backup: graphersal store repair data/ --to <new_dir> ...

Refused (exit 1, the backup unchanged): a backup of another graph, a directory holding a store that is not a backup, a non-empty directory without a backup, --full into a non-empty directory, a rollback of the store behind the backup, a pruned gap, a fork, repair or conversion of the backed-up store (another store id). --zip --full is a usage error (exit 2: "--zip backups are always full: drop --full").

--from-memory is a usage error here (exit 2) that says where it works: a backup from memory writes the graph of a store open in this process (whose files are damaged), and this command runs in a new process. Use the dev server's Store menu (Back up from memory), POST /api/store/backup {"from_memory": true}, or Python store.backup(path, from_memory=True). See Backup and Restore.

restore

graphersal store restore <BACKUP_DIR>
graphersal store restore <FILE.zip> <DIR>

With one argument: makes the backup in BACKUP_DIR the live store, in place, with the original's graph id (a backup directory of an older Graphersal: upgrade it first). With two: unpacks a ZIP backup into the new directory DIR as the live store; a ZIP of an older Graphersal's store is upgraded to the current format as it is unpacked (verified). To keep a backup as it is, fork it instead (store fork BACKUP_DIR NEW_DIR).

$ graphersal store restore backup/
Restored: backup/ is now the live store (the backup up to commit 4, taken 2026-10-08T07:05:09Z; the same graph id). Use it: graphersal --graph backup/
$ graphersal store restore data.zip restored/
Restored into restored/ (the live store). Use it: graphersal --graph restored/

export

graphersal store export <DIR> <FILE.gsnap> [--commit <N>] [--without-models]

Writes the latest stored snapshot (or the one at commit N, which must be a snapshot's commit: store list) as one packed file (Exported the snapshot at commit 3 to data.gsnap.). Load it with --graph FILE.gsnap, store create --from FILE.gsnap, or the playground.

The file carries the store's embedding models with their cards and licences (listed after the first line), unless --without-models. store create --from FILE.gsnap and the playground put them back into a store; Graphersal 0.3.0 loads such a file and ignores them. A damaged model stops the export (exit 1; export --without-models, or remove the model).

models

graphersal store models <DIR>
graphersal store models remove <DIR> <IDENTITY>

Lists the embedding models the store keeps, one line each: the identity a schema's embedder records (model2vec/<repo>@<12 hex>), the size, the licence and where its text comes from (text from the repository, standard text, written by Graphersal, no licence text), gated repository when it applies, and whether the schema uses it; then every model the schema names that the store does not keep (missing). Works while a server has the store open.

$ graphersal store models data/
model2vec/minishlab/potion-base-8M@fac4fa854e68  29.5 MiB  licence mit (standard text, written by Graphersal)  used by the schema

remove deletes one model, by its identity or its id model2vec-<12 hex> (refused while a writer has the store open, and on a backup; an unknown model exits 1). It is the only way a model leaves a store. Models enter a store by graphersal embed-model download <REPO> --into <DIR> and graphersal embed-model import <MODEL_DIR> --into <DIR> (see Embedding Models in a Store).

prune

graphersal store prune <DIR> --up-to <COMMIT> [--drop-marks]

Removes snapshots and WAL only needed for targets before COMMIT; the last two snapshots and the attic's bases always stay (Kept from commit 0; removed 0 snapshot(s) [] and 0 WAL segment(s).). Without --up-to it is a usage error (exit 2: nothing is pruned implicitly). On a backup directory it prunes the backup.

A prune never makes a mark unreachable unless told to: when it would remove the history a mark needs, it names those marks, changes nothing and exits 1:

$ graphersal store prune data --up-to 4
Error: `store prune` would make the mark(s) "m0", "m1" unreachable: it removes the history they need, so they cannot be opened, forked or rolled back to afterwards (only from a backup that holds older snapshots). Nothing was changed.
Help: run it again with --drop-marks to prune anyway, or back the store up first (`graphersal store backup data <BACKUP_DIR>`).

With --drop-marks it prunes and names them on a second line ("No longer reachable (their history was pruned): the mark(s) ..."); store marks no longer lists them. Without affected marks the flag changes nothing. See Prune, Compact and Retention.

compact

graphersal store compact <DIR> [--drop-marks]

Prunes up to the current commit, then, for a single-file store, rewrites the file without its free space (the disk needs room for the live data meanwhile). On a directory the prune is all. Like prune, it refuses (exit 1, nothing changed) when the prune would make marks unreachable, naming them, unless --drop-marks is given; compact-advice lists them beforehand (marks lost m0, m1 (...)).

$ graphersal store compact graph.gstore
Pruned: kept from commit 0; removed 0 snapshot(s) and 0 WAL segment(s).
Compacted the file: 23.7 KiB -> 22.8 KiB (930 B given back).

compact-advice

graphersal store compact-advice <DIR> [--min-ratio <R>] [--min-reclaimable <BYTES>] [--min-size <BYTES>]

Whether compact is worth it now, and the numbers; cheap (reads only names, sizes and small metadata files, no element data) and works while a server has the store open. The rule: at least --min-ratio of the store (0.0..1.0, default 0.5) and --min-reclaimable bytes (default 64 MiB) to gain, in a store of at least --min-size bytes (default 64 MiB), and enough free disk space. Always exit 0 (the answer is in the text: compact now: ... with a Run: graphersal store compact <DIR> line, or no compaction needed: ...).

$ graphersal store compact-advice data/
no compaction needed: the store is smaller than the minimum of 64.0 MiB
store       9.6 KiB (directory: compact = prune)
prune       0 B
reclaimable 0 B (0 % of the store)
decided by  total_bytes

convert

graphersal store convert <DIR> <NEW> [--single-file]

Copies the whole closed store (snapshots, WAL, marks, attic) into NEW, byte for byte: a directory into a single file (NEW ending in .gstore, or --single-file) or back. NEW must not exist (or be an empty directory); the copy is verified; DIR is not changed. The copy is a new store with its own store id (creation parameters): it does not continue the backups of DIR (its first backup is a full one into a new directory).

$ graphersal store convert data/ graph.gstore
Copied the store data/ into the single file graph.gstore: 9 file(s), 9.6 KiB; verified.
Use it: graphersal --graph graph.gstore. data/ is unchanged.

upgrade

graphersal store upgrade <DIR> <NEW> [--single-file]
graphersal store upgrade <DIR> --in-place

Converts a store written by an older Graphersal (store format version 2: Graphersal 0.1.x) to the current format, without the older binary. DIR is a store directory, a single-file store or a backup directory (it stays a backup). With NEW: a new store in NEW (a new or empty directory, or a single file: NEW ending in .gstore, or --single-file); DIR is not changed. With --in-place: DIR itself; back it up first (a copy of the closed directory or file will do): afterwards the older Graphersal refuses it as newer.

Everything is carried: the graph, its schema and catalog, the history (snapshots and WAL), the marks, the lineage, the attic entries and the store's identity and creation parameters; only GRAPH and GRAPH.copy are rewritten, every other file stays byte for byte. DIR is verified first. Exit 1 when it is damaged (nothing is written; store repair DIR --to NEW writes a repaired store of the current format), in use (a server or another writer has it open), of a newer or a pre-release version, or a copy of a store that is already current; exit 2 without NEW or --in-place, or with a NEW that exists. An upgrade in place of a current store prints nothing to do (exit 0). An interrupted upgrade leaves no store in NEW (run it again: it clears what was left), and in place leaves the store either older or upgraded (run it again). A ZIP backup of an older store is upgraded by store restore FILE.zip DIR. See Format Versions.

Which versions are upgraded, and how, is decided by one table (the same in Format Versions and the format specification 15.1); a version without a supported row is refused before anything is written, a row "into a copy only" refuses --in-place (StoreFailure::UpgradeNeedsCopy), and a store with any file of a newer version is refused like every other command does (below):

From store format versionWritten byToUpgrade
1never released (no store id)3unsupported (packed snapshot)
2Graphersal 0.1.x3in place or into a copy (version word)
3Graphersal 0.2.x and later3nothing to do
$ graphersal store upgrade old/ new/
Verified the store old/ (store format version 2): 2 snapshot(s), 2 WAL segment(s), 10 record(s).
Upgraded into new/ (store format version 3): 15 file(s), 21.2 KiB; verified. old/ is unchanged (keep using new/: it is the same store, with the same identity).
Use it: graphersal --graph new/
$ graphersal store upgrade old/ --in-place
Verified the store old/ (store format version 2): 2 snapshot(s), 2 WAL segment(s), 10 record(s).
Upgraded old/ in place to store format version 3: GRAPH rewritten, every other file kept. The older Graphersal no longer opens it.
Use it: graphersal --graph old/

repair

graphersal store repair <DIR> --to <NEW_DIR>

Builds a repaired copy of a damaged store in NEW_DIR (never in place; the damaged files are not changed) and reports what was repaired, lost and diverged. A store of an older released format (Graphersal 0.1.x) is read as it is; the repaired store has the current format. Exit 0 with ok: nothing lost, exit 1 when data is lost or diverged (the repaired store is written anyway: read the lists), exit 2 without --to. The repaired store starts without marks: one mark not carried: name @ commit N line per mark of the damaged store at or before the repaired position. When both GRAPH copies are damaged, repair and verify print the note lineage before commit N is approximate (both GRAPH copies damaged) (verify then exits 1 with the damage report instead of "not a store"). See Damage, Maintenance and Repair.

The Store in the Playground

The web playground runs the engine in the browser (WebAssembly), where there is no disk to write to. It still gives every graph the full Store: a MemDir store, with the same byte format as on disk.

Every graph you load (a sample, the empty graph, a file) is kept as a Store in memory: the loaded state is commit 0 (its first snapshot), every run that changes the graph adds a commit to the store's write-ahead log, and the Store menu in the top bar works on it exactly as the dev server's does on a store directory:

  • the position (commit, time of the last commit) and the sizes: the store's bytes in memory next to the graph's own footprint;
  • Checkpoint (a snapshot of the current state; one is also written automatically after 4 MiB of log since the last one) and Mark (a name for the current position);
  • the marks and the snapshots (each with a .gsnap download; when the store keeps embedding models, a second download .gsnap without models leaves them out, the first one carries them with their licences), the newest five of each; Calendar… (or See all… when there are more) opens the history calendar;
  • on every snapshot and mark, and through Go to commit / Go to time: Open read-only here (queries read that past state, writes are refused, a banner offers Back to the live graph), Fork into a new database and Roll back here (what comes after moves to the attic);
  • the attic: Show changes (100 commits per page with Previous/Next, the totals over all of them; the dialog scrolls in both directions and has a full-screen toggle, Esc restores its size), Restore, Fork, Remove;
  • Databases: the store you loaded and every fork made from it ("fork of Modern (TinkerPop) @ commit 12"), each a store in memory with its own history, with Switch to (the tabs' results may be stale afterwards) and Close (frees its memory);
  • Disk space with Compact: in memory a compaction is a prune up to the current commit (the last two snapshots stay), which frees the memory old snapshots and WAL hold; the button is always enabled (not while another store action runs); when the compaction advice does not recommend it, it asks first, showing what it would free and why it is not recommended;
  • Models (when the store keeps embedding models, or its schema names one it lacks): each model's identity, size, licence and where its text comes from, whether the repository is gated and whether the schema uses it. Handing the store or a snapshot with models on redistributes them. A .gsnap with models loaded on the start page keeps them in its store in memory (the browser cannot run them, but its copies and downloads carry them);
  • Verify the store checks every checksum, and Download current state (.gsnap) saves the state on screen.

The menu after a few commits, three marks and three snapshots (the buttons View, Fork… and Roll back… are the three actions above):

Calendar… shows every mark and snapshot by day, with the same actions:

A running store action is shown in three places (the same on the dev server): its button switches to the running text in bold accent colour with a spinner and the elapsed time ("Verifying the store… 0:42"); the Store button in the top bar shows it while the menu is closed ("Store · verifying… 0:42"); and a toast gives the result at the end (a problem found, such as Verify's damage, has a Details button that opens the menu, where the last Verify's result is listed under its item). Meanwhile every other store action is disabled, its tooltip saying which one to wait for; screen readers hear the start and the end through a polite live region. The engine reports no progress for these actions and none of them can be cancelled: the elapsed time is all there is.

In memory: everything is lost on page reload. Download a .gsnap to keep a state (load it back from the start page). The browser has no disk the playground writes to: syncs are no-ops, and the byte format is the same as on disk, so a downloaded snapshot opens anywhere.

Stop (next to Run) restarts the engine: the graph is restored as it was last loaded or saved, and the store in memory starts over from that state (its history is lost).

To keep a history across reloads, run the same UI on a store on disk with the dev server: graphersal --graph data/ --server.

Python

The Python binding (bindings/py-graphersal, package graphersal) has the packed snapshot, the journal and recovery on graphersal.Graph, and the Store as graphersal.Store. Errors raise graphersal.GraphersalError with the diagnostic and its help text. Build and test instructions: bindings/py-graphersal/README.md.

Packed snapshots, journal and recovery

import graphersal

graph = graphersal.Graph.tinkerpop_modern()
graph.save("g.gsnap")                                     # {"commit_seq", "vertex_count", "edge_count"}; name= optional
graph = graphersal.Graph.load("g.gsnap")                  # no schema re-validation, checksummed
graph = graphersal.Graph.load("g.gsnap", memory_limit="auto")   # refuse a snapshot that does not fit

graph.start_journal("g.wal")                              # durability="every_commit" (default) | "os" | seconds
graph.execute('g.addV("person").property("name", "ann").next()')
graph.mark("after-ann")                                   # {"name", "commit_seq", "time"}

graph, report = graphersal.Graph.recover("g.gsnap", ["g.wal"])                    # to the end
graph, report = graphersal.Graph.recover("g.gsnap", ["g.wal"], mark="after-ann")  # or commit_seq=, time=

Graph.recover takes one target: commit_seq=, time= (microseconds since the Unix epoch) or mark=; without one it replays to the end. An interrupted last write is ignored (report["torn_tail"]); damage raises GraphersalError with its location. The recovered graph has no journal: save and start_journal again to continue (see Journal and Recovery).

The Store

with graphersal.Store.create("data") as store:            # or Store.open("data"); "x.gstore": one file
    store.graph.execute('g.addV("person").property("name", "ann").next()')   # durable when it returns
    store.mark("after-ann")
    store.checkpoint("nightly")
    store.snapshots(); store.marks(); store.verify()       # listings and the scrub
    store.fork("branch", mark="after-ann")                 # a new store (commit_seq=, time=, mark=)
    store.backup("bk")                                     # full, then incremental: {"incremental", "commit_seq", ...}
    store.open_report()                                    # {"clean_close", "commit_seq", "commits_replayed", ...}
MethodDoesPage
Store.create(path, on_damage="maintenance"), Store.open(path)create (missing or empty path; on_damage is the damage policy, fixed for the store's life) / open read-write, with recovery; a second writer raisesOpening and Closing
Store.create_file(path), Store.open_file(path)a single-file store (create/open of a .gstore path do the same)
store.graphthe store's Graph; every commit is durable before it returnsCommits
store.close(), with ...:a clean close; the graph refuses commits afterwards
store.open_report()what the open did
store.workload_report(history=None)the workload statistics: queries, property uses, lock times, jobs (Python's queries under the channel python); history="minutes"|"hours"|"days" adds every row's buckets

store.snapshots()the snapshots, oldest first

store.rollback(commit_seq=, time=, mark=, delete=False)roll back in place; the rest goes to the atticRollback
store.attic(), store.attic_restore(id)the attic entries; undo a rollback
store.backup(path, full=False, from_memory=False)full or incremental backup, every checksum read in the store and in the copy (damage raises, nothing kept); from_memory=True after damage was found: the graph in memory, nothing written to the storeBackup and Restore
store.store_id, store.damage_policy, store.damage_found, store.frozen_by_damagethe store id and the policy, fixed at creation; damage found on disk while the store is open; whether it turned read-onlyDamage

Store.restore_backup(path)make a backup the live store (same graph id)

store.models()the embedding models the store keeps, with their licences (license, license_text), files and used_by_schema; the ones the schema names are registered when the store is opened (an embedders= embedder of the same model wins; a missing model is a UserWarning)Embedding Models in a Store

Store.upgrade(source, target=None, in_place=False, single_file=False)convert a store (or backup) of Graphersal 0.1.x to the current format, into target or in placeFormat Versions
with graphersal.Store.open_backup("bk") as backup:        # read-only; backup.backup_marker
    backup.snapshots()
graphersal.Store.restore_backup("bk")                      # the live store from now on: Store.open("bk")

with graphersal.Store.create("graph.gstore") as store:     # one file
    if store.compaction_advice()["recommended"]:
        store.compact()
graphersal.Store.convert("graph.gstore", "data")           # a closed store into a directory (or back)
graphersal.Store.upgrade("old_store", "new_store")         # a store of Graphersal 0.1.x, upgraded (or in_place=True)

Times in Python are microseconds since the Unix epoch (time=), as in Rust.

| Cannot create a store in data/: the directory is not empty, PersistError::DirectoryNotEmpty | a new store (Store::create, the target of Store::convert) needs a new or empty directory | choose an empty or new directory, or open the existing store if it is one (graphersal store info data/) |

FAQ and Troubleshooting

Choosing

Snapshot, journal or Store? A .gsnap when the application decides when to save (a script, the browser, a download). A journal when you need durability over streams you manage yourself. The Store for everything else: it is a snapshot plus a journal plus recovery, retention, backups and repair. See Persistence.

Directory or single file? A directory for a server (parts can live on other disks, the files are easy to inspect); a .gstore file when the store travels as one document. Both have the same guarantees, and graphersal store convert switches between them.

Is GraphSON or GraphML not enough? They are exchange formats: they do not carry the schema, the commit position or the auto-id sequences, and GraphML loses value types without a schema. A snapshot is lossless.

Errors and what to do

MessageCauseWhat to do
The store data/ is in use: another writer holds its locka dev server, a REPL or a program has the store open read-writeuse the reading commands (they work), the dev server's Store menu, or stop the writer. A crashed writer never leaves a stale lock (the OS releases it)
data/ is not a Graphersal store: no valid GRAPH file (...)the path is not a store (a typo, or not created yet), or both GRAPH copies are unreadablecheck the path; graphersal --graph <dir> --create-store creates a store; for damage see Damage
... is a BACKUP (up to commit N, ...), PersistError::IsBackupa backup opens read-onlygraphersal store restore <dir> makes it the live store, store fork <dir> <new> a writable copy

The commit was rejected by the commit hook 'maintenance'a write to a store in maintenance modethe same: repair into a new directory
The journal is poisoned by an earlier failurean fsync or a write failed (a full disk, an I/O error)fix the cause, then reopen the store (or restart the server): recovery continues from the last durable commit
The journal is poisoned by an earlier failure: a panic while writing a commit record: ...the journal panicked while it wrote a record (a bug, or a store backend that panics); the record was cut off again and the unit rolled backreport the panic; reopen the store (or restart the server): it gives the state before that unit. Every case: Failures while committing
Commit N is too large for the journal: its uncompressed record body is B bytes, more than the limit of 1073741824 bytes per commit / CommitTooLarge (in CommitRejected from the hook journal)one unit changed more than 1 GiB of WAL record (every change with its before and after values: dropping and re-creating a large graph in one script of the dev server or the playground)split the work: drop in a run of its own, load in several runs; see The size of one commit. The unit rolled back; the store keeps working

Nothing of the failed backup was kept

The error's help names the command

Refused store operations (PersistError::Store)

A refused operation reads Cannot <operation>: <reason>. Its cause is one of a closed set (graphersal::persist::StoreFailure, #[non_exhaustive]), so a program or a server can react to it with a match; StoreFailure::name() is the stable name, which the Python exception carries as err.cause (None for every other error). Each cause has its own help:

Cause (name())WhenWhat to do
Closed (closed)the store was closed (close, shutdown)open it again
LockPoisoned (lock_poisoned)a thread panicked while it held a lock of the open storeend the process and reopen the store
NameTaken (name_taken)a snapshot name in use, or a mark name used before (also by a mark a prune made unreachable)choose another name; store list, store marks
NameTooLong (name_too_long)a snapshot name over 255 bytesa shorter name
SnapshotExists (snapshot_exists)a named checkpoint at a commit that already has a snapshot under another namecommit something first, or checkpoint without a name
NoSnapshot (no_snapshot)an export of a commit without a snapshot, a backup of a store without onestore list, store checkpoint
BackupRunning (backup_running)a prune while a backup copies the filesprune again afterwards
PruneRunning (prune_running)a backup while a prune deletes filesback up again afterwards
NothingAfterTarget (nothing_after_target)a rollback to the current commit or lateran earlier target
UnknownAtticEntry (unknown_attic_entry)no attic entry with that idstore attic <dir> lists them
AtticLineageChanged (attic_lineage_changed)a later rollback or restore came after the entry's rollbackrestore the newer entry first, or fork the entry
ChangedSinceRollback (changed_since_rollback)commits or marks since the entry's rollbackfork the entry (store attic <dir> fork <id> <new_dir>)
AtticBaseMissing (attic_base_missing)the snapshot an attic entry continues is gonestore verify; take the entry from a backup or remove it
NotABackup (not_a_backup)a backup-only operation (prune_backup) on a live storeopen and prune it as a store
KeptSnapshotDamaged (kept_snapshot_damaged)a snapshot a prune would keep fails verification; nothing was removedstore verify, then store repair <dir> --to <new_dir>

ChangedConcurrently (changed_concurrently)a store file changed or vanished while the operation read itnever edit a store's files; repeat, then store verify
JournalSyncFailed (journal_sync_failed)writing or syncing the journal failedfix the disk, reopen the store
MissingCapability (missing_capability)the graph's storage does not claim atomic and change_capture, so no journal can be attached (never for TraversalGraph)keep the graph in a storage that claims both
ReloadFailed (reload_failed)the files of a rollback or attic restore changed, but loading the new state into the open graph failed: the graph in memory was emptied and the store stoppedclose the store and open it again (restart the server): the open completes the change
Stopped (stopped)an earlier rollback or attic restore failed part-way, so the store writes nothing more (Store::stopped_reason)close the store and open it again

UnknownModel (unknown_model)store models remove, Store::remove_model or read_model_file of an embedding model the store does not keepgraphersal store models <dir> lists the identities and ids
InvalidModel (invalid_model)an embedding model to add lacks its config, tokenizer or weights file, has a file name that is not allowed, a file over 8 GiB, or a repository or licence that is not a valid name; nothing was addedcheck the model directory (--embedder name=<dir> loads it) and graphersal embed-model import <dir> --into <store> again
AutoCheckpointFailed (auto_checkpoint_failed)read from Store::last_auto_checkpoint_error after an automatic checkpoint run by Store::run_due_checkpoint (the browser) failed with a graph error; the caller of run_due_checkpoint got the error itselfnothing is lost: the commits are in the journal and the checkpoint is tried again at the next commit; graphersal store checkpoint <dir> reports a manual one with its own help

Questions

Can I change the damage policy (or the chunk size) of a store? No. Both are fixed at creation and carried by every fork, repair, conversion and backup. To get another policy, create a new store with it and load the data (for example graphersal store export old/ graph.gsnap, then graphersal store create new/ --from graph.gsnap --on-damage continue).

Does a backup check what it copies? Yes, every checksum, in the store before anything is written and again in the copy. A backup never copies damage silently; see Every checksum, twice.

Is a commit really on disk when the query returns? Yes, with the default Durability::EveryCommit: the WAL record is written and fsynced first; a failed sync rolls the commit back. With Interval or Os a machine crash may lose the last commits (never one in the middle). See Commits and Durability.

The dev server (or my program) was killed. Is the store damaged? No. The next open replays the WAL and cuts an interrupted last write; stderr notes that the store was not closed cleanly, which is harmless. Ctrl+C closes it cleanly in the first place.

Why does the store keep growing? Nothing is deleted implicitly: every commit is in the WAL and every checkpoint adds a snapshot until you prune. store compact-advice tells you what a prune and a compaction would give back.

How do I see the graph as it was yesterday? Store::open_read_only(dir, RecoveryTarget::Time(..)), the dev server's Go to time..., or graphersal store fork data/ yesterday/ --at-time 2026-10-07T18:00:00Z and open the fork. See Point in Time.

I rolled back by mistake. graphersal store attic data/ lists the rolled-back history; store attic data/ restore <ID> undoes the rollback as long as nothing was committed or marked since, otherwise store attic data/ fork <ID> <NEW_DIR> keeps it as a new store. A rollback with --delete cannot be undone (restore a backup).

Can I copy a store with cp or rsync? While no process has it open, yes: no file records a path. While it is open, use graphersal store backup (it copies up to the durable end and pins the files against a concurrent prune); a plain copy of a live store may catch a half-written file.

Can two processes use one store? One writer at a time (an operating-system lock). Any number of readers (info, verify, fork, backup, Store::open_read_only) at the same time as the writer.

Does a backup include the attic? No. It holds the snapshots and the WAL up to the durable end, and the marks.

Where is the time zone? Everything is stored and printed in UTC. --at-time takes any offset, but refuses a time without one.

Does it work in the browser? Snapshots, journals and recovery work over any stream in WebAssembly; the Store works there over a MemDir (the playground does that). There is no disk: download a .gsnap to keep a state.

Can another program read the WAL (change data capture)? Yes. The byte format is public (specification); a reader tails the WAL segments, reads complete records only, and treats records after the writer's durable end as possibly not final. In Rust, store.changes_since(commit) yields the ChangeSets.

Is the format stable? Store format version 3 (with file format version 3) is specified on the specification page; a newer version is refused, never guessed at, and a store of an older released version is upgraded by graphersal store upgrade without the older build (every build keeps the readers of every released format; Format Versions).

Custom Storages

Graphersal's reference storage is TraversalGraph, an in-memory graph. A host (a server, an application) can bring its own in-memory storage instead: any type that implements the GraphStorage trait. The engine, the Rhai DSL, saved queries, the session of the playground and the dev server (graphersal-session) and the persist Store then work over it.

EXPERIMENTAL in 0.4.x. GraphStorage, PersistentStorage, AnyGraph and the conformance crate graphersal-storage-tests may change in any 0.4.x release. Pin the exact versions (graphersal = "=0.4.0", graphersal-storage-tests = "=0.4.0"). graphersal-session is internal and has no stability guarantees at all.

How it fits together

The engine (GraphTraversalSource<'g, S>) is generic over the storage and statically dispatched: a traversal over a host storage is compiled for that storage, with no virtual call per element. Everything above the engine holds one object-safe type per layer instead, and makes one virtual call per operation (a terminal, a schema method, a catalog call, a view):

LayerHoldsImplemented for
Rhai DSL, saved queries (graphersal::script)Arc<dyn AnyGraph>every Graph<S> (sealed blanket implementation)
Session (graphersal-session)Arc<dyn SessionGraph>, Arc<dyn SessionStore>, Arc<dyn GraphFactory>every Graph<S>, every Store<S>, StorageKind<S>
Store (graphersal::persist)Store<S>, internally a non-generic coreevery S: PersistentStorage

Graph<S> (in graphersal::storage, also in the prelude) is the shared form of a storage: S behind a read-write lock, with read()/write() guards that dereference to S. Graph without a parameter means Graph<TraversalGraph>.

What a host implements

  1. GraphStorage (required). Only the read methods, the element-inserting and element-removing methods and the property writes are required; everything else has a default that is correct for a simple, non-transactional storage. The trait's rustdoc ("A guide for storage implementers") is the reference: handles that never alias, the write checks and their public helpers, units of atomicity, capabilities, change capture, statistics, schema and the catalog. The schema's defaults on create come for free: you implement the primitive insert_vertex/insert_edge (store exactly this; imports, change sets, replay and copies call it), and the queries create through the provided add_vertex/add_edge (add_vertex_with/add_edge_with with a pinned time), which fill the defaults in from get_schema() and then call your insert_vertex/insert_edge (override add_vertex_with/add_edge_with only to avoid that schema copy).
  2. Default (required by the DSL and the session). The session builds every new graph (a sample, a file load) by reading it into a TraversalGraph and copying it into an S::default() (through the load sink of a PersistentStorage, through the write methods otherwise). A whole script runs as one unit that its thread holds across locks (Graph::begin_unit), on your storage in place: the graph holds the lock upgradable until the script's first write and only then opens your storage's unit (begin_unit_at with the time it pinned from next_unit_started_at, both defaulted), so opening and closing a unit that never wrote take no exclusive moment. A unit you open yourself through a write guard (graph.write().begin_unit()) must be closed under that same guard, else other threads read its uncommitted changes and a Store checkpoint may persist them.
  3. Send + Sync + 'static, so the graph can be shared between threads.
  4. Change capture (optional; needed for commit hooks, dry runs and the Store). A storage that claims change_capture (and therefore atomic) in capabilities() builds the ChangeSet of every committed unit itself with the public constructors (ChangeSet::builder, one Mutation constructor per kind). There is no reusable undo log or capture component: the storage derives what a unit changed from its own bookkeeping. It embeds a CommitHooks (graphersal::storage) and calls it at its commit point, so the order of the hooks (user hooks in registration order, then the journal) is implemented once; the rustdoc of CommitHooks says when to call each event.
  5. PersistentStorage (optional, feature persist; needed for snapshots and the Store): the lineage id, the commit position, a load sink outside units, clear, the journal slot and replay. See Your Own Storage.

Errors of a backend. Every trait method that reads or changes state returns a Result (since 0.4.0). The element reads (vertex_count, edge_count, vertices, edges, vertices_by_label, edges_by_label, get_vertex_by_id, get_edge_by_id, out_edges, in_edges, vertex_id, edge_id, vertex_label, edge_label, vertex_labels, vertex_has_label, vertex_properties, edge_properties, edge_endpoints, contains_vertex, contains_edge) and unit_started_at answer Ok(None) / Ok(false) / an empty label set for what does not exist and Err only when the backend cannot answer; an iterating one returns Result<impl Iterator>, one Result for starting the iteration, never one per item (a backend that can fail mid-iteration collects first, like the defaults of vertices_by_label and edges_by_label). The query that read fails with the error, located at its step.
