predicatesIS [NOT] NULL, IN [list], STARTS WITH, ENDS WITH, CONTAINS, IS [NOT] LABELED, IS [NOT] SOURCE OF e, IS [NOT] DESTINATION OF e
arithmetic+, -, *, /, %, ^ (Cypher power, always a float: 2 ^ 10 is 1024.0), unary - and +
concatenation|| on two strings or two lists (Cypher +); Cypher + of a list and one other value appends or prepends it ([1] + 2 is [1, 2], 0 + [1] is [0, 1])
conditionalsimple CASE x WHEN v THEN r ... ELSE d END and searched CASE WHEN cond THEN r ... END
conversionCAST(x AS INTEGER | FLOAT | STRING | BOOLEAN) (Conversions)
function callsname(args) (Functions)
map projectionp {.name, .*, f, key: expr} (Cypher, below)
list comprehension[x IN list WHERE cond | expr], either part optional (Cypher)
pattern comprehension[(p)-[:knows]->(f) WHERE cond | expr] (Cypher)

Precedence, loosest first: OR, XOR, AND, NOT, comparison, the predicates (IS NULL, IN, STARTS WITH, ...), + - ||, * / %, ^ (left to right: 2 ^ 3 ^ 2 is 64.0), unary minus (-3 ^ 2 is 9.0), property access and subscripts (x[i], x[a..b], left to right: [1, 2][0] + 1 is 2). x ^ y follows the rules of power(x, y): 0 ^ -1 and (-8) ^ 0.5 are errors (2201F), an overflow is error 22003.

g.gql("MATCH (n:person) WHERE n.age IN [27, 35] RETURN n.name AS name ORDER BY name").to_list()   // #{"name": "peter"}, #{"name": "vadas"}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) WHERE n.name STARTS WITH 'm' OR n.name ENDS WITH 's' OR n.name CONTAINS 'et' RETURN n.name AS name ORDER BY name").to_list()   // marko, peter, vadas
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) WHERE n.age > 30 XOR n.name = 'josh' RETURN n.name AS name ORDER BY name").to_list()   // #{"name": "peter"}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.name || '!' AS a, n.age * 2 + 1 AS b, n.age / 10 AS c, n.age % 10 AS d, n.age / 10.0 AS e ORDER BY a LIMIT 1").to_list()
// #{"a": "josh!", "b": 65, "c": 3, "d": 2, "e": 3.2}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.name AS name, CASE WHEN n.age < 30 THEN 'young' WHEN n.age < 34 THEN 'middle' ELSE 'senior' END AS band ORDER BY name").to_list()
// josh middle, marko young, peter senior, vadas young
g.gql("MATCH (n) RETURN n.name AS name, CASE n.lang WHEN 'java' THEN 'jvm' ELSE 'other' END AS k ORDER BY name LIMIT 2").to_list()
// #{"k": "other", "name": "josh"}, #{"k": "jvm", "name": "lop"}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN {name: n.name, tags: [n.age, NULL, true]} AS m ORDER BY n.name LIMIT 1").to_list()
// #{"m": #{"name": "josh", "tags": [32, (), true]}}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN RECORD {name: n.name, age: n.age} AS m ORDER BY n.name LIMIT 1").to_list()
// #{"m": #{"age": 32, "name": "josh"}}

RECORD {k: v} is the ISO record constructor with its keyword written out; it builds the same map as {k: v}. The word is contextual, not reserved: RECORD (any case) followed by { and then } or name: is the constructor; anywhere else record is an ordinary variable, also before a map projection such as record {.name}. A variable named record whose projection is empty or starts with a key: expr item is back-quoted: `record` {k: 1}.

Integer arithmetic stays integer (/ truncates toward zero, % takes the sign of the dividend); a float operand makes the result a float. An overflow or an integer division by zero is an error, never a wrapped value (Errors); a float divided by zero follows IEEE 754 (1.0 / 0.0 is Infinity, 0.0 / 0.0 is NaN; Semantics).

g.gql("RETURN [1, 2] + 3 AS a, 0 + [1] AS b, [1] + [2] AS c").to_list()   // #{"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [0, 1], "c": [1, 2]}

Indexing and slicing

x[i] reads the item i of a list, counted from 0; a negative index counts from the end (x[-1] is the last item), and an index out of range gives NULL. x[a..b] is the sub-list from a up to b (excluded); either bound may be left out (x[..2], x[1..]), a negative one counts from the end, bounds beyond the list are clamped, and a >= b gives []. On a map m[k] reads the entry of the string key k, and on a node or an edge n[k] reads the property k; a missing key gives NULL. n['name'] with a string literal is the property access n.name (the same plan, so a property index serves it); a computed key (n[$key], n['na' || 'me']) is read per row. A NULL list, map, index or bound gives NULL. These are Cypher forms with their Neo4j meaning, measured against the openCypher TCK (Semantics).

g.gql("RETURN [10, 20, 30][0] AS a, [10, 20, 30][-1] AS b, [10, 20, 30][5] AS c, [10, 20, 30][1..] AS d, [10, 20, 30][..-1] AS e").to_list()
// #{"a": 10, "b": 30, "c": (), "d": [20, 30], "e": [10, 20]}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WITH p ORDER BY p.age RETURN collect(p.name)[0] AS youngest, collect(p.name)[-2..] AS oldest").to_list()
// #{"oldest": ["josh", "peter"], "youngest": "vadas"}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN p['na' || 'me'] AS name, {lang: 'java'}['lang'] AS lang").to_list()
// #{"lang": "java", "name": "marko"}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'josh'}) RETURN p[$key] AS v", #{key: "age"}).to_list()   // #{"v": 32}
g.gql("RETURN 'abc'[0] AS c")   // error: cannot index a string

The index of a list is an integer (x[1.0] and x['1'] are errors, GQLSTATUS 22G03; convert with toInteger(i)), the key of a map or an element a string; a text is no list (use substring(s, start, length)). These errors arise when a row reaches the expression, as for every other operand of the wrong kind (Errors).

Map projections and comprehensions

Three Cypher forms build maps and lists inside an expression. They are not GQL; gql() accepts them with their Neo4j meaning because Cypher users and LLMs write them all the time (Cypher Aliases). Together they give a JSON-shaped answer: one row per entity, its related data nested inside.

v {.key, .*, x, key: expr}                    -- map projection of a vertex, an edge or a map
[x IN list]  [x IN list WHERE cond]  [x IN list | expr]  [x IN list WHERE cond | expr]
[(a)-[:R]->(b) WHERE cond | expr]             -- pattern comprehension, also [p = (a)-->(b) | p]

Map projection. v {...} builds a map from the variable v: .key is its property (NULL when missing, the key kept), .* every stored property (no id, no labels), x the entry x: x, and key: expr any value, all in the written order. Its Gremlin twins are project() and value_map().by(unfold()); the GQL form is the record constructor {name: p.name}, which differs only for a NULL variable (Semantics):

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p {.name, .age, decade: p.age / 10} AS m ORDER BY p.name LIMIT 2").to_list()
// #{"m": #{"age": 32, "decade": 3, "name": "josh"}}, #{"m": #{"age": 29, "decade": 2, "name": "marko"}}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN p {.*} AS m").to_list()   // #{"m": #{"age": 29, "name": "marko"}}
g.v().has("name", "marko").value_map().by(__.unfold()).to_list()   // #{"age": 29, "name": "marko"}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'})-[e:knows]->(f) RETURN e {.*, to: f.name} AS k ORDER BY k.to").to_list()
// #{"k": #{"to": "josh", "weight": 1.0}}, #{"k": #{"to": "vadas", "weight": 0.5}}

List comprehension. [x IN list WHERE cond | expr] walks the list in its order, keeps the items for which cond is TRUE and maps each kept item to expr; leave out WHERE to keep every item, | expr to keep the item itself. x is a new name that exists only inside the brackets. The Gremlin twin is local(__.unfold().is(..).fold()):

g.gql("RETURN [x IN range(1, 5) WHERE x % 2 = 1] AS odd, [x IN range(1, 3) | x * x] AS sq, [x IN [1, 2] | [y IN [10, 20] | x * y]] AS grid").to_list()
// #{"grid": [[10, 20], [20, 40]], "odd": [1, 3, 5], "sq": [1, 4, 9]}
g.inject([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]).local(__.unfold().is(P.gt(2)).fold()).to_list()   // [3, 4, 5]
g.gql("MATCH p = (a {name: 'marko'})-[:knows|created]->{2}(b) RETURN [x IN nodes(p) | x.name] AS names ORDER BY b.name").to_list()
// #{"names": ["marko", "josh", "lop"]}, #{"names": ["marko", "josh", "ripple"]}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, [x IN [p.age, p.age + 10] WHERE x > 30] AS l ORDER BY name LIMIT 2").to_list()
// #{"l": [32, 42], "name": "josh"}, #{"l": [39], "name": "marko"}

A | inside the list or the WHERE part ends that part, so a label alternative there needs parentheses: [x IN l WHERE x:(A|B) | x.name].

Pattern comprehension. [(a)-[:R]->(b) WHERE cond | expr] is the list of expr for every match of the pattern on the row: [] when nothing matches, never NULL. The pattern has at least one edge; it reads the variables bound before it (they are imported, like in EXISTS), and the names it binds itself (b here, or a path variable p = ...) exist only inside the brackets. It is a subquery: the Gremlin twin is project(..).by(__.out("knows").values("name").fold()), and the items come in no defined order.

g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN [(p)-[:knows]->(f) | f.name] AS friends").to_list()   // #{"friends": ["josh", "vadas"]}, in any order
g.v().has("name", "marko").project("friends").by(__.out("knows").values("name").fold()).to_list()   // #{"friends": ["josh", "vadas"]}
g.gql("MATCH (s:software {name: 'ripple'}) RETURN [(s)<-[:created]-(p) WHERE p.age > 30 | p.name] AS older").to_list()   // #{"older": ["josh"]}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE size([(p)-[:created]->(s) | s]) >= 2 RETURN p.name AS name").to_list()   // #{"name": "josh"}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN [q = (p)-[:knows]->() | path_length(q)] AS l").to_list()   // #{"l": [1, 1]}

Together, one row per person with its friends and projects nested inside, the shape a JSON API or an LLM wants (Result Shape):

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p {.name, friends: [(p)-[:knows]->(f) | f.name], projects: [(p)-[:created]->(s) | s {.name, .lang}]} AS person ORDER BY person.name").to_json()
// [{"person": {"name": "josh", "friends": [], "projects": [{"name": "ripple", "lang": "java"}, ...]}}, ...]

All three stand anywhere an expression does (WHERE, RETURN, WITH, LET, FILTER, FOR, ORDER BY, an aggregate's argument) and nest in each other. Their rules:

  • A comprehension variable must be a new name: one that is in scope, or that the query uses anywhere else, is an error (Semantics).
  • No aggregate inside the WHERE or | part (aggregate in a WITH first, or aggregate the list: size([..])).
  • A list-comprehension variable cannot be read inside an EXISTS or a pattern comprehension in its WHERE or | part yet (Not supported yet).
  • A pattern comprehension counts as a subquery: a query holds at most 64 subqueries (Errors).
  • The list predicates all(), any(), none(), single() and reduce() follow the same rules for their variables (below).
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN [p IN [1, 2] | p * 2] AS l")   // error: the comprehension variable `p` shadows the variable `p` in scope
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN [(p)-[:knows]->(f) | count(f)] AS l")   // error: count() cannot be used inside the | part of a pattern comprehension
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS n, [(p)-[:knows]->(f) | f.name] AS l ORDER BY f.name")   // error: `f` is bound inside a pattern comprehension
g.gql("RETURN size([x IN [1, 2, 3] WHERE x > 0]) = size([1, 2, 3]) AS all_positive").to_list()   // #{"all_positive": true}

List predicates and reduce

Cypher's all(x IN l WHERE c), any(..), none(..), single(..) and reduce(acc = init, x IN l | expr) are openCypher compatibility forms (Cypher Aliases has their NULL rules). The predicates are three-valued: a NULL list or, when no item decides the answer, a NULL condition gives NULL. A list comprehension counted with size() gives the same answer when no condition is NULL; over a pattern comprehension they are the Gremlin where(__..) / not(__..) of a pattern. reduce folds a list per row, where FOR and an aggregate fold the rows of a query.

g.gql("RETURN all(x IN [1, 2, 3] WHERE x > 0) AS a, any(x IN [1, NULL] WHERE x > 1) AS b, single(x IN [1, 2] WHERE x > 1) AS c").to_list()   // #{"a": true, "b": (), "c": true}
g.gql("RETURN size([x IN [1, 2, 3] WHERE x > 0]) = size([1, 2, 3]) AS a").to_list()   // #{"a": true}, the count form of all()
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE all(w IN [(p)-[:created]->(s) | s] WHERE w.lang = 'java') AND any(a IN [(p)-[:knows]->(f) | f.age] WHERE a > 30) RETURN p.name AS name").to_list()   // #{"name": "marko"}
g.V().hasLabel("person").not(__.out("created").has("lang", P.neq("java"))).where(__.out("knows").has("age", P.gt(30))).values("name").to_list()   // "marko"
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, reduce(s = 0, a IN [(p)-[:knows]->(f) | f.age] | s + a) AS ages ORDER BY name").to_list()   // josh 0, marko 59, peter 0, vadas 0
g.gql("FOR x IN [1, 2, 3] RETURN sum(x) AS s").to_list()   // #{"s": 6}, one fold over the rows
g.gql("RETURN reduce(s = 0, x IN [1, 2, 3] | s + x) AS s").to_list()   // #{"s": 6}, one fold per row
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN all(p IN [1] WHERE p > 0) AS a")   // error: the variable `p` of all() shadows the variable `p` in scope
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN any(x IN [1] WHERE x > count(*)) AS a")   // error: count() cannot be used inside the WHERE part of all(), any(), none() or single()

Functions

Function names are case-insensitive (toInteger, TOINTEGER). Every function returns NULL for a NULL argument (except coalesce, nullif and the ...OrNull conversions, by their definition) and fails for an argument of the wrong kind (22G03), never with a silent NULL. A position or a length counts characters (Unicode scalar values), never bytes. The aggregates are listed under Aggregation; Semantics has the exact rules and where they differ from Neo4j and from the Gremlin steps of the same name.

The functions come from two sources: the GQL functions (with their Cypher spellings as aliases), and a fixed list of openCypher compatibility functions that GQL has no counterpart for (toInteger, substring, split, round, keys, nodes, ...): they keep their Neo4j meaning (Cypher Aliases).

FunctionReturnsCypher alias
element_id(x)the id of a vertex or edge, a stringelementId(x)
labels(x)a vertex's labels in stored order (primary first); an edge's label as a one-item list
type(e)an edge's label; a vertex is an error (use labels(v))
coalesce(a, b, ...)the first argument that is not NULL
nullif(a, b)NULL when a = b is TRUE, else asame (nullIf)
path_length(p)the number of edges of a pathlength(p)
g.gql("MATCH (n) RETURN element_id(n) AS id, labels(n) AS labels ORDER BY id LIMIT 3").to_list()
// #{"id": "1", "labels": ["person"]}, #{"id": "2", "labels": ["person"]}, #{"id": "3", "labels": ["software"]}
g.gql("MATCH ()-[e]->() RETURN element_id(e) AS id, type(e) AS type, e.weight AS w ORDER BY id LIMIT 2").to_list()
// #{"id": "0", "type": "knows", "w": 0.5}, #{"id": "1", "type": "created", "w": 0.4}
g.gql("MATCH (n) RETURN n.name AS name, coalesce(n.age, n.lang) AS info ORDER BY name LIMIT 2").to_list()
// #{"info": 32, "name": "josh"}, #{"info": "java", "name": "lop"}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.name AS name, nullif(n.age, 29) AS age ORDER BY name").to_list()
// #{"age": 32, "name": "josh"}, #{"age": (), "name": "marko"}, #{"age": 35, "name": "peter"}, #{"age": 27, "name": "vadas"}

Conversions

GQL's CAST is strict: text that is not a value of the target type is an error (22018). The Cypher conversions are lenient: toInteger, toFloat, toBoolean give NULL for such text, and their ...OrNull forms give NULL for a value of any unsupported kind too (Semantics).

FunctionConvertsUnconvertible textWrong kind
CAST(x AS INTEGER) (INT, INT64, BIGINT, SIGNED INTEGER)integer; float truncated toward zero; a decimal text ('42', ' 1.9 ', '1e3')error 22018error 22G03 (a boolean too)
CAST(x AS FLOAT) (FLOAT64, DOUBLE, DOUBLE PRECISION, REAL)number; a decimal text, 'NaN', 'Infinity', '-Infinity'error 22018error 22G03
CAST(x AS STRING) (VARCHAR, CHAR VARYING)any value except a vertex, edge or path-error 22G03
CAST(x AS BOOLEAN) (BOOL)boolean; 'true' / 'false' in any case, 'unknown' is NULLerror 22018error 22G03 (numbers too)
toInteger(x)as CAST, also true / false (1 / 0) and Cypher literals ('0x1F', '0o17', '1_000')NULLerror 22G03
toFloat(x)as CAST, also Cypher literalsNULLerror 22G03
toBoolean(x)as CAST, also integers (0 is FALSE, any other TRUE)NULLerror 22G03
toString(x)as CAST(x AS STRING), scalars only; a temporal value in Neo4j's text (Dates and times)-error 22G03 (a list or a map too)
toIntegerOrNull(x), toFloatOrNull(x), toBooleanOrNull(x), toStringOrNull(x)as their toXNULLNULL (for toStringOrNull a list, map, vertex, edge or path too)

A float's text always shows that it is a float (toString(1.0) is '1.0', Neo4j's form), while Gremlin's as_string() gives "1"; integers and booleans give the same text as as_string(). A list or a map converts to Neo4j's text form ('[29, marko, 1.0, null]', '{a: 1, b: marko}').

g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.name AS name, toString(n.age) AS a, toString(n.age / 10.0) AS b ORDER BY name").to_list()
// #{"a": "32", "b": "3.2", "name": "josh"}, #{"a": "29", "b": "2.9", "name": "marko"}, #{"a": "35", "b": "3.5", "name": "peter"}, #{"a": "27", "b": "2.7", "name": "vadas"}
g.v().has_label("person").values("age").as_string().order().to_list()   // "27", "29", "32", "35"
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN toFloat(n.age) AS f ORDER BY f").to_list()   // #{"f": 27.0}, #{"f": 29.0}, #{"f": 32.0}, #{"f": 35.0}
g.v().has_label("person").values("age").as_number(GType.DOUBLE).order().to_list()   // 27.0, 29.0, 32.0, 35.0
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN CAST('42' AS INTEGER) AS i, CAST(' 1.5 ' AS FLOAT) AS f, CAST('TRUE' AS BOOLEAN) AS b, CAST(1.0 AS STRING) AS s").to_list()
// #{"b": true, "f": 1.5, "i": 42, "s": "1.0"}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN toInteger(' 42 ') AS a, toInteger('1.9') AS b, toInteger('0x1F') AS c, toInteger('abc') AS d, toIntegerOrNull(true) AS e").to_list()
// #{"a": 42, "b": 1, "c": 31, "d": (), "e": 1}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN toBoolean(1) AS a, toBooleanOrNull(1.5) AS b, toFloat('1e3') AS c, toFloatOrNull([1]) AS d").to_list()
// #{"a": true, "b": (), "c": 1000.0, "d": ()}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN CAST([n.age, n.name, 1.0, NULL] AS STRING) AS l, CAST({a: 1, b: n.name} AS STRING) AS m").to_list()
// #{"l": "[29, marko, 1.0, null]", "m": "{a: 1, b: marko}"}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN toString([n.age])")   // error: toString() takes a number, a boolean, a string or another scalar, not a list (22G03)
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN toStringOrNull([n.age]) AS s").to_list()   // #{"s": ()}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.name || ' is ' || toString(n.age) AS s ORDER BY s LIMIT 2").to_list()
// #{"s": "josh is 32"}, #{"s": "marko is 29"}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN CAST('abc' AS INTEGER) AS x")   // error: invalid character value for cast (22018)
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN toFloat(true) AS x")   // error: toFloat() takes a number or a string, not a boolean (22G03)
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN toString(n) AS x")   // error: toString() takes no vertex, edge or path (22G03)

CAST to a GQL type Graphersal has no values of yet (DATE, LIST<..>, DECIMAL, ...) is not supported yet; an unknown type name is a syntax error with a suggestion:

g.gql("MATCH (n) RETURN CAST(n.age AS DATE) AS d")   // error: CAST to DATE is not yet supported
g.gql("MATCH (n) RETURN CAST(n.age AS INTEGR) AS d")   // error: unknown type INTEGR in CAST, did you mean INTEGER

Strings

FunctionReturnsCypher spelling
upper(s), lower(s)the string in upper / lower casetoUpper(s), toLower(s)
char_length(s), character_length(s)the number of characterssize(s)
byte_length(s), octet_length(s)the number of UTF-8 bytes
left(s, n), right(s, n)the first / last n characters (the whole string when n is larger)same
substring(s, start [, length])Cypher: length characters from the 0-based start (to the end without length); past the end ''compatibility function
TRIM([[LEADING | TRAILING | BOTH] [c] FROM] s), trim(s)s without the character c (default: the space) at both ends, the start or the end; c is exactly one charactertrim(s)
btrim(s [, chars]), ltrim(s [, chars]), rtrim(s [, chars])s without any character of the set chars (default: the space) at both ends / the start / the endsame
replace(s, search, replacement [, limit])every occurrence of search replaced, left to right; at most limit of themcompatibility function
split(s, delimiter)the list of the parts between the delimiters (a string or a list of strings); empty parts are keptcompatibility function
reverse(x)a string with its characters reversed, or a list with its items reversedcompatibility function
isEmpty(x)whether a string, list or map has no character / item / entrycompatibility function

A negative position or length is an error (22011), and a TRIM character that is not exactly one character is too (22027). The SQL form SUBSTRING(s FROM a FOR b) is not GQL; it fails with a hint to substring(s, start, length).

g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN left(n.name, 2) AS l, right(n.name, 2) AS r, substring(n.name, 1, 3) AS s, substring(n.name, 2) AS t ORDER BY l").to_list()
// #{"l": "jo", "r": "sh", "s": "osh", "t": "sh"}, #{"l": "ma", "r": "ko", "s": "ark", "t": "rko"}, ... peter, vadas
g.v().has_label("person").values("name").substring(1, 4).order().to_list()   // "ada", "ark", "ete", "osh"
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.name AS name, replace(n.name, 'a', '4') AS r, split(n.name, 'a') AS s ORDER BY name").to_list()
// #{"name": "josh", "r": "josh", "s": ["josh"]}, #{"name": "marko", "r": "m4rko", "s": ["m", "rko"]}, ... #{"name": "vadas", "r": "v4d4s", "s": ["v", "d", "s"]}
g.v().has_label("person").values("name").replace("a", "4").order().to_list()   // "josh", "m4rko", "peter", "v4d4s"
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN reverse(n.name) AS r, reverse([1, 2, 3]) AS l, byte_length('héllo') AS b, char_length('héllo') AS c, isEmpty('') AS e").to_list()
// #{"b": 6, "c": 5, "e": true, "l": [3, 2, 1], "r": "okram"}
g.v().has("name", "marko").values("name").reverse().to_list()   // "okram"
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN trim('  a  ') AS a, TRIM(LEADING 'x' FROM 'xxaxx') AS b, TRIM(TRAILING FROM '  a  ') AS c, btrim('xyaxy', 'xy') AS d, ltrim('  a  ') AS e, rtrim('..a..', '.') AS f").to_list()
// #{"a": "a", "b": "axx", "c": "  a", "d": "a", "e": "a  ", "f": "..a"}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN split('a,,b,', ',') AS a, split('a-b;c', ['-', ';']) AS b, split('abc', '') AS c, replace('abc', '', '.') AS d, replace('aaa', 'a', 'b', 2) AS e").to_list()
// #{"a": ["a", "", "b", ""], "b": ["a", "b", "c"], "c": ["a", "b", "c"], "d": ".a.b.c.", "e": "bba"}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN substring(n.name, -1) AS x")   // error: substring() takes a start of 0 or more (22011)
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN TRIM(BOTH 'ab' FROM 'abxab') AS x")   // error: TRIM(.. FROM ..) removes exactly one character (22027)
g.gql("MATCH (n) RETURN SUBSTRING(n.name FROM 1 FOR 2) AS r")   // error: SUBSTRING(s FROM a FOR b) is SQL, not GQL

Numbers

FunctionReturnsCypher spelling
abs(x)the absolute value, of the argument's typesame
floor(x), ceil(x) / ceiling(x)rounded down / up; an integer stays the integersame
round(x [, precision [, mode]])rounded, always a float; mode one of 'UP', 'DOWN', 'CEILING', 'FLOOR', 'HALF_UP' (the default), 'HALF_DOWN', 'HALF_EVEN'compatibility function
sign(x)-1, 0 or 1, an integercompatibility function
sqrt(x), exp(x)the square root, e to the power x; a floatsame
ln(x), log10(x)the natural / decimal logarithm; a floatlog(x), log10(x)
log(base, x)the logarithm to base; a float
power(x, y)x to the power y; a float(Cypher's ^ is not supported yet)
mod(a, b)the remainder, exactly as a % ba % b

None of them makes NaN or an infinity from finite numbers: the square root of a negative number and power() of 0 to a negative power are errors (2201F), the logarithm of a number <= 0 is an error (2201E), an overflow is 22003. round() with one argument rounds a half toward positive infinity (round(-2.5) is -2.0, Java's and Neo4j's rule); with a precision it rounds the decimal text of the number (round(2.675, 2) is 2.68).

g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.name AS name, sqrt(n.age) AS s ORDER BY name LIMIT 2").to_list()
// #{"name": "josh", "s": 5.656854249492381}, #{"name": "marko", "s": 5.385164807134504}
g.v().has_label("person").order().by("name").limit(2).values("age").math("sqrt(_)").to_list()   // 5.656854249492381, 5.385164807134504
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN abs(-3) AS a, abs(-2.5) AS b, floor(2.7) AS c, ceil(2.1) AS d, ceiling(3) AS e, sign(-0.5) AS f, mod(7, 3) AS g").to_list()
// #{"a": 3, "b": 2.5, "c": 2.0, "d": 3.0, "e": 3, "f": -1, "g": 1}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN round(2.5) AS a, round(-2.5) AS b, round(2.675, 2) AS c, round(-1.55, 1) AS d, round(2.5, 0, 'HALF_EVEN') AS e, round(3) AS f").to_list()
// #{"a": 3.0, "b": -2.0, "c": 2.68, "d": -1.6, "e": 2.0, "f": 3.0}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN exp(1) AS a, ln(1) AS b, log(100) AS c, log10(1000) AS d, log(2, 8) AS e, power(2, 10) AS f").to_list()
// #{"a": 2.718281828459045, "b": 0.0, "c": 4.605170185988092, "d": 3.0, "e": 3.0, "f": 1024.0}
g.inject(100).math("log(_)").to_list()   // 4.605170185988092
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN round(avg(n.age), 1) AS mean").to_list()   // #{"mean": 30.8}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN ln(0) AS x")   // error: ln() of a number <= 0 (2201E)
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN sqrt(-1) AS x")   // error: sqrt() of a negative number (2201F)
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN round(1234.5, -2) AS x")   // error: round() needs a precision >= 0 (22023)

Lists, elements and paths

FunctionReturnsCypher spelling
size(list), cardinality(list)the number of items (size(e) of a group variable counts its edges)size(list)
head(list), last(list)the first / last item; NULL for []compatibility function
tail(list)all items but the firstcompatibility function
trim(list, n)the list without its last n items
range(start, end [, step])the integers from start to end inclusive, by step (default 1)compatibility function
keys(x)the property keys of a vertex or edge (a stored null is no key), or the keys of a mapcompatibility function
properties(x)the properties of a vertex or edge as a map; a map itselfcompatibility function
startNode(e), endNode(e)the stored source / target vertex of the edgecompatibility function
n IS [NOT] SOURCE OF e, n IS [NOT] DESTINATION OF ewhether n is the edge's source / target (a predicate)
nodes(p), relationships(p)the vertices / the edges of a path, in the path's ordercompatibility function

startNode(e) is the edge's stored source, whatever direction the pattern was written in: in (a)-[e]-(b) the variable a may be either end. range() checks its size before it builds the list, so range(0, 9223372036854775807) is a limit error, never an out-of-memory (Errors).

g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN head([1, 2, 3]) AS h, last([1, 2, 3]) AS l, tail([1, 2, 3]) AS t, trim([1, 2, 3], 1) AS tr, range(1, 5) AS r, range(10, 0, -5) AS d, head([]) AS e").to_list()
// #{"d": [10, 5, 0], "e": (), "h": 1, "l": 3, "r": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], "t": [2, 3], "tr": [1, 2]}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person)-[:created]->(s) WITH p, s ORDER BY s.name RETURN p.name AS name, head(collect(s.name)) AS first ORDER BY name").to_list()
// #{"first": "lop", "name": "josh"}, #{"first": "lop", "name": "marko"}, #{"first": "lop", "name": "peter"}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN keys(n) AS k, properties(n) AS p").to_list()   // #{"k": ["name", "age"], "p": #{"age": 29, "name": "marko"}}
g.v().has("name", "marko").properties().key().fold().to_list()   // ["name", "age"]
g.v().has("name", "marko").value_map().by(__.unfold()).to_list()   // #{"age": 29, "name": "marko"}
g.gql("MATCH (a)-[e:knows]-(b) RETURN a.name AS a, b.name AS b, startNode(e).name AS s, endNode(e).name AS t ORDER BY a, b").to_list()
// josh marko: s marko, t josh; marko josh: marko, josh; marko vadas: marko, vadas; vadas marko: marko, vadas
g.e().has_label("knows").project("s", "t").by(__.out_v().values("name")).by(__.in_v().values("name")).to_list()
// #{"s": "marko", "t": "vadas"}, #{"s": "marko", "t": "josh"}
g.gql("MATCH (a)-[e:knows]-(b) RETURN a.name AS a, b.name AS b, a IS SOURCE OF e AS src ORDER BY a, b").to_list()
// josh marko false, marko josh true, marko vadas true, vadas marko false
g.gql("MATCH p = (a {name: 'marko'})-[:knows|created]->{1,2}(b) RETURN b.name AS b, size(nodes(p)) AS n, size(relationships(p)) AS r, last(nodes(p)) = b AS same ORDER BY n, b").to_list()
// josh 2 1 true, lop 2 1 true, vadas 2 1 true, lop 3 2 true, ripple 3 2 true
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN range(0, 9223372036854775807) AS r")   // error: Resource limit 'traversal.max_materialized_bytes' exceeded

A list comprehension maps or filters the items of a list ([x IN nodes(p) | x.name]); FOR walks a list as rows and collect_list() collects them again:

g.gql("MATCH p = (a {name: 'marko'})-[:knows]->(b) RETURN b.name AS b, [x IN nodes(p) | x.name] AS names ORDER BY b").to_list()
// #{"b": "josh", "names": ["marko", "josh"]}, #{"b": "vadas", "names": ["marko", "vadas"]}
g.gql("MATCH p = (a {name: 'marko'})-[:knows]->(b) FOR x IN nodes(p) RETURN b.name AS b, collect_list(x.name) AS names ORDER BY b").to_list()
// #{"b": "josh", "names": ["marko", "josh"]}, #{"b": "vadas", "names": ["marko", "vadas"]}

Dates and times

The temporal values are the engine's six date and time types (date, time, offsettime, localdatetime, datetime, duration): a value gql() builds is the same value a Gremlin step or a stored property holds, and a stored date reads as a date (n.born.year). The functions are openCypher's (Neo4j Cypher 25) with Neo4j's meaning; the constructors also have their ISO GQL names. The places where an answer differs from Neo4j are on Semantics, and the Gremlin step that does the same as each function on Dates in GQL.

ISO GQLCypherGives (engine type)
date(x)date(x)a calendar day (date)
local_time(x)localtime(x)a time of day without an offset (time)
zoned_time(x)time(x)a time of day with its UTC offset (offsettime)
local_datetime(x)localdatetime(x)a date and a time of day without an offset (localdatetime)
zoned_datetime(x)datetime(x)an instant with its UTC offset, and its zone name when built with one (datetime)
duration(x)duration(x)months, days and a time part (duration)

x is ISO 8601 text, a map of fields, or (not for duration) another temporal value, which is projected onto the type (date(datetime(..)) is the date at the value's own offset, datetime(localdatetime(..)) the wall clock at UTC, time(localtime(..)) at UTC, time(datetime(..)) its time of day and offset). With no argument a constructor gives the time the query started (Clocks). A NULL argument, or a NULL field of the map, gives NULL. Values hold nanoseconds, as Neo4j's: up to nine fraction digits and the nanosecond field are kept exactly. A constant can also be written as an ISO GQL literal, DATE '2015-07-21' (Literals).

g.gql("RETURN date('2015-07-21') AS d, localtime('21:40:32.142') AS t, localdatetime('2015-07-21T21:40') AS ldt, datetime('2015-07-21T21:40+01:00') AS dt").to_list()
// #{"d": date("2015-07-21"), "dt": datetime("2015-07-21T21:40:00+01:00"), "ldt": localdatetime("2015-07-21T21:40:00"), "t": time("21:40:32.142")}
g.gql("RETURN local_time('10:00') AS t, local_datetime('2015-07-21T21:40') AS ldt, zoned_datetime('2015-07-21T21:40:32+02:00') AS dt").to_list()
// #{"dt": datetime("2015-07-21T21:40:32+02:00"), "ldt": localdatetime("2015-07-21T21:40:00"), "t": time("10:00:00")}
g.gql("RETURN date(datetime('2015-07-21T23:40:32+02:00')) AS d, localtime(datetime('2015-07-21T23:40:32+02:00')) AS t, datetime(localdatetime('2015-07-21T12:00')) AS dt").to_list()
// #{"d": date("2015-07-21"), "dt": datetime("2015-07-21T12:00:00Z"), "t": time("23:40:32")}
g.gql("RETURN date(null) AS a, date({year: 2015, month: null}) AS b").to_list()   // #{"a": (), "b": ()}

Text. The constructors read ISO 8601 as Neo4j does, in the extended and the basic form:

TypeText forms (examples)
date2015-07-21 / 20150721, 2015-07 / 201507, 2015; week dates 2015-W30-2 / 2015W302, 2015-W30 (its Monday); ordinal dates 2015-202 / 2015202; quarter dates 2015-Q3-21 / 2015Q321, 2015-Q3
localtime21:40:32.142 / 214032.142, 21:40 / 2140, 21; a comma for the fraction (21:40:32,142); no offset (12:00+01:00 is 22007)
timea localtime form, then Z, +01:00, +0100 or +01 (21:40:32.142+0100, 2140-02); no offset is UTC; no zone name
localdatetimea date form, T, a time form: 2015-07-21T21:40, 2015-W30-2T2140, 2015202T21:40:32.142
datetimea local datetime with Z, +01:00, +0100 or +01, and / or a zone in brackets: 2015-07-21T21:40:32.142[Europe/London], ..+01:00[Europe/London] (the offset must be the zone's at that time; the name is kept); a date alone is midnight; no offset and no zone is UTC
durationP14DT16H12M, P5W, -P1D, P-1DT2H; a fraction on any unit (P1.5Y, PT0.75M, PT1.5H); the alternative form P0001-02-03T04:05:06
g.gql("RETURN date('2015W302') AS w, date('2015-202') AS o, date('2015-Q3-21') AS q, date('2015-W30') AS monday").to_list()
// #{"monday": date("2015-07-20"), "o": date("2015-07-21"), "q": date("2015-07-21"), "w": date("2015-07-21")}
g.gql("RETURN datetime('2015-07-21T21:40:32.142[Europe/London]') AS a, datetime('2015-07-21T21:40:32+0100') AS b, datetime('2015-07-21') AS c").to_list()
// #{"a": datetime("2015-07-21T21:40:32.142+01:00[Europe/London]"), "b": datetime("2015-07-21T21:40:32+01:00"), "c": datetime("2015-07-21T00:00:00Z")}
g.gql("RETURN time('21:40:32.142+0100') AS a, time('2140-02') AS b, zoned_time('12:00') AS c").to_list()
// #{"a": offsettime("21:40:32.142+01:00"), "b": offsettime("21:40:00-02:00"), "c": offsettime("12:00:00Z")}
g.gql("RETURN duration('P1Y2M10DT2H30M') AS a, duration('P1.5Y') AS b, duration('PT0.75M') AS c, duration('P0001-02-03T04:05:06') AS d").to_list()
// #{"a": duration("P1Y2M10DT2H30M"), "b": duration("P1Y6M"), "c": duration("PT45S"), "d": duration("P1Y2M3DT4H5M6S")}
g.gql("RETURN date('2015-13-01') AS d")   // fails: the date does not exist (22007)

Maps. A map names the fields; the keys match in any ASCII case:

TypeKeys
dateyear with one group: month / day; week / dayOfWeek (ISO 8601 weeks: year is then the week-numbering year); ordinalDay; quarter / dayOfQuarter. A missing smaller field is its first value ({year: 1984} is January 1)
localtimehour, minute, second, and millisecond, microsecond, nanosecond (added up: {millisecond: 645, microsecond: 876} is .645876)
timethe keys of localtime and timezone (an offset, or a zone name: its offset at the query's instant); no timezone is UTC
localdatetimethe keys of both
datetimethe keys of both and timezone ('+01:00', 'Europe/Stockholm': the name is kept); no timezone is UTC
base valuesdate: d takes the date (of a date, a local datetime or a datetime at its own offset), time: t the time of day (and the offset of a datetime or time t, and the zone name of a datetime t), datetime: x both; the other keys then override single fields ({date: d, day: 28}, {date: d, week: 1} keeps the day of the week), and a base with a zone name is read again in its zone. With a base that has an offset, timezone converts the instant (12:00+01:00 to 16:00+05:00); without one it attaches the zone
durationyears, months, weeks, days, hours, minutes, seconds, milliseconds, microseconds, nanoseconds, each may be fractional and negative; a fraction cascades down (a year is 12 months, a month 2 629 746 seconds, a week 7 days, a day 86 400 seconds, then the whole days of the seconds become days: {months: 0.75} is P22DT19H51M49.5S)

An unknown key, or two groups of date keys together, is 22007; a field out of range (month: 13, day: 30 in February, hour: 25, the year 10000) is 22008.

g.gql("RETURN date({year: 2015, week: 30, dayOfWeek: 2}) AS w, date({year: 1984, quarter: 3, dayOfQuarter: 45}) AS q, localdatetime({year: 1984, ordinalDay: 202, hour: 12}) AS o").to_list()
// #{"o": localdatetime("1984-07-20T12:00:00"), "q": date("1984-08-14"), "w": date("2015-07-21")}
g.gql("RETURN localtime({hour: 12, minute: 31, second: 14, millisecond: 645, microsecond: 876}) AS t, datetime({year: 1984, month: 10, day: 11, hour: 12, timezone: 'Europe/Stockholm'}) AS dt").to_list()
// #{"dt": datetime("1984-10-11T12:00:00+01:00[Europe/Stockholm]"), "t": time("12:31:14.645876")}
g.gql("RETURN date({date: date('2015-07-21'), day: 28}) AS a, localdatetime({date: date('2015-07-21'), time: localtime('12:30')}) AS b, datetime({datetime: datetime('2015-07-21T12:00+01:00'), timezone: '+05:00'}) AS c").to_list()
// #{"a": date("2015-07-28"), "b": localdatetime("2015-07-21T12:30:00"), "c": datetime("2015-07-21T16:00:00+05:00")}
g.gql("RETURN duration({days: 14, hours: 16, minutes: 12}) AS a, duration({years: 1.5, weeks: 2, seconds: 1.25}) AS b, duration({months: 0.75}) AS c").to_list()
// #{"a": duration("P14DT16H12M"), "b": duration("P1Y6M14DT1.250S"), "c": duration("P22DT19H51M49.500S")}
g.gql("RETURN date({year: 2015, month: 2, day: 30}) AS d")   // fails: the field day cannot be 30 (22008)

datetime.fromepoch(seconds, nanoseconds) and datetime.fromepochmillis(milliseconds) give the datetime (UTC) of a time since 1970-01-01T00:00Z. The map form does the same as in Neo4j: datetime({epochSeconds: s}) with an optional millisecond / microsecond / nanosecond, or datetime({epochMillis: ms}), each with an optional timezone (the instant shown in that zone); no other field may stand next to them.

g.gql("RETURN datetime.fromepoch(1416779, 999999000) AS a, datetime.fromepochmillis(237821673987) AS b").to_list()
// #{"a": datetime("1970-01-17T09:32:59.999999Z"), "b": datetime("1977-07-15T13:34:33.987Z")}
g.gql("RETURN datetime({epochSeconds: 1416779, microsecond: 5}) AS a, datetime({epochMillis: 237821673987, timezone: '+01:00'}) AS b").to_list()
// #{"a": datetime("1970-01-17T09:32:59.000005Z"), "b": datetime("1977-07-15T14:34:33.987+01:00")}

Components

x.name reads a component of a temporal value (any ASCII case: d.weekyear is d.weekYear). A name the value's type does not have is 22G03, and the message lists the names it has:

OfComponents
date, localdatetime, datetimeyear, quarter (1-4), month, week and weekYear (ISO 8601: Monday weeks, week 1 holds January 4), dayOfQuarter (also quarterDay), day, ordinalDay (1-366), dayOfWeek (also weekDay; 1 = Monday to 7 = Sunday)
localtime, time, localdatetime, datetimehour, minute, second, millisecond, microsecond, nanosecond, each fraction counted from the start of the second (.645876 gives 645, 645876, 645876000)
datetimetimezone (the zone name, 'Europe/Stockholm', of a value built with one, else the offset text), offset (the offset text: Z, +01:00), offsetMinutes, offsetSeconds, epochSeconds, epochMillis
timetimezone and offset (the offset text), offsetMinutes, offsetSeconds
durationthe totals years, quarters, months, weeks, days, hours, minutes, seconds, milliseconds, microseconds, nanoseconds; the remainders quartersOfYear, monthsOfQuarter, monthsOfYear, daysOfWeek, minutesOfHour, secondsOfMinute, millisecondsOfSecond, microsecondsOfSecond, nanosecondsOfSecond

A duration's months, days and seconds stay apart: years and quarters count its months, weeks its days, hours to nanoseconds its time part (duration('P1M2D').days is 2). The divisions truncate toward zero (duration({months: -16}).years is -1).

g.gql("RETURN date('2017-10-11').year AS y, date('2017-10-11').week AS w, date('2017-10-11').dayOfWeek AS dw, date('1984-01-01').weekYear AS wy, date('1984-10-11').ordinalDay AS o").to_list()
// #{"dw": 3, "o": 285, "w": 41, "wy": 1983, "y": 2017}
g.gql("RETURN datetime('2015-07-21T21:40:32.142+01:00').epochMillis AS e, datetime('2015-07-21T21:40:32.142+01:00').offset AS o, localtime('12:31:14.645876').millisecond AS ms").to_list()
// #{"e": 1437511232142, "ms": 645, "o": "+01:00"}
g.gql("RETURN duration({months: 14, days: 3, seconds: 3725}).years AS y, duration({months: 14, days: 3, seconds: 3725}).monthsOfYear AS my, duration({months: 14, days: 3, seconds: 3725}).hours AS h").to_list()
// #{"h": 1, "my": 2, "y": 1}
g.gql("RETURN date('2015-01-01').hour AS h")   // fails: a date has no component hour (22G03)

Arithmetic and comparison

FormResult
x + dur, dur + x, x - dur (x a date, localtime, time, localdatetime or datetime)a value of x's type: the duration's months (the day clamped to the month's end), then its days, then its time part, each where the type has it
dur + dur, dur - durpart by part (P1D + PT49H is P1DT49H)
dur * n, n * dur, dur / neach part scaled, with the fraction cascade of duration({..}) (P1M * 0.5 is P15DT5H14M33S)
-durevery part negated

A date takes the months, the days and the whole days of the time part (toward zero: PT33H adds one day, PT-33H takes one away), a localtime and a time only the time part, wrapping around midnight (a time keeps its offset). A datetime keeps its offset, or, with a zone name, follows its zone: a day added across a daylight saving change keeps the wall-clock time. Two values that are not both durations cannot be added (22G03: the time between them is duration.between(a, b)); dur / 0 is 22012; a result outside the years -9999 to 9999 is 22008.

g.gql("RETURN date('2024-01-31') + duration('P1M') AS a, date('1997-09-11') + duration('P29DT33H') AS b, localtime('23:00') + duration('PT2H') AS c, localdatetime('2015-07-21T21:40') - duration('PT1H30M') AS d").to_list()
// #{"a": date("2024-02-29"), "b": date("1997-10-11"), "c": time("01:00:00"), "d": localdatetime("2015-07-21T20:10:00")}
g.gql("RETURN duration('P1M') * 0.5 AS a, duration('P1Y') / 2 AS b, duration('P1D') + duration('PT49H') AS c, -duration('P1D') AS d").to_list()
// #{"a": duration("P15DT5H14M33S"), "b": duration("P6M"), "c": duration("P1DT49H"), "d": duration("-P1D")}
g.gql("RETURN date('2015-01-01') + date('2015-01-01') AS x")   // fails: + adds a duration to a temporal value (22G03)

Values of one type compare by calendar and clock, two datetimes by their instant (12:00+01:00 = 11:00Z is TRUE). Two durations are equal when their months, days and time part are, but they are not ordered: <, >, <=, >= on two durations are NULL (a month has no fixed length); ORDER BY still sorts them, by their length with a month of 30 days. Values of different temporal types are never equal (= FALSE) and not ordered (NULL), as values of different kinds are (Comparisons across types).

g.gql("RETURN datetime('2015-07-21T12:00+01:00') = datetime('2015-07-21T11:00Z') AS a, date('2015-01-01') < date('2016-01-01') AS b, duration('P1M') < duration('P30DT1S') AS c, date('2015-01-01') = localdatetime('2015-01-01T00:00') AS d").to_list()
// #{"a": true, "b": true, "c": (), "d": false}
g.gql("FOR d IN [duration('P1M'), duration('P30DT1S'), duration('PT1H')] RETURN d ORDER BY d").to_list()
// #{"d": duration("PT1H")}, #{"d": duration("P1M")}, #{"d": duration("P30DT1S")}

toString(x) writes a temporal value in Neo4j's text ('12:00', '1984-10-11T12:31', 'PT-1M-0.001S': no zero seconds, trailing fraction zeros stripped, a sign per duration component), while CAST(x AS STRING) writes the engine's canonical ISO 8601 text ('12:00:00', '-PT1M0.001S', Text Formats). The constructors read both back.

g.gql("RETURN toString(localtime('12:00')) AS a, CAST(localtime('12:00') AS STRING) AS b, toString(duration({minutes: -1, milliseconds: -1})) AS c, CAST(duration({minutes: -1, milliseconds: -1}) AS STRING) AS d").to_list()
// #{"a": "12:00", "b": "12:00:00", "c": "PT-1M-0.001S", "d": "-PT1M0.001S"}

Truncation

date.truncate(unit, x [, map]), localtime.truncate(..), time.truncate(..), localdatetime.truncate(..) and datetime.truncate(..) cut x to the start of unit and give a value of their type (these qualified names are Cypher's; GQL has no spelling for them):

FunctionUnits (any ASCII case)
date.truncatemillennium, century, decade, year, weekYear, quarter, month, week, day
localdatetime.truncate, datetime.truncatethose, and hour, minute, second, millisecond, microsecond, nanosecond
localtime.truncate, time.truncateday (midnight) to nanosecond
  • millennium and century follow Neo4j: 2017 truncates to 2000, 1984 to 1900 (Gremlin's date_trunc keeps PostgreSQL's 2001 and 1901). weekYear is the Monday of ISO week 1 of the week-numbering year (1984-01-01 gives 1983-01-03); week is a Monday; nanosecond keeps the value (it holds nanoseconds).
  • x may be of another temporal type and is projected first: the date of a datetime at its own offset, the time of day of either, midnight for a date. datetime.truncate keeps the offset of a datetime (and its zone name: the truncated wall clock is read in that zone again) and gives UTC to a value without one; time.truncate keeps the offset of a time or a datetime.
  • The map overrides fields of the truncated value as the constructors' base form does: {day: 2}, {dayOfWeek: 2}, {hour: 1}, {millisecond: 5}, and for datetime.truncate {timezone: ..}, which keeps the wall clock and reads it in that zone (a name is kept), for time.truncate the offset of the result.
  • A unit the type lacks (date.truncate('hour', ..)) or an unknown unit is 22023; a value without the part the type needs (date.truncate('day', localtime(..))) or a duration 22G03.
g.gql("RETURN date.truncate('millennium', date('2017-10-11')) AS m, date.truncate('century', date('1984-10-11')) AS c, date.truncate('weekYear', date('1984-01-01')) AS wy").to_list()
// #{"c": date("1900-01-01"), "m": date("2000-01-01"), "wy": date("1983-01-03")}
g.gql("RETURN date.truncate('week', date('2017-10-11'), {dayOfWeek: 2}) AS a, localdatetime.truncate('quarter', localdatetime('2017-11-11T12:31:14'), {day: 2}) AS b, localtime.truncate('hour', localtime('12:31:14'), {minute: 5}) AS c").to_list()
// #{"a": date("2017-10-10"), "b": localdatetime("2017-10-02T00:00:00"), "c": time("12:05:00")}
g.gql("RETURN datetime.truncate('month', date('2017-11-11')) AS a, datetime.truncate('day', datetime('2017-10-11T12:31:14+01:00'), {timezone: 'Europe/Stockholm'}) AS b").to_list()
// #{"a": datetime("2017-11-01T00:00:00Z"), "b": datetime("2017-10-11T00:00:00+02:00[Europe/Stockholm]")}
g.gql("RETURN date.truncate('hour', date('2017-10-11')) AS d")   // fails: the unit hour is not defined for a date (22023)

Durations between two values

FunctionGives
duration.between(a, b)the whole months from a to b (a month counts once its day of the month and time of day are reached), then the whole days after them, then the rest of the time; every part has the sign of the direction
duration.inMonths(a, b)the whole months only (toward zero)
duration.inDays(a, b)the whole days only (toward zero)
duration.inSeconds(a, b)the elapsed time, as a duration of seconds only

The operands may be of different types; they are aligned first as Neo4j aligns them: when only one has a time of day, the other gets midnight; when only one has a date, the other gets that date (date('1984-10-11') to localtime('16:30') is PT16H30M); when only one has an offset, the other is read at that offset, or in that side's zone when it is a datetime with a zone name (across a daylight saving change, as Neo4j). inMonths / inDays of two localtimes or two times, a duration or a value that is no temporal value is 22G03.

g.gql("RETURN duration.between(date('1984-10-11'), date('2015-06-24')) AS d, duration.inMonths(date('1984-10-11'), date('2015-06-24')) AS m, duration.inDays(date('1984-10-11'), date('2015-06-24')) AS dd, duration.inSeconds(date('1984-10-11'), date('1984-10-12')) AS s").to_list()
// #{"d": duration("P30Y8M13D"), "dd": duration("P11213D"), "m": duration("P30Y8M"), "s": duration("PT24H")}
g.gql("RETURN duration.between(localdatetime('2015-07-21T21:40:32.142'), date('2015-06-24')) AS a, duration.between(date('1984-10-11'), localtime('16:30')) AS b").to_list()
// #{"a": duration("-P27DT21H40M32.142S"), "b": duration("PT16H30M")}
g.gql("RETURN duration.inDays(localtime('10:00'), localtime('12:00')) AS d")   // fails: two local times have no days (22G03)

Clocks

date(), localtime(), time(), localdatetime() and datetime() with no argument (and their ISO names), the ISO clocks CURRENT_DATE, CURRENT_TIME, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, LOCAL_TIME and LOCAL_TIMESTAMP (written without parentheses; current_date() with empty ones is accepted too), and X.statement() / X.transaction() (date.statement(), datetime.transaction(), ...) give the time the query started: one instant per query, the same for every row and every call, so a query is deterministic and repeatable. A zone argument or map gives that instant in the zone (datetime.statement('Europe/Berlin'), date({timezone: '+05:00'})); the default zone is UTC. In a script the instant is the script's own: datetime() in g.gql(..) equals the script's now(), and date() its today() at UTC. X.realtime(), a clock that moves while the query runs, is refused like rand().

g.gql("RETURN date() = date.statement() AS a, datetime.transaction() = datetime() AS b, datetime({timezone: '+05:00'}).timezone AS z").to_list()   // #{"a": true, "b": true, "z": "+05:00"}
g.gql("RETURN CURRENT_DATE = date() AS a, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP = zoned_datetime() AS b, LOCAL_TIMESTAMP = local_datetime() AS c").to_list()   // #{"a": true, "b": true, "c": true}
g.gql("FOR i IN [1, 2, 3] RETURN count(DISTINCT datetime()) AS instants").to_list()   // #{"instants": 1}
g.gql("RETURN datetime.realtime() AS t")   // refused: a clock that moves while the query runs

Literals

The ISO GQL temporal literals are a type word and a string; the string is read as the constructor of that type reads its text:

LiteralValueAs
DATE '2024-01-05'a datedate('2024-01-05')
TIME '10:00:00.5'a local time (no offset in the text)local_time('10:00:00.5')
TIME '10:00+01:00'a zoned time (an offset in the text)zoned_time('10:00+01:00')
DATETIME '2024-01-05T10:00', TIMESTAMP '..'a local datetime (no offset or zone in the text)local_datetime('..')
DATETIME '2024-01-05T10:00+01:00', TIMESTAMP '..[Europe/Berlin]'a zoned datetime (an offset or a zone in the text, a zone name kept)zoned_datetime('..')
DURATION 'P1DT2H'a durationduration('P1DT2H')
ZONED TIME '..', ZONED DATETIME '..' / ZONED TIMESTAMP '..'the zoned type; a text without an offset or zone is a syntax error (42001)zoned_time('..'), zoned_datetime('..')
LOCAL TIME '..', LOCAL DATETIME '..' / LOCAL TIMESTAMP '..'the local type; an offset in the text is 22007local_time('..'), local_datetime('..')

The type follows the text as ISO GQL defines it, never a guess from its content beyond the offset: TIME '10:00' is a local time, TIME '10:00Z' a zoned one. The ZONED / LOCAL forms spell the type out (the words of the GQL type names, as in CAST). A text the type cannot read is 22007. The type words are no reserved words: date stays a variable name wherever no string follows it.

g.gql("RETURN DATE '2024-01-31' + DURATION 'P1M' AS d, TIME '10:00:00.123456789+01:00' AS t, TIMESTAMP '2024-01-05T10:00[Europe/Berlin]' AS z").to_list()
// #{"d": date("2024-02-29"), "t": offsettime("10:00:00.123456789+01:00"), "z": datetime("2024-01-05T10:00:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]")}
g.gql("RETURN ZONED TIME '10:00' AS t")   // error: a ZONED TIME literal needs a UTC offset or a time zone (42001)

Not yet

timestamp() (Neo4j's milliseconds since 1970), date_trunc(), datetime_trunc() and CAST(x AS DATE) (and the other temporal CAST targets). Each is 0A000 with the alternative.

g.gql("RETURN timestamp() AS t")   // error: timestamp() is not yet supported
g.gql("RETURN time('12:00+01:00') AS t").to_list()   // [#{"t": offsettime("12:00:00+01:00")}]

Parameters

$name reads the value of name from the parameter map, the second argument of gql(). A parameter is a value, never query text: it cannot change the query, whatever it holds. A parameter the query reads but the map lacks is an error before the run; extra entries are ignored.

g.gql("MATCH (n:person) WHERE n.age > $min RETURN n.name AS name ORDER BY name", #{min: 30}).to_list()   // #{"name": "josh"}, #{"name": "peter"}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) WHERE n.name IN $names RETURN n.name AS name, n.age AS age ORDER BY name", #{names: ["josh", "vadas"]}).to_list()
// #{"age": 32, "name": "josh"}, #{"age": 27, "name": "vadas"}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: $who})-[:created]->(s) RETURN s.name AS s", #{who: "peter"}).to_list()   // #{"s": "lop"}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.name AS name ORDER BY name SKIP $s LIMIT $l", #{s: 2, l: 5}).to_list()   // #{"name": "peter"}, #{"name": "vadas"}

A parameter may also stand where an index can serve it, so MATCH (p:person {name: $n}) uses a property index on person.name when one exists (Plans and Performance).

Not supported yet

These are part of GQL (or Cypher constructs that LLMs and Cypher users write often) and come in a later version. Each fails before the run with GQLSTATUS 0A000 and a message that names the construct and the alternative.

ConstructUntil then
Cypher's FOREACHFOR x IN list INSERT .. (or SET .., DELETE .., MERGE ..) (Writing with GQL)
a write in an operand of UNION, a path variable in INSERTrun the write on its own; name the nodes and edges
a SET / REMOVE target deeper than a variable (n.a.b = .., head(l).k = .., a computed key n[k] = ..)WITH head(l) AS x SET x.k = ..
NEXT YIELDRETURN the columns to pass on before NEXT
a CALL folder.name(..) of a saved query written in Rhaig.query(name, #{..}) from the DSL, or save it again in GQL (Calling saved queries)
an argument of CALL folder.name(..) that reads the row (CALL people.older(s.age)); a CALL of a saved query inside EXISTS { }, COUNT { }, COLLECT { }a constant or a $parameter; a CALL (s) { .. } subquery or the saved query's pattern in the query
OPTIONAL { ... } / OPTIONAL ( ... ) blocksone OPTIONAL MATCH per optional part
a quantified edge over a list of edges bound before, Cypher's WITH [r1, r2] AS rs MATCH (a)-[rs*]->(b)a new name compared in WHERE: MATCH (a)-[rs2*]->(b) WHERE rs2 = rs
a quantifier nested in a quantified path pattern, (((a)-->(b)){2})+write the inner path out, ((x)-->(y)-->(z))+, or Gremlin repeat()
path search prefixes and match modes (ANY SHORTEST, TRAIL, DIFFERENT EDGES written out)Gremlin path(), repeat()
EXCEPT, INTERSECT, OTHERWISENOT EXISTS { } / EXISTS { } on the rows of the first query, or NEXT
NULLS FIRST / NULLS LASTthe fixed order: NULL last ascending, first descending
gql() after other steps (g.v().gql(..))start with g.gql(..) and continue with Gremlin
a list-comprehension or list-predicate variable read inside a subquery of its WHERE / | parttest the variable outside the subquery, or match the pattern in the query
trigonometric functions (sin, cos, ..., pi(), degrees())Gremlin math() after gql()
timestamp(), date_trunc(), datetime_trunc()datetime().epochMillis, date.truncate(unit, d)
CAST(x AS DATE) and the other temporal CAST targetsDATE '..' for a constant, date(x) for a value
list conversions toIntegerList(), toStringList(), ...FOR t IN list RETURN collect_list(toInteger(t)), or Gremlin unfold() and as_number() after gql()
normalize(s)store normalized text
GQL's elements(p)nodes(p) and relationships(p)
the standard deviations stDev(), stDevP()collect_list(x), then compute after gql()
g.gql("MATCH (((a)-[:knows]->(b)){1,2})+ RETURN b")   // error: a parenthesized path pattern nested in another one is not yet supported
g.gql("MATCH ((a)-[:knows]->(b)){1,3} RETURN [n IN b | n.name] AS b ORDER BY b").to_list()   // #{"b": ["josh"]}, #{"b": ["vadas"]}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN [x IN [p] WHERE (x)-[:created]->() | x.name] AS l")   // error: reading the comprehension variable `x` inside a subquery is not yet supported
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE (p)-[:created]->() RETURN [x IN [p] | x.name] AS l ORDER BY l").to_list()   // #{"l": ["josh"]}, #{"l": ["marko"]}, #{"l": ["peter"]}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS n EXCEPT MATCH (p:person)-[:created]->() RETURN p.name AS n")   // error: EXCEPT is not yet supported
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE NOT EXISTS { (p)-[:created]->() } RETURN p.name AS n").to_list()   // #{"n": "vadas"}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN sin(n.age) AS s")   // error: sin() (a trigonometric function) is not yet supported
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.name AS name, n.age AS a ORDER BY name").select("a").math("sin(_)").to_list()   // 0.5514266812416906, -0.6636338842129675, -0.428182669496151, 0.956375928404503

Semantics

gql() follows ISO GQL. Where the standard leaves a choice to the implementation, or where its text could not be checked yet, Graphersal follows Neo4j's Cypher 25, which implements GQL too; this page says where.

Trail: different edges

Within one MATCH clause an edge is bound at most once (GQL's DIFFERENT EDGES match mode, also called trail semantics; the GQL default and Neo4j's). Vertices may repeat.

g.gql("MATCH (a)-[:created]->(s)<-[:created]-(b) WHERE s.name = 'lop' RETURN a.name AS a, b.name AS b ORDER BY a, b").to_list()
// josh/marko, josh/peter, marko/josh, marko/peter, peter/josh, peter/marko: never a person with themselves
g.gql("MATCH (a {name: 'marko'})-[:knows]->(b)<-[:knows]-(c) RETURN c.name AS c").to_list()   // no rows: c could only be marko again over the same edge

The second query has no rows: every knows edge into b comes from marko, and binding it again for c would use the same edge twice. Gremlin has no such rule, so its twin returns marko:

g.v().has("name", "marko").out("knows").in("knows").values("name").to_list()   // "marko", "marko"

Two separate MATCH clauses are checked separately: an edge bound in the first may be bound again in the second. An edge variable written twice in one MATCH is an error.

g.gql("MATCH (a {name: 'marko'})-[:knows]->(b) MATCH (b)<-[:knows]-(c) RETURN c.name AS c").to_list()   // #{"c": "marko"}, #{"c": "marko"}
g.gql("MATCH (a)-[e]->(b), (b)<-[e]-(a) RETURN a")   // error: the edge variable `e` is used for more than one edge in the same MATCH

Quantified edges

A quantified edge (-[:knows]->{1,3}, The Supported Subset) is part of its MATCH clause like any edge: within one match every edge is different, across the repetitions and from the other edges of the clause (trail). Vertices may repeat, so a quantified edge may walk around a cycle, but never over the same edge twice.

  • The zero-length match of a lower bound 0 ({0,n}, *) binds the far node to the near one; the group variable is then []. {0} matches only that.
  • Cypher's empty interval ([*2..1], [*..0]: the lower bound above the upper one) matches nothing, as in Neo4j: no row, and an OPTIONAL MATCH part gets its NULL row. The GQL form {2,1} is a syntax error (ISO).
  • An upper bound larger than any trail can be (beyond about four billion) means "no bound"; such a quantifier behaves like {m,}.
  • Unbounded quantifiers ({m,}, *, +, Cypher [*]) have no limit of their own: trail ends every walk once it has used every edge it can reach, which on a finite graph always happens. Two general limits still apply: repeat.max_loops (10 000 repetitions) and traversal.max_traversers (live rows between two steps). Reaching either is an error, never a shortened result; its help names the quantifier and how to bound it or raise the limit with g.with(..).gql(..).
g.with("repeat.max_loops", 1).gql("MATCH (a {name: 'marko'})-[:knows|created]->*(b) RETURN b.name AS b")   // error: repeat() exceeded the loop limit of 1 iterations
g.with("repeat.max_loops", 5).gql("MATCH (a {name: 'marko'})-[:knows|created]->*(b) RETURN b.name AS b ORDER BY b").to_list()
// josh, lop, lop, marko, ripple, vadas
g.gql("MATCH (a {name: 'marko'})-[e]->{0}(b) RETURN b.name AS b, e").to_list()   // #{"b": "marko", "e": []}

The help of the first error reads (shortened):

Help: The loop of the quantified edge -[:knows|created]->{0,} of the gql() query ran 1 iterations, the limit of repeat.max_loops. ...
Give the quantifier an upper bound, as in -[:knows|created]->{0,5}, ... Or raise the limit for the query, g.with("repeat.max_loops", 2).gql(..), ...

Each match of a quantified edge is a row of its own (the edges it used keep the rows apart), so the number of rows can grow fast on a densely connected graph: bound the quantifier where the question allows it.

Quantified path patterns

A quantified path pattern ((a) ((x)-[e]->(y)){1,3} (b), The Supported Subset) repeats a whole chain. Graphersal follows ISO GQL and, where a detail is open, Neo4j's Cypher 25, which implements the same construct:

  • Merge rule. The node before the group is the first node of the first iteration, the node after it the last node of the last iteration, and each iteration starts where the previous one ended: in (a) ((x)-->(y)){1,3} (b), a is the first x, b the last y, and the y of one iteration is the x of the next. After zero iterations a and b are one node, so (a) ((x)-->(y))* (a) matches the closed walks from a (the zero-length one included).
  • Trail per body edge. Within one match every edge is different: across the iterations, between the body's edges and from the other edges of the MATCH clause, so a quantified path pattern ends on every finite graph, like a quantified edge. A body edge that a ? part did not bind (zero iterations) clashes with nothing.
  • Group lists. With a quantifier other than ?, each body variable is the list of its elements, one per iteration, in the order the text reads (also when the plan walks the pattern from its far end): x = [x1, x2, ...]. A zero-length match gives []. A property of a group variable has no single value outside the body (42002); inside the body, in its conditions, the variable is the element of the current iteration.
  • ? gives nullable singletons (ISO). ((x)-[e]->(y))? matches its body once or not at all; its variables are single elements, NULL for the match where it did not match (no iteration), not lists. {0,1} matches the same paths but keeps group lists ([] or one element).
  • No quantifier: singletons. A parenthesized path pattern without a quantifier matches its body exactly once; its variables are single elements, as if the parentheses were not there, and its WHERE is a condition on that part of the path.
  • The body condition runs in every iteration and reads only body variables, parameters and values: an iteration whose condition is not TRUE ends that walk.
g.gql("MATCH (a {name: 'marko'})-[e]->(m) ((x)-[f]-(y))? (b) RETURN m.name AS m, b.name AS b ORDER BY m, b").to_list()
// josh/josh, josh/lop, josh/ripple, lop/josh, lop/lop, lop/peter, vadas/vadas: never back to marko over the edge e
g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'vadas'}) ((x)-[:created]->(s))? (q) RETURN s AS s, q.name AS q").to_list()   // #{"q": "vadas", "s": ()}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'vadas'}) ((x)-[:created]->(s)){0,1} (q) RETURN s AS s, q.name AS q").to_list()   // #{"q": "vadas", "s": []}

Limits that hold now (E17; each refused with 0A000 and a help line naming the rewrite): one chain per body, no quantifier nested inside a body (neither a group nor a quantified edge), no path variable inside a body (name the whole path instead), and a body variable is a new name: an outer variable written inside a body, a variable written twice in one body, a body condition reading an outer variable, and a subquery inside a body are not supported yet. Every body edge counts once toward the 64 edge patterns of a MATCH clause, however often the body repeats.

The unbounded quantifiers ({m,}, *, +) are bounded as for a quantified edge: repeat.max_loops counts the iterations of the whole body, traversal.max_traversers the live rows, and reaching either is an error naming the pattern (Errors), never a shortened result.

Reading ((. Where an expression stands, (( followed by a pattern and a closing ) with {..}, ?, a node, an edge, or * / + not followed by an operand reads as a quantified path pattern (a pattern predicate). So ((a)-->(b)) + (c) is the pattern ((a)-->(b))+ (c), not the boolean of the pattern predicate ((a)-->(b)) plus c; with an operand after it (((a)-->(b)) + [1], + x, + 1) it stays arithmetic. Arithmetic on a predicate's boolean is a type error (22G03) in either reading, so no working query changes meaning.

OPTIONAL MATCH and NULL

A row that reaches an OPTIONAL MATCH whose pattern does not match continues once, with every variable the optional part introduces set to NULL: a property of it is NULL, a group variable is NULL (not []), a path variable is NULL. The variables bound before keep their values. The trail rule is checked per clause, so an optional part may bind an edge the MATCH before it bound.

g.gql("MATCH (a {name: 'marko'})-[:knows]->(b) OPTIONAL MATCH (b)-[:created]->(s) RETURN b.name AS b, s.name AS s ORDER BY b, s").to_list()
// #{"b": "josh", "s": "lop"}, #{"b": "josh", "s": "ripple"}, #{"b": "vadas", "s": ()}

NULL and three-valued logic

A property that is missing reads as NULL, exactly like a property stored as null. WHERE uses three-valued logic: a comparison with NULL is NULL (unknown), AND / OR / NOT follow the SQL / GQL truth tables, and a row passes only when the condition is TRUE.

g.gql("MATCH (n) RETURN n.name AS name, n.age > 30 AS old, n.lang = 'java' AS java ORDER BY name").to_list()
// josh: old true, java (); lop: old (), java true; marko: old false, java (); ...
g.gql("MATCH (n) RETURN n.age = NULL AS a, NULL IS NULL AS b, 2 IN [1, NULL] AS c, NULL IN [] AS d LIMIT 1").to_list()
// #{"a": (), "b": true, "c": (), "d": false}
g.gql("MATCH (n) WHERE n.age IS NULL RETURN n.name AS name ORDER BY name").to_list()   // #{"name": "lop"}, #{"name": "ripple"}

(() is how Rhai shows NULL; JSON shows null.) Test for a missing value with IS NULL, never with = NULL.

The consequence that surprises Gremlin users: NOT of an unknown condition is still unknown, so the software (which has no age) passes neither n.age < 30 nor NOT n.age < 30, while Gremlin's not(has(..)) keeps them:

g.gql("MATCH (n) WHERE NOT n.age < 30 RETURN n.name AS name ORDER BY name").to_list()   // #{"name": "josh"}, #{"name": "peter"}
g.v().not(__.has("age", P.lt(30))).values("name").order().to_list()   // "josh", "lop", "peter", "ripple"
g.gql("MATCH (n) WHERE n.age <> 29 RETURN n.name AS name ORDER BY name").to_list()   // josh, peter, vadas (not lop, not ripple)

The same holds for <>: a vertex without age is not "different from 29", its comparison is unknown.

EXISTS and pattern predicates

A row is kept once, however often the body matches. EXISTS (and a pattern predicate, The Supported Subset) is a semi-join: it asks whether there is a match and adds no rows. The same pattern in MATCH gives one row per match, so josh, who created two programs, comes twice:

g.gql("MATCH (p:person)-[:created]->() RETURN p.name AS name ORDER BY name").to_list()   // josh, josh, marko, peter
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE (p)-[:created]->() RETURN p.name AS name ORDER BY name").to_list()   // josh, marko, peter

TRUE or FALSE, never NULL. A body that matches is TRUE, one that does not is FALSE, also when it reads a variable that is NULL on the row (an import from an OPTIONAL MATCH that did not match): a NULL element matches nothing, so EXISTS is FALSE and NOT EXISTS TRUE. Around it, three-valued logic works as usual: NULL OR EXISTS {..} is TRUE when the body matches and NULL otherwise. (This follows Neo4j; the ISO text is still to be checked.)

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s WHERE s.name = 'ripple') RETURN p.name AS name, EXISTS { (s)<-[:created]-() } AS made, NOT EXISTS { (s)<-[:created]-() } AS not_made ORDER BY name").to_list()
// josh: made true, not_made false; marko, peter, vadas (s is NULL): made false, not_made true
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, p.lang = 'x' OR EXISTS { (p)-[:knows]->() } AS a ORDER BY name").to_list()
// josh (), marko true, peter (), vadas ()

A pattern alone is a condition, not a value. A pattern predicate such as (p)-[:knows]->() stands only where WHERE (or FILTER, a comprehension's WHERE, a WHEN of a searched CASE) expects a condition, also under NOT, AND, OR and XOR there. Anywhere else (a RETURN or WITH item, a function argument, a SET value) it is a syntax error (42001), as in Neo4j: write EXISTS { .. } for whether it matches, COUNT { .. } for how often, or a pattern comprehension for what it matches (stage 3f, the openCypher TCK Pattern1, List6):

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, (p)-[:knows]->() AS k")   // error: the pattern stands where a value is expected (42001)
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, EXISTS { (p)-[:knows]->() } AS k, COUNT { (p)-[:knows]->() } AS n, [(p)-[:knows]->(f) | f.name] AS fs ORDER BY name").to_list()
// josh: false, 0, []; marko: true, 2, ["vadas", "josh"]; ...

Trail per body clause. Each MATCH clause inside a body is its own clause for the trail rule (Trail): its edges are different from each other, but they may repeat an edge of the query outside the body (an imported edge variable is that same edge) or of another body clause. (Neo4j's rule; the ISO text is still to be checked.)

g.gql("MATCH (a {name: 'marko'}) WHERE EXISTS { MATCH (a)-[:knows]->(x)<-[:knows]-(a) } RETURN a.name AS a").to_list()   // no rows: one clause, one edge twice
g.gql("MATCH (a {name: 'marko'}) WHERE EXISTS { MATCH (a)-[:knows]->(x) MATCH (x)<-[:knows]-(a) } RETURN a.name AS a").to_list()   // #{"a": "marko"}
g.gql("MATCH (a {name: 'marko'})-[e:knows]->(b) WHERE EXISTS { MATCH (b)<-[e]-(x) } RETURN b.name AS b ORDER BY b").to_list()   // josh, vadas: e imported

Evaluated only when needed, at most once per row. A body stops at its first match. Where EXISTS stands inside a larger expression, a row runs the body only when the evaluation reaches it (a OR EXISTS {..} runs nothing when a is TRUE), and once even when several columns or keys of the row hold the same subquery. A body that imports nothing (EXISTS { (:robot) }) is still run per row; its answer is not cached yet.

Filter order. The conditions of one element (or one WHERE) run in this order: those pushed into has(), the other plain conditions, then those holding a subquery, which cost the most (a subquery inside a larger expression before a plain [NOT] EXISTS). The result does not depend on the order, only the work does. The global optimizer rule filter_reorder may still move a subquery's step before a gql:filter by its own cost estimate, as it does for the same Gremlin steps (Plans and Performance).

Map projections and comprehensions

A NULL variable projects to NULL. A map projection v {..} of a NULL variable (an OPTIONAL MATCH that did not match) is NULL, and its entries are not evaluated at all, while the GQL record constructor {name: v.name} builds a map whose values are NULL. A pattern comprehension that imports a NULL variable matches nothing and gives [], never NULL:

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s {name: 'ripple'}) RETURN p.name AS name, s {.name} AS projection, {name: s.name} AS record, [(s)<-[:created]-(c) | c.name] AS creators ORDER BY name").to_list()
// josh: projection #{"name": "ripple"}, record #{"name": "ripple"}, creators ["josh"]
// marko, peter, vadas: projection (), record #{"name": ()}, creators []
g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'vadas'}) OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN s {k: 1 / 0} AS m").to_list()   // #{"m": ()}: the entry never runs

Keys. The entries come in the written order. .* puts every stored property at its place, in stored order, without the id and the labels; a property stored as null is left out, as in properties(). A key written twice (also through .*) keeps its first place and takes the later value. The variable of a projection must be a vertex, an edge or a map; any other value is the data error 22G03. An element inside the map (friend: f) stays the live element (Result Shape).

g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN p {.name, age: 1, .age} AS m").to_json()   // [{"m": {"name": "marko", "age": 29}}]
g.gql("WITH {a: 1, b: 2} AS m RETURN m {.a, .c, .*, d: 3} AS x").to_json()   // [{"x": {"a": 1, "c": null, "b": 2, "d": 3}}]
g.gql("WITH 1 AS m RETURN m {.a} AS x")   // error: a map projection reads a node, an edge or a map, not a number (22G03)

List comprehension. A NULL list gives NULL, a value that is not a list the data error 22G03. WHERE keeps an item only when the condition is TRUE: FALSE and NULL drop it (three-valued logic). The result keeps the list's order.

g.gql("RETURN [x IN [1, NULL, 3] WHERE x > 1] AS kept, [x IN [1, NULL, 3] | x] AS every, [x IN NULL | x] AS none").to_list()
// #{"every": [1, (), 3], "kept": [3], "none": ()}
g.gql("RETURN [x IN 5 | x] AS m")   // error: a list comprehension iterates over a list, not a number (22G03)

List predicates and reduce. all(), any(), none() and single() are three-valued, not counts: a NULL list gives NULL; an item that decides the answer wins (all FALSE at a FALSE item, any TRUE and none FALSE at a TRUE one, single FALSE at a second TRUE one) and the later items are not evaluated; otherwise a NULL condition gives NULL. This is the openCypher TCK (Quantifier1 to Quantifier4), which Neo4j Cypher 25 follows; Neo4j's manual words the NULL rule of any() like that of all(), but its implementation and the TCK give any(x IN [NULL, 2] WHERE x = 2) TRUE, as here. reduce(acc = init, x IN l | expr) gives NULL for a NULL list, init for an empty one, and lets NULL items flow through expr. Their variables are new names like a comprehension's.

g.gql("RETURN any(x IN [NULL, 2] WHERE x = 2) AS a, all(x IN [NULL, 2] WHERE x = 2) AS b, single(x IN [2, NULL] WHERE x = 2) AS c, single(x IN [2, NULL, 2] WHERE x = 2) AS d").to_list()
// #{"a": true, "b": (), "c": (), "d": false}
g.gql("RETURN reduce(s = 0, x IN [1, NULL] | s + x) AS a, reduce(s = 0, x IN [] | s + x) AS b, reduce(s = 0, x IN NULL | s + x) AS c").to_list()
// #{"a": (), "b": 0, "c": ()}

A comprehension variable hides no name in scope. It may not shadow a variable or column in scope, nor the variable of a comprehension around it. A name that is no longer in scope (one a WITH dropped, one bound inside a subquery) may be used again, as in Neo4j (stage 3f, the openCypher TCK Quantifier1..4). One exception keeps a LET / WITH value right: a name that the expression of such a value in scope reads is refused too, since gql() substitutes the value by its expression, which still refers to the dropped variable by that name. So MATCH (n) WITH n AS m RETURN [n IN [1] | n], which runs in Neo4j, is an error here; pick another name ([x IN [1] | x]). The variable exists only inside its brackets.

g.gql("MATCH (n:person) WITH n AS m RETURN [n IN [1] | n] AS l")   // error: the comprehension variable `n` is a name that a LET or WITH value in scope still reads
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) WITH collect(n) AS ns RETURN [n IN ns | n.name] AS names").to_list()   // #{"names": ["marko", "vadas", "josh", "peter"]}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) WITH n AS m RETURN [x IN [1] | x] AS l ORDER BY l LIMIT 1").to_list()   // #{"l": [1]}

Pattern comprehension: one item per match, in no defined order. The list holds one item per match of the pattern, so the same value may come several times (josh created two programs in java). Like any subquery it runs on the row's imports, with the trail rule inside its own pattern (EXISTS); its items come in the order the matches are found, which depends on the plan. When the order matters, match the pattern in the query, sort the rows and collect them with collect_list(), or sort the list after gql().

g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'josh'}) RETURN [(p)-[:created]->(s) | s.lang] AS langs").to_list()   // #{"langs": ["java", "java"]}
g.gql("MATCH (a {name: 'marko'}) RETURN [(a)-[:knows]->(x)<-[:knows]-(a) | x.name] AS one").to_list()   // #{"one": []}: one pattern, one edge twice

Evaluated when reached, once per row. A pattern comprehension runs its pattern only for the rows whose evaluation reaches it, at most once per row, like EXISTS; one that imports nothing still runs per row. Comprehensions nested from the same element multiply the work: [(m)-->(a) | [(m)-->(b) | ..]] runs the inner pattern once for every match of the outer one, like nested Gremlin map(..fold()) children, and only the resource limits bound a deep chain of them (Resource limits).

COUNT and COLLECT

An aggregating answer for every row. COUNT { } and COLLECT { } run their body once per row, like EXISTS, but read it to the end: COUNT { } is the number of rows the body returns (0, never NULL, when there are none) and COLLECT { } the list of its one RETURN item ([] when there are none). An imported NULL variable matches nothing, as in EXISTS, so both give 0 and []. COLLECT { } keeps NULL items, unlike collect_list(), and keeps the body's row order, so an ORDER BY inside it orders the list; without one the order is unspecified, as for a pattern comprehension.

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s {name: 'ripple'}) RETURN p.name AS name, COUNT { (s)<-[:created]-() } AS n, COLLECT { MATCH (s)<-[:created]-(c) RETURN c.name } AS l ORDER BY name").to_list()
// josh 1 ["josh"]; marko, peter, vadas (s is NULL): 0 []
g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN COLLECT { MATCH (p)-[:knows]->(f) RETURN f.lang } AS l, [(p)-[:knows]->(f) | f.lang] AS c").to_list()   // #{"c": [(), ()], "l": [(), ()]}

A deviation: the RETURN of a counted body is not evaluated. When a COUNT { } body is one query whose final RETURN only projects (no aggregate, DISTINCT, ORDER BY or UNION, which need the values), gql() counts the body's rows without evaluating the RETURN items, nor the values a projecting WITH names only for them: the count is the same, but an expression there that would fail on a row (a division by zero, a value of the wrong kind) raises no error, while the same body run as a query (or in CALL) raises it. EXISTS and COLLECT { } evaluate theirs.

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, COUNT { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN 1 / 0 AS x } AS n ORDER BY name").to_list()   // josh 2, marko 1, peter 1, vadas 0
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN COUNT { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN DISTINCT 1 / 0 AS x } AS n")   // error: division by zero: DISTINCT needs the value
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE EXISTS { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN 1 / 0 AS x } RETURN p.name AS name")   // error: division by zero: EXISTS evaluates its RETURN

UNION and NEXT

Columns by name. The operands of a UNION are matched by column name, not by position: an operand may list the same names in another order, and the result takes the first operand's order. (Whether the standard also allows another order is still to be checked; gql() takes the permissive reading.) UNION removes duplicate rows with GQL's equality, as DISTINCT does (1 and 1.0 are one value, DISTINCT); which of two equal rows is kept is unspecified.

g.gql("RETURN 1 AS x UNION RETURN 1.0 AS x").to_list()   // #{"x": 1}: one row
g.gql("RETURN 1 AS x UNION ALL RETURN 1.0 AS x").to_list()   // #{"x": 1}, #{"x": 1.0}

Per operand. Each operand is a query of its own: its variables are its own, and its ORDER BY, OFFSET and LIMIT apply to it before the union. The rows of a union come in no defined order: the operands' rows are not interleaved in any documented way, so an order within an operand is not an order of the result. Sort or page the whole union after NEXT.

NEXT passes on the columns, not the variables. After NEXT the next statement sees the RETURN columns of the statement before it as its variables and nothing else; an element column is the live element, so a MATCH after NEXT continues from it. NEXT after one plain query is that query with a WITH of the same items, so it gives the same rows and the same plan; after a UNION the union's rows are the input. The order a RETURN .. ORDER BY makes before NEXT is not kept by later clauses (Ordering): sort in the last RETURN.

CALL subqueries

Per row, joined. A CALL runs its body once for each incoming row, with the imported variables set to the row's values, and each row the body returns extends the incoming row: an incoming row with three results becomes three rows, one with none is dropped (OPTIONAL CALL keeps it once, the returned names NULL).
