The whole pattern is matched or created: MATCH (p:person) MERGE (p)-[:in]->(g:group {name: 'x'}) creates a group for every person without such an edge, because the pattern with the edge does not match for them; to share one group, MERGE the group first and the edge second:

g.gql("FOR n IN ['Rome', 'Rome', 'Oslo'] MERGE (c:city {name: n}) RETURN count(*) AS rows, count(DISTINCT c) AS cities").to_list()   // #{"cities": 2, "rows": 3}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE p.age > 30 MERGE (g:group {name: 'over30'}) MERGE (p)-[:in]->(g) RETURN count(DISTINCT g) AS groups").to_list()   // #{"groups": 1}

ON CREATE SET and ON MATCH SET. After the pattern, ON CREATE SET <items> changes the elements of a row that the MERGE created, and ON MATCH SET <items> those of a row it found. The items are the items of SET and may read every variable of the row (the pattern's and the earlier ones). Both may be written several times and in any order; they apply in the order written, each in its own case.

g.gql("FOR name IN ['marko', 'ann'] MERGE (p:person {name: name}) ON CREATE SET p.visits = 1 ON MATCH SET p.visits = coalesce(p.visits, 0) + 1").iterate();
g.gql("FOR name IN ['marko', 'ann'] MERGE (p:person {name: name}) ON CREATE SET p.visits = 1 ON MATCH SET p.visits = coalesce(p.visits, 0) + 1 RETURN p.name AS name, p.visits AS visits ORDER BY name").to_list()   // ann 2, marko 2

g.gql("MERGE (p:person {name: 'marko'}) ON CREATE SET p.new = true ON MATCH SET p.new = false RETURN p.new AS new").to_list()   // #{"new": false}
g.gql("MERGE (p:person {name: 'marko'}) ON MATCH SET p.seen = 1 ON MATCH SET p.seen = p.seen + 1 RETURN p.seen AS seen").to_list()   // #{"seen": 2}

NULL in the pattern. MERGE cannot look for or create a NULL property value: a property of the pattern that is NULL on a row (a missing parameter, an OPTIONAL MATCH that found nothing) fails the query with 22004 when that row runs, and nothing of the query is kept. Keep such rows away with FILTER x IS NOT NULL, or give a default with coalesce():

g.gql("FOR x IN [1, NULL] MERGE (n:num {v: x})")   // error: MERGE cannot match or create `{v: NULL}` (22004)
g.gql("FOR x IN [1, NULL] FILTER x IS NOT NULL MERGE (n:num {v: x}) RETURN count(*) AS n").to_list()   // #{"n": 1}

A MERGE that only finds changes nothing. It commits no change: a commit hook and the journal see nothing, and the dev server's answer reports no change summary and no commit. An ON MATCH SET that runs is a change, as a SET is.

The same in Gremlin: merge_v() finds or creates a vertex, merge_e() an edge between given vertices, and the fold().coalesce(__.unfold(), __.add_v(..)) idiom does it by hand. Their onCreate option map replaces the creation map, while ON CREATE SET changes the created element afterwards.

g.merge_v(#{"T.label": "city", name: "Berlin"}).values("name").to_list()   // "Berlin"
g.v().has_label("city").has("name", "Berlin").fold().coalesce(__.unfold(), __.add_v("city").property("name", "Berlin")).values("name").to_list()   // "Berlin"

The same in plain GQL, without the compatibility form: a CALL body that inserts only when nothing exists yet, then a MATCH that reads the result:

g.gql("CALL { FILTER NOT EXISTS { MATCH (:city {name: 'Berlin'}) } INSERT (:city {name: 'Berlin'}) } MATCH (c:city {name: 'Berlin'}) RETURN count(c) AS cities").to_list()   // #{"cities": 1}

Once per row

A write clause runs once for each row that reaches it, so the clauses before it decide how many elements an INSERT creates and how often a SET applies (SET n.c = n.c + 1 over two rows of the same node adds 2). A MATCH gives one row per match, FOR (Cypher UNWIND) one per list item, and a variable of the row connects the new elements to what it matched:

g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) INSERT (p)-[:likes]->(f:fruit {name: 'apple'}) RETURN f.name AS fruit").to_list();   // #{"fruit": "apple"}
g.gql("FOR n IN $names INSERT (:person {name: n, born: $year})", #{names: ["ann", "bob"], year: 1990}).iterate();
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE p.born = 1990 RETURN p.name AS name ORDER BY name").to_list()   // #{"name": "ann"}, #{"name": "bob"}

A write clause may stand after MATCH, OPTIONAL MATCH, FOR, WITH, LET, FILTER and another write clause, and further clauses may follow it: a MATCH after the INSERT sees the new elements, and a new node can be connected to every row a later MATCH finds:

g.gql("INSERT (c:city {name: 'Berlin'}) MATCH (p:person) INSERT (p)-[:lives_in]->(c) RETURN count(*) AS n").to_list()   // #{"n": 4}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WITH p, p.age + 1 AS later INSERT (p)-[:turns]->(:age {years: later}) RETURN p.name AS name, later ORDER BY name").to_list()
// #{"later": 33, "name": "josh"}, #{"later": 30, "name": "marko"}, #{"later": 36, "name": "peter"}, #{"later": 28, "name": "vadas"}

A node an OPTIONAL MATCH left NULL cannot be an edge's endpoint: the query fails (22004) and changes nothing. Keep only the bound rows with FILTER x IS NOT NULL first:

g.gql("OPTIONAL MATCH (p:person {name: 'nobody'}) INSERT (p)-[:knows]->(:person)")   // error: the source node `p` of the inserted `:knows` edge is NULL
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) FILTER s IS NOT NULL INSERT (p)-[:made]->(s) RETURN count(*) AS n").to_list()   // #{"n": 4}

Inside CALL. A CALL body may end with its write instead of RETURN (a unit subquery): it runs once per incoming row and passes the row on unchanged, also when the body found nothing:

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { INSERT (p)-[:likes]->(:fruit {name: p.name}) } RETURN count(*) AS c").to_list()   // #{"c": 4}

A subquery expression (EXISTS { }, COUNT { }, COLLECT { }) and a comprehension cannot write (42001), and a write in an operand of UNION is not supported yet.

What a row sees

Each clause sees every write of the clauses before it, for all rows; within one clause the rows are processed in order, and each row sees the writes of the rows before it. A query never sees its own writes while it is still finding the rows of an earlier clause: MATCH (n) INSERT (:X) creates exactly one node per node that existed before, and MATCH (a)-[e]->(b) INSERT (a)-[:copy]->(b) copies each existing edge once, never the copies.

g.gql("MATCH (n) INSERT (:X)").iterate();
g.v().has_label("X").count().next()   // 6

g.gql("FOR i IN range(1, 3) INSERT (:n {i: i}) WITH count(*) AS made MATCH (m:n) RETURN made, count(m) AS seen").to_list()   // #{"made": 3, "seen": 3}

A value a row carried before a SET keeps the value it had: WITH p.age AS old SET p.age = 0 still returns the old age in old, while p.age reads the new one.

g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) WITH p, p.age AS old SET p.age = 0 RETURN old, p.age AS now").to_list()   // #{"now": 0, "old": 29}

The details, and how this follows from the executor, are on Semantics.

One query is one unit

A gql() query is one traversal and so one unit (Transactions): when any row fails (a data error on the last row, a schema violation, a permission, a resource limit, cancellation), nothing the query wrote stays. Here the second item divides by zero, and the node of the first item is rolled back with it (execute() keeps the error instead of raising it, so the script goes on):

let run = g.gql("FOR x IN [1, 0] INSERT (:n {v: 1 / x})").execute();   // fails: division by zero
g.v().has_label("n").count().next()   // 0

A SET that fails on one row leaves the rows before it unchanged too:

let set = g.gql("MATCH (p:person) SET p.score = 100 / (p.age - 27)").execute();   // fails on vadas (27)
g.v().has("score").count().next()   // 0

Commit hooks see the query's ChangeSet and may veto it, a dry run shows its changes without keeping them, and a Store's journal records it like any Gremlin write (Change capture).

Schema

An INSERT creates each element in one storage call with all its properties, so a schema sees the whole element (Schemas): defaults on create are filled in, a required property is satisfied by the map, write-time coercion applies, and a closed schema refuses undeclared labels and properties. SET and REMOVE are checked like the Gremlin steps that do the same: a value of the wrong type, removing a required property (also with SET n.k = NULL or a SET n = {..} without it) and a label the schema does not allow fail the query. A violation fails the query (and changes nothing), with a help line written for GQL:

g.set_schema(#{mode: "open", vertices: #{person: #{schema: #{type: "object", properties: #{
    name: #{type: "string"}, age: #{type: "integer"}, active: #{type: "boolean", default: true}},
    required: ["name"]}}}});
g.gql("INSERT (:person {name: 'alice'})").iterate();
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, p.active AS active").to_list()   // #{"active": true, "name": "alice"}

Caused by: Missing required property 'name' on vertex 'person'
Help: Give 'name' a value in the property map of the INSERT, as in g.gql("INSERT (:person {name: 'value'})"); a NULL value (such as a property the matched element lacks) is not stored and so is missing too: give it a fallback, as in {name: coalesce(n.name, 'unknown')}. Or remove it from the label's "required" in the schema, or give it a "default" (or "defaultFunction") in the schema: it is stored when an element is created without the property.

A MERGE that creates creates like an INSERT of its pattern: the schema's defaults are filled in and the pattern's map must satisfy required. Its ON CREATE SET items run afterwards, as a second write in the same query, so a required property given only there is missing when the element is created and fails the query; put it into the pattern's map instead (where it is also part of what MERGE looks for):

g.set_schema(#{mode: "open", vertices: #{person: #{schema: #{type: "object", properties: #{
    name: #{type: "string"}, active: #{type: "boolean", default: true}}, required: ["name"]}}}});
g.gql("MERGE (p:person {name: 'ann'}) RETURN p.active AS active").to_list()   // #{"active": true}

A value of the wrong type is not converted, and GQL never infers a type from text. Convert it where the INSERT writes it:

Caused by: Type mismatch on vertex 'person.age': expected int64, got string
Help: Convert the value to the type 'int64' where the INSERT writes it, with toInteger(), as in g.gql("INSERT (:person {age: toInteger($v)})", #{v: "29"}). toInteger() gives NULL for a value it cannot convert, and a NULL value is not stored; CAST(x AS ..) fails the query for it instead.

Permissions

The permission check sees the lowered plan before anything runs: an INSERT asks Create on Data(vertex "label") per label of each new node and Create on Data(edge "label") per new edge, exactly as add_v(labels) and add_e(label) do, plus the reads of its MATCH clauses. SET and REMOVE ask Update, as property(), remove_property(), add_label() and drop_label() do: on Data(vertex) for a node (any label, since a node's label set is not fixed by the pattern), on Data(edge "label") for an edge whose pattern names its labels, and on any element when the kind is not known before the run (an item of a FOR list). It asks nothing for the properties: they are part of creating the element. DELETE asks Delete, as drop() does: on Data(vertex) for a node, on Data(edge "label") for an edge whose pattern names its labels, and on any element for a path, a list or a value whose kind is known only at run time; DETACH asks nothing more (as drop() of a vertex, which removes its edges too). MERGE asks what its two halves need, whether a row will find or create: Read for the search (as a MATCH of its pattern), Create per label of every element the pattern can create (as the INSERT of it), and, only when it has ON CREATE SET / ON MATCH SET items, their Updates (as SET). The step's own Create and Update requests are checked first, then the Reads of its search; a policy that denies Create refuses a MERGE even where every row would only find. merge_v() and merge_e() ask Read on what they search first, then Create and Update on any vertex or edge (no labels, and Update even without on_create / on_match options). (Gremlin's add_v(..).property(..) asks Create and Update, because the check runs before the optimizer folds the property into the creation; a policy that denies only Update allows the INSERT and refuses its Gremlin twin.) A read-only host (AccessPolicy::read_only(), the MCP server's --mcp-read-only, a read-only view of a past state) refuses a GQL write before it runs.

Saved queries and the DSL

A saved query may be written in GQL itself (Saved queries in GQL): the body is the plain query text, its $parameters are the declared ones, and an INSERT, SET, REMOVE, DELETE or MERGE makes it a query that writes, whose effects name what its plan creates, changes and deletes. A call writes in one unit and returns the rows. A GQL query calls it with CALL hire('lop', 'ann') YIELD name (the arguments in the order the body first reads them: $company, then $name); its writes then belong to the calling query's unit (Calling saved queries):

g.define_query(#{name: "hire", language: "gql", params: #{name: "string", company: "string"},
    body: "MATCH (c:software {name: $company}) INSERT (p:person {name: $name})-[:created]->(c) RETURN p.name AS name"});
g.get_query("hire")["effects"].map(|e| e.text);   // ["Create Data(vertex \"person\")", "Create Data(edge \"created\")"]
g.query("hire", #{name: "ann", company: "lop"}).select("name").to_list()   // "ann"

g.define_query(#{name: "birthday", language: "gql", params: #{name: "string"},
    body: "MATCH (p:person {name: $name}) SET p.age = p.age + 1 RETURN p.age AS age"});
g.get_query("birthday")["effects"].map(|e| e.text);   // ["Update Data(vertex)"]
g.query("birthday", #{name: "vadas"}).select("age").to_list()   // 28

g.define_query(#{name: "unlink", language: "gql", params: #{}, body: "MATCH ()-[e:knows]->() DELETE e"});
g.get_query("unlink")["effects"].map(|e| e.text)   // ["Delete Data(edge \"knows\")"]

g.define_query(#{name: "visit", language: "gql", params: #{name: "string"},
    body: "MERGE (p:person {name: $name}) ON MATCH SET p.visits = coalesce(p.visits, 0) + 1 RETURN p.name AS name"});
g.get_query("visit")["effects"].map(|e| e.text)   // ["Create Data(vertex \"person\")", "Update Data(vertex)"]

A saved query in Rhai whose body runs g.gql("INSERT ...") with a literal query text is a writing query too: its effects name what it creates, changes and deletes. A computed query text claims every write; pass values as $parameters instead.

In a script, a writing gql() takes the write lock like a Gremlin write (is_mutating() is true), and the playground asks before running it again. Gremlin steps may follow:

g.gql("INSERT (c:city {name: 'Berlin'}) RETURN c").select("c").values("name").to_list()   // "Berlin"

In Rust

Run a writing query on the writing source, traversal_mut(), under the write lock. The read source refuses it with the error a Gremlin write gets there:

use graphersal::prelude::*;

let graph = Graph::new(TraversalGraph::tinkerpop_modern());
graph
    .write()
    .traversal_mut()
    .gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) INSERT (p)-[:likes]->(:fruit {name: 'apple'})")
    .iterate()?;

// The read source cannot write:
let error = graph.read().traversal().gql("INSERT (:x)").iterate().unwrap_err();
assert_eq!(
    error.root_cause().to_string(),
    "Invalid element state: Cannot mutate immutable graph reference"
);

The plan

An INSERT lowers to the internal steps gql:insert_node and gql:insert_edge, one per element of the pattern, in text order (Plans and Performance); a SET clause to one gql:set step and a REMOVE clause to one gql:remove step with its items, which pass the row on unchanged. A DELETE clause lowers to one gql:delete step: it collects the targets of all its rows first (the NODETACH check sees the whole clause), removes the edges, then the nodes, and passes the rows on unchanged. A MERGE lowers to one gql:merge step with two children: the search (the plan of a MATCH of the pattern, starting from a bound node or using a property index where one serves it) and the creation (the gql:insert_node / gql:insert_edge chain of the pattern); .profile() shows both under the step. Because the plan writes, its traversers are never merged into one with a higher bulk: each row creates its own elements and applies its own changes.

g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) SET p.age = 1 RETURN p").profile()
g.gql("MERGE (c:city {name: 'Rome'}) RETURN c").profile()

Not yet

ConstructUntil then
FOREACH (x IN list | ...)FOR x IN list INSERT ...
a write in a UNION operand, a path variable in INSERTrun the write on its own; name the nodes and edges
a deeper SET / REMOVE target (n.a.b, head(l).k), Cypher's dynamic n[key]name the element with WITH .. AS x and write the item on x; for a nested value Gremlin property() with a jpath key
g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) SET p.address.city = 'Rome'")   // error: `p.address.city` as a SET target is not yet supported

Writing GQL in Rhai Strings

In the Gremlin DSL (the command line, the playground, Python scripts, saved queries) a GQL query is a Rhai string passed to g.gql(..). GQL has quotes and backticks of its own, and Rhai gives some characters a meaning inside strings, so this page shows which string form to use and how to write values, names and comments inside it. Through the MCP tool gql none of this applies: the query is plain text.

Short queries: "..." with GQL '...' literals

A query on one line goes into a Rhai double-quoted string. Write GQL string literals with single quotes, so nothing needs escaping:

g.gql("MATCH (s:software) WHERE s.name = 'lop' RETURN s.lang AS lang").to_list()   // #{"lang": "java"}

GQL accepts "..." string literals too, but inside a Rhai "..." string each one must be escaped as \":

g.gql("MATCH (s:software) WHERE s.name = \"lop\" RETURN s.lang AS lang").to_list()   // #{"lang": "java"}

A single quote inside a GQL '...' literal is doubled ('it''s'), the GQL rule. Rhai processes backslash escapes in "..." strings first, so a backslash that GQL should see is written \\.

g.gql("MATCH (s:software) RETURN 'it''s' AS t LIMIT 1").to_list()   // #{"t": "it's"}

Long queries: backtick strings

A Rhai backtick string may span lines and processes no backslash escapes, so a multi-line query reads as it would in any GQL editor. Line breaks are whitespace for GQL; the error positions count lines and columns inside the query.

g.gql(`MATCH (p:person)-[:created]->(s:software)
       WHERE p.age > 30
       RETURN p.name AS who, s.name AS what
       ORDER BY who, what`).to_list()
// #{"what": "lop", "who": "josh"}, #{"what": "ripple", "who": "josh"}, #{"what": "lop", "who": "peter"}

Inside a backtick string both GQL quote forms work unescaped ('lop' and "lop"). Two characters are special to Rhai there:

  • ${ starts a Rhai interpolation: ${expr} is replaced by the value of a Rhai expression. GQL never needs ${, so this only matters when you use it on purpose (next section). A $ followed by a name, a GQL parameter such as $min, is left alone.
  • A backtick ends the string. A backtick that GQL should see is doubled: Rhai reads `` inside a backtick string as one backtick. GQL back-quoted identifiers are therefore written with doubled backticks there:
g.gql(`MATCH (s:software) RETURN s.name AS ``the name`` ORDER BY ``the name```).to_list()   // #{"the name": "lop"}, #{"the name": "ripple"}

The same query in a "..." string needs no doubling, because a backtick means nothing to a Rhai double-quoted string:

g.gql("MATCH (s:software) RETURN s.name AS `the name` ORDER BY `the name`").to_list()   // #{"the name": "lop"}, #{"the name": "ripple"}
g.gql("MATCH (`my var`:software) RETURN `my var`.name AS n ORDER BY n").to_list()   // #{"n": "lop"}, #{"n": "ripple"}

Values: parameters, not interpolation

Put values into a query as parameters: $name in the query, the value in the map after it. A parameter is a typed value that can never change the query text, whatever it contains:

g.gql(`MATCH (s:software) WHERE s.lang = $lang RETURN s.name AS name ORDER BY name`, #{lang: "java"}).to_list()   // #{"name": "lop"}, #{"name": "ripple"}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) WHERE n.age > $min RETURN n.name AS name ORDER BY name", #{min: 30}).to_list()   // #{"name": "josh"}, #{"name": "peter"}

Interpolation (${..}) and string concatenation ("..." + x + "...") paste the value in as query text. It runs, but a value with a quote in it breaks the query (or changes it), a number becomes text, and nothing is checked:

{ let name = "o'brien"; g.gql(`MATCH (p:person) WHERE p.name = '${name}' RETURN p.age AS age`).to_list() }   // error: unterminated string literal
{ let name = "o'brien"; g.gql(`MATCH (p:person) WHERE p.name = $name RETURN p.age AS age`, #{name: name}).to_list() }   // no rows, no error

In the first query the quote in the value ends the GQL string literal early; in the second the value is compared as it is.

Parameters also keep the plan reusable and let a property index serve the lookup (Index use). A parameter name that is not an identifier is back-quoted: $`my value` (in a backtick string $``my value``).

Comments

GQL has three comment forms, and all of them work inside both Rhai string forms (Rhai does not look for comments inside a string):

  • // ... to the end of the line;
  • /* ... */, not nested;
  • -- ... to the end of the line, the ISO GQL form.
g.gql(`-- people older than 30
MATCH (p:person)            // every person
  WHERE p.age > 30          /* only the older ones */
RETURN p.name AS name       -- one column
ORDER BY name`).to_list()
// #{"name": "josh"}, #{"name": "peter"}

The -- rule. -- is a comment in GQL but an edge in Cypher ((a)--(b)). Graphersal reads -- as an edge when the next character is > or ( (-->, --(), or when the token before it is a ) on the same line ((a)--(b), (a) -- (b)); everywhere else it starts a comment. So a -- comment on a line of its own or after a value is a comment, and an edge pattern is never misread. The one trap: a -- comment written right after a node pattern on the same line becomes an edge and the query fails loudly; use // there.

g.gql(`MATCH (a:person)--(b:software) RETURN a.name AS a, b.name AS b ORDER BY a, b`).to_list()
// josh/lop, josh/ripple, marko/lop, peter/lop

g.gql(`MATCH (p:person) -- every person
       RETURN p.name AS name`)   // error: unexpected `every`: this -- is read as an edge

Which string to use

QueryUse
one line, string literals"..." with GQL '...' literals
several lines, commentsa backtick string
values from your program$name parameters, never ${..} or +
a back-quoted GQL name"..." (no doubling), or doubled backticks in a backtick string

The MCP tool gql: no Rhai string at all

An agent connected to the dev server's MCP endpoint can call the tool gql with the query as plain text and the parameters as a JSON object, so none of the quoting above applies:

{
  "query": "MATCH (p:person)-[:knows]->(f) WHERE p.name = $name RETURN f.name AS friend ORDER BY friend",
  "params": {"name": "marko"},
  "max_rows": 100
}

It runs the same g.gql(..) call with the parameters as values and returns the rows like the query tool, in written column order. Like the query tool it may write (INSERT; the answer says that it changed the graph, with a one-line summary such as +3 vertices, +2 edges), and a server started with --mcp-read-only still offers it but refuses its writes. Prefer it whenever an agent writes GQL: there is no Rhai string to escape and no interpolation to get wrong. To continue a GQL result with Gremlin steps, use the query tool with g.gql(..) in the script.

Cypher Aliases

gql() speaks ISO GQL. Common Cypher spellings are accepted as aliases where they are unambiguous and mean exactly the same: an alias is translated to its GQL form while the query is parsed, so both spellings give the same plan and the same rows. An alias never has a meaning of its own. This table lists every accepted alias; Cypher functions without any GQL counterpart are the compatibility functions below, and Cypher's map projections and comprehensions, COUNT { }, COLLECT { }, SET n += .. and MERGE the compatibility forms (Map projections and comprehensions, COUNT and COLLECT, SET and REMOVE, MERGE); any other Cypher spelling is either not supported yet or refused.

Cypher spellingGQL formNotes
SKIP nOFFSET n
a != ba <> b
s1 + s2 on two stringss1 || s2also on two lists; + of a string and a number is an error (no implicit conversion: write s + toString(n) or s || CAST(n AS STRING))
(n:A:B)(n:A&B)plain names only; mixing :A:B with |, & or ! is an error (write it with &)
-[:A|:B]->-[:A|B]->a colon after the | of a label disjunction
n:A in an expressionn IS LABELED A
-->->abbreviated edge pointing right
<--<-abbreviated edge pointing left
---abbreviated edge, either direction (the -- rule)
<--><->either direction
elementId(x)element_id(x)the id as a string
toUpper(s)upper(s)
toLower(s)lower(s)
size(s) on a stringchar_length(s)size(list) is the item count, as cardinality(list)
collect(x)collect_list(x)also collect(DISTINCT x)
percentileCont(x, p), percentileDisc(x, p)percentile_cont(x, p), percentile_disc(x, p)ISO's binary set functions, value first (Aggregation)
length(p)path_length(p)the number of edges of a path
log(x) (one argument)ln(x)the natural logarithm; the two-argument log(base, x) is GQL's general logarithm
-[e:T*]->-[e:T]->{1,}Cypher's lower bound is 1: not GQL's postfix *, which is {0,}
-[e:T*n]->-[e:T]->{n}
-[e:T*m..n]->-[e:T]->{m,n}
-[e:T*..n]->-[e:T]->{1,n}lower bound 1 again
-[e:T*m..]->-[e:T]->{m,}
-[e:T*m..n]-> with m > n, -[e:T*..0]->no matchthe empty interval matches nothing (no row; OPTIONAL MATCH gives its NULL row); the GQL {3,1} is a syntax error
a < b <= c, a chained comparisona < b AND b <= cany mix of =, <>, <, <=, >, >=; the middle operand is evaluated once per comparison
WHERE (a)-[:T]->(b), a pattern predicateWHERE EXISTS { (a)-[:T]->(b) }where a condition stands (WHERE, FILTER, under NOT / AND / OR / XOR, a comprehension's WHERE, a searched CASE WHEN; elsewhere 42001); it may name only variables bound before it (EXISTS)
UNWIND list AS xFOR x IN listone row per item; WITH ORDINALITY / WITH OFFSET only after FOR
CREATE <pattern>INSERT <pattern>the same clause: once per row, nodes with label conjunctions (:A:B as :A&B), directed edges with one label (Writing with GQL); CREATE INDEX / CONSTRAINT / GRAPH are refused catalog commands
CALL { WITH a, b ... }, the importing WITHCALL (a, b) { ... }the first WITH of the body, when it lists plain variables only, is the variable scope clause (CALL subqueries)
SET n:A:B, REMOVE n:A:BSET n:A, n:B, REMOVE n:A, n:Bthe labels in order; SET n IS A & B likewise (Writing with GQL)
SET (n).k = v, REMOVE (n).kSET n.k = v, REMOVE n.ka parenthesized variable as the target
localtime(x), localdatetime(x), datetime(x)local_time(x), local_datetime(x), zoned_datetime(x)the temporal constructors (Dates and times)

Each pair below returns the same rows:

g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.name AS name ORDER BY name SKIP 2").to_list()   // #{"name": "peter"}, #{"name": "vadas"}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.name AS name ORDER BY name OFFSET 2").to_list()   // #{"name": "peter"}, #{"name": "vadas"}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) WHERE n.age != 29 RETURN n.name AS name ORDER BY name").to_list()   // josh, peter, vadas
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) WHERE n.age <> 29 RETURN n.name AS name ORDER BY name").to_list()   // josh, peter, vadas
g.gql("MATCH (p {name: 'marko'})-->(x) RETURN x.name AS x ORDER BY x").to_list()   // josh, lop, vadas
g.gql("MATCH (p {name: 'marko'})->(x) RETURN x.name AS x ORDER BY x").to_list()   // josh, lop, vadas
g.gql("MATCH (n) WHERE n:software RETURN n.name AS name ORDER BY name").to_list()   // lop, ripple
g.gql("MATCH (n) WHERE n IS LABELED software RETURN n.name AS name ORDER BY name").to_list()   // lop, ripple
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN elementId(n) AS id, toUpper(n.name) AS up, size(n.name) AS len, n.name + '?' AS q ORDER BY id LIMIT 1").to_list()
// #{"id": "1", "len": 5, "q": "marko?", "up": "MARKO"}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN element_id(n) AS id, upper(n.name) AS up, char_length(n.name) AS len, n.name || '?' AS q ORDER BY id LIMIT 1").to_list()
// #{"id": "1", "len": 5, "q": "marko?", "up": "MARKO"}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person)-[:created]->(s) RETURN p.name AS name, collect(s.name) AS sw ORDER BY name").to_list()
// #{"name": "josh", "sw": ["ripple", "lop"]}, #{"name": "marko", "sw": ["lop"]}, #{"name": "peter", "sw": ["lop"]}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person)-[:created]->(s) RETURN p.name AS name, collect_list(s.name) AS sw ORDER BY name").to_list()
// #{"name": "josh", "sw": ["ripple", "lop"]}, #{"name": "marko", "sw": ["lop"]}, #{"name": "peter", "sw": ["lop"]}
g.gql("MATCH p = (a {name: 'marko'})-[*1..2]->(b) RETURN b.name AS b, length(p) AS len ORDER BY len, b").to_list()
// josh 1, lop 1, vadas 1, lop 2, ripple 2
g.gql("MATCH p = (a {name: 'marko'})-[]->{1,2}(b) RETURN b.name AS b, path_length(p) AS len ORDER BY len, b").to_list()
// josh 1, lop 1, vadas 1, lop 2, ripple 2
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN log(100) AS l").to_list()   // #{"l": 4.605170185988092}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN ln(100) AS l").to_list()   // #{"l": 4.605170185988092}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE (p)-[:created]->() RETURN p.name AS name ORDER BY name").to_list()   // josh, marko, peter
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE EXISTS { (p)-[:created]->() } RETURN p.name AS name ORDER BY name").to_list()   // josh, marko, peter
g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) UNWIND [p.age, p.age + 1] AS a RETURN a ORDER BY a").to_list()   // #{"a": 29}, #{"a": 30}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) FOR a IN [p.age, p.age + 1] RETURN a ORDER BY a").to_list()   // #{"a": 29}, #{"a": 30}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL { WITH p MATCH (p)-[:knows]->(f) RETURN count(f) AS n } RETURN p.name AS name, n ORDER BY name").to_list()   // josh 0, marko 2, peter 0, vadas 0
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-[:knows]->(f) RETURN count(f) AS n } RETURN p.name AS name, n ORDER BY name").to_list()   // josh 0, marko 2, peter 0, vadas 0
g.gql("CREATE (c:city:capital {name: 'Rome'}) RETURN labels(c) AS l").to_list()   // #{"l": ["city", "capital"]}
g.gql("INSERT (c:city&capital {name: 'Rome'}) RETURN labels(c) AS l").to_list()   // #{"l": ["city", "capital"]}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) SET p:admin:staff RETURN labels(p) AS l").to_list()   // #{"l": ["person", "admin", "staff"]}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) SET p:admin, p:staff RETURN labels(p) AS l").to_list()   // #{"l": ["person", "admin", "staff"]}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) WHERE 27 <= n.age < 32 RETURN n.name AS name ORDER BY name").to_list()   // marko, vadas
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) WHERE 27 <= n.age AND n.age < 32 RETURN n.name AS name ORDER BY name").to_list()   // marko, vadas
g.gql("MATCH (a {name: 'marko'})-[*2..1]->(b) RETURN b.name AS b").to_list()   // [] (the empty interval)

The importing WITH passes the variables on unchanged; a first WITH that renames, computes or filters (WITH p AS q, WITH p WHERE ..) is an ordinary WITH of a body that imports nothing, so reading p there is an error (write CALL (p) { .. }). A CALL { } without a scope clause and without that WITH imports nothing, as in Neo4j Cypher 25.

Mind the Cypher *: -[*]-> starts at one edge, GQL's -[]->* at zero, so the GQL form also returns marko himself:

g.gql("MATCH (a {name: 'marko'})-[*]->(b) RETURN b.name AS b ORDER BY b").to_list()   // josh, lop, lop, ripple, vadas
g.gql("MATCH (a {name: 'marko'})-[]->*(b) RETURN b.name AS b ORDER BY b").to_list()   // josh, lop, lop, marko, ripple, vadas

The Cypher clause WITH

WITH is Cypher; GQL writes the same with its linear statements (LET, FILTER, and RETURN ... NEXT, UNION and NEXT). gql() accepts WITH with Cypher's meaning: it passes on only its items, may take DISTINCT, aggregates, ORDER BY, SKIP / OFFSET, LIMIT and a WHERE (applied last), and a later clause continues from its columns (The Supported Subset). A WITH that only passes values on is the same as LET plus a narrower scope, and its WHERE the same as FILTER:

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WITH p, p.age / 10 AS d WHERE d = 3 RETURN p.name AS name ORDER BY name").to_list()   // #{"name": "josh"}, #{"name": "peter"}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) LET d = p.age / 10 FILTER d = 3 RETURN p.name AS name ORDER BY name").to_list()   // #{"name": "josh"}, #{"name": "peter"}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p, p.age / 10 AS d NEXT FILTER d = 3 RETURN p.name AS name ORDER BY name").to_list()   // #{"name": "josh"}, #{"name": "peter"}

Spellings that are GQL as well

These look like Cypher but are GQL too, so they are not aliases: : before a label expression (GQL also has IS), ASC / DESC (also ASCENDING / DESCENDING), string literals in '...' and "...", // and /* */ comments, $name parameters, back-quoted names.

The functions abs, floor, ceil, sqrt, exp, log10, left, right, ltrim, rtrim, btrim, trim(s), nullif (Cypher nullIf; names are case-insensitive) and coalesce have the same name in both languages and are GQL functions. Where Neo4j's version differs, GQL's meaning wins: trim(s), ltrim(s) and rtrim(s) remove spaces only (Cypher removes any whitespace), and floor(3) / ceil(3) of an integer stay integers (Neo4j returns floats that compare equal). ceiling(x) is GQL's second spelling of ceil(x).

Compatibility functions

Some Cypher functions have no GQL counterpart at all, so they cannot be aliases. gql() accepts a fixed list of them, because Cypher users and LLMs write them all the time, with their openCypher / Neo4j Cypher 25 meaning: a query using them means the same as in Neo4j, except where Semantics says otherwise. They never get a meaning of their own, and no vendor function joins them (apoc.*, text.* are refused).

FunctionFamilyGQL nearest form
toInteger(x), toFloat(x), toBoolean(x), toString(x)conversionsCAST(x AS INTEGER | FLOAT | BOOLEAN | STRING), but stricter (below)
toIntegerOrNull(x), toFloatOrNull(x), toBooleanOrNull(x), toStringOrNull(x)conversionsnone
substring(s, start [, length])stringsleft(s, n), right(s, n)
replace(s, search, replacement [, limit]), split(s, delimiter), reverse(x), isEmpty(x)strings, listsnone
round(x [, precision [, mode]]), sign(x)numbersnone
head(list), last(list), tail(list), range(start, end [, step])liststrim(list, n) drops items from the end
keys(x), properties(x)elementsx.key reads one property
startNode(e), endNode(e)elementsthe predicates n IS SOURCE OF e, n IS DESTINATION OF e
nodes(p), relationships(p)pathsGQL's elements(p) (not supported yet)
all(x IN l WHERE c), any(..), none(..), single(..)list predicatesnone; a list comprehension counted with size() (below)
reduce(acc = init, x IN l | expr)listsnone; FOR x IN l and an aggregate fold the rows of a query, not a list per row
date.truncate(unit, x) and the other X.truncate(), duration.between(a, b), duration.inMonths() / inDays() / inSeconds(), X.statement(), X.transaction(), datetime.fromepoch(), datetime.fromepochmillis(), toString(temporal)dates and timesthe constructors date(), local_time(), ... and duration() (Dates and times)

CAST is not an alias of toInteger(). Both convert with the same rules, but they treat a text that does not convert differently: GQL's CAST fails the query with 22018, Cypher's toInteger / toFloat / toBoolean give NULL, and the ...OrNull forms also give NULL for a value of the wrong kind. toInteger and toFloat also read Cypher literals ('0x1F', '1_000'), CAST only decimal text. Use CAST to catch dirty data, toInteger to skip it (Semantics).

g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN toInteger('42') AS a, CAST('42' AS INTEGER) AS b").to_list()   // #{"a": 42, "b": 42}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN toInteger('forty') AS a").to_list()   // #{"a": ()}
g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN CAST('forty' AS INTEGER) AS b")   // error: invalid character value for cast (22018)
g.gql("MATCH (a)-[e:knows]-(b) WHERE startNode(e) = a RETURN a.name AS a, b.name AS b ORDER BY b").to_list()   // #{"a": "marko", "b": "josh"}, #{"a": "marko", "b": "vadas"}
g.gql("MATCH (a)-[e:knows]-(b) WHERE a IS SOURCE OF e RETURN a.name AS a, b.name AS b ORDER BY b").to_list()   // #{"a": "marko", "b": "josh"}, #{"a": "marko", "b": "vadas"}

List predicates and reduce

all(x IN l WHERE c), any(..), none(..) and single(..) test the items of a list, and reduce(acc = init, x IN l | expr) folds them: acc starts at init and takes the value of expr for each item in list order. x (and acc) exist only inside the call and must be new names, like a list comprehension's variable. The WHERE is required; an aggregate may stand in the list and in init, not in the condition or after |. Their NULL rules are the three-valued ones of the openCypher TCK, which Neo4j Cypher 25 follows:

  • a NULL list gives NULL (reduce too), a value that is not a list is error 22G03;
  • a decided answer wins and stops at once: all is FALSE at the first FALSE item, any TRUE and none FALSE at the first TRUE one, single FALSE at the second TRUE one (later items are not evaluated);
  • otherwise an item whose condition is NULL makes the answer NULL;
  • otherwise all and none are TRUE, any FALSE, single whether exactly one item was TRUE; so for an empty list all / none are TRUE, any / single FALSE, and reduce gives init.

A list comprehension counted with size() gives the same answer when no condition is NULL (it drops a NULL condition instead): all is size([x IN l WHERE c]) = size(l), any is > 0, none is = 0, single is = 1. Over a pattern comprehension the predicates test the matches of a pattern per row, the Gremlin where(__..) / not(__..):

g.gql("RETURN all(x IN [1, NULL] WHERE x > 0) AS a, any(x IN [1, NULL] WHERE x > 0) AS b, single(x IN [1, 2] WHERE x > 1) AS c, none(x IN [] WHERE x > 1) AS d").to_list()   // #{"a": (), "b": true, "c": true, "d": true}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE any(a IN [(p)-[:knows]->(f) | f.age] WHERE a > 30) RETURN p.name AS name").to_list()   // #{"name": "marko"}
g.V().hasLabel("person").where(__.out("knows").has("age", P.gt(30))).values("name").to_list()   // "marko"
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE none(w IN [(p)-[:created]->(s) | s] WHERE w.name = 'lop') RETURN p.name AS name").to_list()   // #{"name": "vadas"}
g.V().hasLabel("person").not(__.out("created").has("name", "lop")).values("name").to_list()   // "vadas"
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, reduce(total = 0, w IN [(p)-[e]->() | e.weight] | total + w) AS weight ORDER BY name").to_list()
// josh 1.4, marko 1.9, peter 0.2, vadas 0 (reduce starts at 0)
g.V().hasLabel("person").order().by("name").project("name", "weight").by("name").by(__.out_e().values("weight").fold().sum(Scope.local)).to_list()
// josh 1.4, marko 1.9, peter 0.2, vadas without "weight" (the sum of no values is no value)
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN reduce(s = '', n IN collect_list(p.name) | s || n) AS names").to_list()   // one string of the four names

Map projections and comprehensions

Three Cypher expression forms have no GQL counterpart with the same meaning, so they are not aliases either. gql() accepts them as compatibility forms, like the compatibility functions: with their openCypher / Neo4j Cypher 25 meaning, because they are how Cypher users and LLMs ask for nested, JSON-shaped answers (The Supported Subset).

Cypher formGQL nearest formDifference
map projection p {.name, .age, .*, f, k: expr}the record constructor {name: p.name, age: p.age, f: f, k: expr} (or RECORD {..})for a NULL p the projection is NULL, the record {name: NULL, ...}; .* has no record form (properties(p) is the map of all properties)
list comprehension [x IN list WHERE cond | expr]none; FOR x IN list FILTER cond RETURN collect_list(expr) gives one list per query, not per row
pattern comprehension [(p)-[:R]->(f) WHERE cond | expr]none; OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:R]->(f) WHERE cond + collect_list(expr) groups the rows insteadthe comprehension keeps the row and gives [] when nothing matches

The projection and the record give the same map whenever the variable is not NULL:

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p {.name, .age} AS m ORDER BY p.name LIMIT 1").to_list()   // #{"m": #{"age": 32, "name": "josh"}}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN {name: p.name, age: p.age} AS m ORDER BY p.name LIMIT 1").to_list()   // #{"m": #{"age": 32, "name": "josh"}}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, [(p)-[:created]->(s) | s.name] AS sw ORDER BY name").to_list()
// josh [ripple, lop] (in any order), marko [lop], peter [lop], vadas []
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN p.name AS name, collect_list(s.name) AS sw ORDER BY name").to_list()
// josh [ripple, lop], marko [lop], peter [lop], vadas []

Cypher's list predicates all(), any(), none(), single() and reduce() bind a variable the same way; they are compatibility functions.

COUNT and COLLECT

Cypher's COUNT { } and COLLECT { } subqueries have no GQL counterpart either; gql() accepts them as compatibility forms with their Neo4j Cypher 25 meaning (COUNT and COLLECT). They take the bodies of EXISTS: a pattern, MATCH clauses, or a whole query ending in RETURN (one item for COLLECT).

Cypher formGQL nearest formDifference
COUNT { <pattern or query> }CALL (p) { OPTIONAL MATCH .. RETURN count(x) AS n }, or OPTIONAL MATCH + count()the subquery keeps the row and stands in any expression; COUNT { } > 0 is EXISTS { }
COLLECT { <query> RETURN x }CALL (p) { OPTIONAL MATCH .. RETURN collect_list(x) AS l }COLLECT keeps NULL items, collect_list() skips them
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, COUNT { (p)-[:created]->() } AS n ORDER BY name").to_list()   // josh 2, marko 1, peter 1, vadas 0
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN count(s) AS n } RETURN p.name AS name, n ORDER BY name").to_list()   // josh 2, marko 1, peter 1, vadas 0
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, COLLECT { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN s.name ORDER BY s.name } AS sw ORDER BY name").to_list()
// josh [lop, ripple], marko [lop], peter [lop], vadas []
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) WITH s ORDER BY s.name RETURN collect_list(s.name) AS sw } RETURN p.name AS name, sw ORDER BY name").to_list()
// josh [lop, ripple], marko [lop], peter [lop], vadas []

One difference from Neo4j: a COUNT { } body whose final RETURN only projects is counted without evaluating its items (Semantics).

SET and REMOVE

GQL's SET items are a property (SET n.k = v), all properties from a braced map (SET n = {k: v}) and a label (SET n:A / SET n IS A); REMOVE takes a property or a label. Two Cypher forms have no GQL counterpart and are accepted as compatibility forms with Cypher's meaning:

  • SET n += map merges the map into the properties: the keys of the map are set (a NULL value removes its key), the other properties stay.
  • SET n = expr with an expression that is not a braced map: a $parameter or any map value replaces every property, and a node or an edge stands for its properties, so SET n = m copies them (SET n = n changes nothing). Write SET n = properties(m) for the same as a plain map.

A NULL on the right of = or += is an error (22004) rather than an empty map; write coalesce($map, {}) (Semantics). This is our choice for the compatibility form, where Neo4j removes every property: standard GQL has no such form, since its SET n = {..} takes a braced map only.

g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) SET p += {city: 'Rome'} RETURN properties(p) AS props").to_list()   // #{"props": #{"age": 29, "city": "Rome", "name": "marko"}}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) SET p = $props RETURN properties(p) AS props", #{props: #{name: "marko", city: "Rome"}}).to_list()   // #{"props": #{"city": "Rome", "name": "marko"}}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}), (q:person {name: 'josh'}) SET p = q RETURN properties(p) AS props").to_list()   // #{"props": #{"age": 32, "name": "josh"}}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) SET p += $more", #{more: ()})   // error: the right side of SET p += .. is NULL, not a map

MERGE

Cypher's MERGE ("find or create") has no ISO GQL counterpart. gql() accepts it as a compatibility form with Neo4j Cypher 25's meaning, and with it its ON CREATE SET and ON MATCH SET actions:

CypherIn gql()Notes
MERGE <pattern>supported as a compatibility formone path pattern per clause; per row, every match is a row, or the whole pattern is created; each row sees the rows before it (Writing with GQL)
ON CREATE SET <items>, ON MATCH SET <items>supported as a compatibility formthe items of SET, several actions in any order, applied in the order written
MERGE p = <pattern>supportedthe path found or created
MERGE (a)-[:T]-(b) without a directionsupportedmatches either direction, creates from left to right

Plain GQL writes the same with a CALL body that inserts only when nothing exists:

g.gql("MERGE (c:city {name: 'Berlin'}) RETURN c.name AS name").to_list()   // #{"name": "Berlin"}
g.gql("CALL { FILTER NOT EXISTS { MATCH (:city {name: 'Berlin'}) } INSERT (:city {name: 'Berlin'}) } MATCH (c:city {name: 'Berlin'}) RETURN c.name AS name").to_list()   // #{"name": "Berlin"}

The differences from Neo4j are on Semantics.

Dates and times

The temporal constructors have an ISO GQL name and a Cypher name; the Cypher names are aliases (the same function, the same value). The qualified Cypher functions have no ISO spelling: they are compatibility functions with Neo4j's meaning (Dates and times).

CypherISO GQLNotes
date(x)date(x)the same name
localtime(x)local_time(x)a time of day without an offset
localdatetime(x)local_datetime(x)
datetime(x)zoned_datetime(x)an instant with its UTC offset (and its zone name)
time(x)zoned_time(x)a time of day with its UTC offset
duration(x)duration(x)the same name
date.truncate(), localtime.truncate(), time.truncate(), localdatetime.truncate(), datetime.truncate()nonecompatibility functions
duration.between(), duration.inMonths(), duration.inDays(), duration.inSeconds()nonecompatibility functions; ISO's duration_between() is an unknown function that suggests duration.between()
X.statement(), X.transaction(); datetime.fromepoch(), datetime.fromepochmillis()nonecompatibility functions; the clocks give the time the query started

| X.realtime() | none | refused: a clock that moves while the query runs |

g.gql("RETURN datetime('2015-07-21T21:40+01:00') = zoned_datetime('2015-07-21T21:40+01:00') AS a, localtime('12:00') = local_time('12:00') AS b, localdatetime('2015-07-21T21:40') = local_datetime('2015-07-21T21:40') AS c").to_list()
// #{"a": true, "b": true, "c": true}
g.gql("RETURN zoned_time('12:00+01:00') = time('12:00+01:00') AS t").to_list()   // #{"t": true}

Cypher spellings that are not aliases

CypherIn gql()
id(n)refused: an integer in Neo4j, Graphersal ids are strings; use element_id(n)
nodes(p), relationships(p)supported as compatibility functions, not aliases: GQL has no such functions
x ^ ysupported as a compatibility operator: GQL has no operator for it; it means power(x, y) (always a float, the same errors), binding tighter than * and looser than a unary minus
rand(), randomUUID()refused: gql() functions are deterministic
time(), time.*(); date.realtime() and the other X.realtime()time() not supported yet (no time-with-offset type: use localtime() or datetime()); X.realtime() refused, like rand() (Dates and times)
map projections, list and pattern comprehensionssupported as compatibility forms, not aliases
any() / all() / none() / single(), reduce()supported as compatibility functions, not aliases: GQL has no such functions
COUNT { }, COLLECT { }supported as compatibility forms, not aliases
CALL { } IN TRANSACTIONSrefused: a write form; the CALL itself is supported
exists(n.p) (Cypher 4)refused: EXISTS takes a pattern; test a property with n.p IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY (not Cypher)ISO GQL, accepted after the RETURN items (optional: grouping is implicit); after WITH an error that explains implicit grouping
MERGEsupported as a compatibility form, with ON CREATE SET / ON MATCH SET
FOREACHnot supported yet (Writing with GQL); CREATE is an alias of INSERT; SET and REMOVE are supported, += as a compatibility form
DELETE, DETACH DELETEthe same in GQL, supported (Writing with GQL); GQL also writes the default explicitly as NODETACH DELETE
SET n[key] = v, SET n:$(expr) (Cypher 25 dynamic keys and labels)not supported; name the key and the label in the query
CALL proc(..) YIELD ..supported for saved queries written in GQL: CALL folder.name(..) with YIELD, YIELD * and the standalone forms of Cypher (Calling saved queries)
CALL db.*(), dbms.*, apoc.*, gds.*, SHOW ...refused: vendor extensions
a--1 (minus minus one)a comment starts at -- (GQL wins): RETURN n.age--1 AS x returns the column n.age; write n.age - -1

Refused Constructs

Some constructs gql() refuses for good, not just for now. A refused construct fails before the traversal runs, with GQLSTATUS 0A000, a caret under it and a help line naming what to use instead. (Constructs that are only not supported yet are listed on The Supported Subset.) GROUP BY is neither: it is accepted after the RETURN items, and grouping is implicit anyway; after WITH (no ISO counterpart) it is a syntax error whose help shows the query without it (Aggregation).

ConstructWhyInstead
undirected edges ~[e]~, <~[e]~, ~[e]~>, ~, <~, ~>Graphersal edges are always directed; there is no undirected edge to match-[e]-, an edge in either direction
catalog commands CREATE INDEX, CREATE CONSTRAINT, CREATE GRAPH, CREATE DATABASEnot part of a query: indexes, schemas and graphs are the host'sg.create_index(..), g.set_schema(..), opening another graph
LOAD CSVa vendor extension, not GQLthe host's import (GraphSON, GraphML), or the rows as a list parameter: FOR row IN $rows INSERT (..)
vendor procedures: the namespaces db, dbms, apoc and gds (CALL db.labels(), CALL apoc.*)vendor extensions, not GQL (an inline CALL { } subquery is supported, and any other CALL folder.name(..) calls a saved query)the Gremlin steps that do the same, such as g.v().label().dedup(), or a saved GQL query that does it
CALL { ... } IN TRANSACTIONScommits the writes of a subquery in batches; a gql() query is one unit, which commits at once or not at allthe same CALL without IN TRANSACTIONS
SHOW ...a vendor command, not GQLthe catalog steps (indexes(), queries(), get_schema(), statistics())
vendor path search *BFS, *WSHORTEST, *ALLSHORTESTvendor extensions, not GQLGremlin repeat()
id(n)Cypher's id() is an integer; Graphersal ids are strings, and returning a different type under the same name would misleadelement_id(n), the id as a string
exists(n.p), the Cypher 4 property testEXISTS is GQL's subquery predicate and takes a graph pattern; reading it as a property test as well would give one keyword two meaningsn.p IS NOT NULL; EXISTS { (n)-[:T]->() } tests a pattern (EXISTS)
USE graphgql() runs on the graph of its traversal sourceopen the other graph and run there
non-deterministic functions rand(), randomUUID()every gql() function is pure, so a LET or WITH name may stand for its expression and the plan stays deterministic; a random value would differ between its usesGremlin after gql(): sample(n) or coin(p) to pick rows at random
vendor and namespaced functions apoc.*, db.*, gds.*, text.*, ...vendor extensions, not GQL; the accepted Cypher functions are a fixed list (compatibility functions)a gql() function, or Gremlin steps after gql()
g.gql("MATCH (a)~[e]~(b) RETURN a")   // refused: undirected edges (`~`) are not supported
g.gql("CALL db.labels() YIELD label RETURN label")   // refused: the vendor procedures of db, dbms, apoc and gds are vendor extensions
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN s.name AS sw } IN TRANSACTIONS RETURN sw")   // refused: CALL { } IN TRANSACTIONS commits writes in batches
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN s.name AS sw } RETURN sw ORDER BY sw").to_list()   // lop, lop, lop, ripple
g.gql("SHOW INDEXES")   // refused: SHOW commands are vendor extensions
g.gql("CREATE INDEX FOR (n:person) ON (n.name)")   // refused: CREATE INDEX is a catalog command
g.gql("LOAD CSV FROM 'people.csv' AS row RETURN row")   // refused: LOAD CSV is a vendor extension
g.gql("MATCH (n) RETURN id(n)")   // refused: use element_id(n)
g.gql("MATCH (a)-[:knows*BFS]->(b) RETURN b")   // refused: *BFS is a vendor path search extension
g.gql("USE g MATCH (n) RETURN n")   // refused: USE is not supported
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) WHERE exists(n.age) RETURN n.name AS name")   // refused: exists(value) is the Cypher 4 property test
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) WHERE n.age IS NOT NULL RETURN n.name AS name ORDER BY name").to_list()   // josh, marko, peter, vadas
g.gql("MATCH (n) RETURN rand() AS r")   // refused: rand() is a non-deterministic function
g.gql("MATCH (n) RETURN apoc.text.join(['a', 'b'], ',') AS r")   // refused: apoc.text.join() is a vendor function
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.name AS name ORDER BY name").sample(1).count().next()   // 1
g.gql("MATCH (n) RETURN element_id(n) AS id ORDER BY id LIMIT 2").to_list()   // #{"id": "1"}, #{"id": "2"}

Writes are supported (INSERT, SET, REMOVE, DELETE, and Cypher's MERGE as a compatibility form: Writing with GQL); Cypher's FOREACH is not supported yet and is listed there. The full message of a refused construct reads:

Error: GQL unsupported construct at line 1, column 1: CREATE INDEX is a catalog command, not part of a gql() query (step #1 'gql:error("0A000")' refused the query before the traversal ran)
  at #1: v().gql:error("0A000")
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  query:     CREATE INDEX FOR (n:person) ON (n.name)
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^
  GQLSTATUS: 0A000
Help: create a property index with g.create_index(#{label: "person", key: "age"}); every query that can use it then does. gql() does not support this construct; write this part of the query as Gremlin steps.

Errors

A GQL error is a TraverserError::Gql (feature gql) with a kind, a message, the position (line and column inside the query), a caret under the offending text, the expected tokens, a "did you mean" suggestion where one fits, and a GQLSTATUS code, the five-character status code of ISO GQL (derived from SQL's SQLSTATE). Like every Graphersal error it has a Help: line that names the fix.

Errors before the run

A query that does not parse or bind fails before the traversal runs, even when no traverser would ever reach the step, as math() does with an equation. On the empty graph, where nothing matches, the query is still checked:

g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.name +")   // error: unexpected end of input

Error: GQL syntax error at line 1, column 33: unexpected end of input (step #1 'gql:error("42001")' refused the query before the traversal ran)
  at #1: v().gql:error("42001")
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  query:     MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.name +
                                             ^
  expected:  an expression
  GQLSTATUS: 42001
Help: Expected an expression at the marked position. Fix the query at the marked position: a GQL read query is MATCH <pattern> [WHERE <condition>], then any further MATCH, OPTIONAL MATCH, WITH, LET or FILTER clauses, then RETURN <items>, for example g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE p.age > 30 RETURN p.name") or g.gql("MATCH (p:person) OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) WITH p, count(s) AS n RETURN p.name, n"). CALL (p) { .. RETURN .. } runs a query for each row, UNION combines the records of two queries and NEXT continues after a RETURN, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p NEXT MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN p.name, s.name"). FOR x IN <list> (Cypher UNWIND <list> AS x) gives one row per item of a list, and a query may also start with FOR, LET, WITH, FILTER or RETURN, as in g.gql("FOR n IN ['marko', 'josh'] MATCH (p:person {name: n}) RETURN n, p.age").

The plan of a query that failed this way is the marker step gql:error("<GQLSTATUS>"), which raises the error before anything runs; the query: line, not the plan, shows the position. In a multi-line query the error names the line and shows only that line:

g.gql(`MATCH (n:person)
       WHERE n.age >
       RETURN n`)   // error: unexpected keyword RETURN at line 3

Error: GQL syntax error at line 3, column 8: unexpected keyword RETURN (step #1 'gql:error("42001")' refused the query before the traversal ran)
  at #1: v().gql:error("42001")
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  line 3:           RETURN n
                    ^^^^^^
  expected:  an expression
  GQLSTATUS: 42001

Misspelt keywords, functions and variables get a suggestion:

g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETRUN n")   // error: unexpected `RETRUN`, did you mean RETURN
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN m.name")   // error: the variable `m` is not defined, did you mean n
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) WHERE n.age > $min RETURN n.name AS name")   // error: the parameter `$min` has no value

Error: GQL syntax error at line 1, column 18: unexpected `RETRUN` (step #1 'gql:error("42001")' refused the query before the traversal ran)
  at #1: v().gql:error("42001")
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  query:        MATCH (n:person) RETRUN n
                                 ^^^^^^
  expected:     `,`, WHERE, MATCH, OPTIONAL MATCH, WITH, LET, FILTER, FOR, UNWIND, CALL, RETURN
  did you mean: RETURN
  GQLSTATUS:    42001
Help: Did you mean RETURN? Expected `,`, WHERE, MATCH, OPTIONAL MATCH, WITH, LET, FILTER, FOR, UNWIND, CALL, ... at the marked position. ...

Errors while the query runs

A valid query can still fail on a row of the data: a division by zero, an overflow, an operand of the wrong kind. These fail the traversal when the row reaches the expression (kind Data, GQLSTATUS class 22), with the caret under the expression and the step that ran it:

g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.age / 0 AS x")   // error: division by zero
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.name + 1 AS x")   // error: + joins two strings or adds two numbers, not a string and a number
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN type(n) AS x")   // error: type() takes an edge, not a node

Error: Step #1 'gql:project("x")' execution failed
  at #1: v().has_label("person").gql:project("x")
                                 ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  plan:  v(labels: ["person"]).gql:project("x")
                               ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
Caused by: GQL data exception at line 1, column 25: division by zero
  query:     MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.age / 0 AS x
                                     ^^^^^^^^^
  GQLSTATUS: 22012
Help: A row of the data made the marked expression fail. Keep such rows away from it with a WHERE condition or a CASE expression, ...

Comparisons never fail: = of values of different kinds is FALSE (<> TRUE), an ordering < of them is NULL, and any comparison with NULL is NULL (Semantics).

+ of a string and a number names the explicit conversions in its help:

Help: Convert the number or boolean to text first, with toString(x) or CAST(x AS STRING), and join text with ||, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name || ' is ' || toString(p.age) AS s"); or compute with numbers only, converting text with toInteger(x) or toFloat(x). ...

Function errors

A function fails on an argument it cannot take, with a GQLSTATUS that says why and a help line that leads with the fix for that function, then the general advice above:

g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN CAST(n.name AS INTEGER) AS x")   // error: invalid character value for cast (22018)
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN substring(n.name, -1) AS x")   // error: substring() takes a start of 0 or more (22011)
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN TRIM(BOTH 'ab' FROM n.name) AS x")   // error: TRIM(.. FROM ..) removes exactly one character (22027)
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN ln(n.age - 29) AS x")   // error: ln() of a number <= 0 (2201E)
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN sqrt(27 - n.age) AS x")   // error: sqrt() of a negative number (2201F)
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN range(1, n.age, 0) AS x")   // error: range() step 0 (22023)
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN toFloat(n.age > 30) AS x")   // error: toFloat() takes a number or a string, not a boolean (22G03)

Caused by: GQL data exception at line 1, column 30: invalid character value for cast: 'marko' is not an INTEGER (expected a decimal number, surrounding spaces allowed)
  query:     MATCH (n:person) RETURN CAST(n.name AS INTEGER) AS x
                                          ^^^^^^
  GQLSTATUS: 22018
Help: CAST is strict: text that is not a value of the target type fails the query. The Cypher conversions are lenient: toInteger(x), toFloat(x) and toBoolean(x) give NULL for such text, and toIntegerOrNull(x), toFloatOrNull(x) and toBooleanOrNull(x) give NULL for a value of any other kind too, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name, toInteger(p.name) AS n"). A row of the data made the marked expression fail. ...

A function gql() knows but does not support gets a message with the reason and the alternative instead of "unknown function", and a misspelt name a suggestion:

g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN sin(n.age) AS x")   // error: sin() (a trigonometric function) is not yet supported
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN rand() AS x")   // refused: rand() is not supported: a non-deterministic function
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN toInt(n.age) AS x")   // error: unknown function toInt(), did you mean toInteger()

Error: GQL construct not supported yet at line 1, column 25: sin() (a trigonometric function) is not yet supported in this version (step #1 'gql:error("0A000")' refused the query before the traversal ran)
  ...
  GQLSTATUS: 0A000
Help: Gremlin math() after gql(), for example g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.age AS a").select("a").math("sin(_)"). This construct comes in a later version of gql(); until then, write the query without it or as Gremlin steps.

Dates and times

The temporal functions fail with these codes; the help line shows the accepted forms with a runnable example:

CodeWhen
22007text that is no value of the type (date('nonsense'), date('2015-13-01'), an offset in localtime('12:00+01:00'), an offset that is not the zone's in '..+02:00[Europe/London]'); a map with an unknown key or with two groups of date keys; an unknown time zone
22008a field out of range (month: 13, day: 30 in February, hour: 25) or a value outside the years -9999 to 9999, also as the result of arithmetic (date('9999-12-31') + duration('P1D'))
22G03a component the value's type does not have (date(..).hour; the message lists the components it has); a constructor argument of the wrong kind (date(42), localdatetime(date(..))); arithmetic without a meaning (date + date, date * 2); a truncation or difference of a value without the part it needs (date.truncate('day', localtime(..)), duration.inDays() of two local times)
22023a truncation unit the type does not have (date.truncate('hour', ..)) or an unknown unit
22012a duration divided by zero
0A000X.realtime() (refused)
g.gql("RETURN date('nonsense') AS d")   // error: cannot parse "nonsense" as a date (22007)
g.gql("RETURN date({year: 2015, mnth: 3}) AS d")   // error: the map has an unknown field mnth (22007)
g.gql("RETURN datetime({year: 2015, timezone: 'Mars/Olympus'}) AS d")   // error: unknown time zone (22007)
g.gql("RETURN date({year: 2015, month: 13, day: 1}) AS d")   // error: the field month cannot be 13 (22008)
g.gql("RETURN date('9999-12-31') + duration('P1D') AS d")   // error: the result is outside the supported range (22008)
g.gql("RETURN date('2015-01-01').foo AS x")   // error: a date has no component foo; its components are year, quarter, ... (22G03)
g.gql("RETURN date('2015-01-01') * 2 AS x")   // error: * with a temporal value takes a duration and a number (22G03)
g.gql("RETURN date.truncate('fortnight', date('2017-10-11')) AS d")   // error: unknown unit 'fortnight' (22023)
g.gql("RETURN duration('P1D') / 0 AS d")   // error: division by zero (22012)
g.gql("RETURN datetime.realtime() AS t")   // error: datetime.realtime() is not supported (0A000)

Caused by: GQL data exception at line 1, column 13: date(): the field month cannot be 13
  query:     RETURN date({year: 2015, month: 13, day: 1}) AS d
                         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  GQLSTATUS: 22008
Help: Temporal fields stay within their ranges (month 1 to 12, day within its month, week within its week-numbering year, hour 0 to 23, minute and second 0 to 59, millisecond 0 to 999) and every value within the years -9999 to 9999, as in g.gql("RETURN date({year: 1984, month: 10, day: 11}) AS d, localtime({hour: 23, minute: 59, second: 59, millisecond: 999}) AS t"). A row of the data made the marked expression fail. ...

Scope, grouping and limits

The help of a semantic error explains the rule behind it. A variable that a WITH did not carry on, a value read outside an aggregate that is not a grouping key, and a GROUP BY that leaves out a grouping key each name the fix:

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WITH p.name AS name RETURN p.age")   // error: the variable `p` is not in scope: the WITH before does not carry it
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS n, count(p.age) + p.age AS x")   // error: `p` is read outside an aggregate and is not a grouping key
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS n, p.age AS a, count(*) GROUP BY n")   // error: the RETURN item `a` has no aggregate, so it is a grouping key, and GROUP BY does not list it

Help: add `p` to the WITH items, as in WITH ..., p. WITH passes on only its columns: a variable it does not list is out of scope after it (only the WHERE of a WITH without an aggregate still reads it), so list every variable a later clause reads, ...
Help: add `p` to the RETURN items (it then becomes a grouping key), or read it inside an aggregate, as in collect(p). A RETURN or WITH with an aggregate groups the rows by its other items (the grouping keys): ...
Help: add it to GROUP BY (GROUP BY ..., a), or remove GROUP BY: grouping is implicit, the items without an aggregate are the keys. ...

A FOR (or UNWIND) defines new names; reusing a name in scope, giving the item and its position one name, or using the position as a node is an error whose help says what FOR defines:

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) FOR p IN [1] RETURN p")   // error: the variable `p` is already defined; FOR defines a new variable
g.gql("FOR x IN [3, 1, 2] WITH OFFSET x RETURN x")   // error: `x` names both the item and its position

Help: choose another name, as in FOR p2 IN <list>. FOR x IN <list> (Cypher UNWIND <list> AS x) gives one row per item of the list, which it reads on the row before the FOR; the item x and, with WITH ORDINALITY i (from 1) or WITH OFFSET i (from 0), its position i are two new variables with names of their own; ...

An unbounded quantifier that reaches repeat.max_loops or traversal.max_traversers fails with the ordinary limit error (RepeatLimitExceeded, ResourceLimitExceeded; no GQLSTATUS), never with fewer rows. Its help is written for GQL: it names the quantified edge, an upper bound to give it and the g.with(..).gql(..) that raises the limit (Semantics):

g.with("traversal.max_traversers", 3).gql("MATCH (a)-[:knows|created]->{1,}(b) RETURN b.name AS b")   // error: traversal.max_traversers exceeded

Caused by: Resource limit 'traversal.max_traversers' exceeded (limit 3, reached 6)
Help: The gql() query kept more traversers (rows in the making) alive between two steps than 'traversal.max_traversers' allows (3). Each path a quantified edge (-[:knows|created]->{1,}) matches is a traverser of its own (trail keeps them apart, so they do not merge), ... give it a lower upper bound, as in -[:knows|created]->{1,5}. ...

A function whose result can be larger than its arguments (range(), split(), replace(), toString() of a list or map, ||) checks the size of its result before it builds it, against traversal.max_materialized_bytes and the memory budget, like collect_list(). A result that is too large fails with the ordinary limit error (ResourceLimitExceeded, no GQLSTATUS: the option and its lock are the engine's), never with a shortened value; inside gql() its help names the growing functions, a bound for them and the g.with(..).gql(..) that raises the limit:

g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN range(0, 9223372036854775807) AS r")   // error: Resource limit 'traversal.max_materialized_bytes' exceeded
g.with("traversal.max_materialized_bytes", 100).gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN split(n.name, '') AS s")   // error: Resource limit 'traversal.max_materialized_bytes' exceeded

Caused by: Resource limit 'traversal.max_materialized_bytes' exceeded (limit 1073741824, reached 18446744073709551615)
Help: The gql() query built a value larger than 'traversal.max_materialized_bytes' allows (1073741824 bytes); ... A function whose result can be larger than its arguments (range(), split(), replace(), || and CAST(x AS STRING) of a list or map) and the list of collect_list() are checked before they are built, so the query stops instead of running out of memory; the result is never cut short. Build smaller values: bound range() and replace() by the data, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN range(1, p.age / 10) AS r"), ... or raise the limit for the query, g.with("traversal.max_materialized_bytes", 2147483648).gql(..), ...

Subqueries

The errors of an EXISTS subquery or a pattern predicate share one help text that explains subqueries: TRUE or FALSE, never NULL; the body reads the variables bound before it, and the variables it binds stay inside it; a pattern predicate binds no new variable. Before it, each names its own fix:

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE (p)-[:knows]->(q) RETURN p.name AS name")   // error: the pattern predicate introduces the new variable `q`
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, (p)-[:knows]->() AS k")   // error: the pattern stands where a value is expected (42001)
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE EXISTS { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) } RETURN s.name AS s")   // error: the variable `s` is not in scope: it is bound inside a subquery
g.gql("MATCH (a:person) WHERE EXISTS { MATCH (a)-->() WHERE b.age > 1 MATCH (b) } RETURN a")   // error: `b` is bound by a later MATCH clause of the subquery

Help: write it as EXISTS { MATCH (p)-[:knows]->(q) }, whose MATCH may bind new variables, or leave `q` out of the pattern. A subquery, EXISTS { MATCH <pattern> [WHERE <condition>] }, EXISTS { <pattern> } or a Cypher pattern predicate such as (p)-[:created]->(), is TRUE when its body has a match and FALSE otherwise, never NULL; its body reads the variables bound before it, and the variables it binds itself stay inside it. A pattern predicate binds no new variable: name new elements in an EXISTS { MATCH .. }, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE NOT EXISTS { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) WHERE s.lang = 'java' } RETURN p.name"), and bind an element in the MATCH clause of the query to read it after the subquery, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person)-[:created]->(s) RETURN p.name, s.name").
Help: write EXISTS { (p)-[:knows]->() } for whether it has a match, COUNT { (p)-[:knows]->() } for the number of matches, or a pattern comprehension such as [(n)-->(m) | m] for the list of what it matches, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name, COUNT { (p)-[:knows]->() } AS friends, [(p)-[:created]->(s) | s.name] AS made"). A subquery, ...
Help: bind `s` in the MATCH clause of the query to use it here, or test it inside the subquery. A subquery, ...
Help: move the condition to the WHERE of that later MATCH clause inside the subquery. A subquery, ...

A query holds at most 64 subqueries (EXISTS, pattern predicates, pattern comprehensions, COUNT { } and COLLECT { }, nested ones included) and runs at most 1024 subquery bodies, where a LET or WITH variable holding a subquery counts once for every place that reads it. A CALL { } body counts toward neither; CALL bodies and whole-query subquery bodies nest at most 16 levels (UNION, NEXT and CALL). Either limit is 54001 before the run, and its help names both bounds and the forms that need fewer subqueries:

Error: GQL limit exceeded at line 1, column 785: the query holds more than 64 subqueries (EXISTS and pattern predicates), pattern comprehensions included, as are COUNT { } and COLLECT { } ...
Help: join the patterns into fewer subqueries (one EXISTS { MATCH .. } may hold several MATCH clauses and patterns), or add the patterns to the MATCH clause of the query; a pattern comprehension is a subquery too: collect the matches of several patterns with OPTIONAL MATCH and collect_list() instead. The query is larger than gql() accepts: one query holds at most 64 subqueries (EXISTS, pattern predicates, pattern comprehensions, COUNT { } and COLLECT { }, nested ones included) and runs at most 1024 subquery bodies, where a LET or WITH variable holding a subquery counts once for every place that reads it; a CALL { } body counts toward neither (CALL bodies nest at most 16 levels). One EXISTS may hold several MATCH clauses and patterns, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE EXISTS { MATCH (p)-[:knows]->(f) MATCH (f)-[:created]->(s) } RETURN p.name"), and one CALL may compute what several COUNT { } and COLLECT { } over the same pattern do, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN count(s) AS n, collect_list(s.name) AS names } RETURN p.name, n, names").

A quantified edge inside a subquery that reaches repeat.max_loops or traversal.max_traversers fails like one outside, and the help says where it stands and why a subquery may loop long:

g.with("repeat.max_loops", 1).gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE EXISTS { (p)-[:knows|created]->{1,}(x) } RETURN p.name AS n")   // error: repeat() exceeded the loop limit of 1 iterations

Help: The loop of the quantified edge -[:knows|created]->{1,} inside an EXISTS subquery (or pattern predicate) of the gql() query ran 1 iterations, the limit of repeat.max_loops. ... A subquery stops at its first match, so its loop runs this long on a row that has no match, or only a late one. Give the quantifier an upper bound, as in -[:knows|created]->{1,5}, ...

COUNT { } and COLLECT { } follow the same rules (a variable bound inside one is named as bound inside that COUNT { } or COLLECT { }, and the help explains the two forms); a COLLECT { } body must end in a RETURN of exactly one column. Cypher 4's exists(n.p) is refused:

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN COLLECT { MATCH (p)-[:knows]->(f) RETURN f.name, f.age } AS l")   // error: COLLECT { } needs a body that ends in a RETURN of exactly one column
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN COUNT { MATCH (p)-[:knows]->(f) } AS n, f.name AS x")   // error: the variable `f` is not in scope: it is bound inside a COUNT { } subquery
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN exists(p.age) AS a")   // refused: exists(value), the Cypher 4 property test, is not supported

Help: return the one value to collect, as in MATCH (p:person) RETURN COLLECT { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN s.name } AS names. A subquery, ...
Help: bind `f` in the MATCH clause of the query to use it here, or test it inside the COUNT { } body. COUNT { <body> } is the number of matches of its body (or of the records its RETURN gives), and COLLECT { <body> RETURN <expression> } the list of the values it returns; the body reads the variables bound before it, and the variables it binds itself stay inside it, ...
Help: test a property with n.p IS NOT NULL, here p.age IS NOT NULL; EXISTS tests a graph pattern, as in MATCH (p:person) WHERE EXISTS { (p)-[:created]->() } RETURN p.name. ...

Map projections and comprehensions

A pattern comprehension is a subquery, so its errors follow the rules above with their own help text: the variables it binds stay inside it (read them in its | part), and its | part holds no aggregate (aggregate the list, size([..]), or use OPTIONAL MATCH and an aggregate). A list-comprehension variable must be a new name, and its WHERE and | parts hold no aggregate either. Each help names the form that works:

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS n, [(p)-[:knows]->(f) | f.name] AS l ORDER BY f.name")   // error: `f` is bound inside a pattern comprehension
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN [(p)-->(f) | count(f)] AS l")   // error: count() cannot be used inside the | part of a pattern comprehension
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN [p IN [1, 2] | p * 2] AS l")   // error: the comprehension variable `p` shadows the variable `p` in scope
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN [x IN [1, 2] | count(x)] AS l")   // error: count() cannot be used inside the WHERE or | part of a list comprehension
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN [x IN [1, 2] WHERE x:A|B | x] AS a")   // error: unexpected `|`

Help: bind `f` in the MATCH clause of the query to use it here, or read it in the | part of the comprehension, as in [(a)-->(f) | f.name]. A pattern comprehension, [(a)-[:knows]->(f) WHERE <condition> | <expression>], is the list of its | part evaluated for every match of its pattern (the empty list when nothing matches); its pattern reads the variables bound before it, and the variables it binds itself stay inside it. ...
Help: aggregate the list the comprehension builds, as in MATCH (p) RETURN size([(p)-->(f) | f.age]) AS n, or aggregate in a WITH after an OPTIONAL MATCH, as in MATCH (p) OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-->(f) RETURN p, count(f.age) AS n. ...
Help: give the comprehension its own variable, as in [p2 IN list WHERE p2 > 0 | p2]. ...
Help: aggregate in a WITH first and use its column in the comprehension, as in MATCH (p)-->(f) WITH p, count(f.age) AS n RETURN [x IN [1, 2, 3] WHERE x < n]. ...
Help: a `|` in a comprehension ends its list or its WHERE condition; write a label alternative there in parentheses, as in [x IN l WHERE x:(A|B) | x.name]. ...

A map projection of a value that is not an element or a map, and a list comprehension over a value that is not a list, are data errors (22G03) of the row; so is all(), any(), none(), single() or reduce() over a value that is not a list, and the message names the function. Their variables are new names like a comprehension's (42002), and an aggregate inside their condition or | part is 42002 with a WITH example of the same form. A list-comprehension variable read inside an EXISTS or a pattern comprehension of its own WHERE or | part is not supported yet (0A000), the variables of the list predicates and reduce() neither:

g.gql("WITH 1 AS m RETURN m {.a} AS x")   // error: a map projection reads a node, an edge or a map, not a number
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN [x IN [p] WHERE (x)-->() | x.name] AS l")   // error: reading the comprehension variable `x` inside a subquery is not yet supported
g.gql("RETURN any(x IN 5 WHERE x > 1) AS a")   // error: any() iterates over a list, not a number (22G03)
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN reduce(p = 0, x IN [1] | p + x) AS a")   // error: the accumulator `p` of reduce() shadows the variable `p` in scope

Help: test `x` outside the subquery, as in [x IN list WHERE x > 0 AND EXISTS { MATCH (n)-->() }]. ...
Help: give reduce() an accumulator of its own, as in reduce(p2 = 0, item IN list | p2 + item). ... The same holds for the variable of all(), any(), none() and single() and for both variables of reduce(), as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name, all(a IN [p.age] WHERE a > 30) AS old, reduce(s = 0, a IN [p.age, 1] | s + a) AS total").

A resource limit reached inside a pattern comprehension names it. A quantified edge in its pattern loops until the row's last match is found (unlike EXISTS, which stops at its first), and its list is checked against traversal.max_materialized_bytes and the memory budget before it is built, like collect_list():

g.with("repeat.max_loops", 1).gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS n, [(p)-[:knows|created]->{1,}(x) | x.name] AS r")   // error: repeat() exceeded the loop limit of 1 iterations
