g.with("traversal.max_materialized_bytes", 100).gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN [(p)-[:created]->(s) | s.name] AS r")   // error: Resource limit 'traversal.max_materialized_bytes' exceeded

Help: The loop of the quantified edge -[:knows|created]->{1,} inside a pattern comprehension [(a)-->(b) | ..] of the gql() query ran 1 iterations, the limit of repeat.max_loops. ... A pattern comprehension collects every match of its pattern for each row, so its loop runs until the row's last match is found. Give the quantifier an upper bound, as in -[:knows|created]->{1,5}, ...
Help: ... A function whose result can be larger than its arguments (range(), split(), replace(), || and CAST(x AS STRING) of a list or map) and the list of collect_list() are checked before they are built, as is the list of a pattern comprehension [(a)-->(b) | b.name], so the query stops instead of running out of memory; the result is never cut short. ... count the values instead of collecting them, ... or, for the matches of a pattern, g.gql("MATCH (p:person) OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-->(f) RETURN p.name, count(f) AS n"), ...

UNION, NEXT and CALL

The errors of a composite query share one help text that explains UNION and NEXT: the operands return the same column names in any order (the result keeps the first operand's order), UNION removes duplicates and UNION ALL keeps them, one chain uses one kind, each operand has its own variables, ORDER BY and LIMIT, and NEXT passes on only the RETURN columns. The column mismatch names both column sets:

g.gql("RETURN 1 AS x UNION RETURN 2 AS y")   // error: the operands of UNION must return the same column names
g.gql("RETURN 1 AS x UNION RETURN 2 AS x UNION ALL RETURN 3 AS x")   // error: UNION ALL is mixed with UNION in one query
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name NEXT RETURN p.age")   // error: the variable `p` is not in scope: the RETURN before NEXT does not return it
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN s")   // error: MATCH after RETURN: RETURN ends the query

Error: GQL semantic error at line 1, column 21: the operands of UNION must return the same column names: the first returns `x`, this one returns `y` (`x` is missing) ...
Help: name the columns alike with AS in every operand (their order may differ), as in MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name UNION MATCH (s:software) RETURN s.name AS name. UNION combines the records of queries that return the same column names, in any order (the result keeps the order of the first query): UNION (or UNION DISTINCT) removes duplicate records, UNION ALL keeps them, and one chain of UNIONs uses one kind. Each query of a UNION has its own variables, ORDER BY, OFFSET and LIMIT. NEXT passes the records of the statement before it on by their column names (only those), so it sorts, filters or aggregates a UNION as a whole, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name UNION MATCH (s:software) RETURN s.name AS name NEXT RETURN name ORDER BY name LIMIT 3").
Help: write the same kind between every operand, or combine the parts with NEXT, as in RETURN 1 AS x UNION ALL RETURN 1 AS x NEXT RETURN x UNION RETURN 2 AS x. UNION combines ...
Help: add `p` to the RETURN items before NEXT, as in RETURN ..., p NEXT ... UNION combines ...
Help: put every MATCH before the RETURN, or continue with NEXT, which passes the columns of the RETURN on to the next statement, as in MATCH (p:person) RETURN p NEXT MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN p.name, s.name, or chain Gremlin steps after gql(). ...

The errors of a CALL share a help text on its scope: the body reads only the variables its scope clause names (CALL (*) all, CALL { } none, Cypher's CALL { WITH a .. } those of its first WITH), returns new names, aggregates per row, and drops a row without records unless the CALL is OPTIONAL. Cypher's importing WITH lists plain variables only, as in Neo4j: a first WITH with a WHERE, an alias, an expression, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, OFFSET or LIMIT is no importing WITH, so the body imports nothing and the error says so. A body without RETURN (a unit subquery, which only a write could use) is not supported, and IN TRANSACTIONS is refused:

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-[:knows]->(f) RETURN f AS p } RETURN p")   // error: the CALL body returns `p`, which is already defined outside it
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL { WITH p AS q MATCH (q)-->(s) RETURN s.name AS sw } RETURN sw")   // error: the variable `p` is not imported into the CALL body: its first WITH is not an importing WITH
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL { WITH p WHERE p.age > 30 MATCH (p)-->(s) RETURN s.name AS sw } RETURN sw")   // error: the variable `p` is not imported into the CALL body: its first WITH is not an importing WITH
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) } RETURN p")   // error: a CALL { } body without RETURN (a unit subquery) only makes sense for writes, and this body writes nothing
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-->(s) RETURN s.name AS sw } IN TRANSACTIONS RETURN sw")   // refused: CALL { } IN TRANSACTIONS commits writes in batches

Help: rename the column inside the body, as in RETURN ... AS p2. A CALL subquery, CALL (a, b) { <query ending in RETURN, or in a write (INSERT, SET, REMOVE, DELETE, MERGE / FINISH)> }, runs its query once for each incoming row: the body reads only the variables its scope clause names (CALL (*) imports all of them, CALL { } none, and Cypher's CALL { WITH a .. } those of its first WITH), and passes on only the columns of its RETURN, which must be new names; its aggregates, ORDER BY and LIMIT apply to each row's records, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN count(s) AS made } RETURN p.name, made"). A row whose body returns no record is dropped; OPTIONAL CALL keeps it with NULL columns.
Help: import `p` with a variable scope clause, as in CALL (p) { MATCH ... WHERE ... }, or in Cypher with a WITH of plain variables first and the rest of the body after it, as in CALL { WITH p MATCH ... WHERE ... }. A CALL subquery, ...
Help: end the body with RETURN and the columns the query reads after it, for example MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN count(s) AS made } RETURN p.name, made. A CALL subquery, ...
Help: remove IN TRANSACTIONS: the whole query commits at once, and a query that fails changes nothing. A CALL subquery, ...

CALL bodies and whole-query subquery bodies (EXISTS, COUNT or COLLECT with WITH, RETURN, ...) nest at most 16 levels (54001); the help shows how to un-nest them. A resource limit reached inside a CALL body names it: the body runs for each incoming row and keeps every record, so a quantified edge in it loops until the row's last match:

g.with("repeat.max_loops", 1).gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-[:knows|created]->{1,}(x) RETURN count(x) AS n } RETURN p.name AS who, n")   // error: repeat() exceeded the loop limit of 1 iterations

Error: GQL limit exceeded at line 1, column 113: the query nests CALL { } and subquery bodies deeper than 16 levels ...
Help: un-nest the bodies: a CALL body may follow another in the same query, as in CALL { .. RETURN a } CALL (a) { .. RETURN b }, and NEXT passes the result of one query to the next. The query is larger than gql() accepts.

Help: The loop of the quantified edge -[:knows|created]->{1,} inside a CALL { } subquery of the gql() query ran 1 iterations, the limit of repeat.max_loops. ... A CALL { } subquery runs its body for each incoming row and keeps every record it returns, so its loop runs until the row's last match is found. Give the quantifier an upper bound, as in -[:knows|created]->{1,5}, ...

A limit inside an operand of a UNION or a block after NEXT at the top level keeps the plain text of a top-level clause; inside a subquery the place named is the innermost subquery (CALL, COUNT, COLLECT, EXISTS or a pattern comprehension).

Calls of saved queries

The errors of a CALL folder.name(..) of a saved query are found before the run and point at the call; they share one help text that explains the call (folder and name, positional arguments, YIELD, the standalone form, g.queries()), after a fix of their own:

GQLSTATUSWhen
42002no saved query of that name in that folder (with "did you mean" when it is in another folder); too many arguments, or too few for parameters without a default; a standalone call without parentheses whose parameter has no value; an in-query call without parentheses of a query with parameters; an in-query call of a query with columns without YIELD; YIELD of a column the query does not return, of a name already in scope or twice, YIELD on a query without RETURN; an aggregate in an argument; a saved query that calls itself, directly or through others
42001YIELD * inside a query (only a standalone call takes it)
22G03an argument that does not fit its parameter's schema (CALL people.older('x') for an integer)
0A000a saved query written in Rhai (the help names g.query(..)); an argument that reads the row; a call inside EXISTS { }, COUNT { } or COLLECT { }; the vendor namespaces db, dbms, apoc, gds (refused); a read-only saved query that would write through a call
54001saved queries that call each other more than 16 levels deep, or more than 1024 calls in one query and the queries it calls
g.gql("CALL people.older(26) YIELD name RETURN name")   // error: there is no saved query `older` in the folder `people`
g.gql("CALL db.labels()")   // refused: procedure calls of the vendor namespaces are vendor extensions

With the saved query people.older($min) of Saved Queries, returning name and age:

Error: GQL semantic error at line 1, column 6: there is no saved query `older` in the folder `people` ...
Help: save it first with g.define_query(#{name: "older", folder: "people", language: "gql", body: ".."}); g.queries() lists the saved queries. CALL folder.name(args) runs the saved query `name` of the catalog folder `folder` (the segments before the name, joined by /; CALL name() calls one of the root folder), written in GQL. Its arguments are constants or $parameters, in the order its query first reads its parameters (a trailing one left out takes the parameter's default). YIELD names the columns of its RETURN the query reads after the call (YIELD a AS x renames one; each must be a new name), and a call alone is a whole query returning every column, as in g.define_query(#{name: "adults", folder: "people", language: "gql", body: "MATCH (p:person) WHERE p.age >= $min RETURN p.name AS name", params: #{min: "integer"}}); g.gql("CALL people.adults(30) YIELD name RETURN name ORDER BY name"). g.queries() lists the saved queries with their folders and parameters; a saved query written in Rhai runs with g.query(name, #{..}).

Error: GQL semantic error at line 1, column 25: CALL people.older inside a query names the columns it reads with YIELD: the saved query returns `name`, `age` ...
Help: add YIELD, as in CALL people.older(..) YIELD name, age. CALL folder.name(args) runs ...

Call an inner saved query directly, as in g.gql("CALL people.adults(30) YIELD name RETURN name"), or write a part of the chain in the query itself; g.get_query(name) shows a saved query's body.

Error: GQL unsupported construct at line 1, column 1: CALL: procedure calls are vendor extensions, not part of GQL ...
Help: write what the procedure does as Gremlin steps, for example g.v().label().dedup() instead of CALL db.labels(), or save it as a query in GQL and call that one, CALL folder.name(args), which runs a saved query of the graph's catalog. ...

An error inside the called query keeps its own text and caret (under the saved query's text) and gains the line in saved query: "name".

Quantified path patterns

The forms a quantified path pattern does not take yet are refused before the run with 0A000; each help names the rewrite. A body variable is a new name (42002), and outside a quantified body it is a list, so a property of it is an error whose help offers the body's WHERE or a list comprehension:

g.gql("MATCH (a) ((x)-[:knows]->{1,2}(y)){1,3} (b) RETURN b")   // error: a quantified edge inside a parenthesized path pattern is not yet supported
g.gql("MATCH (a) ((x)-->(y) WHERE y.age > a.age){1,3} (b) RETURN b")   // error: a condition inside a parenthesized path pattern that reads a variable declared outside it is not yet supported
g.gql("MATCH (a) ((a)-->(y)){1,2} (b) RETURN b")   // error: `a` is already bound; a variable of a quantified path pattern must be a new name
g.gql("MATCH (a) ((x)-->(y)){1,3} (b) RETURN x.name")   // error: `x` is a group variable of the quantified path pattern

Help: write the edge out as often as needed inside the parentheses, as in ((x)-->()-->(y)){1,3}, or quantify the edge outside them, as in MATCH (a)-[:knows]->{1,3}(b) RETURN b. ...
Help: compare the body's variables with each other, with values or with parameters inside it, as in ((x)-[e]->(y) WHERE e.weight > $w){1,3}, and test the outer variable in the WHERE of the MATCH clause. ...
Help: give the element inside its own variable: the node before a parenthesized path pattern is the first node of its first iteration and the node after it the last node of its last iteration, as in (a) ((x)-->(y)){1,3} (b). ...
Help: test each element inside the parenthesized path pattern, with WHERE x.name ... before its closing parenthesis, or read the list, as in [v IN x | v.name]. ...

An unbounded quantified path pattern that reaches repeat.max_loops or traversal.max_traversers fails like a quantified edge (RepeatLimitExceeded, ResourceLimitExceeded, no GQLSTATUS), never with fewer rows, and its help names the pattern as the plan walks it: read back from the lowered repeat() body, so it shows each node's labels but not its variable (a node without a label is ()), each edge with its labels in the direction of the walk (the plan may walk the pattern from its far end), and a body of one edge with nothing on its nodes as the quantified edge it equals (-[:knows]->{1,}):

g.with("repeat.max_loops", 1).gql("MATCH (a {name: 'marko'}) ((x:person)-[:knows]->(m)-[:created]->(y))+ (b) RETURN b.name AS b")   // error: repeat() exceeded the loop limit of 1 iterations

Help: The loop of the quantified path pattern ((:person)-[:knows]->()-[:created]->()){1,} of the gql() query ran 1 iterations, the limit of repeat.max_loops. A quantifier without an upper bound ({m,}, *, + or Cypher [*]) repeats the pattern until every path has used all the edges it can reach (trail), ... Give the quantifier an upper bound, as in ((:person)-[:knows]->()-[:created]->()){1,5}, ... Or raise the limit for the query, g.with("repeat.max_loops", 2).gql(..), ...

A MATCH clause holds at most 64 edge patterns; an edge in a quantified body counts once, however often the body repeats, so the help of that limit names a quantified path pattern as one of the fixes:

Help: split the pattern into several MATCH clauses that share a variable, for example MATCH (a)-->(b)-->(c) MATCH (c)-->(d)-->(e) RETURN e (edge uniqueness then holds within each clause only), repeat a chain as a quantified path pattern, whose body edges count once however often it repeats, for example MATCH (a) (()-->()){65} (z) RETURN z, or walk a long path with Gremlin repeat(), for example g.v().repeat(__.out()).times(100). The query is larger than gql() accepts.

INSERT

An INSERT pattern that cannot create what it says fails before the run; its help shows the accepted form and ends with one shared paragraph on INSERT:

g.gql("INSERT (a:x)-[:r]-(b:y)")   // error: INSERT needs a direction; write -[e:T]-> or <-[e:T]-
g.gql("INSERT (:a)-[:r|s]->(:b)")   // error: an edge in INSERT has exactly one label
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) INSERT (p:admin)")   // error: the variable `p` is already bound
g.gql("INSERT (:x {a: 1, a: 2})")   // error: the key `a` appears twice in this map
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) INSERT (:x {n: count(p)})")   // error: the aggregate function count() cannot be used in INSERT
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE EXISTS { INSERT (:a) } RETURN p")   // error: INSERT inside EXISTS { }: a subquery expression or a comprehension cannot write

Error: GQL syntax error at line 1, column 13: INSERT needs a direction; write -[e:T]-> or <-[e:T]- (step #1 'gql:error("42001")' refused the query before the traversal ran)
  at #1: v().gql:error("42001")
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  query:     INSERT (a:x)-[:r]-(b:y)
                         ^^^^^^
  GQLSTATUS: 42001
Help: give the new edge its direction, from the node before it (-[:r]->) or to it (<-[:r]-); for example g.gql("INSERT (a:person {name: 'ann'})-[:knows]->(b:person:admin)"). INSERT (Cypher CREATE) creates its pattern once for each row: a new node with the labels written, joined by & or :, and a property map; a new edge with a direction and exactly one label; and a variable bound before, written alone as (p), connects the existing node, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) INSERT (p)-[:likes]->(f:fruit&food {name: 'apple'}) RETURN f.name"). A query may end with the INSERT (it then returns no rows), and FOR gives it one row per item, as in g.gql("FOR n IN ['ann', 'bob'] INSERT (:person {name: n})"). To create a pattern only where it is missing, MERGE finds it or creates it, as in g.gql("FOR n IN ['ann', 'marko'] MERGE (:person {name: n})").

While the query runs, a row whose endpoint is NULL (22004) or no node (22G03), or whose property value is a node, an edge or a path (22G03), fails the query, and it changes nothing:

g.gql("OPTIONAL MATCH (p:person {name: 'nobody'}) INSERT (p)-[:knows]->(:person)")   // error: the source node `p` of the inserted `:knows` edge is NULL
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) INSERT (:x {v: p})")   // error: the value of property `v` is a node

Caused by: GQL data exception at line 1, column 51: the source node `p` of the inserted `:knows` edge is NULL
  query:     …person {name: 'nobody'}) INSERT (p)-[:knows]->(:person)
                                              ^^^
  GQLSTATUS: 22004
Help: keep only the rows where it is bound before the INSERT: FILTER p IS NOT NULL. A row of the data gave the marked endpoint of the new edge no node: an edge connects two nodes, so a variable that OPTIONAL MATCH may leave NULL is filtered first, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) FILTER s IS NOT NULL INSERT (p)-[:made]->(s)"), and a value that is no node is turned into one by a MATCH, as in g.gql("FOR n IN ['lop'] MATCH (s:software {name: n}) INSERT (:review {stars: 5})-[:about]->(s)").

A schema violation of an INSERT is the schema's error, with a help line written for GQL: a missing required property names the INSERT map and coalesce(), a type mismatch the conversion function (toInteger(), ...) with a $parameter example (Writing with GQL). A bound node written with labels or properties (MATCH (p:person) INSERT (p:admin)) gets the SET that changes it, built from the query, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) SET p:admin"), beside the Gremlin steps. The write clause that is not supported yet (FOREACH) is 0A000 with a help line naming the GQL form:

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) FOREACH (x IN [1] | SET p.k = x)")   // error: FOREACH is not yet supported in this version

Help: write FOR x IN <list> followed by the write clause, for example FOR name IN ['ann', 'bob'] INSERT (:person {name: name}). DELETE takes a list itself, as in MATCH p = (:person)-[:knows]->() DETACH DELETE nodes(p). This construct comes in a later version of gql(); until then, write the query without it or as Gremlin steps.

SET and REMOVE

A SET / REMOVE item of the wrong form fails before the run: a label item joined by |, ! or % (42001), a label item on a variable known to be an edge, an aggregate in a value, or a target that is undefined, a LET / WITH value, a path, a group variable or a FOR position (42002); a deeper target such as p.a.b or head(l).k is not supported yet (0A000). Each help names the accepted form and ends with one shared paragraph on SET / REMOVE:

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) SET p:A|B")   // error: `|` (a label alternative) cannot stand in SET
g.gql("MATCH (a)-[e:knows]->(b) SET e:met")   // error: `e` is an edge: an edge has exactly one label
g.gql("MATCH (p) SET p.k = count(*)")   // error: the aggregate function count() cannot be used in SET
g.gql("MATCH (p) SET p.a.b = 1")   // error: `p.a.b` as a SET target is not yet supported in this version

Error: GQL syntax error at line 1, column 24: `|` (a label alternative) cannot stand in SET: a label item names the labels, joined by `:` or `&` (step #1 'gql:error("42001")' refused the query before the traversal ran)
  at #1: v().gql:error("42001")
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  query:     MATCH (p:person) SET p:A|B
                                    ^^^
  GQLSTATUS: 42001
Help: write the labels, as in SET p:A:B. SET changes the nodes and edges of each row, item by item from left to right: n.k = <value> sets a property (a NULL value removes it), n = {map} replaces every property, n += {map} merges the map into them, and n:A:B adds labels to a node (an edge has exactly one label); REMOVE n.k removes a property and REMOVE n:A a label, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) SET p.age = p.age + 1, p:employee REMOVE p.nick RETURN p.age"). A variable that OPTIONAL MATCH leaves NULL is skipped, and a query may end with the SET or REMOVE (it then returns no rows), as in g.gql("MATCH (s:software) SET s += {open: true}").
Help: change the type of the edge with the Gremlin step set_label(), as in g.gql("MATCH (a)-[e:knows]->(b) RETURN e").select("e").set_label("met"). In a MATCH clause a node variable names one node ...

While the query runs, a NULL right side of n = .. or n += .. (22004), a right side that is no map, node or edge, a node, edge or path as a property value, a target that holds no element, and a label item on a value that turns out to be an edge (22G03) fail the query, and it changes nothing. The help rewrites the failing query where it can:

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) SET p = NULL")   // error: the right side of SET p = .. is NULL, not a map
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) SET p.best = p")   // error: the value of property `best` is a node
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) SET p = 1")   // error: the right side of SET p = .. is a single value
g.gql("FOR x IN [1] SET x.k = 1")   // error: SET changes a node or an edge, but `x` holds a value of type 'int64'

Caused by: GQL data exception at line 1, column 26: the right side of SET p = .. is NULL, not a map
  query:     MATCH (p:person) SET p = NULL
                                      ^^^^
  GQLSTATUS: 22004
Help: SET p = {} removes every property; to keep them when the map is NULL, give it the element's own properties as a default with coalesce($p, properties(p)), as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) SET p = coalesce(NULL, properties(p))"). A row of the data gave the marked SET or REMOVE item a value it cannot write; keep such rows away from it with FILTER or WHERE, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) FILTER p.age IS NOT NULL SET p.next = p.age + 1"). SET changes the nodes and edges of each row, ...
Help: store a value of it instead, such as its id, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) SET p.best = element_id(p)"), or its properties with properties(..). A row of the data gave the marked SET or REMOVE item a value it cannot write; ...

A schema violation of a SET / REMOVE gets a help line written for GQL too: a type mismatch names the conversion function in a SET of the label and key, a removed required property (REMOVE, a NULL value, SET n = {map} without the key) the map that keeps it and +=, and a label whose required property the node lacks the SET that writes the key before the label.

DELETE

A DELETE target that cannot hold an element fails before the run: a label test such as n:person or n IS person (42001: it is a boolean, and DELETE removes whole elements), a literal, a computed value, a map or a FOR position (42002). DROP n, the Gremlin step written as a clause, is a syntax error naming DETACH DELETE, and REMOVE n without an item names it too. Each help rewrites the failing query and ends with one shared paragraph on DELETE:

g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'vadas'}) DELETE n:person")   // error: `n:person` is a label test (a boolean), not an element
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) DELETE 1 + 1")   // error: `1 + 1` is a computed value, not a node, an edge, a path or a list of them
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) DROP p")   // error: GQL has no DROP clause: DELETE removes nodes and edges

Error: GQL syntax error at line 1, column 41: `n:person` is a label test (a boolean), not an element; DELETE removes whole nodes and edges (step #1 'gql:error("42001")' refused the query before the traversal ran)
  at #1: v().gql:error("42001")
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  query:     MATCH (n:person {name: 'vadas'}) DELETE n:person
                                                     ^^^^^^^^
  GQLSTATUS: 42001
Help: delete the element itself with DELETE n, as in g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'vadas'}) DELETE n"), or remove the label and keep the element with REMOVE n:person, as in g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'vadas'}) REMOVE n:person"). DELETE removes, for each row, the nodes and edges its targets give: a node or edge variable, a path (all its nodes and edges) or a list of them; a NULL target is skipped, and an element given twice is removed once. A node that still has edges is removed only together with them: DETACH DELETE removes its edges too, as in g.gql("MATCH (s:software {name: 'lop'}) DETACH DELETE s"). The rest of the query can no longer read what it deleted, so read what it needs first, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'vadas'}) WITH p, p.name AS name DETACH DELETE p RETURN name"); a query may end with the DELETE (it then returns no rows).
Help: name the element to remove by its variable, as in g.gql("MATCH (n:person) DETACH DELETE n"). DELETE removes, for each row, ...
Help: write DETACH DELETE (the GQL form of the Gremlin step drop()), as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) DETACH DELETE p"). DELETE removes, for each row, ...

While the query runs, a plain (or NODETACH) DELETE of a node that still has an edge the same clause does not delete fails with G1001; the help names DETACH DELETE in the failing query and the form that deletes the edges in the same clause. A target that turns out to hold no element (a WITH value, a property) is 22G03. Either failure changes nothing:

g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) DELETE n")   // error: `n` is a node that still has edges
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) WITH 1 AS x DELETE x")   // error: DELETE removes nodes, edges and paths, but `1` gives a number on this row

Caused by: GQL data exception at line 1, column 41: `n` is a node that still has edges, and DELETE removes only nodes without edges (besides the edges deleted in the same clause)
  query:     MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) DELETE n
                                                     ^
  GQLSTATUS: G1001
Help: remove the node together with its edges with DETACH DELETE, as in g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) DETACH DELETE n"), or delete its edges in the same clause, as in g.gql("MATCH (s:software {name: 'ripple'})<-[r]-() DELETE r, s").
Help: give DELETE a node, an edge, a path or a list of them, and keep the rows where the target holds something else away from it with FILTER or WHERE, as in g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) DETACH DELETE n"). DELETE removes, for each row, ...

After a DELETE, a later part of the query that reads a deleted element (a property, labels(), element_id(), a SET, REMOVE or INSERT on it) or returns it fails, and the query changes nothing. The error is the storage's (ElementRemoved), with a help line written for GQL: read what the query needs before the DELETE, for example with properties(n). count(n), n IS NULL and type(r) of a deleted edge still work, and a pattern from a deleted node matches nothing:

g.gql("MATCH (n:software) DETACH DELETE n RETURN n.name")   // error: the node was deleted earlier in this query
g.gql("MATCH ()-[r:created]->() DELETE r RETURN r.weight")   // error: the edge was deleted earlier in this query

Caused by: The vertex was removed earlier in this query; its id, label and value are no longer available
Help: The node was deleted earlier in this query (by DELETE or DETACH DELETE, or together with a node a DETACH DELETE removed), but a later part of the query still reads it: a deleted node has no properties, labels or id any more and cannot be returned or changed, and a pattern from it matches nothing; only count(n) and n IS NULL still work. Read what you need before the DELETE and keep that instead, for example g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) WITH n, properties(n) AS p DETACH DELETE n RETURN p"), or run the DELETE as a separate query after reading.
Help: The edge was deleted earlier in this query (...); only count(r), r IS NULL and type(r) still work. Read what you need before the DELETE and keep that instead, for example g.gql("MATCH (:person)-[r:knows]->() WITH r, properties(r) AS p DELETE r RETURN p"), or for a node g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) WITH n, properties(n) AS p DETACH DELETE n RETURN p"), or run the DELETE as a separate query after reading.

MERGE

A MERGE pattern that cannot be matched or created as written fails before the run: a second pattern after ,, an edge without its one label or with a label expression, a quantifier (42001); a node bound before written with labels or properties, a bound edge variable, and a pattern that is only a node bound before (MATCH (a) MERGE (a): nothing to find or create) (42002). Each help rewrites the failing query where it can and ends with one shared paragraph on MERGE:

g.gql("MERGE (a:x), (b:y)")   // error: MERGE takes exactly one pattern
g.gql("MATCH (a) MERGE (a)")   // error: MERGE (a) with `a` bound earlier has nothing to find or create
g.gql("MATCH (a:person) MERGE (a:admin)-[:r]->(:b)")   // error: the variable `a` is already bound
g.gql("MERGE (a:x)-[:r|s]->(b)")   // error: an edge in MERGE has exactly one label

Error: GQL syntax error at line 1, column 12: MERGE takes exactly one pattern: a second pattern after `,` cannot stand here (step #1 'gql:error("42001")' refused the query before the traversal ran)
  at #1: v().gql:error("42001")
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  query:     MERGE (a:x), (b:y)
                        ^
  GQLSTATUS: 42001
Help: write one MERGE for each pattern, as in g.gql("MERGE (a:x) MERGE (b:y)"), or connect the patterns with an edge into one. MERGE looks for its whole pattern for each row: every match is a row, and when nothing matches the whole pattern is created, reusing the nodes bound before. Its one pattern has nodes with the labels written, joined by & or :, and a property map, edges with exactly one label (an edge without a direction matches either direction and is created from left to right), and a node bound before written alone, as (p); ON CREATE SET and ON MATCH SET items change what was created or matched, as in g.gql("MERGE (p:person {name: 'ann'}) ON CREATE SET p.new = true ON MATCH SET p.new = false RETURN p.new"). Each row sees what the rows before it created, so FOR creates a repeated item once, as in g.gql("FOR n IN ['ann', 'ann'] MERGE (:person {name: n})").
Help: to find or create a connection, give the pattern an edge, as in g.gql("MATCH (a) MERGE (a)-[:T]->(:Label)"); to find or create another node, give it its own name, as in g.gql("MATCH (a) MERGE (a2:Label)"). MERGE looks for its whole pattern for each row: ...
Help: write (a) to connect the node, or give a new node its own name, as in MERGE (a)-[:T]->(a2:Label {k: 1}); to change the bound node itself use SET on it, as in g.gql("MATCH (a:person) SET a:admin"), or the Gremlin steps add_label() and property() on it, as in g.gql("MATCH (a) RETURN a").select("a").add_label("admin"). MERGE looks for its whole pattern for each row: ...
Help: give the new edge one label, as in -[:r]->; for example g.gql("MERGE (a:person {name: 'ann'})-[:knows]->(b:person:admin)"). MERGE looks for its whole pattern for each row: ...

While the query runs, a property value of the pattern that is NULL (22004: MERGE can neither match nor create {k: NULL}, checked for each row before the match), a node bound before that is NULL (22004) or no node (22G03), and a node, edge or path as a property value (22G03) fail the query, and it changes nothing, also what earlier rows created. The help names the FILTER before the MERGE or the coalesce() default in the failing query:

g.gql("FOR x IN [1, NULL] MERGE (:n {k: x})")   // error: MERGE cannot match or create `{k: NULL}`
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) MERGE (p)-[:made]->(s)")   // error: the destination node `s` of the merged `:made` edge is NULL
g.gql("MERGE (p:person {name: NULL})")   // error: MERGE cannot match or create `{name: NULL}`

Caused by: GQL data exception at line 1, column 34: MERGE cannot match or create `{k: NULL}`: a property value is NULL
  query:     FOR x IN [1, NULL] MERGE (:n {k: x})
                                              ^
  GQLSTATUS: 22004
Help: keep only the rows where it has a value with FILTER x IS NOT NULL before the MERGE, or give it a default with coalesce(), as in g.gql("FOR x IN [1, NULL] MERGE (:n {k: coalesce(x, 0)})"). A row of the data gave the marked part of the MERGE pattern a value it can neither match nor create: a property value that is NULL or a graph element, or a node bound before that is NULL or no node. A variable that OPTIONAL MATCH may leave NULL is filtered first, and a value that is no node is turned into one by a MATCH, as in g.gql("FOR n IN ['lop'] MATCH (s:software {name: n}) MERGE (:review {stars: 5})-[:about]->(s)"). MERGE looks for its whole pattern for each row: ...
Help: keep only the rows where it is bound before the MERGE: FILTER s IS NOT NULL, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) FILTER s IS NOT NULL MERGE (p)-[:made]->(s)"). A row of the data gave the marked part of the MERGE pattern a value it can neither match nor create: ...
Help: MERGE matches and creates only property values that are not NULL: leave `name` out of the pattern, and find the elements that lack it with a MATCH, as in g.gql("MATCH (n) FILTER n.name IS NULL RETURN n"). A row of the data gave the marked part of the MERGE pattern a value it can neither match nor create: ...

A schema violation of a MERGE gets a help line written for GQL too. One raised by the create names the MERGE pattern and keeps its node variable: a type mismatch the conversion function, as in g.gql("MERGE (p:person {w: toFloat($v)})", #{v: "1.5"}), and a missing required property the pattern's property map, because the ON CREATE SET items run after the create and cannot give it (or a "default" in the schema, to match on other keys only). One raised by an ON CREATE SET / ON MATCH SET item gets the SET fix in MERGE form, as in g.gql("MERGE (n:person) ON MATCH SET n.w = toFloat($v)", #{v: "1.5"}).

GQLSTATUS codes

CodeKindWhen
42001syntaxthe query does not parse: an unexpected token, a missing RETURN, an unclosed bracket, a quantifier with m > n, GROUP BY after WITH (grouping is implicit) or after ORDER BY; an unknown function or CAST type name (with a suggestion), a function called with the wrong number of arguments, the SQL form SUBSTRING(s FROM a FOR b); a ZONED TIME '..' / ZONED DATETIME '..' literal whose text has no offset or zone; WITH ORDINALITY / WITH OFFSET after UNWIND; an INSERT edge without a direction or with a label expression, an INSERT node label other than a conjunction, WHERE or a quantifier in an INSERT pattern, a SET / REMOVE label item joined by `
42002semantican undefined variable, a variable used as a node and an edge, an edge variable bound twice in one MATCH, a duplicate column name, a missing parameter, an ORDER BY key that RETURN DISTINCT dropped; a variable a WITH did not carry on, a LET name bound again; a variable read outside an aggregate that is not a grouping key, an aggregate in WHERE / FILTER / LET or inside another aggregate, ORDER BY after an aggregation reading something other than a column; a GROUP BY key that is not an item without an aggregate, or such an item missing from GROUP BY; a path or group variable bound twice; a variable of a quantified path pattern that is not a new name, or a property of one read outside its body; a FOR / UNWIND name already in scope, one name for the item and its position, the position used as a node or edge, an aggregate in the FOR list; a new variable in a pattern predicate, a variable bound inside a subquery (EXISTS, a pattern predicate, COUNT { }, COLLECT { }) read outside it, a condition in a subquery reading a variable of a later MATCH clause of the body, a subquery in an aggregating item reading a variable outside the aggregates that is not a grouping key; a variable bound inside a pattern comprehension read outside it, a comprehension variable named like another variable of the query, an aggregate inside a comprehension's WHERE or | part; a COLLECT { } body that does not return exactly one column; UNION operands with different column names, UNION mixed with UNION ALL in one chain, a variable read after NEXT that the RETURN before it does not return; a CALL body returning a name already in scope, reading a variable it does not import (also through a first WITH that is no importing WITH), importing one twice; a CALL folder.name(..) of a saved query that does not exist in that folder, with too many or too few arguments, a missing parameter value, an aggregate in an argument, without YIELD inside a query, or with a YIELD of a column it does not return or of a name already in scope, a recursive call (Calls of saved queries); in INSERT, a bound variable with labels or properties, a bound edge variable, a duplicate key in a property map, an aggregate in a property value; in SET / REMOVE, an undefined target, a target that is a LET / WITH value, a path, a group variable or a FOR position, a label item on an edge variable, an aggregate in a value; in DELETE, a target known to hold no element (a literal, a computed value, a map, a FOR position), an aggregate in a target; in MERGE, a bound node with labels or properties, a bound edge variable, a pattern that is only a node bound before
0A000refused / not yeta refused construct or one not supported yet (also a function: sin(), rand(), elements(), CAST to DATE; X.realtime(); EXCEPT, INTERSECT, OTHERWISE; a CALL body without RETURN that writes nothing, CALL { } IN TRANSACTIONS; Cypher 4's exists(n.p); a CALL of a saved query written in Rhai, with an argument that reads the row, or inside EXISTS / COUNT / COLLECT, a vendor procedure (db, dbms, apoc, gds); a SET / REMOVE target deeper than a variable (p.a.b, head(l).k), the write clause FOREACH, a subquery in a MERGE property value, an INSERT in a UNION operand or with a path variable; LOAD CSV, CREATE INDEX / CONSTRAINT / GRAPH; a list-comprehension or list-predicate variable read inside a subquery; inside a parenthesized path pattern: a nested group or quantified edge, a path variable, several patterns, no edge, a variable written twice or bound outside, a condition reading an outer variable, a subquery); also gql() after other steps
54001limitthe query nests too deeply (more than 128 levels of parentheses, or an expression taller than 512)
54001limitmore than 64 subqueries (EXISTS, pattern predicates, pattern comprehensions, COUNT { } and COLLECT { }, nested ones included), or more than 1024 subquery bodies to run (a LET / WITH variable holding a subquery counts once per reader); CALL bodies and whole-query subquery bodies nested more than 16 levels; saved queries calling each other more than 16 levels deep, or more than 1024 calls of saved queries in one query
54001limita MATCH clause holds more than 64 edge patterns (over all its comma-separated paths; a quantified body's edges count once); split it into several MATCH clauses that share a variable, repeat a chain as a quantified path pattern, or use Gremlin repeat()
22004dataan endpoint of an INSERT edge is NULL (from an OPTIONAL MATCH); the right side of SET n = .. / SET n += .. is NULL; a property value of a MERGE pattern or a node bound before it is NULL
22G02dataa negative OFFSET / LIMIT (literal or parameter value)
22G03dataa value of the wrong type, before the run when the kind is certain from the query text (static kind checks: false AND 123, 1 IN true, type(n) of a node variable, p.name of a path, WITH 123 AS x RETURN x.num), else when a row reaches it: OFFSET / LIMIT not an integer, 'a' + 1, type() of a vertex, a non-boolean condition, IN with a right operand that is no list, sum() / avg() of a non-number; a map projection of a value that is no element or map, a list comprehension over a value that is no list; a temporal component the type lacks (date(..).hour), temporal arithmetic without a meaning (date + date); an argument of a CALL of a saved query that does not fit its parameter's schema; a function argument of the wrong kind (toFloat(true), a float where an integer is required, toString() of a list, map, vertex, edge or path, trim(s, x) with a string s); an INSERT endpoint that is no node, a node, edge or path as an INSERT or SET property value; a SET / REMOVE target that holds no node or edge, a label item on an edge at run time, a right side of SET n = .. / += that is no map, node or edge; a DELETE target that holds no node, edge or path; a node bound before a MERGE that is no node, a node, edge or path as a MERGE property value
G1001dataa DELETE / NODETACH DELETE of a node that still has an edge the same clause does not delete (use DETACH DELETE)
22012datainteger division or % by zero (a float one gives Infinity or NaN), also mod(a, 0); a duration divided by zero
22007datatemporal text that is no value of the type, a temporal map with an unknown key or conflicting date keys, an unknown time zone (Dates and times)
22008dataa temporal field out of range, a temporal value or result outside the years -9999 to 9999
22003dataa numeric result out of range (integer overflow, also of sum(), abs(), exp(), power()); a conversion out of range (toInteger(1.0e19), CAST('1e400' AS FLOAT))
22018dataCAST of text that is no value of the target type (CAST('abc' AS INTEGER))
22011dataa negative position or length in substring(), left(), right()
22027dataa TRIM(c FROM s) character c that is not exactly one character
2201Edatathe logarithm of a number <= 0, or to a base <= 0 or 1 (ln, log, log10)
2201Fdatasqrt() of a negative number, power() of 0 to a negative power or of a negative number to a non-integer power
22023dataan argument outside the function's values: a truncation unit the type lacks or an unknown one (date.truncate('hour', ..)), range() step 0, a negative round() precision or an unknown rounding mode, a negative replace() limit, a negative n in the list trim(list, n)

42001 is fixed; the other codes are provisional: they follow the standard's classes and may still be refined before the GQL support is complete. The function codes (22018, 22011, 22027, 2201E, 2201F, 22023, 22007, 22008) are the ISO / SQL-heritage subclasses of class 22; Neo4j reports the same failures with its own vendor subclasses (22N38, 22N03, ...). Match on the kind (GqlErrorKind) in code, and treat the code as diagnostic information.

g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.name AS name ORDER BY name LIMIT $l", #{l: -1})   // error: LIMIT must be a non-negative integer (22G02)
g.v().gql("MATCH (n) RETURN n")   // error: gql() starts a traversal in this version (0A000)

In Rust

use graphersal::error::GqlErrorKind;
use graphersal::prelude::*;

let graph = TraversalGraph::tinkerpop_modern();
let error = graph.traversal().gql("MATCH (n:person) RETRUN n").to_list().unwrap_err();
if let TraverserError::Gql { kind, gqlstatus, line, column, .. } = error.root_cause() {
    assert_eq!(*kind, GqlErrorKind::Syntax);
    assert_eq!(gqlstatus, "42001");
    assert_eq!((*line, *column), (1, 18));
}

The DiagnosticError trait gives the help text (help()) and the labelled lines (details(): query, expected, did you mean, GQLSTATUS) shown above.

Plans and Performance

gql() has no executor of its own. A query is parsed, its variables bound, a planner picks where each pattern starts and in which order it expands, and the result is lowered into an ordinary traversal plan: Gremlin steps (v(), has_label(), has(), out(), as(), where(), skip(), limit(), ...) plus a few internal steps. That plan then goes through the same optimizer, path analysis, property indexes, limits, cancellation, permissions and storages as a hand-written traversal. .profile() shows it.

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE p.age > 30 RETURN p.name AS name").profile()

Step                                                         Call      In     Out
==================================================================================
v(labels: ["person"])                                           1       0       4
has("age", P.gt(30))                                            1       4       2
gql:project("name")                                             1       2       2
Optimizer rules applied: source_filter_pushdown

(The profiles on this page leave out the time columns.) The query became v().has_label("person").has("age", P.gt(30)) plus a projection, and the optimizer folded the label into the scan, exactly as it does for the Gremlin form.

The internal steps

StepDoes
gql:project("a", "b", ...)builds the row map of RETURN (or of a WITH that builds rows) in written order, keeping NULL columns
gql:aggregate([keys], [aggregates], [columns])groups the rows by the key values and builds one row map per group (a barrier)
gql:distinct()DISTINCT on the row maps, with GQL's equality (1 = 1.0)
gql:bind("p")continues the pattern from the element in a WITH column
gql:trail("#1", ...)the trail check of a quantified edge or of an edge in the body of a quantified path pattern: the edge is none of the edges already bound under these labels
gql:filter("<condition>")a WHERE condition, or the part of it that cannot become has(), with GQL's three-valued logic
gql:order("<keys>")ORDER BY with GQL's NULL placement and type order; stable
gql:not_self_loop()keeps a self-loop from matching twice in an either-direction edge
gql:for("x IN <list>")FOR / UNWIND: one row per item of the list (unfold() with GQL's NULL rule); with an ordinal the row is the record of item and position
gql:lookup("(n:label)", "<equality>")starts a pattern at the vertices an equality with a value of the row finds, by id ([id]) or through a property index ([index: vertex label.key])
gql:value("<expression>")the last step of a pattern comprehension's child: the value of its | part for one match, which the host step collects into the list
gql:insert_node(["label", ...], "{props}")INSERT of one node: creates it per row, with all its properties in one storage call, and makes it the current element (Writes)
gql:insert_edge("label", "from", "to", "{props}")INSERT of one edge between the nodes of the row named from and to ((#n) for an unnamed node of the pattern)
gql:set("<items>"), gql:remove("<items>")one SET / REMOVE clause: applies its items per row to the elements the row's variables hold and passes the row on unchanged
gql:delete("[DETACH] DELETE <targets>")one DELETE clause: collects the targets of every row, checks the NODETACH rule for the whole clause, removes the edges, then the nodes, and passes the rows on unchanged
gql:merge("<pattern>", <search>, <creation>[, "ON CREATE SET ..", "ON MATCH SET .."])one MERGE clause: per row, runs the search child (a MATCH of the pattern from the row) and emits a row per match, or runs the creation child (the insert chain) once; then its ON items
gql:error("<GQLSTATUS>")the marker of a query that failed to parse or bind; raises the error before the run

gql:filter, gql:project, gql:value, gql:order, gql:aggregate and gql:for may hold the bodies of the EXISTS, COUNT { } and COLLECT { } subqueries and pattern comprehensions their expressions contain as child traversals, shown as \> lines under the step (EXISTS and pattern predicates, comprehensions, COUNT and COLLECT). UNION and CALL need no step of their own: they are Gremlin's union(), flat_map() and optional() (UNION, NEXT and CALL). They exist only in plans of gql(); they are not DSL steps. Everything else in a GQL plan is an ordinary step.

What becomes has()

A WHERE condition is split at its top-level ANDs. A part of the form var.key <op> value, where the value is a literal or a $parameter, is pushed into has() right at the scan or the edge it reads, where the optimizer and the property indexes see it; the rest runs in gql:filter. Pushed: = (as P.eq), <, <=, >, >=, IN (with NULL items removed), STARTS WITH, ENDS WITH, CONTAINS with a string, IS NOT NULL. Never pushed: <>, IS NULL, OR, NOT, conditions over two variables, NULL or list operands: there the semantics of has() and GQL's three-valued logic differ.

g.gql("MATCH (n:person) WHERE n.age > 30 AND n.name STARTS WITH 'j' RETURN n.name AS n").profile()
g.gql("MATCH (n) WHERE n.age <> 29 RETURN n.name AS n").profile()

v(labels: ["person"])                                           1       0       4
has("name", TextP.starting_with("j"))                           1       4       1
has("age", P.gt(30))                                            1       1       1
gql:project("n")                                                1       1       1

v()                                                             1       0       6
gql:filter("n.age <> 29")                                       1       6       3
gql:project("n")                                                1       3       3

Index use

When a property index exists, the planner starts at the node with an indexed equality (or IN), then one with a label and a property condition, then one with a label, then the first node; and the property index rule of the optimizer serves the scan. A parameter works as well as a literal:

{ g.create_index(#{label: "person", key: "name"}); g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: $n})-[:created]->(s) RETURN s.name AS s ORDER BY s", #{n: "josh"}).to_list() }   // #{"s": "lop"}, #{"s": "ripple"}

v(labels: ["person"]) [index: vertex person.name]               1       0       1
has("name", P.eq("josh"))                                       1       1       1
out("created")                                                  1       1       2
gql:project("s")                                                1       2       2
Optimizer rules applied: source_filter_pushdown, property_index

The planner reads only what every storage offers (statistics() and the index catalog), so a host's own storage gets the same plans.

Edges: out() when nothing reads the edge

An edge that is not named, filtered or read becomes a plain out("T") / in("T"), the cheapest form. A named, filtered or trail-checked edge becomes out_e("T") ... in_v(), with its filters on the edge in between. An either-direction edge is a union() of both directions with the self-loop guard:

g.gql("MATCH (a:person)-[e:created]->(s) WHERE e.weight > 0.5 RETURN a.name AS a, s.name AS s ORDER BY a").profile()
g.gql("MATCH (a:person)-[:knows]-(b) RETURN b.name AS b").profile()

v(labels: ["person"])                                           1       0       4
as("a") [path: labels(a)]                                       1       4       4
out_e("created") [path: labels(a)]                              1       4       4
has("weight", P.gt(0.5)) [path: labels(a)]                      1       4       1
in_v() [path: labels(a)]                                        1       1       1
gql:project("a", "s")                                           1       1       1
gql:order("a")                                                  1       1       1

v(labels: ["person"])                                                     1       0       4
union(__.out("knows"), __.in_e("knows").gql:not_self_loop().out_v())      1       4       4
gql:project("b")                                                          1       4       4

as() only where needed

A variable gets a path label (as("a")) only when something reads it while the traversal has moved past it: a RETURN column of an earlier node, a join, a trail check, a condition over two variables. MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name records no path at all. The [path: ...] note in the profile shows what is recorded (Path Requirement Analysis). Return only what you need: each returned earlier variable is one more label per traverser.

Merge points

Between two hops the lowering places a lazy_barrier(), a merge point: traversers that reached the same vertex with the same recorded labels merge into one with a higher bulk, so the next hop runs once for all of them (Bulk and Barriers). The rows stay the same; the work shrinks. Here four authors (josh twice) become three traversers:

g.gql("MATCH (s:software)<-[:created]-(p)<-[:knows]-(m) RETURN m.name AS m").profile()

Step                                                         Call      In     Out Bulk
=======================================================================================
v(labels: ["software"])                                         1       0       2    2
in("created")                                                   1       2       4    4
lazy_barrier()                                                  1       4       3    4
in("knows")                                                     1       3       1    2
gql:project("m")                                                1       1       1    2

Merging needs equal labels, so it pays off where the middle node is not returned. Returning p labels it, and traversers at the same vertex still merge only with the same p.

Trail checks and merging. The trail rule (an edge is bound once per MATCH) is checked with where(P.neq("#1")) against the earlier edge, which must therefore be labelled. When two edges of one MATCH can have the same label, the first is labelled and the traversers stay apart until the check has run. The planner skips the check when the label sets cannot overlap (-[:knows]-> then -[:created]->), so name edge labels in multi-hop patterns where you can:

g.gql("MATCH (a)-[:created]->(s)<-[:created]-(b) RETURN a.name AS a, b.name AS b").profile()

v()                                                             1       0       6
as("a") [path: labels(a)]                                       1       6       6
out_e("created") [path: labels(a)]                              1       6       4
as("#1") [path: labels(#1,a)]                                   1       4       4
in_v() [path: labels(#1,a)]                                     1       4       4
lazy_barrier() [path: labels(#1,a)]                             1       4       4
in_e("created") [path: labels(#1,a)]                            1       4      10
where(P.neq("#1")) [path: labels(a)]                            1      10       6
out_v() [path: labels(a)]                                       1       6       6
gql:project("a", "b")                                           1       6       6

Disconnected patterns are not optimized yet

Patterns that share no variable (MATCH (a:person), (s:software)) are a Cartesian product, built with a second v() in the middle of the traversal. The optimizer does not fold labels or use indexes for a v() there yet, so the second scan runs in full once per row of the first:

g.gql("MATCH (a:person), (s:software) RETURN a.name AS a, s.name AS s").profile()

v(labels: ["software"])                                         1       0       2
as("s") [path: labels(s)]                                       1       2       2
v() [path: labels(s)]                                           1       2      12
has_label("person") [path: labels(s)]                           1      12       8
gql:project("a", "s")                                           1       8       8

A pattern after the first with an equality an id or index serves is the exception: it starts with a gql:lookup instead of the second v(). Otherwise, connect patterns through a shared variable where the question allows it; the planner prefers connected patterns and starts the product at the smaller side. The same holds for a pattern after a WITH or inside an OPTIONAL MATCH that shares no variable with what came before, and for a leading OPTIONAL MATCH (its scan runs inside optional()).

LET, FILTER and WITH

LET, FILTER and a WITH that only passes values on add no steps: the planner treats their names as the expressions they stand for and their conditions like WHERE, so a condition on a LET value can still become has() where it reads a property directly, and the plan is that of the same query written without them:

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) LET d = p.age / 10 FILTER d = 3 AND p.name STARTS WITH 'j' RETURN p.name AS name").profile()

v(labels: ["person"])                                           1       0       4
has("name", TextP.starting_with("j"))                           1       4       1
gql:filter("d = 3")                                             1       1       1
gql:project("name")                                             1       1       1

A WITH with DISTINCT, an aggregate, ORDER BY, OFFSET or LIMIT builds its rows with the same steps as a RETURN. When a later clause reads them, the row is labelled once (#w1) and gql:bind moves to the element of a column to continue the pattern; the barrier starts fresh paths, so nothing recorded before it is carried on:

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WITH p ORDER BY p.age DESC LIMIT 2 MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN p.name AS name, s.name AS sw").profile()

v(labels: ["person"])                                           1       0       4
as("p") [path: labels(p)]                                       1       4       4
gql:project("p") [path: labels(p)]                              1       4       4
gql:order("p.age DESC")                                         1       4       4
limit(2)                                                        1       4       2
as("#w1") [path: labels(#w1)]                                   1       2       2
gql:bind("p") [path: labels(#w1)]                               1       2       2
out("created") [path: labels(#w1)]                              1       2       3
gql:project("name", "sw")                                       1       3       3

FOR and the correlated lookup

FOR (and UNWIND) becomes one gql:for step; the item is the current object of each row, and as("x") labels it only when a later step reads it after the row moved on. A query that does not start with MATCH starts from one empty row, inject(0):

g.gql("FOR x IN [10, 20] WITH ORDINALITY i RETURN x, i").profile()

inject(0)                                                       1       0       1
gql:for("x IN [10, 20] WITH ORDINALITY i")                      1       1       2
gql:project("x", "i")                                           1       2       2

A MATCH after FOR runs once per row. Without help that is a scan per item, so a list of 1000 names reads the whole label 1000 times:

g.gql("FOR n IN $names MATCH (p:person {name: n}) RETURN n, p.age AS age", #{names: ["vadas", "marko", "nobody"]}).profile()

inject(0)                                                       1       0       1
gql:for("n IN $names")                                          1       1       3
as("n") [path: labels(n)]                                       1       3       3
v() [path: labels(n)]                                           1       3      18
has_label("person") [path: labels(n)]                           1      18      12
gql:filter("name: n") [path: labels(n)]                         1      12       2
gql:project("n", "age")                                         1       2       2

When an equality between the pattern's vertex and a value of the row can be answered directly, the planner starts the pattern with gql:lookup instead: by element id always (element_id(n) = id, either operand order), by a property ({name: n}, n.name = x) when a property index on that key exists for every label of the node. Each row then reads only the vertices the value finds:

g.gql("FOR id IN $ids MATCH (n) WHERE element_id(n) = id RETURN id, n.name AS name", #{ids: ["1", "3", "42"]}).profile()

inject(0)                                                          1       0       1
gql:for("id IN $ids")                                              1       1       3
as("id") [path: labels(id)]                                        1       3       3
gql:lookup("(n)", "element_id(n) = id") [id] [path: labels(id)]    1       3       2
gql:project("id", "name")                                          1       2       2

{ g.create_index(#{label: "person", key: "name"}); g.gql("FOR n IN $names MATCH (p:person {name: n}) RETURN n, p.age AS age", #{names: ["vadas", "marko", "nobody"]}).profile() }

inject(0)                                                                            1       0       1
gql:for("n IN $names")                                                               1       1       3
as("n") [path: labels(n)]                                                            1       3       3
gql:lookup("(p:person)", "name: n") [index: vertex person.name] [path: labels(n)]    1       3       2
has_label("person") [path: labels(n)]                                                1       2       2
gql:project("n", "age")                                                              1       2       2

The lookup checks every vertex it finds with GQL's =, so it returns exactly the rows of the scan (Semantics); a NULL value finds nothing, and a value an index cannot serve (a list, NaN, a non-string id, a storage that reports no index) falls back to scanning the label. The same lookup starts any pattern that is not the first one: a second, disconnected pattern with an indexed equality (MATCH (a:person {name: 'marko'}), (b:person) WHERE b.age = a.age + 3 with an index on person.age), or a MATCH after a WITH. The first pattern of a query is never a lookup: it is a scan the optimizer serves with the index as usual. Edges are not looked up (an equality on element_id(e) stays a filter).

Aggregation

An aggregating RETURN (or WITH) becomes one gql:aggregate in place of gql:project. It does not use Gremlin's group() / count() / fold(), whose rules for missing values and empty input differ from GQL's (Semantics). It counts a merged traverser by its bulk, so merge points before it save work without changing a count:

g.gql("MATCH (s:software)<-[:created]-(p) RETURN s.name AS sw, count(p) AS authors ORDER BY sw").profile()
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN DISTINCT p.age > 30 AS old").profile()

v(labels: ["software"])                                         1       0       2
as("s") [path: labels(s)]                                       1       2       2
in("created") [path: labels(s)]                                 1       2       4
gql:aggregate(["s.name"], ["count(p)"], ["sw", "authors"])      1       4       2
gql:order("sw")                                                 1       2       2

v(labels: ["person"])                                           1       0       4
gql:project("old")                                              1       4       4
gql:distinct()                                                  1       4       2

OPTIONAL MATCH

An OPTIONAL MATCH is Gremlin's optional() around the lowered part, its WHERE inside. Where the part does not match, the row continues unchanged and the labels set inside are absent, which reads as NULL. A leading OPTIONAL MATCH starts from one row, inject(0):

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN p.name AS name, count(s) AS n").profile()
g.gql("OPTIONAL MATCH (n:robot) RETURN n").profile()

v(labels: ["person"]) [path: labels(s)]                                   1       0       4
as("p") [path: labels(p,s)]                                               1       4       4
optional(__.out("created").as("s")) [path: labels(p,s)]                   1       4       5
  \> out("created") [path: labels(p)]                                     4       4       4
  \> as("s") [path: labels(p,s)]                                          4       4       4
gql:aggregate(["p.name"], ["count(s)"], ["name", "n"])                    1       5       4

inject(0) [path: labels(n)]                                               1       0       1
optional(__.v(labels: ["robot"]).as("n")) [path: labels(n)]               1       1       1
  \> v(labels: ["robot"])                                                 1       1       0
  \> as("n") [path: labels(n)]                                            1       0       0
gql:project("n")                                                          1       1       1

After an optional part every later read goes through a label, since the current element differs between the rows that matched and those that did not.

Quantified edges

A quantified edge is a repeat() of the single edge, with emit() and times() for its bounds: {1,2} is repeat(..).emit().times(2), {0,n} emit().repeat(..).times(n), {n} repeat(..).times(n), {m,n} with m > 1 emit(__.loops().is(P.gte(m))), an unbounded one has no times(). Inside the loop each edge is labelled and checked with gql:trail against the edges of the match so far (trail):

g.gql("MATCH (a {name: 'marko'})-[:knows|created]->{1,2}(b) RETURN b.name AS b").profile()

v() [path: labels(#1)]                                                                  1       0       6
has("name", P.eq("marko")) [path: labels(#1)]                                           1       6       1
repeat(__.out_e("knows", "created").gql:trail("#1").as("#1").in_v()).times(2).emit()    1       1       5
[loops: 2, max_depth: 2, avg_loops: 1.4]
  \> out_e("knows", "created") [path: labels(#1)]                                       2       4       5
  \> gql:trail("#1") [path: labels(#1)]                                                 2       5       5
  \> as("#1") [path: labels(#1)]                                                        2       5       5
  \> in_v() [path: labels(#1)]                                                          2       5       5
gql:project("b")                                                                        1       5       5

The labels keep the traversers of different matches apart, so there is no merge point after a quantified edge: a quantified pattern costs more than the plain repeat() that ignores trail. The plan never records full paths ([path: labels(..)], never full).

Quantified path patterns

A quantified path pattern is a repeat() of its whole body, with the same emit() / times() modulators as a quantified edge. Inside the loop each body edge is labelled and checked with gql:trail against every edge of the match so far that could be the same edge (the earlier iterations of each body edge, the other body edges, the edges of the clause outside), and each body variable the query reads is labelled with as(): the list of a group variable is read back from those labels, one per iteration. The plan records labels only, never full paths:

g.gql("MATCH (a {name: 'marko'}) ((x)-[e:knows]->(m)-[f:created]->(y)){1,2} (b) RETURN b.name AS b, [n IN m | n.name] AS via").profile()

{p1}

The two gql:trail steps check one label each here: a knows edge can never be a created edge. A body condition on one element runs where it is matched, as a has() or gql:filter; one that reads several body elements runs as a gql:filter at the end of the body, in every iteration.

? is emit().repeat(B).times(1) and a body without a quantifier is inlined, its steps run once in the plan as if the parentheses were not there:

g.gql("MATCH (a {name: 'josh'}) ((x)-[:created]->(s))? (q) RETURN s.name AS s, q.name AS q").profile()
g.gql("MATCH ((x:person)-[:created]->(s) WHERE s.name = 'ripple') RETURN x.name AS who").profile()

{p2}

{p3}

The planner may walk a quantified path pattern from its far end when that end is the cheaper start (a label, an indexed property); the body then runs in reverse, and the group lists are still given in the order the text reads.

Path variables

A path variable is assembled from labels, not from Gremlin's path() (which would record the full path at every step): every element of the named pattern is labelled, and for a quantified edge also the vertices inside the loop (#gv..):

g.gql("MATCH p = (a {name: 'marko'})-[:knows]->{1,2}(b) RETURN p").profile()

v() [path: labels(#2,#gv2)]                                                                                       1       0       6
has("name", P.eq("marko")) [path: labels(#2,#gv2)]                                                                1       6       1
as("a") [path: labels(#2,#gv2,a)]                                                                                 1       1       1
repeat(__.out_e("knows").gql:trail("#2").as("#2").in_v().as("#gv2")).times(2).emit() [path: labels(#2,#gv2,a)]    1       1       2
[loops: 2, max_depth: 2, avg_loops: 1.0]
  \> out_e("knows") [path: labels(#2,#gv2,a)]                                                                     2       3       2
  \> gql:trail("#2") [path: labels(#2,#gv2,a)]                                                                    2       2       2
  \> as("#2") [path: labels(#2,#gv2,a)]                                                                           2       2       2
  \> in_v() [path: labels(#2,#gv2,a)]                                                                             2       2       2
  \> as("#gv2") [path: labels(#2,#gv2,a)]                                                                         2       2       2
as("b") [path: labels(#2,#gv2,a,b)]                                                                               1       2       2
gql:project("p")                                                                                                  1       2       2

A path variable that nothing reads labels nothing.

EXISTS and pattern predicates

A subquery is lowered in one of two ways.

The fast path. A [NOT] EXISTS (or pattern predicate) that is a condition of its own in a WHERE or FILTER (alone, or joined to the others by AND) becomes Gremlin's filter(__.<body>) or not(__.<body>), the step Gremlin's where(__..) / not(__..) would run. The body starts where the row stands: a body that starts at the element the row is on needs no step and no label, so the "who has no ..." question is exactly its Gremlin twin:

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE NOT (p)-[:created]->() RETURN p.name AS name").profile()
g.gql("MATCH (a:person), (b:person) WHERE (a)-[:knows]->(b) RETURN a.name AS a, b.name AS b").profile()
g.gql("MATCH (s:software) WHERE EXISTS { (p:person) WHERE p.age > 33 } RETURN s.name AS s").profile()

v(labels: ["person"])                                                     1       0       4
not(__.out("created"))                                                    1       4       1
  \> out("created")                                                       4       4       4
gql:project("name")                                                       1       1       1

v(labels: ["person"])                                                     1       0       4
as("a") [path: labels(a)]                                                 1       4       4
v() [path: labels(a)]                                                     1       4      24
has_label("person") [path: labels(a)]                                     1      24      16
filter(__.in("knows").where(P.eq("a"))) [path: labels(a)]                 1      16       2
  \> in("knows") [path: labels(a)]                                       16      16       8
  \> where(P.eq("a"))                                                     8       8       2
gql:project("a", "b")                                                     1       2       2

v(labels: ["software"])                                                   1       0       2
filter(__.v(labels: ["person"]).has("age", P.gt(33)))                     1       2       2
  \> v(labels: ["person"])                                                2       2       8
  \> has("age", P.gt(33))                                                 2       8       2
gql:project("s")                                                          1       2       2

A body that reads a second imported variable joins it with where(P.eq("a")) (or starts from it with select(), or with gql:bind from a WITH column); a body that imports nothing starts with its own scan, which the optimizer folds and pushes down as anywhere else. The optimizer treats the child like any Gremlin child: between two hops it may add a lazy_barrier(), as it does for where(__.out("knows").out("created")).

The expression hook. Anywhere else (under OR, XOR, CASE, in a RETURN or WITH column, an ORDER BY key, an aggregate, a FOR list) the gql:* step that evaluates the expression holds the body as a child and runs it when the evaluation of a row needs the answer: the Call and In columns of the child show how many rows ran it. Here only the two rows that p.age > 30 did not already decide ran in("knows"):

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE p.age > 30 OR (p)<-[:knows]-() RETURN p.name AS name").profile()
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, EXISTS { (p)-[:knows]->() } AS knows").profile()

v(labels: ["person"])                                                     1       0       4
gql:filter("p.age > 30 OR (p)<-[:knows]-()")                              1       4       3
  \> in("knows")                                                          2       2       1
gql:project("name")                                                       1       3       3

v(labels: ["person"])                                                     1       0       4
gql:project("name", "knows")                                              1       4       4
  \> out("knows")                                                         4       4       2

Both forms run the same body, so they give the same rows. On an element, the subquery steps come last (Semantics): after the pushed has() and the plain gql:filter, and after the element's as(), so a body that reads the element through its label (a second body clause starting at it) finds it:

g.gql("MATCH (a:person) WHERE CASE WHEN EXISTS { MATCH (a)<-[:knows]-() MATCH (a)--() } THEN true ELSE false END RETURN a.name AS name ORDER BY name").profile()

v(labels: ["person"])                                                                         1       0       4
as("a") [path: labels(a)]                                                                     1       4       4
gql:filter("CASE WHEN EXISTS { MATCH (a)<-[:knows]-() MATCH (a)--() } THEN t…" (82 chars))    1       4       2
  \> in("knows") [path: labels(a)]                                                            4       4       2
  \> select("a")                                                                              2       2       2
  \> union(__.out(), __.in_e().gql:not_self_loop().out_v())                                   2       2       4
...
gql:project("name")                                                                           1       2       2
gql:order("name")                                                                             1       2       2

The global optimizer rule filter_reorder may still move a fast-path child before a gql:filter by its cost estimate (WHERE NOT (p)-->() AND p.name <> 'x' runs not(__.out()) before gql:filter("p.name <> 'x'")), as it would in a Gremlin plan; the rows are the same.

Map projections and comprehensions

A map projection and a list comprehension add no step: the gql:* step that evaluates the expression builds the map or the list from the row's values, with no allocation per item beyond the result.

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p {.name, .age} AS m, [x IN [p.age, 30] WHERE x > 28] AS l").profile()

v(labels: ["person"])                                           1       0       4
gql:project("m", "l")                                           1       4       4

A pattern comprehension is a subquery that collects: like an EXISTS in an expression, its body is a child of the step evaluating it, and the child ends in gql:value(..), the value of the | part per match. The host runs it once per row that reaches it and builds the list from the child's results (here 4 rows ran out("knows"), which found 2 friends), the plan of its Gremlin twin project(..).by(__.out("knows").values("name").fold()):

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, [(p)-[:knows]->(f) | f.name] AS friends").profile()
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p {.name, projects: [(p)-[:created]->(s) | s {.name, n: size([(s)<-[:created]-(c) | c])}]} AS m").profile()

v(labels: ["person"])                                                     1       0       4
gql:project("name", "friends")                                            1       4       4
  \> out("knows")                                                         4       4       2
  \> gql:value("f.name")                                                  4       2       2

v(labels: ["person"])                                                     1       0       4
gql:project("m")                                                          1       4       4
  \> out("created")                                                       4       4       4
  \> gql:value("s {.name, n: size([(s)<-[:created]-(c) | c])}")           4       4       4
        \> in("created")                                                  4       4      10
        \> gql:value("c")                                                 4      10      10

A comprehension nested in the | part is a child of the inner gql:value, so it runs once per match of the outer pattern: nested comprehensions from the same element multiply the work, as nested Gremlin fold() children do (Semantics). The collected list is checked against the limits before it is built (Limits).

COUNT and COLLECT

COUNT { } and COLLECT { } are hosted like an EXISTS in an expression: the step evaluating the expression holds the body as its child and runs it once per row that reaches it. A COUNT child ends in count(), which counts the body's traversers with their bulk, and a COLLECT child in gql:value(..), the RETURN item, which the host collects in arrival order (after the body's own gql:order). A COUNT body whose RETURN only projects keeps its gql:project, which count() never reads, so its items are not evaluated (Semantics):

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS who, COUNT { (p)-[:created]->() } AS n").profile()
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS who, COLLECT { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN s.name ORDER BY s.name } AS sw").profile()
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE COUNT { (p)-[:created]->() } > 1 RETURN p.name AS who").profile()

v(labels: ["person"])                                                     1       0       4
gql:project("who", "n")                                                   1       4       4
  \> out("created")                                                       4       4       4
  \> count()                                                              4       4       4

v(labels: ["person"])                                                     1       0       4
gql:project("who", "sw")                                                  1       4       4
  \> out("created")                                                       4       4       4
  \> gql:project("s.name")                                                4       4       4
