  \> gql:order("s.name")                                                  4       4       4
  \> gql:value("s.name")                                                  4       4       4

v(labels: ["person"])                                                     1       0       4
gql:filter("COUNT { (p)-[:created]->() } > 1")                            1       4       1
  \> out("created")                                                       4       4       4
  \> count()                                                              4       4       4
gql:project("who")                                                        1       1       1

A whole-query body (WITH, an aggregate, RETURN) is lowered like a top-level query onto the child, so an EXISTS with one keeps the fast path when it stands alone in a WHERE; the child ends in the body's own steps, and filter() asks only whether one traverser comes out:

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE EXISTS { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) WITH count(s) AS c WHERE c > 1 RETURN c } RETURN p.name AS who").profile()

v(labels: ["person"])                                                                                    1       0       4
filter(__.out("created").gql:aggregate([], ["count(s)"], ["c"]).gql:filter("c > 1").gql:project("c"))    1       4       1
  \> out("created")                                                                                      4       4       4
  \> gql:aggregate([], ["count(s)"], ["c"])                                                              4       4       4
  \> gql:filter("c > 1")                                                                                 4       4       1
  \> gql:project("c")                                                                                    4       1       1
gql:project("who")                                                                                       1       1       1

A body that starts from an import with an equality the id or a property index serves starts with gql:lookup, as a later pattern of the query does (FOR and the correlated lookup); this holds for EXISTS, COUNT, COLLECT, pattern comprehensions and CALL bodies alike.

UNION, NEXT and CALL

UNION is Gremlin's union() as the start step: each operand is lowered onto its own child exactly as a query of its own, so its scan keeps the label, the pushed has() and an index, and UNION (not ALL) adds gql:distinct() after it. Each operand's ORDER BY and LIMIT stay inside its child:

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE p.age > 30 RETURN p.name AS name UNION MATCH (s:software) RETURN s.name AS name").profile()

union(__.v(labels: ["person"]).has("age", P.gt(30)).gql:project("name"), __.v(labels: ["software"]).gql:project("name"))    1       1       4
  \> v(labels: ["person"])                                                                                                  1       1       4
  \> has("age", P.gt(30))                                                                                                   1       4       2
  \> gql:project("name")                                                                                                    1       2       2
  \> v(labels: ["software"])                                                                                                1       1       2
  \> gql:project("name")                                                                                                    1       2       2
gql:distinct()                                                                                                              1       4       4

NEXT adds no step. After a plain query it is the WITH of the same items, so it gives the same plan (here the FILTER after NEXT became the has() of the scan); after a UNION the next statement continues from the union's row maps:

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, p.age AS age NEXT FILTER age > 30 RETURN name").profile()
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name UNION ALL MATCH (s:software) RETURN s.name AS name NEXT RETURN name ORDER BY name LIMIT 3").profile()

v(labels: ["person"])                                           1       0       4
has("age", P.gt(30))                                            1       4       2
gql:project("name")                                             1       2       2

union(__.v(labels: ["person"]).gql:project("name"), __.v(labels: ["software"]).gql:project("name"))    1       1       6
  \> v(labels: ["person"])                                                                             1       1       4
  \> gql:project("name")                                                                               1       4       4
  \> v(labels: ["software"])                                                                           1       1       2
  \> gql:project("name")                                                                               1       2       2
gql:project("name")                                                                                    1       6       6
gql:order("name")                                                                                      1       6       6
limit(3)                                                                                               1       6       3

CALL is flat_map(__.<body>): the body is lowered onto the child from the row's current element, so a body that continues from an import needs no step to reach it, and its gql:order and limit() run per call (Call 4: once per person). OPTIONAL CALL wraps it in optional(..) and labels the body's row (as("#c<k>")) so a row without results reads NULL columns. After a CALL, the outer variables are read through their labels (as("p")):

g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-[e:created]->(s) RETURN s.name AS top ORDER BY e.weight DESC LIMIT 1 } RETURN p.name AS who, top").profile()
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) OPTIONAL CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN s.name AS sw } RETURN p.name AS who, sw").profile()

v(labels: ["person"])                                                                                                    1       0       4
as("p") [path: labels(p)]                                                                                                1       4       4
flat_map(__.out_e("created").as("e").in_v().gql:project("top").gql:order("e.weight DESC").limit(1)) [path: labels(p)]    1       4       3
  \> out_e("created")                                                                                                    4       4       4
  \> as("e") [path: labels(e)]                                                                                           4       4       4
  \> in_v() [path: labels(e)]                                                                                            4       4       4
  \> gql:project("top") [path: labels(e)]                                                                                4       4       4
  \> gql:order("e.weight DESC")                                                                                          4       4       4
  \> limit(1)                                                                                                            4       4       3
gql:project("who", "top")                                                                                                1       3       3

v(labels: ["person"]) [path: labels(#c2)]                                                     1       0       4
as("p") [path: labels(#c2,p)]                                                                 1       4       4
optional(__.flat_map(__.out("created").gql:project("sw")).as("#c2")) [path: labels(#c2,p)]    1       4       5
  \> flat_map(__.out("created").gql:project("sw")) [path: labels(p)]                          4       4       4
        \> out("created")                                                                     4       4       4
        \> gql:project("sw")                                                                  4       4       4
  \> as("#c2") [path: labels(#c2,p)]                                                          4       4       4
gql:project("who", "sw")                                                                      1       5       5

flat_map() builds the results of one call before the first moves on, so an outer LIMIT does not shorten a call that has started (Semantics); a body that imports nothing still runs once per row. A UNION or NEXT inside a body is a union() or the next steps inside the flat_map child, run per row.

Writes

An INSERT becomes one gql:insert_node per new node and then one gql:insert_edge per new edge, in text order; a query that ends in a write ends with discard(), which drops the rows. A leading INSERT starts from one empty row, inject(0):

g.gql("INSERT (:city {name: 'Berlin'})").profile()

Step                                                         Call      In     Out
==================================================================================
inject(0)                                                       1       0       1
gql:insert_node(["city"], "{name: 'Berlin'}")                   1       1       1
discard()                                                       1       1       0

After a MATCH, the variables the insert reads are labelled with as():

g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) INSERT (p)-[:likes]->(f:fruit {name: 'apple'})").profile()

Step                                                            Call      In     Out
=====================================================================================
v(labels: ["person"])                                              1       0       4
has("name", P.eq("marko"))                                         1       4       1
as("p") [path: labels(p)]                                          1       1       1
gql:insert_node(["fruit"], "{name: 'apple'}") [path: labels(p)]    1       1       1
gql:insert_edge("likes", "p", "f")                                 1       1       1
discard()                                                          1       1       0
Optimizer rules applied: source_filter_pushdown

A SET or REMOVE clause becomes one gql:set / gql:remove step with its items as written; the variables it changes are labelled with as() before it, like those an insert reads:

g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) SET p.age = p.age + 1, p:admin").profile()

A DELETE clause becomes one gql:delete step with the clause as written. It is a barrier: it takes every row before it removes anything, so the NODETACH check sees the whole clause:

g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) DETACH DELETE p").profile()

A MERGE clause becomes one gql:merge step holding two children, shown as \> lines: the search, planned like a MATCH of the pattern that starts from a bound node of the row (or from a lookup by id or a property index), and the creation, the insert chain of the pattern; both end in the same gql:project of the pattern's variables, so a found and a created row look alike:

g.gql("MATCH (a:person {name: 'marko'}) MERGE (a)-[:likes]->(f:fruit {name: 'apple'})").profile()

A plan that writes never merges traversers, so the lowering places no merge points in it; a lazy_barrier() the optimizer adds between two hops passes every traverser on unmerged (In = Out). The write steps run only after the steps before them consumed their whole input, which is what makes the visibility rule of Semantics hold. A CALL body that ends in a write is optional(__.<body>.discard()): it runs per row and keeps the row.

Limits, cancellation, permissions

A GQL query is a traversal, so everything that bounds a traversal bounds it too: resource limits and query limits, cancellation, the memory budget, and the permission check, which sees the reads and writes of the lowered plan (an INSERT asks Create per new label, like add_v() and add_e(), a SET or REMOVE Update like property(); Writing with GQL): reading a denied label through gql() is refused as the equivalent Gremlin is (also a label reached only through a quantified edge, the body of a quantified path pattern or an optional part, or only inside an EXISTS, COUNT or COLLECT body, a pattern comprehension, a CALL body or a later UNION operand, whichever way it is lowered: a subquery's child is checked like a Gremlin child, even when no row reaches it). An unbounded quantifier (on an edge or a path pattern) is bounded by repeat.max_loops and traversal.max_traversers (Semantics), also inside a subquery. The list of a pattern comprehension expands the bulk of its child's results under bulk.max_expansion and is checked against traversal.max_materialized_bytes and the memory budget before it is built, like collect_list(). The parser bounds nesting (128 levels, 54001) so no query can exhaust the stack, CALL bodies and whole-query subquery bodies nest at most 16 levels, and a query holds at most 64 subqueries (pattern comprehensions, COUNT { } and COLLECT { } included; CALL bodies are not counted) and runs at most 1024 subquery bodies (Errors).

GQL Conformance

This page lists which parts of ISO/IEC 39075 (GQL) gql() supports, in the style of the conformance appendices that GQL implementations publish. It is maintained by hand together with the code; when a construct lands, its row moves here in the same change.

GQL names its optional features with identifiers such as G036 (graph pattern features), GQ.. (query features), GE.. (expressions), GF.. (functions), GA.. (additional behaviour), GB.. (lexical), GL.. (literals), GH.. (other). This page cites only those identifiers and short descriptive names of our own; it does not reproduce the standard. An identifier marked (provisional) could not be checked against the standard text yet and may be corrected.

How far the Cypher compatibility forms agree with Neo4j's behaviour is measured against the openCypher TCK: TCK Compliance.

Status: supported, partial (what is missing is named), not yet (planned), no (refused for good; see Refused Constructs).

Core language

The mandatory core of a GQL query, by construct.

ConstructStatusNotes
MATCH with node and edge patterns, comma-separated patterns, several MATCH clausessupportedtrail (DIFFERENT EDGES) match mode per clause
WHERE after MATCH, inline WHERE and property maps in element patternssupported
RETURN, RETURN *, RETURN DISTINCT, ASsupportedRETURN is mandatory unless the last clause writes; FINISH ends a query without a result
ORDER BY ... ASC / DESCsupportedNULL last ascending, first descending
label expressions &, |, !, ( )supported
property reference x.keysupported
comparison, AND / OR / NOT, IS [NOT] NULLsupportedthree-valued logic
arithmetic + - * / %, string concatenation ||supported
simple and searched CASE, COALESCE, NULLIFsupported
UPPER, LOWER, CHAR_LENGTH / CHARACTER_LENGTH, LEFT, RIGHT, TRIM(s)supportedTRIM removes spaces by default; NORMALIZE not yet
BYTE_LENGTH / OCTET_LENGTH of a character stringsupportedthe number of UTF-8 bytes; Graphersal has no byte strings
list trim TRIM(list, n)supporteddrops the last n items
parameters $namesupportedvalues only, never text
aggregate functions COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, COLLECT_LIST, with DISTINCTsupportedimplicit grouping by the items without an aggregate; Cypher collect alias
binary set functions PERCENTILE_CONT, PERCENTILE_DISCsupportedvalue first, then the percentile (0.0 to 1.0, 22003 outside); Cypher percentileCont / percentileDisc aliases (stage 3f)
OPTIONAL MATCHsupportedalso as the first clause
EXISTS predicate: EXISTS { MATCH ... }, EXISTS { <pattern> }, EXISTS ( ... ) (provisional: whether the standard makes it core or an optional feature, and its identifier, are still to be checked)supportedanywhere an expression stands, nested too; TRUE or FALSE, never NULL; the body is a pattern, MATCH clauses, or a whole query ending in RETURN (EXISTS); Cypher pattern predicates as aliases
Cypher WITHsupportednot GQL; accepted with Cypher's meaning (Cypher Aliases)
record constructor {k: expr, ...} / RECORD {k: expr, ...} and list value constructor [a, b]supportedRECORD is contextual: a variable named record stays usable, back-quoted before a projection that starts with key: or is empty (Expressions)
Cypher map projections p {.k, .*, x, k: expr}, list comprehensions [x IN l WHERE c | e], pattern comprehensions [(a)-->(b) WHERE c | e]supportednot GQL; accepted as compatibility forms with Cypher's meaning (Cypher Aliases); a pattern comprehension is a subquery; all() / any() / none() / single() / reduce() likewise, three-valued as the openCypher TCK (Cypher Aliases)
Cypher COUNT { } and COLLECT { } subqueriessupportednot GQL; compatibility forms with Cypher's meaning (Cypher Aliases); bodies as for EXISTS, COLLECT returns one item; one deviation below
a query without MATCH (RETURN 1)supporteda query may start with FOR, LET, WITH, FILTER or RETURN; it starts from one empty row
data-modifying statements: INSERTsupportednodes with label conjunctions and properties, directed edges with one label, once per row; Cypher CREATE as an alias (Writing with GQL)
data-modifying statements: SET, REMOVEsupportedproperty items n.k = v, all properties n = {..}, label items n:A / n IS A; once per row, items left to right, NULL removes; Cypher's += and SET n = <expression> as compatibility forms (Writing with GQL)
data-modifying statements: DELETEsupportedDETACH DELETE and [NODETACH] DELETE of nodes, edges, paths and lists of them, once per row; NODETACH checked per clause (G1001); reading a deleted element afterwards is an error (Writing with GQL, Semantics)
Cypher MERGE with ON CREATE SET / ON MATCH SETsupportednot GQL; a compatibility form with Cypher's meaning (Cypher Aliases): one pattern, per row every match a row or the whole pattern created, rows see earlier rows' creations, NULL in the pattern 22004 (Writing with GQL, Semantics)
catalog statements (CREATE GRAPH, CREATE GRAPH TYPE, ...), session and transaction commandsnothe host application manages graphs, schemas and transactions
value typespartialthe GQL types Graphersal has (integers, floats, strings, booleans, lists, records/maps, dates and times, NULL); path values; no byte strings

Optional features

IDFeatureStatusNotes
G002different-edges match modepartialthe semantics is the default and only mode; writing DIFFERENT EDGES is not accepted yet
G004path variablessupportedp = (a)-->(b), path_length(p) (Cypher length); Cypher's nodes(p) / relationships(p) as compatibility functions

G013advanced path modes: ACYCLICnot yet

G018any shortest path searchnot yetGremlin repeat()
G019counted shortest path searchnot yet
G035quantified paths (provisional)partiala parenthesized path pattern with {m,n}, {n}, {m,}, {,n}, *, + (Quantified path patterns); body variables are group variables (lists), the outer nodes merge with the body's first and last node, trail per body edge; one chain per body, no quantifier, path variable, path mode or search prefix inside a body, a body variable is a new name (each refused with 0A000)

G074label expression: wildcard labelsupported%

G114SAME predicate (provisional)not yet
G115PROPERTY_EXISTS predicate (provisional)not yetx.key IS NOT NULL tests a property
GA03explicit ordering of nullsnot yetNULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST
GA04universal comparison (provisional)partial= / <> between values of different kinds are FALSE / TRUE, the orderings NULL (Neo4j's reading, see Differences from the standard); there is no total order across kinds outside ORDER BY
GA05cast specificationpartialCAST(x AS INTEGER | FLOAT | STRING | BOOLEAN) and their synonyms (INT, BIGINT, DOUBLE, VARCHAR, BOOL, ...); the other target types (DATE, LIST<..>, DECIMAL, ...) not yet; strict: unconvertible text is 22018
GA07ordering by discarded binding variables (provisional)supportedORDER BY may read variables that RETURN does not return (not after RETURN DISTINCT)
GB02double minus sign commentssupported-- ..., with the edge rule of Writing GQL in Rhai Strings
GB03double solidus commentssupported// ...
GD01updatable graphs (provisional)partialINSERT (Cypher CREATE), SET, REMOVE, DELETE; Cypher's MERGE (no ISO counterpart) as a compatibility form (Writing with GQL); the Cypher forms pass every in-scope case of the openCypher TCK's write clauses (TCK Compliance)
GD02graph label set changes (provisional)supportedSET n:A / SET n IS A and REMOVE n:A add and remove node labels; an edge's single label is not changed by them (Writing with GQL)
GD03DELETE statement: subquery support (provisional)supporteda DELETE item may hold a subquery, as in DETACH DELETE COLLECT { MATCH (s)<-[e]-() RETURN e }; a CALL { } body may end with a DELETE (Writing with GQL)
GD04DELETE statement: simple expression support (provisional)supporteda DELETE item is an expression: a variable, a path, a list (collect(n)), a map member, a function result; NULL is skipped, another value is 42002 / 22G03 (Semantics)
GE07Boolean XORsupported
GF01enhanced numeric functionssupportedABS, FLOOR, CEIL / CEILING, SQRT, MOD; an integer argument keeps its type
GF02trigonometric functions (provisional)not yetGremlin math() after gql()
GF03logarithmic functionssupportedEXP, LN, LOG10, LOG(base, x) (provisional), POWER; an argument outside the domain is an error (2201E, 2201F), never NaN
GF04enhanced path functionspartialPATH_LENGTH; ELEMENTS(p) (provisional) not yet (Cypher's nodes(p) / relationships(p) instead)
GF05multi-character trim functionssupportedBTRIM, LTRIM, RTRIM with an optional set of characters (default: the space)
GF06explicit TRIM functionsupportedTRIM([LEADING | TRAILING | BOTH] [c] FROM s); c is one character (22027 otherwise), the space by default
GF12CARDINALITY functionsupported
GF13SIZE functionsupportedalso on strings as the Cypher alias of CHAR_LENGTH
GH02undirected edge patternsnoGraphersal edges are directed; -[e]- matches either direction
GL01hexadecimal literalssupported0x1F
GL02octal literalssupported0o17
GL03binary literalssupported0b101
GQ01USE graph clausenogql() runs on the graph of its traversal source
GQ02composite query: OTHERWISE (provisional)not yet
GQ03composite query: UNIONsupportedUNION, UNION DISTINCT, UNION ALL; operands return the same column names in any order; one kind per chain; ORDER BY / OFFSET / LIMIT per operand (UNION and NEXT)
GQ04composite query: EXCEPT DISTINCT (provisional)not yet
GQ06composite query: INTERSECT DISTINCT (provisional)not yet
GQ08FILTER statementsupportedFILTER [WHERE] <condition>
GQ09LET statementsupported
GQ10FOR statement: list value supportsupportedFOR x IN <list> (Cypher UNWIND <list> AS x), also as the first clause; a NULL list gives no row, a value that is not a list one row (Semantics)
GQ11FOR statement: WITH ORDINALITY (provisional)supportedthe position from 1
GQ24FOR statement: WITH OFFSET (provisional)supportedthe position from 0
GQ12ORDER BY and page statement: OFFSET clausepartialOFFSET / SKIP after RETURN and in WITH; the standalone statement form not yet
GQ13ORDER BY and page statement: LIMIT clausepartialLIMIT after RETURN and in WITH; the standalone statement form not yet
GQ14complex expressions in sort keys (provisional)supportedORDER BY element_id(e), ORDER BY n.age * 2
GQ15GROUP BY clause (provisional)supportedafter the RETURN items, GROUP BY () included; the keys must be the items without an aggregate (grouping is implicit, so it is optional); a key may also repeat an item's expression (GROUP BY p.name), beyond ISO's variable references
GQ18scalar subqueries (provisional)not yet
GQ20advanced linear composition with NEXTpartialRETURN .. NEXT .., also after a UNION and inside subquery bodies; NEXT YIELD not yet
GQ21OPTIONAL: multiple MATCH statements (provisional)not yetone OPTIONAL MATCH per optional part is supported; the block form OPTIONAL { MATCH ... MATCH ... } is not
GP01inline procedure (provisional)supported[OPTIONAL] CALL { <query> }, run once per incoming row, the body ending in RETURN (CALL subqueries) or, as a unit subquery, in a write (Writing with GQL); IN TRANSACTIONS refused
GP02inline procedure with implicit nested variable scope (provisional)partialCALL { } without a scope clause is accepted but imports nothing (Neo4j Cypher 25's reading; the ISO scoping is still to be checked); import with CALL (*) or Cypher's importing WITH
GP03inline procedure with explicit nested variable scope (provisional)supportedCALL (a, b) { }, CALL (*) { }, CALL () { }
GP04named procedure calls (provisional)partial[OPTIONAL] CALL folder.name(args) [YIELD ..] calls a saved query written in GQL of the graph's catalog, once per row, standalone or inside a query (Calling saved queries); arguments are constants or parameters; a saved query in Rhai and a call inside EXISTS / COUNT / COLLECT not yet; vendor procedures (CALL db.*, dbms.*, apoc.*, gds.*) are refused
GV39temporal types: date, local datetime and local time (provisional)partialdate(), local_time(), local_datetime() (Cypher localtime(), localdatetime()) from ISO 8601 text, a map of fields or another temporal value, components (d.year), arithmetic with durations, comparison (Dates and times); values hold nanoseconds; the literals DATE '..', TIME '..' / LOCAL TIME '..', TIMESTAMP '..' / LOCAL DATETIME '..' and the clocks CURRENT_DATE, LOCAL_TIME, LOCAL_TIMESTAMP (Literals); CAST(x AS DATE) not yet
GV40temporal types: zoned datetime and zoned time (provisional)partialzoned_datetime() (Cypher datetime()) keeps a UTC offset and the zone name it was built with, its arithmetic following the zone; zoned_time() (Cypher time()) keeps a time of day and its offset (Dates and times); the literals TIME '10:00+01:00', DATETIME '..+01:00' (also ZONED TIME '..', ZONED DATETIME '..') and the clocks CURRENT_TIME, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP (Literals); CAST(x AS ZONED TIME) not yet
GV41temporal types: duration (provisional)partialduration() from text or a map, the literal DURATION '..', + / - / * / /, components; ISO DURATION_BETWEEN not yet (the Cypher compatibility function duration.between() instead); < on two durations is NULL

Every feature not listed here is not supported. Cypher spellings that GQL does not have, and the openCypher functions accepted without a GQL counterpart (toInteger, substring, split, round, keys, nodes, the temporal date.truncate(), duration.between(), ...), are on Cypher Aliases.

Implementation-defined choices

Where the standard leaves a choice to the implementation, gql() makes this one (Neo4j's, where it has one):

TopicChoice
NULL in ORDER BYlast ascending, first descending
order of values of different typesmap, vertex, edge, list, date/time, UUID, string, boolean, number, vector, NULL
row order without ORDER BYunspecified
item order of a pattern comprehensionunspecified: the order the matches are found, which depends on the plan
item order of COLLECT { }the order of the body's rows: its ORDER BY when it has one, unspecified otherwise
UNION operands with the same column names in another orderaccepted, matched by name; the result has the first operand's column order (provisional)
order of the rows of a UNIONunspecified, also when the operands are sorted: sort after NEXT
a CALL body that imports nothingstill run once per incoming row; its rows are not cached
the RETURN items of a projecting COUNT { } bodynot evaluated: the rows are counted, an expression that would fail raises no error (a deviation, Semantics)
a comprehension variable named like another variable of the queryan error (42002) for a name in scope or one a LET / WITH value in scope still reads (stricter than Neo4j only there); a name no longer in scope may be used again (Semantics)
DISTINCT, grouping keys, DISTINCT in aggregatesGQL equality: 1 and 1.0 are one value, NULLs form one group
aggregates of no rows (no grouping keys)one row: count 0, sum 0, collect_list [], avg / min / max NULL (Neo4j's values, which the openCypher TCK confirms; the ISO text is still to be checked)
min / max over values of different kindsthe ORDER BY order, never an error
sum of integersan integer; overflow is an error (22003)
unbounded quantifiersno own limit: trail ends them; repeat.max_loops and traversal.max_traversers are errors, never a shortened result (quantified edges and quantified path patterns alike)
outer nodes next to a quantified path patternmerged with the body's first node of the first iteration and last node of the last iteration (Neo4j Cypher 25's reading)
order of a group variable's listthe iterations in the order the text reads, also when the plan walks the pattern from its far end
WITH ... LIMIT ... WHEREthe WHERE filters after ORDER BY / OFFSET / LIMIT (Cypher's order; provisional)
name of an unaliased columnthe expression as written (Neo4j's names, such as count(*), which the openCypher TCK confirms; the ISO text is still to be checked)
element idsstrings, the same as Gremlin's id(); vertex and edge ids are separate spaces
integer divisiontruncates toward zero; % takes the sign of the dividend
temporal precisionnanoseconds
default time zoneUTC: a datetime without an offset or zone, and the clocks without a zone
the current date and timeone instant per query, taken when it starts; X.realtime() is refused
ORDER BY of durationsby length, a month counted as 30 days (< on two durations is NULL)
CAST(temporal AS STRING)the engine's ISO 8601 text ('12:00:00'); Cypher's toString() writes Neo4j's ('12:00')
integer overflowan error (22003), never a wrap
text and numbersno implicit conversion: 'a' + 1 is an error (22G03); convert with CAST(x AS STRING)
CAST of a float to INTEGER, of text with surrounding spacestruncated toward zero; the spaces are skipped (provisional)
CAST to STRING of a float, a boolean, a list or a mapJava's float text ('1.0', '1.0E7'), 'true' / 'false', Neo4j's list and map text (provisional)
CAST(x AS BOOLEAN) of a number; of 'unknown'22G03; NULL (provisional)
default character of TRIM, BTRIM, LTRIM, RTRIMthe space U+0020 only (provisional)
BTRIM / LTRIM / RTRIM with charactersany character of the set is removed (Neo4j's semantics; provisional)
functions and NULLa NULL argument gives NULL, before the kinds are checked
strings in functionspositions and lengths count characters (Unicode scalar values)
GQLSTATUS codes42001 for syntax errors; the others provisional (Errors)
order of the writes of one INSERTper row: its nodes in text order, then its edges in text order
property values of INSERTNULL is not stored; maps and lists of any kinds are stored as given (a difference from Neo4j)

Differences from the standard

Where ISO GQL and Neo4j disagree and the openCypher TCK measures the Neo4j behaviour, gql() follows Neo4j in these places (user decision, stage 3f):

TopicISO GQLgql()
= / <> / IN / simple CASE between values of different kindsnot comparable= FALSE, <> TRUE (1 = '1', [1] = 1, 1 IN ['1']); the orderings < .. >= stay NULL (Semantics)
< <= > >= on two listsnot comparablelexicographic, three-valued
a float divided by zero22012IEEE 754: Infinity, -Infinity or NaN; an integer divided by zero stays 22012
NaN in a comparison(no NaN arises: every division by zero is 22012)never equal (NaN = NaN FALSE), every ordering against a number FALSE

The deliberate differences from Neo4j are listed on Semantics.

TCK Compliance

Graphersal's GQL is measured against the openCypher TCK (Technology Compatibility Kit): Gherkin scenarios that each set up a graph, run one query and state the exact expected result, side effects or error. They exercise the Cypher compatibility forms that gql() accepts (CREATE, MATCH ... RETURN, WITH, UNWIND, ...) with Neo4j's semantics, so the kit works as a ready-made differential test. It serves three purposes:

  1. Compliance measure: what passes, what does not, and why.
  2. Regression gate: a test case that passed must keep passing; cargo test fails otherwise.
  3. Backlog generator: the report ranks the missing constructs and lists every wrong behaviour.

Graphersal's GQL is not a Cypher implementation; the TCK measures how far its compatibility forms agree with the behaviour the kit specifies.

The kit

  • Pinned version: openCypher TCK release 2024.3 (commit 677cbafabb8c3c5eed458fd3b1ec0daec8d67d23), vendored unmodified under crates/graphersal/tests/opencypher/ (features/, the named graphs in graphs/, its licence and notice). The directory's README.md records the upgrade procedure. A test case is a scenario, or one Examples row of a scenario outline.
  • Runner: the integration test target crates/graphersal/tests/opencypher_tck.rs (feature gql), with its harness in crates/graphersal/tests/opencypher/harness/. Every case runs on a fresh graph through the Rust GQL API: the setup queries (having executed, the named graphs) run through gql()'s own writes, the query runs with its parameters, then its rows, its side effects (a state diff) and its error are compared. Every query runs under resource limits and a wall-clock guard.
  • Gate: crates/graphersal/tests/opencypher/baseline.toml lists every in-scope case that does not pass yet, with its class and a one-line reason.

Out of scope

Some cases are excluded from the scope: they are not run, get the class excluded, have no baseline entry and are in no total or percentage. They are listed by case id, grouped by reason, in crates/graphersal/tests/opencypher/harness/scope.rs (ids, never tags or content, so a case that a kit upgrade adds is never excluded silently). Merely unimplemented constructs are never excluded: they stay missing, the backlog.

CodeWhyDocsTest cases
upstream-ignoremarked @ignore by the TCK itself ("does not work in Cypher")gql/tck_compliance.md#out-of-scope1
w21-property-kindsa list of maps is a valid property value (maps and lists of any kinds are stored as given); Neo4j raises a TypeError (deliberate deviation)gql/semantics.md#writes1
parameter-at-compile-timeparameters are bound when the query is compiled: a negative or non-integer SKIP / LIMIT parameter is refused then (22G02 / 22G03), not at runtime (deliberate deviation)gql/semantics.md#parameters-are-bound-when-the-query-is-compiled6
year-rangetemporal values hold the years -9999 to 9999; a year beyond them is a data error (22008), Neo4j reads years up to 999999999 (deliberate deviation)gql/semantics.md#where-dates-and-times-differ-from-neo4j2
all10
  • upstream-ignore: the one scenario that the kit itself marks @ignore.
  • w21-property-kinds (a deliberate deviation, user decision): a list of maps is a valid property value in Graphersal, where Neo4j raises a TypeError (Semantics).
  • parameter-at-compile-time (a deliberate deviation, user decision): a negative or non-integer $parameter of SKIP / LIMIT is refused when the query is compiled, since parameters are bound then; the kit expects the SyntaxError at runtime. The user sees the same thing, an error before any row (Semantics).

Every difference from Neo4j, also those the kit has no case for, is listed on Semantics.

The deliberate deviations run in a guard test (deviation_cases_still_deviate): it fails when one of them passes, so it moves back into scope. id() (an integer in Neo4j, a string id here) does not occur in the pinned kit.

Classes

ClassMeaning
passevery expectation holds: rows (and their order where stated), column names, side effects, the error type and phase
missingthe query uses a construct that gql() refuses or does not support yet (GQLSTATUS 0A000); the report ranks the constructs
setupa setup step (having executed, a named graph, a parameter value) does not run, usually for the same reason
excludedout of the scope (above): not run, in no total
wrong_resultthe rows differ
wrong_columnsthe column names differ
wrong_side_effectsthe side effects differ, or a failed query changed the graph
wrong_erroran error was expected and another one (type or phase), or none, came
unexpected_erroran error where a result was expected
timeouta time or resource budget of the harness fired
panica panic was caught (a rule-1 violation, top priority)

The headline groups them: Unsupported = missing + setup; Wrong behaviour of supported constructs = the seven classes from wrong_result to panic. An unimplemented construct is fine; a supported construct must behave as the kit specifies, unless a user decision says otherwise (then the case is excluded with its reason and documented as a difference from Neo4j). The wrong-behaviour count is driven to 0.

Errors match by type and phase only, never by the detail text. The phase comes from where the error arose: compile time is an error of parsing, binding or planning, before the traversal runs; runtime is an error while it runs.

Running and regenerating

# Run the kit (also part of the plain `cargo test --package graphersal --features script,io,display,serde,persist,gql`)
cargo test --package graphersal --features script,io,display,serde,persist,gql --test opencypher_tck

# Rewrite the baseline AND the generated blocks of this page after intended changes; review the diff like code
OPENCYPHER_UPDATE_BASELINE=1 cargo test --package graphersal --features script,io,display,serde,persist,gql --test opencypher_tck

Every run prints a summary to stderr and writes the full report to target/opencypher-report.md: the headline, the per-directory table, the exclusions with their ids, the full wrong-behaviour list by class, the missing constructs ranked by the number of cases they block, the setup failures by reason and the baseline class changes. OPENCYPHER_DETAILS=1 prints one line per in-scope case that does not pass; OPENCYPHER_LANES=<n> sets the number of parallel lanes (default: one per core).

The test fails when:

  • a case that is not in the baseline does not pass (a regression);
  • a case in the baseline passes now, no longer exists or is excluded (the entry is stale; remove it in the same change);
  • an id of the scope table does not exist, an @ignore case is not in it, or a deliberate deviation passes now (scope_table_is_consistent, deviation_cases_still_deviate);
  • a generated block of this page (scope, headline, directories, excluded) differs from what the run computes. Only trailing whitespace is ignored.

A case still failing under another class than recorded is reported, not failed. GRAPHERSAL_TEST_STORAGE=forwarding runs the whole kit on a storage that is not TraversalGraph (the Forwarding wrapper of graphersal-storage-tests): the same gate against the same baseline and page, it additionally fails when a case changes class, never rewrites either and writes target/opencypher-report-forwarding.md.

Writing Queries

This part describes the Gremlin DSL in detail, topic by topic. The DSL is the text form of a query: what the command line, the playground, Python, saved queries and AI agents run, and what script::eval_value evaluates in Rust. It is Gremlin embedded in Rhai.

The shape of a script

A script is a sequence of Rhai statements. g is the graph, __ starts an anonymous traversal, and the token classes (P, T, Order, Scope, Column, Pop, ...) are predefined:

let min_age = 30;
let names = g.v().has_label("person").has("age", P.gt(min_age)).values("name").to_list();
names.len()                                        // 2
  • Terminals run a traversal. to_list(), next() and iterate() run it and return native values; a traversal that is the last value of a script is displayed instead. A traversal in the middle of a script without a terminal is only built, not run.
  • Two spellings for TinkerPop's steps. Every TinkerPop step and function is available in snake_case (has_label, out_e) and in Gremlin camelCase (hasLabel, outE), with the same overloads. Graphersal's own extensions (create_index, memory_report, remove_property, glob_path, define_query, the Fake methods, ...) are snake_case only (since 0.3.0); a camelCase call of one fails with a help that names the snake_case name.
  • Strings in double quotes. Single quotes are Rhai character literals; maps are written #{key: value}.
  • Anonymous traversals start with __.: where(__.out("knows")), repeat(__.both()).
  • Every traversal is atomic. A failing traversal leaves nothing it wrote (Transactions).

An error names the failing step with its position in the plan, and most errors come with a help text that suggests a fix built from the failing query.

The following chapters cover traversal patterns, changing the graph, schemas, saved queries and profiling; every single step is in the Step Reference.

Displaying Results

A traversal's result is either data or display:

  • Data is what to_list(), next(), a script variable, and the Rust data API return. It is never cut: let xs = g.v().to_list(); xs.len() counts every vertex. iterate() runs a traversal for its side effects (g.add_v("x").property("a", 1).iterate()) and returns nothing: its results are discarded, never materialized, so nothing is shown.
  • Display is every rendering of results into text: a traversal left without a terminal (the session visualizer), a list or map that is a script's final value, and the explicit visualizers to_table(), to_markdown(), to_json(), to_tree(), to_mermaid(), to_plantuml(), to_json_schema() and visualize(fmt).

Display can be bounded by two limits:

LimitWhat it bounds
max_rowstop-level results: table rows, traversers, list items
max_itemsitems of every nested collection inside a row, at any depth (a fold() list, the keys of one group() row)

Where the limits come from

  • The library is unbounded by default. A Rust caller of visualize_with and a script engine built without render options get everything.
  • Front ends set a session default. graphersal and the web playground show at most 100 rows and 100 nested items, for every kind of display, including an explicit to_table(): the DSL cannot write a string to a file, so in a front end such a call is for viewing.
  • A single call overrides the session default with an options map.

Per-call options (DSL)

g.v().to_table(#{max_rows: 20})             // other limits for this call
g.v().to_json(#{max_items: 5})
g.v().visualize(V.Markdown, #{no_limit: true})  // no limit at all for this call
g.with("render.max_rows", 10).v()           // session default for one query

max_rows: 0 / max_items: 0 is an error: no_limit: true is the one way to say "unlimited". no_limit: true together with max_rows or max_items is an error too. no_limit: false keeps the session default. Both spellings work: max_rows/maxRows, max_items/maxItems, no_limit/noLimit.

Session default (embedding the DSL)

A host passes its limits as scope options, and can change them later (a REPL /set):

use std::sync::Arc;
use graphersal::prelude::*;
use graphersal::auth::AllowAll;
use graphersal::exec::RenderOptions;
use graphersal::script::{graph_scope_with_options, render_scope_options, set_scope_render_options};

let limits = RenderOptions::new().with_max_rows(100).with_max_items(100);
let graph = Arc::new(GraphSource::tinkerpop_modern());
let mut scope =
    graph_scope_with_options(graph, &render_scope_options(&limits), Arc::new(AllowAll));
// ... later: remove the limits for the rest of the session.
set_scope_render_options(&mut scope, &RenderOptions::unlimited());

render_value / try_render_value take the host's RenderOptions for final lists and maps and return a RenderedOutput.

Rust API

use graphersal::prelude::*;
use graphersal::exec::RenderOptions;

let graph = TraversalGraph::tinkerpop_modern();
let rendered = graph
    .traversal()
    .v(None::<()>)
    .visualize_with(VisualizeFormat::Table, &RenderOptions::new().with_max_rows(2))
    .unwrap();
println!("{}", rendered.text);
if let Some(notice) = rendered.notice() {
    eprintln!("{notice}");
}

visualize(fmt), to_table(), to_json(), ... are always unbounded and return a String; visualize_with, to_table_with and to_markdown_with take RenderOptions and return a RenderedOutput. RenderOptions::unlimited() / .with_no_limit() remove both limits.

How a cut is shown

The truncation is never part of the result text. RenderedOutput::truncation reports it (rows_shown, more_rows, items_cut, max_items; there is no total count, because counting would cost a full execution), and Truncation::notice() builds the one notice text every front end prints:

… showing the first 100 rows; more exist. Use .limit(n), #{no_limit: true}, /set no-limit (--no-limit), or to_list() for the data.
… nested collections were cut to 100 items. Use #{max_items: n}, /set max-items <n> (--max-items <n>), or /set no-limit (--no-limit).
  • Tables, markdown and trees mark a nested cut inside the cell with …, for example [1, 2, 3, …], or with a └─ … line in a tree. A row with more keys than max_items shows max_items columns and a … column.
  • Maps with typed keys in JSON: a map with a non-string key (groupCount().by("age")) is written in the GraphSON shape {"@type": "g:Map", "@value": [29, 1, 27, 1]}; a string-keyed map is a plain object. Tables and trees print such keys as text (29, v[1]); see Maps With Non-String Keys.
  • Non-finite floats in JSON: JSON has no number for NaN, Infinity or -Infinity, so a result holding one (math("0 / 0"), 0.0 / 0.0, a stored NaN property) writes it in GraphSON's typed form, {"@type": "g:Double", "@value": "NaN"} (payloads "NaN", "Infinity", "-Infinity"), at any depth, the same form a GraphSON export writes. The tag keeps it apart from the string "NaN", which stays a plain string. This holds for to_json(), --format json, execute().to_json(), the playground's and the dev server's answers and the MCP query tool; tables and trees print the number itself (NaN, inf, -inf), and the playground shows NaN, Infinity, -Infinity in its Table view and inspector. The tag is written, not read: plain JSON read back (serde of a value, GraphML's embedded JSON) does not turn it into a float; GraphSON import does. The serde Serialize of a value itself stays strict and refuses a non-finite float, and GraphML export refuses one (with a help naming the fix).
  • JSON stays valid JSON: an array of the first max_rows results, with nested collections cut and no marker inside, since a sentinel element would break the data's types. The only signal is the notice. The JSON-per-line fallback formats (jsonschema, mermaid, plantuml on traversal results) follow the same rules.
  • A schema (g.get_schema(), g.infer_schema()) and a profile() result are never bounded.

Graph values

A graph as a script's final value (g.e(0).to_graph(), g.e().subgraph("sg").cap("sg").next(), GraphSource::empty(), g itself) is shown as one result {"vertices": [..], "edges": [..]}, each element materialized like a g.v()/g.e() result: exactly what cap("sg") shows for a graph inside a traversal. A table prints the elements in their short form ([v[1], v[2]]), JSON with all their properties:

graphersal> g.e(0).to_graph()
╭────────────────────┬──────────────╮
│ edges              │ vertices     │
├────────────────────┼──────────────┤
│ [e[0][1-knows->2]] │ [v[1], v[2]] │
╰────────────────────┴──────────────╯

max_items bounds both lists, and only max_items + 1 vertices and edges are read, so even g on a large graph shows its first elements and the cut notice instead of materializing everything. This is display only: next() and to_graph() still return the graph itself, a source you traverse (sub.v().count().next()). The web playground shows the same result (and draws it in the Graph panel).

A single list-valued result

A traversal that yields ONE list-valued traverser (g.v().values("age").fold(), cap("a") of an aggregate("a")) is a list of one element in every terminal: to_list().len() is 1 and to_json() is [[29, 27, 32, 35]]. Nothing is unwrapped. The only difference you may see is in the graphersal printer: it prints a returned script array one element per line, so the list of one list prints as [29, 27, 32, 35] (the single element), while the flat list [29, 27, 32, 35] prints as four lines. Use to_json() or .len() to tell them apart.

Tokens and anonymous traversals

A DSL token shows as the DSL text that builds it, wherever a script prints it: as the final value (also inside a list or map), through to_string() and in string interpolation ${..}. The text is the canonical dotted spelling, and evaluating it gives the same token back:

ScriptShows
Scope::localScope.local
Order::DescOrder.desc
keys, firstColumn.keys, Pop.first
T.id, By.CountT.id, By.Count
GType.INTGType.LONG (the same type)
Operator.sum, Barrier.normSackOperator.sum, Barrier.normSack
P.gt(1).and(P.lt(3))P.gt(1).and(P.lt(3))
TextP.containing("a")TextP.containing("a")
Cardinality.single(5), CastPolicy.Default("x")the same text
__.out().has("name", "x")__.out().has("name", "x")
Scope, P (a class itself)Scope, P

An anonymous traversal (__...) is a template for a child position, not a query of your graph, so a script that returns one shows its text instead of running it; the steps read like .profile() names them. The session's step-name spelling (--spelling camel, render.spelling) applies to a displayed result (__.outE(), TextP.startingWith("a")); to_string() and ${..} always give the canonical snake_case text. A UUID is a value, not a token: it shows its canonical text.

Early stop

With max_rows = n, the visualizer appends an internal limit(n + 1) to the pipeline before it is optimized and executed, so only n + 1 results are produced and materialized. The extra one only tells whether more exist. Barriers before it (group(), order(), ...) still see the whole stream. In the executed plan it is the step limit(n + 1) [display].

An error location never shows it: the at #N: line with its caret, the plan: line, step_location() and the query a help text rewrites show the traversal as you wrote it, so g.inject(1).math("value + 1") fails with

Error: Step #1 'math("value + 1")' execution failed
  at #1: inject(1).math("value + 1")
                   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

and not with a .limit(101) [display] you never wrote. The display step is appended last, so leaving it out changes no step number. It is shown only when the failure is that step itself.

No limit is appended, and the traversal runs completely with only the output cut, when the pipeline mutates the graph (so g.v().property("x", 1) still updates every vertex) or already ends on a single-result step such as count(), fold() or group().

graphersal

  • Defaults: 100 rows, 100 nested items, the same in the REPL, -e and --in.
  • Flags: --max-rows <N>, --max-items <N> (N ≥ 1), and --no-limit. --no-limit together with either of the others is an invalid invocation (exit code 2).
  • REPL: /set max-rows <N>, /set max-items <N>, /set no-limit. Setting a limit after /set no-limit turns limits back on.
  • In -e / --in the notice goes to stderr, so stdout carries only the result (and --format json stays parseable) and the exit code stays 0. The REPL prints it after the output.
graphersal --graph large -e 'g.v()'                         # 100 rows, notice on stderr
graphersal --graph large --no-limit -e 'g.v()' > all.txt    # everything
graphersal --graph large --format json -e 'g.v()' | jq length   # 100

Web playground

The web playground uses the same defaults (changeable in its settings). It runs a traversal without a terminal as execute() and keeps all results as data; its Table, JSON and Raw views show them within the limits (Raw is the text the CLI prints), and a cut result shows the same notice above them. g.with("render.max_rows", n) and to_table(#{max_rows: n}) override the limits for one query there too.

Predicates: Comparison and Resolution

This page lists where Graphersal's predicates (P.eq, P.neq, P.lt, P.lte, P.gt, P.gte, P.within, P.without, P.inside, P.outside, P.between), their composition (and, or, not, negate) and the id order of elements differ from Apache TinkerPop 3.8.2 or settle what TinkerPop leaves open. The Deviations table at the end collects them.

One comparison core

All of these predicates compare through one rule set (TinkerPop's semantics/Comparability).

  • Numbers compare by value across int64 and float64; NaN is incomparable with everything, itself included.
  • Strings compare with strings, booleans with booleans (false < true), UUIDs with UUIDs, null only with null.
  • A string is never read as a number, a date or a UUID.
  • Incomparable means false, never an error. Every test except neq is false for an incomparable pair. A vertex, edge, path or collection on the stream against a number is false as well; for example g.V().where(P.eq(111)) is an empty result, not a cast error.
g.V().where(P.eq(111)).count().next()          // 0, no error
g.V().has("age", P.gt("x")).count().next()     // 0, a number never compares with a string

Operands are single values: a string, a number, a boolean, a date or time, a UUID, a vector or () (the items of P.within([..]) / P.without([..]) each). A list, a map or a traversal as an operand is an ArgumentMismatch naming the predicate when the step is built, never compared as its text. Comparing a list or map inside a predicate is not supported; to match a list or map property as a whole, pass the value itself, as in has("tags", ["a", "b"]). P.within() / P.without() without arguments are the empty set.

g.V().has("name", P.gt(["a"])).count().next()          // error: Argument mismatch for step 'P.gt'
g.V().has("name", P.within(["a", "b"])).count().next()  // 0: the list holds the values
g.V().has("name", P.without()).count().next()           // 6

Text predicates match strings only

TextP.startingWith, endingWith, containing and their negations (also spelled P.startingWith(..)) test a string. Any other value on the stream (a number, a UUID, a list from fold(), a map, a path, a vertex or an edge) is not one, so the predicate is false and its negation true. This is never an error, matching TinkerPop, where TextP only matches a String:

g.V().values("age").is(TextP.startingWith("2")).count().next()   // 0
g.V().fold().is(TextP.startingWith("a")).count().next()           // 0
g.V().fold().is(TextP.notStartingWith("a")).count().next()        // 1

A property handle (values("name")) and a property element (properties("name")) are tested by their stored value.

Regular expressions

TextP.regex(pattern) holds for a string in which pattern matches somewhere; TextP.notRegex(pattern) is its complement (also spelled not_regex, and bare regex(..)/notRegex(..)). Like the other text predicates, a value that is not a string makes regex false and notRegex true. The match is unanchored, as Java's Matcher.find() is; write ^...$ to match the whole string.

g.V().has("name", TextP.regex("^[jp]")).values("name").to_list()   // josh, peter
g.V().has("name", TextP.regex("(?i)^MAR")).values("name").to_list() // marko

Deviation from TinkerPop: Graphersal compiles the expression with the Rust regex crate and uses that crate's dialect, not Java's java.util.regex. Look at the crate's syntax page for what an expression may contain. Matching takes linear time in the input. The expression is compiled once, when the predicate is built: an invalid one is a script error (ValueError::InvalidRegex) before the traversal runs. In Rust the predicate is P::regex("^mar")? / P::not_regex(..)?.

Resolution of a string operand

  • where(P): a bare string operand of eq/neq/lt/lte/gt/gte/within/without is resolved in this order: a path label (as("a")), then a side effect (aggregate, store, withSideEffect), then the literal string. A side effect holding a collection compares as a whole value for eq/neq and is false for the ordering predicates. An unknown name stays a literal.
  • has(key, P), is(P), hasValue(P), all(P), any(P), none(P): operands are always literal values, as in TinkerPop; they never resolve to a label or side effect, so a name that exists as a step label or side-effect key cannot change the meaning of a property filter: g.V().as("vadas").out("knows").has("name", P.eq("vadas")) finds vadas.
  • eq/neq with a string on a vertex compares the vertex's id (is(P.eq("1")), kept from the original implementation); under where(P) a step label of that name comes first.
  • Changed in 0.2.2: before, a value filter compared a string naming a step label with the labelled element (so the first query below returned nothing). TinkerPop compares the literal; only where(P) resolves labels.
g.v(1).as("vadas").out("knows").has("name", P.eq("vadas")).values("name").to_list()   // ["vadas"]: a value filter compares the string
g.v(1).as("a").out("created").in("created").where(P.eq("a")).values("name").to_list()   // ["marko"]: where() reads the label a

hasId(P), hasLabel(P), hasKey(P)

hasId(P.neq("1")) and its siblings evaluate the predicate instead of stringifying it. A lone P.eq(x)/P.within(xs) is rewritten to the literal step so source-filter pushdown still applies.

  • Operands are always literal. No step label or side effect is consulted, so a label named like an id cannot shadow it.
  • Label and key sets. A vertex carries a set of labels, a map a set of keys. A positive predicate (eq, within, lt, ...) holds if any label or key satisfies it; a negated one (neq, without, notStartingWith, ...) holds only if all do. For a single-label vertex this is TinkerPop's behaviour.
  • A predicate mixed with other arguments (hasId(P.eq("1"), "2")) is an ArgumentMismatch.
  • Ids are strings. An order predicate (P.gt, P.gte, P.lt, P.lte, P.between, P.inside, P.outside) with a number operand in hasId(P) / has(T.id, P) is an error before the query runs, not a filter that silently matches nothing; the help shows the string form. Compare with a string instead, hasId(P.gt("3")), and mind the string order: "10" sorts before "9". Equality forms (hasId(3), hasId(P.eq(3)), hasId(P.neq(3)), hasId(P.within(1, 2)), hasId(P.without(1, 2)), also nested as in hasId(P.eq(1).or(P.eq(2)))) take numbers and compare their literal text, in the DSL and the Rust API (has_id_p(P::Neq(3))): 3 matches the id "3", a float 3.0 the id "3.0".
g.V().hasId(P.neq("1")).count().next()                     // 5
g.V().hasId(P.gt("3")).count().next()                      // 3 ("4", "5", "6")
g.V().hasId(P.without(1, 2)).count().next()                // 4
g.V().hasLabel(P.within("person", "x")).count().next()     // 4

Element order

  • TinkerPop: vertices and edges order by id; its ids are typically numbers, so 9 sorts before 10.
  • Graphersal: ids are stored as strings and compared as strings (a string is never parsed into a number), so "10" sorts before "9". Elements with equal or missing ids fall back to a structural comparison.
g.V().order().by(T.id).id().toList()   // "1", "2", ... ; with ids up to 10: "1", "10", "2", ...

Composing predicates: and, or, not, negate

g.V().has("age", P.gt(18).and(P.lt(30)).or(P.gt(35))).values("name").toList()   // marko, vadas
g.V().has("name", TextP.containing("o").and(P.lt("m"))).values("name").toList() // lop, josh
g.V().hasLabel(P.not(P.eq("person"))).count().next()                            // 2
g.V("1").out().aggregate("a").out().where(P.not(P.within("a"))).values("name").toList()
  • p.and(q) and p.or(q) are binary and left-associative: a.and(b).or(c) means (a and b) or c, a.or(b).and(c) means (a or b) and c. Evaluation is left to right and short-circuits, as TinkerPop's AndP/OrP do: P.eq(1).or(q) never evaluates q for a value equal to 1, so a runtime error on the right is not raised when the left side decides.
  • P.not(p) (also P::not(p) and a bare not(p)) and p.negate() are the complement of the result for the same stream value. TextP predicates compose with P ones.
  • The logic is two-valued. An incomparable pair is plain false (see above), so P.lt(NaN) is the "error" column of the Comparability scenarios and reduces to false; there is no third value.
  • Over a label or key set (hasLabel(P), hasKey(P)) a leaf keeps the rule above (positive: any, negated: all); a composite combines the set results: and is &&, or is ||, not is ! of the child's set result.
  • In where(P) each child resolves a string operand on its own (step label, then side effect, then literal), and the path analysis records the union of the labels of the children (P.eq("a").or(P.eq("d")) records a and d).
  • A composite is never pushed into an index or a source filter (.profile() shows has("age", P.gt(27).and(P.lt(33))) with no optimizer rule named); the results are identical with g.with("optimizer.disabled", [...]).
  • A non-predicate operand (P.gt(1).and(__.out()), P.not("x")) is an ArgumentMismatch whose help names the predicate and the traversal combinators (__.and(..), __.or(..)).
  • Not part of this feature: the infix steps g.V().has(..).and().has(..) (TinkerPop's ConnectiveStrategy) and the two-argument where("a", P) with by() modulators.

Type predicates

P.typeOf(GType.X) keeps a value of the given type (GType.STRING, GType.LONG, GType.NUMBER, GType.LIST, GType.VERTEX, ...). TinkerPop 3.8 also accepts a type name, and so does Graphersal, for a fixed list of names:

g.V().values("name").is(P.typeOf("String")).count().next()   // 6
g.V().values("age").is(typeOf("Long")).count().next()         // 4
g.V().values("age").is(P.typeOf("Byte"))                      // script error: unknown type name
NameToken
StringGType.STRING
Integer, LongGType.LONG (every integer is an int64)
Double, FloatGType.DOUBLE (every float is a float64)
OffsetDateTimeGType.DATETIME (TinkerPop's date type; see Dates and Times)
DurationGType.DURATION
LocalDate, LocalDateTime, LocalTimeGType.DATE, GType.LOCALDATETIME, GType.TIME (Graphersal's other date and time types, by their java.time names)
Boolean, UUID, Number, List, Map, Vertex, Edge, Path, Graphthe token of the same name

Both forms take the same values in both spellings (P.typeOf(GType.LONG), P::typeOf(GType::LONG), typeOf("Long") select the same ages). The names are Java's simple class names, as TinkerPop registers them, not the token names: "LONG" is not a type name, in TinkerPop either. The names are case-sensitive. Any other name is a script error (ArgumentMismatch listing the accepted names), as TinkerPop rejects a name it has not registered. In Rust, the same lookup is GType::from_type_name.

Deviations

AreaTinkerPop behaviourGraphersal behaviourWhyScenarios affected
P.typeOf(name)any name in TinkerPop's registered-type cache, custom types includeda fixed list of names (above)Graphersal has no type registry; one width per number kindnone (the suite uses "String" and an unregistered name)
negate() / P.not(p)Compare.negate() flips the operator (gt becomes lte), so the result differs from the complement for incomparable operandsThe plain complement of the result: P.not(P.gt(1)) is true for "foo" and NaNOne rule for every predicate (text, typeOf, composites); operator flipping would need a per-variant inverseNone (every vendored scenario negates a comparable number)
Error value in and/orComparability scenarios call a NaN comparison an "error" columnThere is no error value: incomparable is false, the logic is two-valuedThe expected results reduce to boolean and/or18 Comparability
Numeric widths in the test surfacebyte, short, BigInteger, BigDecimal are distinct typesOnly int64/float64 exist; the harness maps 1b/1s/1n to an integer and 1m to a float (documented in tests/tinkerpop/README.md)Widths cannot be told apart; equality is by value8 Equality, Sum, AsNumber, Inject with width literals
Composites and indexesn/aA composite predicate is not index-pushableOnly a single comparison can be folded into a rangenone
Incomparable pairsSome comparisons raisefalse for every test but neq, never an errorSee "One comparison core"Comparability, where(111) on a vertex
Element id orderNumeric ids order numericallyIds compare as strings, "10" sorts before "9"; an order predicate on a number in hasId(P)/has(T.id, P) (P.gt(3)) is an error naming the string form P.gt("3")A string is never parsed into a number; a number comparison against a string id could never holdorder().by(T.id) on ids with different digit counts
nullProperty null handling depends on the @AllowNullPropertyValues flavournull is a real stored valueGraphersal has a null typeAddVertex/AddEdge/MergeEdge null-property scenarios
Property cardinalitylist/set propertiesOne value per property keyBy design@MultiProperties scenarios

Id Arguments of V(), E() and hasId()

g.V(ids...), g.E(ids...), the nested __.V(ids...)/__.E(ids...) and hasId(ids...) take element ids. This page lists where Graphersal differs from Apache TinkerPop 3.8.2.

Arrays flatten in the first position only

  • TinkerPop: hasId(id, otherIds...) treats a list in a later position as one id that matches nothing; a list as the first argument is flattened.
  • Graphersal: the same observable result, modelled explicitly. Only the first argument flattens an array (recursively); an array in any later position contributes the empty id, which matches no element.
  • Why: the TinkerPop scenario HasId::g_VX1X_out_hasIdX2_listXid3_id4XX depends on it.
g.V(["1", "2"]).values("name").toList()      // "marko", "vadas"
g.V("1", ["2", "3"]).values("name").toList() // "marko" only

null is the empty id

  • TinkerPop: a null id is not a defined element id.
  • Graphersal: () (the DSL's null) contributes the empty id, which matches nothing, so g.E(()) and hasId(()) stay empty instead of widening to every element.

Elements and maps as ids (extension)

A map with an "id" key, as returned by next()/toList(), contributes that id, so g.E(e) works with a previously fetched edge. Any other map is rejected with an ArgumentMismatch error instead of being turned into an id that never matches.

Predicates

hasId(P) evaluates the predicate over the id; see Predicates: Comparison and Resolution.

Type Conversion and length()

Deviations of length(), as_string(), as_bool(), as_number() and cast() from Apache TinkerPop 3.8.2.

length() accepts strings only

  • TinkerPop: length() is a string step; any other input is a cast error.
  • Graphersal: the same. A list, map, path, vertex, edge or number raises a cast error, in both scopes; null stays null. Use count(Scope.local) for the size of a collection. Earlier Graphersal versions also measured lists and paths; that was removed.
g.V().fold().length().toList()            // error: expected type [string], got type 'array'
g.V().fold().count(Scope.local).toList()  // 6
  • Deviation: the length counts Unicode scalar values (Rust chars().count()). TinkerPop counts Java chars (UTF-16 code units). The two agree for every character in the Basic Multilingual Plane ("é" is 1, "日本語" is 3, in both). They differ for astral-plane characters such as emoji: "😀" is 1 here and 2 in TinkerPop. The same applies to length(Scope.local) and to length() of a label.

null: asString() and asBool() raise, asNumber() and cast() keep it

  • TinkerPop: asString() and asBool() reject null ("Can't parse null"); asNumber() keeps it.
  • Graphersal: the same, per step. as_string() and as_bool() raise a cast error on null (the configured CastPolicy still applies); as_number() and the Graphersal extension cast() keep null as null. The behaviour is deliberately not uniform.
g.inject(()).asString().toList()   // error: expected type [string], got type 'null'
g.inject(()).asNumber().toList()   // null

asBool() and asNumber() are explicit conversions

as_bool() and as_number(GType.INT | GType.LONG) follow TinkerPop's own rules, not the schema coercion matrix. The matrix (used when a declared property is written) and the Graphersal extension cast() stay strict: cast(GType.BOOLEAN) of 2 or of "TRUE" and cast(GType.INT) of 5.43 still fail, because a lossy conversion there would corrupt stored data.

asBool():

InputResult
true, falseunchanged
0, 0.0, -0.0, NaNfalse
any other number (1, -1, 3.14, Infinity)true
the texts true / false in any ASCII letter case ("tRUe", "FALSE")true / false
any other text ("hello", "1", "", " true"), null, a uuid, a collectionerror

asNumber(GType.INT) and asNumber(GType.LONG) (the same int64 target):

InputResult
an integerunchanged
a floattruncated toward zero (5.67 is 5, -5.67 is -5)
a text that parses as a whole integer ("5"), a boolean5, 1/0
nullnull
"5.7", NaN, infinity, a float outside the int64 rangeerror
  • Deviation (asNumber): TinkerPop's Integer target wraps or narrows to its own width; Graphersal has one integer width, so a NaN, infinite or out-of-range float is an error instead.
  • Deviation (asBool): only the two literals true and false convert from text, never "1" or "yes": a string is not interpreted by its content.
g.inject(-1, 0.0, "tRUe").asBool().toList()        // [true, false, true]
g.inject(5.67, -5.67).asNumber(GType.INT).toList() // [5, -5]
g.inject(5.43).cast(GType.INT).toList()            // error: stays strict

trim(), lTrim() and rTrim()

  • Deviation: the three steps strip Unicode whitespace (the White_Space property, Rust str::trim), while Java's String.trim() strips only characters up to U+0020. A no-break space (U+00A0) or an ideographic space (U+3000) at the end of a string is removed here and kept by TinkerPop. No vendored scenario depends on it.

Math Expressions

math("<equation>") evaluates an arithmetic equation for every traverser and emits the result, always as a double. Graphersal follows TinkerPop's math() step, which uses the exp4j expression language: the same operators, precedence, functions and constants, the same variable resolution and the same errors. The equation is parsed once, when the traversal is built, by Graphersal's own expression engine; it does not need the script feature.

Every example on this page was run with graphersal on the default modern graph; the line after // is its real output.

Quick reference

g.V("1").values("age").math("_ / 2").toList()                                  // 14.5
g.V().math("_ + 1").by("age").toList()                                         // 30.0, 28.0, 33.0, 36.0
g.V().as("a").out("knows").as("b").math("a + b").by("age").toList()            // 61.0, 56.0
g.V("1").project("a", "b").by("age").by(__.out().count()).math("a / b").toList()  // 9.666666666666666
g.withSideEffect("x", 100).V("1").values("age").math("_ + x").toList()          // 129.0
g.inject(1).math("2^3").toList()                                                // 8.0

In Rust the step is math(expr) on GraphTraversalSource, AnonymousTraversal and __, with the same by() modulators as in the DSL.

Syntax

An equation is built from:

  • numbers: 12, 1.5, .5, 5., 1e3, 1.2E-3, 2.5e+2 (no sign, hex or inf literal; a sign is the unary operator);
  • the current value _ and variables (a, price_2): a name [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]* that is not a function;
  • operators, functions and constants from the tables below;
  • parentheses: (, [ and { all group and call (sqrt[_]), but a closer must match its opener.

There is no implicit multiplication, as in TinkerPop (which turns it off): 2 pi, 2(3) and 2 _ are errors; write 2 * pi.

A function name without parentheses applies to everything to its right up to the end of the enclosing group, as in exp4j: sin _ is sin(_), sin _ + 1 is sin(_ + 1), and (sin _ + 1) * 2 is sin(_ + 1) * 2.

g.inject(2).math("sin _ + 1").next()           // 0.1411200080598672  (= sin(3))
g.inject(100).math("log10(_) + log(e)").next() // 3.0

Operators

Higher precedence binds tighter. Unary operators never take a pending binary operator, so -2^2 is -(2^2) and 2^-2^2 is 2^(-(2^2)).

OperatorPrecedenceAssociativityMeaning
a + b500leftaddition
a - b500leftsubtraction
a * b1000leftmultiplication
a / b1000leftdivision; a zero divisor is an error
a % b1000leftremainder with the sign of the dividend (Java %); a zero divisor is an error
a ^ b10000rightpower (right-associative)
-a5000rightnegation
+a5000rightidentity
g.inject(1).math("-2^2").next()   // -4.0
g.inject(1).math("2^3^2").next()  // 512.0
g.inject(-7).math("_ % 3").next() // -1.0

+ and - are unary at the start, after an opening bracket, after , and after another operator; everywhere else they are binary (2--2 is 4).

Functions

The exp4j 0.4.8 built-in set. All take one argument except pow. Domain errors are not errors: sqrt(-1) and log(-1) are NaN and log(0) is negative infinity, as in Java.

FunctionMeaning
abs(x)absolute value
acos(x)arc cosine (radians)
asin(x)arc sine (radians)
atan(x)arc tangent (radians)
cbrt(x)cube root
ceil(x)round up to an integer
cos(x)cosine (radians)
cosh(x)hyperbolic cosine
cot(x)cotangent; an error where tan(x) = 0
exp(x)e raised to x
expm1(x)exp(x) - 1
floor(x)round down to an integer
log(x)natural logarithm
log10(x)base-10 logarithm
log1p(x)log(1 + x)
log2(x)base-2 logarithm
pow(x, y)x raised to y
signum(x)sign: -1, 0 or 1
sin(x)sine (radians)
sinh(x)hyperbolic sine
sqrt(x)square root
tan(x)tangent (radians)
tanh(x)hyperbolic tangent

There is no round; use floor(_ + 0.5). cot, expm1, log1p and pow are exp4j built-ins that TinkerPop's math() cannot use (it declares their names as variables, which exp4j rejects); Graphersal accepts them.

Constants

ConstantValueMeaning
pi3.141592653589793π
π3.141592653589793π
e2.718281828459045Euler's number
φ1.61803398874golden ratio (exp4j's 12-digit value)

pi and e are variables with a fallback, as in exp4j: a map key, side effect or step label named e wins, and the constant is used only when the name resolves to nothing else (TinkerPop fails in that case). π and φ are always constants.

g.withSideEffect("e", 2).inject(1).math("e + _").next()  // 3.0

Variables and by()

_ is the current traverser's value. Any other variable is resolved as in TinkerPop's Scoping, in this order:

  1. a key of the current value when it is a map (project(), select(), valueMap(), elementMap(), group() results, a map-valued property);
  2. a side effect (withSideEffect(), aggregate(), store());
  3. a step label (as()); the last object with that label on the path.

The by() modulators form a ring over the distinct variables in order of first appearance: the first by() applies to the first variable, the second to the second, and so on, cycling when there are fewer by()s than variables. A variable used twice takes one slot. _'s by() runs on the current traverser; any other variable's by() runs on the resolved object.

// b appears first: b takes in("created").count(), a takes age
g.V().as("a").out("created").as("b").math("b + a").by(__.in("created").count()).by("age").toList()
// 32.0, 33.0, 35.0, 38.0

A traverser for which a by() produces nothing (by("age") on a vertex without age) is filtered out, as in TinkerPop 3.6+.

Every variable must resolve to a number. A string, a list or a map is an error; convert a numeric string with as_number(GType.DOUBLE) first.

Nested access (Graphersal extension)

Graphersal extends the language with nested access after any variable, with no whitespace before . or [. It is not part of exp4j or TinkerPop: exp4j rejects every such equation, so no TinkerPop equation changes its meaning.

FormReads
_.keya key of a map (or a property of a vertex or edge)
_["unit price"], _['k']a key that is not an identifier (escapes \\, \", \')
_[0], _[-1]an element of a list; a negative index counts from the end

The path is applied after the variable's by() projection and reads the value in place, without materializing the element.

g.V("1").elementMap().math("_.age * 2").toList()        // 58.0
g.V("1").valueMap().math("_.age[0] + 1").toList()       // 30.0  (valueMap() values are lists)
g.inject(#{price: #{total: 10, items: [1, 2.5, 4]}}).math("_.price.total * 2 + _.price.items[-1]").toList()
// 24.0
g.inject(#{"unit price": 3}).math("_[\"unit price\"] * 4").toList()  // 12.0

Errors

An equation that does not parse fails before the traversal runs, even when no traverser reaches the step. Every other problem fails the traversal for the traverser that hits it. The diagnostic underlines the offending token:

g.inject(1).math("2 pi")
// Error: math("2 pi") failed at column 3: missing operator before name 'pi'; implicit multiplication is not supported, write '*' explicitly
//   equation: math("2 pi")
//                     ^
ProblemExampleMessage
syntaxmath("2 +* 3")unexpected '*'; expected a number, a variable, a function or '('
unknown functionmath("sqr(_)")unknown function 'sqr'; ... (the help suggests sqrt)
unknown variablemath("_ + x") with no x anywherevariable 'x' is not '_', a key of the current map, a side effect or a step label
bad pathelementMap().math("_.agee")_.agee leads to no value: no key 'agee'; the available keys are: id, label, name, age
not a numbervalues("name").math("_ + 1")the variable _ for math() must resolve to a number, but it is a string
nulla null valuethe variable _.a for math() must resolve to a number, but it is null
division by zeromath("_ / 0")Division by zero! (exp4j's message; also % and cot)

The current value is _

The current value is _, as in TinkerPop; there is no other name for it. math("value + 1") fails with an unknown-variable error whose help shows the rewritten query. Results are doubles (math("2 + 2") is 4.0), and ^ is the power operator.

Map Keys and Values

group(), group_count(), project(), element_map() and select("a", "b") produce maps. This page covers how a query reads a map's keys and values generically: unfold() turns a map into its entries, and select(Column.keys) / select(Column.values) (TinkerPop select(Column)) reads keys or values.

Quick reference

On the modern graph:

g.V().group().by("name").by(__.out().count())                                 // one map
g.V().group().by("name").by(__.out().count()).unfold()                        // 6 entries: marko=3, vadas=0, ...
g.V().group().by("name").by(__.out().count()).unfold().select(Column.keys)    // "marko", "vadas", "lop", ...
g.V().group().by("name").by(__.out().count()).unfold().select(Column.values)  // 3, 0, 0, 2, 0, 1
g.V().group().by("name").by(__.out().count()).select(Column.keys)             // ONE list: ["marko", "vadas", ...]
g.V().group().by("name").by(__.out().count()).select(Column.keys).unfold()    // "marko", "vadas", "lop", ...

The order is the map's own order. group() keeps first-seen order. The index-backed group_count().by(T.label) pushdown does not guarantee any order.

unfold() of a map

unfold() emits one traverser per map entry. It still unrolls a list into its elements, and any other value passes through unchanged. An entry is its own kind of stream value (TinkerPop's Map.Entry). When an entry reaches a terminal (to_list(), next(), a table), it becomes a single-key map, which is how the Gremlin console prints marko=3:

g.V().groupCount().by(T.label).unfold().toList()
// #{"person": 4}
// #{"software": 2}

unfold() of an entry passes it through unchanged. An entry is not a collection.

select(Column.keys) / select(Column.values)

Inputselect(Column.keys)select(Column.values)
a map (group(), group_count(), project(), element_map(), a nested object property)one list of all keysone list of all values, types kept
an entry (from unfold() of a map)the keythe value
a path (from path())one list holding the step labels of each positionnot implemented: cast error
anything elsecast errorcast error

Map or entry? The rule depends on the kind of value, not on how many keys it has. A map is always a map, even with one key:

g.V("1").groupCount().by("name").select(keys).toList()            // [["marko"]]: one list
g.V("1").groupCount().by("name").unfold().select(keys).toList()   // ["marko"]: the key itself

This follows TinkerPop, where Map and Map.Entry are different types. A rule based on the number of keys ("a single-key map is an entry") would make one-group group() results behave differently from every other group() result. Only unfold() creates entries. A single-key map that went through a terminal and came back into a query (for example through inject()) is a map again, and values(k), select(k) and has(k, v) read its keys like those of a project() result:

let m = #{name: "x", age: 3};
g.inject(m).values("name").toList()        // ["x"]
g.inject(m).select("name", "age").toList() // [#{age: 3, name: "x"}]
