 .add_v("chunk").property("text", "Graphersal runs Gremlin in Rhai.").property("emb", vector([0.9, 0.2]))
   .add_e("part_of").to("d")
 .add_e("mentions").from("d").to("e")
 .iterate();
g.v().has_label("chunk").nearest("emb", vector([1.0, 0.1]), 5).as("hit")
 .out("part_of").as("doc")
 .out("mentions").has_label("entity").as("ent")
 .select("hit", "doc", "ent").by("text").by("title").by("name")
 .to_list()

The embedding of the question comes from the host (the model is never called by the engine), as a query parameter or the argument of a saved query: params: #{q: #{schema: #{type: "array", format: "vector", dimension: 384}}} with the body g.v().has_label("chunk").nearest("emb", q, k). MCP clients and the AI Chat call such a query with run_saved_query.

More like this

The query vector can come from the graph itself: label it, then search with __.select(..):

g.add_v("doc").property("id", "d42").property("emb", vector([1.0, 0.0])).iterate();
g.add_v("doc").property("id", "d7").property("emb", vector([0.9, 0.1])).iterate();
g.add_v("doc").property("id", "d9").property("emb", vector([0.0, 1.0])).iterate();
g.v().has("id", "d42").as("me").values("emb").as("q")
 .v().has_label("doc").where(P.neq("me"))
 .nearest("emb", __.select("q"), 2)
 .values("id").to_list()   // ["d7", "d9"]

Recommendations with vector_mean()

vector_mean() is a reducing barrier (like mean()): the component-wise mean of the incoming vectors, as an f32 vector. An incoming list of vectors (fold()) counts each of its vectors, null is skipped, quantized vectors count with their values, an empty stream gives no result, and vectors of different dimensions fail. local(__.unfold().vector_mean()) averages each list on its own. The mean of what a user liked is a taste vector to search with:

g.add_v("user").property("name", "u7").as("u")
 .add_v("article").property("title", "Graphs").property("emb", vector([1.0, 0.0])).as("a")
 .add_v("article").property("title", "Trees").property("emb", vector([0.8, 0.4])).as("b")
 .add_v("article").property("title", "Cooking").property("emb", vector([0.0, 1.0]))
 .add_v("article").property("title", "Forests").property("emb", vector([0.9, 0.3]))
 .add_e("liked").from("u").to("a").add_e("liked").from("u").to("b").add_e("read").from("u").to("a")
 .add_e("read").from("u").to("b")
 .iterate();
g.v().has("name", "u7").out("liked").values("emb").fold().vector_mean().as("taste")
 .v().has_label("article")
 .where(__.in("read").has("name", "u7").count().is(0))
 .nearest("emb", __.select("taste"), 1)
 .values("title").next()   // "Forests"

Performance

The search is an exact scan: its time grows with the number of scored elements times the dimension, and it needs no index, so it costs nothing to keep up to date and answers the same at every commit, mark and snapshot. Measured with the bench nearest_10k_x_384 (cargo bench -p graphersal --bench graph --features io,script,display,serde -- nearest_10k_x_384): 10 000 vertices with a random 384-dimensional embedding, v().has_label("doc").nearest("emb", q, 10), on an Apple M3:

Stored elementMetricMedianPer vector
f32cosine1.3 ms130 ns
f16cosine2.3 ms230 ns
i8cosine1.8 ms180 ns
bithamming0.21 ms21 ns

So about 13 ms per 100 000 f32 vectors of 384 components: enough for most in-memory graphs, and a filter before the search (above) scores fewer. There is no approximate (ANN) index yet (see Current Limitations). These figures come from a source build, not from the musl-linked prebuilt Linux binary (Performance of the prebuilt Linux binaries).

Quantization: memory against accuracy

A quantized property takes less memory and gives approximately the same answers. Measured by the test quantized_search_recall_against_f32 on 2 000 random 128-dimensional vectors (20 queries, recall@10 against the f32 search with cosine); random vectors are the hardest case, real embeddings usually keep more:

Stored asBytes per 384 componentsrecall@10
f321 5361.00 (exact)
f167681.00
i8384 (+ 4 for the scale)0.99
bit (hamming)480.30
bit top 100, re-ranked by f3248 + 1 5360.74

Bit vectors are a coarse, very fast prefilter: keep both properties and re-rank the prefilter's hits exactly, nearest("emb_bit", q.quantize("bit"), 100, #{metric: "hamming"}) followed by nearest("emb", q, 10).

Embeddings

An embedder turns text into vectors. The step embed() embeds the incoming string, embed(key) the string property key (a name or a jpath(..)) of the incoming element, and the function embed(text) makes a query vector before any traversal runs. Each takes an option map naming the embedder, #{embedder: "name"}; without it the host's default runs. g.embedders() lists what is registered:

g.embedders()[0].name   // "hash-ngram/1"
embed("graph").dimension   // 256
g.v().has_label("person").embed("name").count().next()   // 4
g.v().embed("name", #{embedder: "hash-ngram/1"}).count().next()   // 6
g.v().values("age").embed().next()   // error: embed() takes a string, not int64
g.v().embed("name", #{embedder: "nope"}).next()   // error: there is no embedder "nope"

Rules of the step:

  • an element without the property is dropped (like values(key)); a value that is not a string fails: nothing is converted implicitly, write as_string() first;
  • an empty text, or one with no word at all, fails (has(key, P.neq("")) leaves them out);
  • the step hands the embedder batches (up to the embedder's max_batch traversers per call), each traverser once whatever its bulk, and keeps the order;
  • .profile() names the embedder that ran: embed("name", embedder: "hash-ngram/1");
  • writing the vectors (property("emb", __.embed("text"))) happens inside the traversal's unit under the graph's write lock, which suits a fast local embedder such as the built-in one;
  • a property declared {"type": "array", "format": "vector", "dimension": 384} refuses a vector of another dimension or element kind, as for any write (Vectors in a schema).

A fuzzy name search on the modern graph:

g.v().has_label("person").property("name_emb", __.embed("name")).iterate();
g.v().has_label("person").nearest("name_emb", embed("Markus"), 2).values("name").to_list()   // ["marko", "vadas"]

What g.embedders() returns for each embedder:

Key
namethe registry name, what #{embedder: ..} takes
modelthe stable identity of what computes the vectors (hash-ngram/1, acme/minilm@3f2a9c41b7de), independent of the host's name for it and of any file path: two embedders of one model give comparable vectors
dimension, elementthe shape of every vector it returns
metricthe metric it recommends for comparing them
max_batchthe most texts per call
deterministicwhether the same text always gives the same bits
localwhether the texts stay in the process
defaultwhether it runs without an embedder option

Running an embedder asks Execute on the resource Embedder("name"), for every embedder including the built-in one (Permissions); AccessPolicy::read_only() allows it, and a saved query may embed. A computed vector is stored as a plain value: replay, recovery, change sets and loads never call an embedder, so an embedder that is not deterministic is safe to use.

Embedding a property: embed_property()

g.embed_property(#{label, from, to}) embeds the string property from (a name or a jpath(..)) of every element with label and stores the vector in its top-level property to. It is a job, not a traversal step, and returns a report:

g.set_schema(g.infer_schema(), SchemaMode.open);
let report = g.embed_property(#{label: "person", from: "name", to: "emb"});
[report.embedded, report.units, report.schema_changed]   // [4, 1, true]
OptionDefault
label(required)the label of the elements
from(required)the text property, a name or a jpath(..)
to(required)the vector property, a top-level name
element"vertex""edge" embeds edges
embedderthe host's defaultthe registry name of the embedder
only_missingtrueskip elements that have to already; false embeds every element again
batchthe embedder's max_batchelements per page (one embedder call and one unit each)

The report counts embedded, skipped_no_text (no such property, null, or a text with nothing to embed), not_text (a value that is not a string: nothing is converted), skipped_changed and skipped_removed (see below), the committed units, whether the job declared the property in the schema (schema_changed), elapsed_ms, and the embedder and model that ran.

How it runs. The job works in pages so that a slow embedder (a model in another process, a network service) never blocks the graph:

  1. it collects the ids of the elements to embed (a short read lock);
  2. per page it reads their texts (a short read lock), calls the embedder without any lock of the graph, so other queries and writers go on meanwhile, and then writes the page's vectors in one unit under the write lock;
  3. before writing an element it reads its text again: a text another writer changed since step 2 is skipped (skipped_changed), as is an element removed meanwhile (skipped_removed), so a stale vector is never stored.

Each page is atomic; the job as a whole is not. When it fails (the embedder fails, a schema refuses a write, the run is cancelled), the pages before stay committed, the failing page is rolled back, and the error stops the script; since only_missing is the default, running the job again continues where it stopped. A text the embedder finds nothing in (an empty one, punctuation only) is skipped and counted, never a failure.

Inside an open unit (an explicit transaction, and every script of the playground, which runs as one unit) the job releases nothing: it runs every phase under the unit's lock, its pages are savepoints of that unit, and it commits or rolls back with it. The CLI runs it two-phase.

The job asks Read and Update on the label's data, Execute on the embedder and, when it declares the property, Update on Schema (Permissions); a saved query cannot run it (it may write data only, never the schema). From Rust it is Graph::embed_property(&EmbedJob, &Embedders, &CancelToken, &mut progress) (two-phase, a progress callback after every page, a partial report in the error) or EmbedJob::run_in(&mut storage, ..) inside a transaction you hold.

Which model produced a property

Vectors of different models cannot be compared: a cosine between a hash-ngram/1 vector and one of a semantic model means nothing. The schema therefore records, per label and property, which model produced the vectors: the keyword embedder of a vector declaration holds the embedder's model identity (model in g.embedders(), never a registry name or a file path):

{"type": "array", "format": "vector", "element": "f32", "dimension": 256, "metric": "cosine", "embedder": "hash-ngram/1"}

embed_property needs an attached schema (mode open or closed) and keeps it right; it never creates or attaches one itself (g.set_schema(g.infer_schema(), SchemaMode.open) attaches the structure a graph has):

  • to undeclared for the label: the job declares it (type, format: vector, element, dimension, metric from the embedder, embedder its model), in the unit of the first page, so the declaration and the first vectors commit together (and travel together through the journal, a rollback, a fork);
  • declared as a vector of the embedder's dimension (or of any dimension) without embedder: the job adds embedder;
  • declared with the same model: nothing to change;
  • declared with another model: refused ("the schema declares "doc"."emb" as vectors of the model ..."): embed into another property, or change the schema deliberately and embed again with only_missing: false;
  • declared as something else (not a vector, or another dimension): refused with the schema's own type mismatch, before the embedder runs;
  • declared with another element kind (i8, f16, bit) than the embedder returns: fine, each vector is quantized to the declared element on write, exactly as a schema write of a vector of another element is, so an f32 model can fill an i8 property (a quarter of the memory) directly.

Different labels and properties may use different models: doc.emb from one, doc.title_emb or person.emb from another. A plain write of a vector (property("emb", vector)) still checks only the element kind and the dimension: the provenance is kept by embed_property and used by the text queries, not checked on every write.

Text queries

With the provenance recorded, nearest() and similarity() take the query as text: the text is embedded once per execution, with the registered embedder whose model the schema declares for the property, so the query vector always comes from the model of the stored ones:

g.set_schema(g.infer_schema(), SchemaMode.open);
g.embed_property(#{label: "person", from: "name", to: "emb"});
g.v().has_label("person").nearest("emb", "Markus", 2).values("name").to_list()   // ["marko", "vadas"]
  • The model is read per element from the attached schema (the element's labels, the property); every element the query meets must declare the same model, else the query fails naming both (filter by label first: has_label("doc")).
  • No schema attached, or no embedder declared for the property: the query fails, and its help shows how to attach a schema or run embed_property; passing a vector, nearest("emb", embed("Markus"), 2), keeps working without any schema.
  • No registered embedder of the declared model (Embedders::by_model): the query fails, and its help shows how a host registers one.
  • The key form only: similarity("emb", "text") and nearest("emb", "text", k), with a top-level property name.
  • On a property declared i8 or f16 the embedded (f32) query is compared with the stored vectors as a vector query is; on a bit property, which compares only with bit vectors, the query is quantized to bits first, with the quantizer of a write (the same as nearest("emb", g.inject(embed("text")).quantize("bit").next(), k)).
  • It asks Execute on the embedder it resolves (on each one, when the schema declares several models for the property on different labels), and .profile() names it: nearest("emb", "Markus", 2, embedder: "hash-ngram/1").

The built-in hash-ngram/1

hash-ngram/1 needs no model file and no dependency and gives the same bits on every target (the CLI, Python, the dev server, the browser playground). It lowercases the text, splits it into words (runs of letters and digits), and hashes each word and its character 3-, 4- and 5-grams (of the word framed as <word>) into 256 signed buckets, then scales the result to length 1 (f32 components, metric cosine).

It measures lexical similarity: typos, word forms and shared stems come out close, in any script ("Graph" and "grahp", "Москва" and "Москве"), meaning does not ("car" and "automobile" are unrelated). Uses: fuzzy lookup, entity matching, deduplication, and a baseline before a semantic model.

The algorithm is frozen: the output of hash-ngram/1 never changes (a different algorithm would be a new name, hash-ngram/2), and tests pin its bits. Two caveats: there is no Unicode normalization (a precomposed "é" and "e" followed by a combining accent are different words), and lowercasing and the letter/digit classes follow the Unicode version of the Rust toolchain the binary was built with.

Its time grows with the length of the text. Measured with the bench embed_hash_ngram_1000 (cargo bench -p graphersal --bench graph --features io,script,display,serde -- embed_hash_ngram_1000, 1000 texts per call, Apple M-series, source build): about 0.84 µs per short title (5 words) and about 18.5 µs per paragraph of about 1 KB, so embedding a property of 100 000 short texts takes well under a second.

Embedders for hosts

A host plugs in its own embedder (a model loaded from a file, an HTTP client, a binding language's function) by implementing the Rust trait graphersal::vector::Embedder (an embedder that holds a model in memory may also override memory_bytes(), which a host's process memory report shows): info() returns its EmbedderInfo (name, model identity, dimension, element kind, metric, batch size, determinism, locality; built at runtime, so a dimension learnt from a model file is fine), and embed(texts, ctx) returns one vector per text, calling ctx.check() between pieces of work so a cancelled or timed-out query stops. A constructor that cannot load its model returns EmbedError::unavailable(..). The host registers it in an Embedders registry and hands that to its traversals:

use std::sync::Arc;
use graphersal::prelude::*;
use graphersal::vector::{Embedders, HashNgram};

// Any `Embedder`; here the built-in algorithm with 64 components under the host's own name.
let small = HashNgram::with_dimension("acme/small", 64).unwrap();
let embedders = Arc::new(
    Embedders::builder()
        .with(Arc::new(small))
        .unwrap()
        .default_name("acme/small")
        .unwrap()
        .build(),
);
// The Rust API.
let graph = GraphSource::tinkerpop_modern();
let n = graph
    .read()
    .traversal()
    .with_embedders(embedders.clone())
    .v(None::<()>)
    .embed("name", None)
    .count()
    .next()
    .unwrap();
assert_eq!(n.and_then(|n| n.as_i64()), Some(6));
// A script host: the engine (embed(text), GraphSource::x()) and the scope (g, _g, __).
let mut engine = graphersal::script::engine();
graphersal::script::set_engine_embedders(&mut engine, embedders.clone());
let mut scope = graphersal::script::graph_scope(Arc::new(graph));
graphersal::script::set_scope_embedders(&mut scope, embedders);

The script entry points that build their own engine and scope (eval_value_with_limits, eval_value_atomic, eval_value_dry_run, ...) take the registry from Embedders::scope: embedders.scope(|| eval_value_atomic(graph, script, params, &limits, authorizer)) gives every engine, scope and traversal created inside the closure on that thread the host's registry (an explicit with_embedders/set_*_embedders wins). The Python binding runs its scripts this way.

The registry always keeps hash-ngram/1; hash-ngram and every hash-ngram/* name are reserved, a name is unique and made of letters, digits and . _ - / : (such as minishlab/potion-base-8M), and Embedders::by_model finds an embedder by its model identity. graphersal-session takes the registry in SessionPresets::with_embedders, which the dev server (its MCP query tool and the AI Chat's tools included) and the WebAssembly playground run under.

Model2Vec models (feature model2vec)

graphersal::vector::Model2Vec is a ready-made embedder for Model2Vec static embedding models (one vector per token, averaged over the text; semantic, fast on a CPU), behind the feature model2vec of the graphersal crate (off by default, native targets only; the graphersal command line has it on: Real models: Model2Vec). It loads from a local directory only and never touches the network:

use std::sync::Arc;
use graphersal::vector::{Embedder, Embedders, Model2Vec};

let model = Model2Vec::options()
    .with_max_tokens(256) // a longer text is cut (default 512)
    .load("potion", "models/minishlab/potion-base-8M")?;
assert_eq!(model.info().dimension, 256);
let embedders = Embedders::builder().with(Arc::new(model))?.default_name("potion")?.build();
Ok::<(), graphersal::vector::EmbedError>(())

  • Layouts: config.json, tokenizer.json and model.safetensors in the directory (the Model2Vec layout), or config_sentence_transformers.json beside them or beside a 0_StaticEmbedding directory holding them (the sentence-transformers layout).

  • Info: the model's dimension, f32, metric cosine, 256 texts per call, local, and deterministic: false: one build gives the same bits for the same text, but they depend on the versions of model2vec-rs and tokenizers it was built with. Vectors are L2-normalized when the model's config says so (with_normalize overrides it).

  • Model identity: model2vec/<repo>@<12 hex digits>, where <repo> comes from the manifest graphersal-embed-model.json that graphersal embed-model download writes or from Model2VecOptions::with_repo("minishlab/potion-base-8M") for a directory the host downloaded itself (the same identity as the download of the same files; a repository differing from the manifest's refuses the load), else model2vec@<12 hex digits>. The digits start a SHA-256 over the three files (Model2Vec::model_identity(dir) computes it without loading the model); no path is part of it, so a copied or moved directory keeps its identity. A normalization other than the config's adds ?normalize=false.

  • Load failures are EmbedError::Unavailable with the reason (a missing file, a file that does not parse, a tokenizer whose vocabulary does not fit the embedding matrix) and the hint to download a model. The checks at load make every later lookup safe; a tokenizer failure while embedding is EmbedError::Failed, never a panic. A text with no known token (an empty text, or only unknown words) fails like an empty text for hash-ngram/1.

  • Models in a Store: a Store keeps the models its schema needs beside the graph (Store::add_model, CLI graphersal embed-model download <repo> --into <store>), carries them in every copy with their licences, and Store::stored_embedders(&registered) registers the ones the schema names at open, an embedder the host registered for the same model winning: Embedding Models in a Store.

Storage and exchange

FormatA vector
Graphersal's binary format (snapshots, the Store, the journal)its own value tag: the element kind, the dimension, for i8 the scale, then the packed components (format spec 3)
Serialized ChangeSetexact, tagged: {"@type": "graphersal:Vector", "@value": {"element": "f32", "data": [..]}} (Transactions)
JSON results, to_json()the list of its values (an i8 or bit vector dequantized)
GraphSON exporta g:List of g:Float, which TinkerGraph loads
GraphSON importa list stays a list; it becomes a vector where the target schema declares one (mode open/closed); the exact graphersal:Vector tag is read too (GraphSON)
GraphMLthe JSON text of the list; a vector again where the target graph's schema declares one (any mode)

Exporting an i8 or bit vector as its values loses nothing that matters: a declared i8 property quantizes them back to the same codes. memory_usage() counts a vector's components exactly (plus a small header), and the memory budget of a query estimates them the same way.

From Python

A vector property is a graphersal.Vector in Python, built from a list of numbers or from any one-dimensional float32/float64 buffer such as a numpy array (the extension does not depend on numpy):

import numpy as np
from graphersal import Graph, Vector

g = Graph()
emb = np.array([0.12, -0.5, 0.33], dtype=np.float32)      # model.encode(text) in practice
g.execute('g.add_v("doc").property("emb", e).iterate()', params={"e": Vector(emb)})
v = g.query('g.v().values("emb").next()')                # graphersal.Vector
v.element, v.dimension, v.tolist()                       # ('f32', 3, [0.12, -0.5, 0.33])
Vector(emb, element="i8")                                # quantized, 1 byte per component

q = np.array([0.1, -0.4, 0.3], dtype=np.float32)          # the question's embedding
g.query('g.v().nearest("emb", q, 10).to_list()', params={"q": q})

A one-dimensional float32/float64 numpy array passed as a parameter arrives as an f32 vector, like Vector(array). See the Python binding's README for the details.

Python registers its own embedders: graphersal.Embedder(name, fn, dimension=..) wraps any Python model (fn(texts) returns the rows, or one 2-D numpy array), graphersal.Model2Vec(name, path, model="minishlab/potion-base-8M") loads a Model2Vec model from a directory you downloaded (the same model identity as the command line's download), and Graph(embedders=[..]), graph.register_embedder, graph.embed_property(label=.., source=.., target=..) and text queries work as described above (Python Quick Start: Embedders).

In the playground and the CLI

The result table shows a vector as vector[768 f32] with an expandable preview of its first values; the JSON view holds all of them. The property editor edits a vector as a JSON list of numbers (a declared vector property offers the type vector). The CLI's tables show the kind and the first values (vector[768 f32] [0.012, -0.5, 0.33, 0.1, …]), and a final vector prints as its literal.

Dates and Times

Graphersal has six date and time types. They are values of their own, like numbers and UUIDs: a property holds a date, not a string that looks like one, and a query compares, sorts and computes with it. The model follows PostgreSQL and the SQL standard; the part TinkerPop defines (datetime(), asDate(), dateAdd(), dateDiff(), DT.second to DT.day) behaves exactly as TinkerPop 3.8 specifies it (TinkerPop compatibility).

The six types

Graphersal (type_of, GType)What it isLiteralPostgreSQLSQL standardPythonTinkerPop / java.time
datetime (GType.DATETIME)an instant with the UTC offset it was written with, and the IANA zone name when it was written with onedatetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00"), datetime("2023-08-02T09:30[Europe/Berlin]")timestamptz (keeps no offset)TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONEaware datetime.datetime (a zoneinfo.ZoneInfo for a zone name)datetime, OffsetDateTime, ZonedDateTime
localdatetime (GType.LOCALDATETIME)a wall-clock date and time, no zonelocaldatetime("2023-08-02T09:30")timestampTIMESTAMPnaive datetime.datetimeLocalDateTime
date (GType.DATE)a calendar daydate("2023-08-02")dateDATEdatetime.dateLocalDate
time (GType.TIME)a time of day, no zonetime("09:30:15.5")timeTIMEnaive datetime.timeLocalTime
offsettime (GType.OFFSETTIME)a time of day with a UTC offsetoffsettime("09:30:15.5+02:00")timetzTIME WITH TIME ZONE (GQL ZONED TIME)datetime.time with a datetime.timezoneOffsetTime
duration (GType.DURATION)months, days and nanoseconds, each with its own signduration("P1Y2M3DT4H")intervalINTERVALdatetime.timedelta, or graphersal.Interval with monthsDuration, Period
type_of(datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00"))   // "datetime"
date("2024-02-29").day   // 29
duration("P1Y2M3DT4H").months   // 14
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T09:30Z")).is(P.typeOf(GType.DATETIME)).count().next()   // 1
  • Resolution: one nanosecond for every type with a time, as in java.time and TinkerPop (PostgreSQL and Python stop at the microsecond). TinkerPop's millisecond views (as_number() of a datetime, date_diff()) round down to milliseconds. Python's datetime holds microseconds: a value with a part below them comes back as a pandas.Timestamp / pandas.Timedelta (From Python). The store format, GraphSON, GraphML and the serialized change set keep every nanosecond (Storage and Exchange). The clock behind now() has the digits the platform gives (nanoseconds on Linux, microseconds on macOS, milliseconds in the browser: Clock precision).
  • Range: the years -9999 to 9999 in the proleptic Gregorian calendar (date("-0044-03-15") is year 44 BC counted astronomically, year 0 = 1 BC). A value outside the range, or a result that would leave it, is an error, never a wrapped value.
  • Offsets: a datetime keeps its offset (±18:00, whole seconds) and shows it, unlike PostgreSQL's timestamptz, which keeps only the instant. A datetime written with an IANA zone name keeps the name too (2024-03-31T12:00:00+02:00[Europe/Berlin]) and follows the zone's daylight saving rules in its calendar arithmetic; a step given an IANA zone (at_zone("Europe/Berlin")) returns a value carrying that name, one given a fixed offset (at_zone("+02:00")) a value with the offset only (Time Zones). An offsettime keeps its offset.
  • A duration is not normalized: P1M, P30D and PT720H are three different values. A month has no fixed length and a day is not always 24 hours in a time zone, so the three fields stay apart, as in PostgreSQL's interval.
  • Duration range: the months and the days are 32-bit integers each; the time part has the range of java.time.Duration (TinkerPop) and of Neo4j's duration, a 64-bit count of seconds plus the nanoseconds of one second: from -PT9223372036854775808S to PT9223372036854775807.999999999S (about ±292 billion years). Adding such a duration to a date or time whose result leaves the years -9999 to 9999 is an error.
  • No guessing: a string stays a string whatever it looks like. A date comes from a constructor, a conversion step (Conversions), a schema that declares the property (Schema), a typed value in a file (Storage and Exchange) or a Python datetime (From Python).

Script values

In a script each type is a value of its own Rhai type with getters and operators:

TypeGetters
datetimeyear, month, day, hour, minute, second, microsecond, nanosecond (on its own wall clock), offset (seconds), timezone (the zone name, else the offset text), epoch_millis
localdatetimeyear, month, day, hour, minute, second, microsecond, nanosecond
dateyear, month, day
timehour, minute, second, microsecond, nanosecond
offsettimehour, minute, second, microsecond, nanosecond (of its local time), offset (seconds), timezone (the offset text)
durationmonths, days, micros (the time part in whole microseconds), nanos (in nanoseconds); micros beyond a 64-bit integer (about 292,000 years) and nanos beyond one (about 292 years) are a range error

microsecond is the whole microseconds of the second (0-999999), nanosecond all its nanoseconds (0-999999999): time("12:00:00.123456789") has microsecond 123456 and nanosecond 123456789.

let d = datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:15.25+02:00"); [d.hour, d.offset, d.microsecond]   // [9, 7200, 250000]
datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z") + duration("P1M")   // datetime("2023-09-02T12:00:00Z")
date("2023-08-02") - date("2023-01-01")   // duration("P213D")
time("10:00") - time("09:30")   // duration("PT30M")
offsettime("10:00+02:00") - offsettime("07:30Z")   // duration("PT30M")
datetime("2024-03-30T12:00[Europe/Berlin]") + duration("P1D")   // datetime("2024-03-31T12:00:00+02:00[Europe/Berlin]")
datetime("2023-08-02T09:30+02:00").as_string()   // "2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00"

+ and - with a duration work as date_add() does; the difference of two values of one type is a duration (two datetimes or localdatetimes give days of 24 hours and a time part, two dates days, two times the elapsed time, two offsettimes the time between their UTC times of day). as_string() is the canonical text, to_string() the DSL literal. A value printed or shown as a script value is its literal (date("2023-08-02")); tables, JSON and the playground show the canonical text.

The pages of this part

  • Comparing and Sorting: equality by instant (and by UTC time of day), field-wise durations, the order of types.
  • Text Formats: the canonical output, what is read, strict and lenient input.
  • Time Zones: the bundled IANA database, offsets, zone names kept in a value, daylight saving.
  • Arithmetic: date_add(), date_diff(), age().
  • Truncation and Parts: date_trunc(), date_part().
  • Conversions: as_date(), as_duration(), as_number(), as_string().
  • now() and today(): the evaluation's start time and how a host pins it.
  • Dates in a Schema: the date formats, bounds and coercion.
  • Storage and Exchange: the binary format, GraphSON, GraphML, change sets.
  • From Python: the datetime mapping.
  • TinkerPop Compatibility: what is TinkerPop and what is an extension.
  • Dates in GQL: the openCypher temporal functions of gql() (date(), x.year, date.truncate(), duration.between()) beside the steps of this part.

The steps have generated reference pages: as_date, as_duration, date_add, date_diff, age, date_trunc, date_part, at_zone and as_local; the constructors, now(), today() and DT are on Functions, Tokens and Values.

Comparing and Sorting

Every comparison of dates goes through one set of rules: == in a script, the predicates (P.eq, P.gt, P.between, P.within, ...), dedup(), group() and group_count() keys, order(), min()/max() and the schema bounds.

datetime: by its instant

Two datetimes are equal when they are the same instant, whatever their offsets (12:00Z equals 14:00+02:00). This is PostgreSQL's equality and TinkerPop's ("dates are evaluated based on the numerical comparison of Unix Epoch time"). The offset is kept and shown, but never compared:

datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z") == datetime("2023-08-02T14:00+02:00")   // true
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z"), datetime("2023-08-02T14:00+02:00")).dedup().count().next()   // 1
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T14:00+02:00")).is(P.gt(datetime("2023-08-02T11:00Z"))).count().next()   // 1

A zone name is shown but never compared either: 2023-08-02T14:00+02:00[Europe/Berlin] equals 2023-08-02T12:00Z (as Neo4j and the openCypher TCK compare instants).

datetime("2023-08-02T14:00[Europe/Berlin]") == datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")   // true

Of two values with the same instant and different offsets the first one met is kept (dedup(), a group() key); their order in a sort is unspecified. To compare the wall clocks instead, convert first: as_local() gives the wall-clock localdatetime (Time Zones).

offsettime: by its UTC time of day

Two offsettimes are equal when they are the same time of day in UTC (12:00+01:00 equals 11:00Z), and order by it, as a datetime compares by its instant (java.time OffsetTime.isEqual / isBefore). The offset is kept and shown, never compared; the UTC time is not wrapped around midnight (01:00+02:00 is before 00:00Z, the previous day's 23:00 in UTC).

offsettime("12:00+01:00") == offsettime("11:00Z")   // true
offsettime("01:00+02:00") < offsettime("00:00Z")   // true

duration: field-wise equal, ordered by length

Two durations are equal when their months, days and nanoseconds are equal: P1M is not P30D, and P1D is not PT24H (a day in a time zone may have 23 or 25 hours). Sorting compares their length as PostgreSQL does for an interval, counting a month as 30 days and a day as 24 hours; equal lengths are ordered by months, then days, then the time part:

duration("P1M") == duration("P30D")   // false
g.inject(duration("P1M"), duration("P30D"), duration("PT719H")).order().to_list()   // [PT719H, P30D, P1M]

The other types: by calendar and clock

A date, a localdatetime and a time compare by their calendar or clock value.

g.inject(time("10:00")).is(P.between(time("09:00"), time("17:00"))).count().next()   // 1
g.inject(date("2023-08-02")).is(P.within(date("2023-08-02"), date("2023-08-03"))).count().next()   // 1

Different types

Values of different types are never equal, and an ordering predicate between them does not match (no error): a date is not a datetime, and a date is never equal to a string, as a UUID is not. Convert one side first (Conversions).

g.inject(date("2023-08-02")).is(P.eq("2023-08-02")).count().next()   // 0
g.inject(date("2023-08-02")).is(P.lt(datetime("2024-01-01T00:00Z"))).count().next()   // 0
g.inject(date("2023-08-02")).as_date().is(P.lt(datetime("2024-01-01T00:00Z"))).count().next()   // 1

order() of a mixed stream puts the dates after the numbers and before the strings (TinkerPop's orderability places its date type there), in the order date, localdatetime, datetime, time, duration, offsettime:

g.inject("x", 1, duration("P1D"), time("01:00"), datetime("2023-08-02T00:00Z"), date("2023-08-02")).order().to_list()

Property indexes

A property index on a key holding dates and times serves has() with these same rules: an equality or P.within reads the values equal to the operand (a datetime by its instant, an offsettime by its UTC time of day, a duration field by field), a range (P.gt, P.between, ...) reads the values of the operand's type in that range. The results are always the same as without the index.

g.create_index(#{label: "person", key: "joined"});
g.v().has("name", "marko").property("joined", datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).iterate();
g.v().has_label("person").has("joined", datetime("2023-08-02T14:00+02:00")).count().next()   // 1

Text Formats

Dates are read and written as ISO 8601 text (RFC 3339 for a datetime, with the RFC 9557 zone suffix). No locale formats, no two-digit years, no guessing: a text is read as a date only where a date is asked for (a constructor, a conversion step, a declared schema format, a typed value in a file).

Canonical output

Every value has one text, the one tables, JSON, GraphML, GraphSON and as_string() write. It is the text java.time writes, so other tools read it back:

TypeCanonical text
date2023-08-02; a year before 1 or after 9999 with its sign: -0044-03-15
time09:30:00; a fraction only when it is not zero, in groups of three digits (milliseconds, microseconds or nanoseconds): 09:30:00.500, 09:30:00.123456, 09:30:00.123456789
localdatetime2023-08-02T09:30:00 (the date, T, the time)
datetime2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00; Z for a zero offset; an offset with seconds as +00:19:32; a zone name after the offset in brackets: 2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00[Europe/Berlin]
offsettime09:30:00+02:00, 09:30:00Z: the time as for a time, then the offset
durationP1Y2M3DT4H5M6S: years and months from the months, days, then the time part; a zero part is left out, a zero duration is PT0S; a sign before P when every part is negative (-P1M2D), else a sign per part (P1M-2D)
time("09:30:00.1").as_string()   // "09:30:00.100"
datetime("2023-08-02 09:30+00:00").as_string()   // "2023-08-02T09:30:00Z"
duration("PT90M").as_string()   // "PT1H30M"
duration("P2W").as_string()   // "P14D"

A duration keeps its three fields as they are: PT36H stays PT36H (not P1DT12H), and weeks are read as 7 days. Years and months are one field, months: P1Y2M is 14 months.

What is read

TypeAccepted text
dateYYYY-MM-DD; a year before 1 with its sign (-0044-03-15)
timeHH:MM, HH:MM:SS, HH:MM:SS.f with 1 to 9 fraction digits, kept to the nanosecond
localdatetimea date, optionally followed by T (or t, or a space) and a time; a date alone is midnight
datetimea local date-time, then an offset (Z, +02:00, +0200, +02, +00:19:32) and/or a zone in brackets ([Europe/Berlin], kept in the value)
offsettimea time as for a time, then an offset (Z, +02:00, +0200, +02), which it must have; no zone name
duration[+-]P[nY][nM][nW][nD][T[nH][nM][n[.f]S]], a sign per number allowed (P1M-2D), letters in either case
datetime("2023-08-02T09:30+0200")   // datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00")
datetime("2023-08-02T09:30[Europe/Berlin]")   // datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00[Europe/Berlin]")
datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00.123456789Z")   // datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00.123456789Z")
offsettime("09:30+0200")   // offsettime("09:30:00+02:00")
offsettime("09:30")   // error: an offsettime needs its UTC offset
date("10000-01-01")   // error: expected a four-digit year
duration("1 day")   // error: not an ISO 8601 duration

A datetime with only a zone is resolved in it (a wall-clock time the zone skips moves forward, one it repeats takes the earlier offset, see Time Zones); with an offset and a zone the offset must be the zone's at that instant.

Strict and lenient: a datetime without an offset

TinkerPop reads a date-time text without an offset as UTC (asDate("2023-08-02") is midnight UTC). Graphersal does that only where a query asks for a conversion:

  • lenient (no offset = UTC, a date alone = midnight UTC): the datetime() / DateTime() constructor and the conversion steps as_date() and as_date(GType.DATETIME);
  • strict (an offset or a zone is required): every place a text is stored as a datetime, namely a property declared "format": "date-time" in the schema, the formatMinimum/formatMaximum bounds, a typed gx:OffsetDateTime in GraphSON or a change set, a saved query argument declared as a date-time, and the playground's property editor.
datetime("2023-08-02T09:30")   // datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00Z")
g.inject("2023-08-02").as_date().next()   // datetime("2023-08-02T00:00:00Z")

A stored instant without its offset would be a guess about where it was written; the strict rule turns that guess into an error that names the expected form. The other types have no offset (an offsettime always needs its offset), so they read the same everywhere.

Time Zones

A datetime carries the UTC offset it was written with. Written with an IANA zone name (datetime("2024-03-30T12:00[Europe/Berlin]"), a GQL timezone: 'Europe/Berlin', a Python zoneinfo.ZoneInfo), it keeps the name as well, and its calendar arithmetic follows the zone (Zone names in a value). An operation can also take a zone as an argument and give back a datetime with the zone's offset at that instant, carrying the zone's name when the argument is an IANA name: the PostgreSQL model (AT TIME ZONE, a session zone for the calendar arithmetic), with the zone passed explicitly instead of a session setting, and the java.time model (atZoneSameInstant gives a ZonedDateTime that keeps its zone).

Zone arguments

A zone argument is one of:

  • an IANA zone name: "Europe/Berlin", "America/New_York", "UTC"; a datetime the step returns keeps the name (+02:00[Europe/Berlin], Z[UTC]);
  • a fixed offset: "+02:00", "-0530", "Z"; a datetime the step returns has that offset and no name.
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).at_zone("Europe/Berlin").next()   // datetime("2023-08-02T14:00:00+02:00[Europe/Berlin]")
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).at_zone("+02:00").next()   // datetime("2023-08-02T14:00:00+02:00")

The IANA rules come from the time zone database bundled with Graphersal (the jiff-tzdb crate). Every machine, and the browser playground, gives the same answer to the same query, and a replayed journal computes what it computed when it was written; the database changes only with a Graphersal release, not with an operating system update. An unknown name is an error, found before any value is read:

g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).at_zone("Mars/Olympus").next()   // error: unknown time zone

The steps that take a zone: at_zone(zone), as_local(zone), date_add(.., zone), date_diff(.., zone), age(.., zone), date_trunc(.., zone), date_part(.., zone), and today(zone). Only a datetime (and the localdatetime of at_zone) takes one; the other types have no instant, and a zone argument for them is an error.

Zone names in a value

A text with a zone in brackets (RFC 9557, java.time ZonedDateTime) keeps the zone's name beside the offset; the value prints it back:

datetime("2024-03-30T12:00[Europe/Berlin]")   // datetime("2024-03-30T12:00:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]")
datetime("2024-03-30T12:00[Europe/Berlin]").timezone   // "Europe/Berlin"
datetime("2024-03-30T12:00+01:00").timezone   // "+01:00"

Such a value computes in its zone wherever a zone argument could be given and none is: adding days, weeks, months or years keeps the wall-clock time and takes the zone's offset at the new day, while hours and smaller units (and the time part of a duration) move the instant. A difference in days or larger units, age(), date_trunc() and date_part() read the wall clock of the zone. The result keeps the name.

datetime("2024-03-30T12:00[Europe/Berlin]") + duration("P1D")   // datetime("2024-03-31T12:00:00+02:00[Europe/Berlin]")
datetime("2024-03-30T12:00[Europe/Berlin]") + duration("PT24H")   // datetime("2024-03-31T13:00:00+02:00[Europe/Berlin]")
g.inject(datetime("2024-03-31T12:00[Europe/Berlin]")).date_trunc(DT.day).next()   // datetime("2024-03-31T00:00:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]")

A zone argument wins over the value's own zone (at_zone(), date_add(.., zone), ...): the result carries the argument's name when it is an IANA zone and no name when it is a fixed offset, whatever zone the input had. To drop a name and keep the instant, pass the offset: at_zone("+02:00"). Equality and order ignore the name, as they ignore the offset (Comparing and Sorting). The name is the database's spelling (europe/berlin reads as Europe/Berlin); a fixed offset in brackets ([+01:00]) is no name. The store, GraphSON, GraphML (through a schema), the change set and Python keep the name (Storage and Exchange).

Moving between a datetime and its wall clock

  • at_zone(zone) on a datetime: the same instant, written with the zone's offset at it (PostgreSQL AT TIME ZONE, java.time atZoneSameInstant).
  • at_zone(zone) on a localdatetime: the wall-clock time read in the zone, the datetime of that instant (java.time atZone).
  • as_local() / as_local(zone): the wall-clock localdatetime a datetime shows on its own offset or in the zone (toLocalDateTime).
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).at_zone("America/New_York").next()   // datetime("2023-08-02T08:00:00-04:00[America/New_York]")
g.inject(localdatetime("2023-08-02T12:00")).at_zone("+02:00").next()   // datetime("2023-08-02T12:00:00+02:00")
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).as_local("Asia/Tokyo").next()   // localdatetime("2023-08-02T21:00:00")

Daylight saving: gaps and folds

Where a zone moves its clocks, a wall-clock time can be missing (a spring-forward gap) or happen twice (a fall-back fold). Graphersal resolves both as PostgreSQL and java.time do (the "compatible" rule), never with an error:

  • a time in a gap moves forward by the length of the gap: 02:30 on 2023-03-26 in Berlin becomes 03:30+02:00;
  • a time in a fold takes the earlier offset: 02:30 on 2023-10-29 in Berlin is 02:30+02:00, the first of the two.
g.inject(localdatetime("2023-03-26T02:30")).at_zone("Europe/Berlin").next()   // datetime("2023-03-26T03:30:00+02:00[Europe/Berlin]")
g.inject(localdatetime("2023-10-29T02:30")).at_zone("Europe/Berlin").next()   // datetime("2023-10-29T02:30:00+02:00[Europe/Berlin]")

The same rule applies to a text with only a zone (datetime("2023-03-26T02:30[Europe/Berlin]")) and to every result a zone computes on the wall clock.

Calendar arithmetic in a zone

Without a zone a datetime is computed on its own fixed offset: date_add(DT.day, 1) adds 24 hours, as TinkerPop specifies. With a zone, calendar units work on the zone's wall clock, so a day stays a calendar day across a daylight saving change (23 or 25 hours long), while hours stay hours:

g.inject(datetime("2023-03-25T12:00+01:00")).date_add(DT.day, 1).next()   // datetime("2023-03-26T12:00:00+01:00")
g.inject(datetime("2023-03-25T12:00+01:00")).date_add(DT.day, 1, "Europe/Berlin").next()   // datetime("2023-03-26T12:00:00+02:00[Europe/Berlin]")
g.inject(datetime("2023-03-25T12:00+01:00")).date_add(DT.hour, 24, "Europe/Berlin").next()   // datetime("2023-03-26T13:00:00+02:00[Europe/Berlin]")

The same holds for date_diff() in days and larger units, age(), date_trunc() and date_part(): they read the wall clock of the zone. Without a zone, date_diff() and age() read both operands on the wall clock of the second operand's offset:

g.inject(datetime("2023-03-26T12:00+02:00")).date_diff(datetime("2023-03-25T12:00+01:00"), DT.day).next()   // 0 (23 hours)
g.inject(datetime("2023-03-26T12:00+02:00")).date_diff(datetime("2023-03-25T12:00+01:00"), DT.day, "Europe/Berlin").next()   // 1
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_trunc(DT.day, "America/New_York").next()   // datetime("2023-08-02T00:00:00-04:00[America/New_York]")

GQL has no zone argument of a step: a zone name in its text (datetime('..[Europe/Berlin]')), in a map (timezone: 'Europe/Berlin') or given to a clock (datetime('Europe/Berlin')) is kept in the value, as Neo4j keeps it, and its arithmetic then follows the zone (Dates in GQL).

Arithmetic

Three steps compute with dates: date_add() moves a value, date_diff() measures the distance between two values as a number, age() as a duration. All of them are checked: a result outside the years -9999 to 9999 is an error, never a wrapped value. In a script the operators + and - do the same (script values). In GQL, + with a duration and duration.between() follow Neo4j's rules instead (Dates in GQL).

Units: the DT token

DT.second, DT.minute, DT.hour and DT.day are TinkerPop's (the bare names second, minute, hour and day work too, as in the TinkerPop scenarios). Graphersal adds the smaller and the calendar units, with PostgreSQL's field names:

UnitKindAdding it
DT.nanosecond, DT.microsecond, DT.millisecond, DT.second, DT.minute, DT.houra fixed lengthmoves the instant (or the clock) by that many units
DT.day, DT.weekcalendar daysmoves the wall-clock date; in a zone the time of day is kept across a daylight saving change
DT.month, DT.quarter, DT.year, DT.decade, DT.century, DT.millenniumcalendar months (1, 3, 12, 120, 1200, 12000)moves the month and clamps the day to the end of the target month

DT.day_of_week, DT.iso_day_of_week, DT.day_of_year, DT.iso_year, DT.epoch and DT.offset are parts, not units: only date_part() takes them.

date_add()

date_add(DT.unit, n) adds n units (a negative n subtracts); date_add(duration) adds a duration. Both take an optional zone as the last argument (Time Zones).

g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_add(DT.hour, 36).next()   // datetime("2023-08-04T00:00:00Z")
g.inject(date("2023-08-02")).date_add(day, 3).next()   // date("2023-08-05")
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_add(DT.millisecond, 1500).next()   // datetime("2023-08-02T12:00:01.500Z")

Month ends. Adding months keeps the day of the month where it exists and otherwise takes the last day of the target month, as PostgreSQL and java.time do. Each step clamps on its own, so two single months can end earlier than two months at once:

g.inject(date("2024-01-31")).date_add(DT.month, 1).next()   // date("2024-02-29")
g.inject(date("2024-01-31")).date_add(DT.month, 2).next()   // date("2024-03-31")
g.inject(date("2024-01-31")).date_add(DT.month, 1).date_add(DT.month, 1).next()   // date("2024-03-29")

A duration is added in PostgreSQL's order: its months first (clamped), then its days, then its time part.

g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_add(duration("P1M1DT1H")).next()   // datetime("2023-09-03T13:00:00Z")
g.inject(date("2024-02-29")).date_add(duration("P1Y1D")).next()   // date("2025-03-01")

What each type accepts:

TypeDT unitsA duration
datetimeall units; a fixed length moves the instant and keeps the offset (TinkerPop: a day is 24 hours at a fixed offset), with a zone the result takes the zone's offset (and its name, for an IANA zone); a datetime with a zone name computes in its zone and keeps the name when no zone is given (Time Zones)any
localdatetimeall units, on the wall clockany
dateday and largerwithout a time part
timehour and smaller; the clock wraps around midnight (PostgreSQL time + interval)without months or days
offsettimeas a time, on its local time; the offset stayswithout months or days
durationall units: adds to the matching fieldany (field by field)
g.inject(time("23:00")).date_add(DT.hour, 2).next()   // time("01:00:00")
g.inject(date("2024-02-29")).date_add(DT.hour, 2).next()   // error: adding the unit hour is not defined for a date

date_diff()

date_diff(other) is TinkerPop's dateDiff(): the incoming value minus other in milliseconds, an int64, each operand's epoch milliseconds rounded down. other is a value or a child traversal whose first result is the operand; () (null) stands for the epoch.

g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_diff(datetime("2023-08-01T00:00Z")).next()   // 129600000
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_diff(__.constant(datetime("2023-08-01T00:00Z"))).next()   // 129600000
g.inject(datetime("1970-01-01T00:00:01Z")).date_diff(()).next()   // 1000

Graphersal extends it to the other types (both operands of one type: a date counts from midnight, a time within the day; () is 1970-01-01 or midnight) and adds date_diff(other, DT.unit[, zone]): the difference in whole units, truncated toward zero.

  • Units below a day count the elapsed time.
  • Days and weeks count wall-clock days (a datetime on the wall clock of other's offset, or of the zone).
  • Months and larger count as java.time's ChronoUnit.between: a month is complete when the day of the month (and the time) is reached again, so January 31 to February 28 is 0 months.
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_diff(datetime("2023-08-01T00:00Z"), DT.hour).next()   // 36
g.inject(time("10:00")).date_diff(time("09:00"), DT.minute).next()   // 60
g.inject(date("2024-02-28")).date_diff(date("2024-01-31"), DT.month).next()   // 0
g.inject(date("2024-03-31")).date_diff(date("2024-02-29"), DT.month).next()   // 1

age()

age(other[, zone]) is PostgreSQL's age: the difference as a duration of whole years and months, days and a time part, all with the same sign. It is counted down from the incoming value to other with PostgreSQL's borrowing rules, so swapping the operands negates the result. Both operands have the same type; () is an error.

g.inject(date("2001-04-10")).age(date("1957-06-13")).next()   // duration("P43Y9M27D")
g.inject(date("1957-06-13")).age(date("2001-04-10")).next()   // duration("-P43Y9M27D")
g.inject(datetime("2024-02-29T00:00Z")).age(datetime("2023-01-31T12:00Z")).next()   // duration("P1Y28DT12H")

To get a plain number of days, years or hours, use date_diff(other, DT.unit); to get a duration of elapsed time without calendar units, subtract the two values in a script (a - b).

Truncation and Parts

date_trunc(DT.unit) is PostgreSQL's date_trunc, and date_part(DT.unit) is its extract. Both are Graphersal extensions; TinkerPop has neither. GQL's X.truncate() and x.year do the same with Neo4j's names, but truncate millennia and centuries as Neo4j does (Dates in GQL). A datetime is read on its own wall clock, or on the wall clock of a zone given as the last argument (Time Zones).

date_trunc()

The fields below the unit become their first value: the start of the hour, the day, the month. A truncated datetime keeps its offset (or, with a zone, takes the zone's offset at the new instant, and the zone's name when it is an IANA zone).

g.inject(datetime("2023-08-17T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_trunc(DT.hour).next()   // datetime("2023-08-17T15:00:00+02:00")
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-17T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_trunc(DT.week).next()   // datetime("2023-08-14T00:00:00+02:00")
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-17T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_trunc(DT.day, "UTC").next()   // datetime("2023-08-17T00:00:00Z")
g.inject(date("2023-08-17")).date_trunc(DT.quarter).next()   // date("2023-07-01")
g.inject(duration("P1Y2M3DT4H5M")).date_trunc(DT.day).next()   // duration("P1Y2M3D")
UnitTruncates to
nanosecond ... hourthe start of that unit of the clock (nanosecond keeps the value)
daymidnight
weekMonday, midnight (ISO 8601 weeks)
month, quarter, yearthe first day of the month, of the quarter (January, April, July, October), of the year
decadethe first day of a year divisible by 10 (2020-01-01)
century, millenniumthe first day of a year ending in 01/001: centuries and millennia start at year 1, as PostgreSQL counts them (2001-01-01 starts the 21st century)

A date takes day and larger, a time and an offsettime hour and smaller (the offset stays), a duration keeps the fields at and above the unit (month and larger keep whole multiples of the unit's months and drop the days and the time part).

date_part()

One field as a number: an int64, except DT.epoch, a float64 of seconds.

PartValue
DT.year, DT.month (1-12), DT.day (1-31), DT.hour, DT.minute, DT.second (0-59)the field
DT.millisecond (0-999), DT.microsecond (0-999999), DT.nanosecond (0-999999999)the fraction of the second in that unit; unlike PostgreSQL, not the seconds with the fraction
DT.quarter (1-4)the quarter
DT.week (1-53)the ISO 8601 week number
DT.iso_yearthe ISO 8601 week-numbering year (2023-01-01 is in week 52 of 2022)
DT.day_of_week0 = Sunday to 6 = Saturday (PostgreSQL dow)
DT.iso_day_of_week1 = Monday to 7 = Sunday (PostgreSQL isodow)
DT.day_of_year (1-366)the day of the year
DT.decade, DT.century, DT.millenniumas PostgreSQL counts them (the 21st century is 2001-2100)
DT.epochseconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z (a localdatetime read as UTC); for a duration its length with a year of 365.25 days and a month of 30 days
DT.offsetthe UTC offset of a datetime or an offsettime in seconds
g.inject(date("2023-08-17")).date_part(DT.day_of_week).next()   // 4
g.inject(datetime("2023-01-01T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_part(DT.week).next()   // 52
g.inject(datetime("2023-01-01T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_part(DT.iso_year).next()   // 2022
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-17T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_part(DT.epoch).next()   // 1692280032.5
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-17T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_part(DT.offset).next()   // 7200
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T02:00Z")).date_part(DT.day, "America/New_York").next()   // 1

A date has no clock parts (hour and smaller), a time only those (and epoch, the seconds since midnight). A duration gives PostgreSQL's interval fields: year and month from its months (14 months are 1 year and 2 months), day its days, hour and smaller from its time part; it has no week, day-of parts, iso_year or offset:

g.inject(duration("P1Y2M3DT4H5M6.5S")).date_part(DT.month).next()   // 2
g.inject(date("2023-08-17")).date_part(DT.hour).next()   // error: the part hour is not defined for a date

Conversions

A value becomes a date only through an explicit step; nothing is converted by guessing (a string that looks like a date stays a string).

as_date(): TinkerPop's asDate()

as_date() converts to a datetime exactly as TinkerPop's asDate() does:

IncomingResult
a datetimeunchanged
a stringread leniently as ISO 8601 / RFC 3339: without an offset it is UTC, a date alone is midnight UTC (Text Formats)
an int64milliseconds since the epoch, in UTC
a date, a localdatetimethe datetime at UTC (Graphersal: TinkerPop has no such types)
anything else (a float64, (), a list, a map, a time, a duration, an element)an error starting with "Can't parse", as in TinkerPop
g.inject("2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00", 1690000000000, date("2023-08-02")).as_date().to_list()   // [2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00, 2023-07-22T04:26:40Z, 2023-08-02T00:00:00Z]
g.inject(1.5).as_date().next()   // error: Can't parse float64 1.5 as a datetime

as_date(GType.X): to another date type

as_date(GType.DATETIME | DATE | LOCALDATETIME | TIME | OFFSETTIME) converts to that type (a Graphersal extension, spelled like as_number(GType.LONG)):

Incoming →DATETIMEDATELOCALDATETIMETIMEOFFSETTIME
stringlenient, as as_date()strict: a date textstrict: a local date-time textstrict: a time textstrict: a time text with its offset
datetimeunchangedits wall-clock date (at its own offset)its wall clockits wall-clock timeits wall-clock time and offset
localdatetimeat UTCits dateunchangedits timeits time at UTC
datemidnight UTCunchangedmidnightan erroran error
timean erroran erroran errorunchangedat UTC
offsettimean erroran erroran errorits local timeunchanged
int64epoch milliseconds, UTCan erroran erroran erroran error
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T09:30+02:00")).as_date(GType.OFFSETTIME).next()   // offsettime("09:30:00+02:00")
g.inject(offsettime("09:30+02:00")).as_date(GType.TIME).next()   // time("09:30:00")

GType.DURATION is not a target here: use as_duration(). To read a datetime's wall clock in another zone, use as_local(zone) first (Time Zones).

g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T23:30-07:00")).as_date(GType.DATE).next()   // date("2023-08-02")
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T23:30-07:00")).as_local("UTC").as_date(GType.DATE).next()   // date("2023-08-03")
g.inject("2023-08-02").as_date(GType.DATE).next()   // date("2023-08-02")
g.inject("2023-08-02T09:30").as_date(GType.DATE).next()   // error: unexpected text after the value

as_duration()

as_duration() reads an ISO 8601 duration text; a duration passes unchanged, anything else fails with "Can't parse".

g.inject("PT90M").as_duration().next()   // duration("PT1H30M")

To numbers and text

  • as_number() of a datetime is its epoch milliseconds (TinkerPop), rounded down; the other date types are not numbers (use date_part(DT.epoch) or date_diff()).
  • as_string() of any date is its canonical text; in a script, x.as_string() does the same.
  • cast(GType.DATETIME) (and the other date tokens) parses a string or, for DATETIME, reads an int64 as epoch milliseconds, like as_date(GType.X).
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T00:00Z")).as_number().next()   // 1690934400000
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T09:30+02:00")).as_string().next()   // "2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00"
g.inject(date("2023-08-02")).as_number().next()   // error: Cast exception

Storing text as a date

A property written as a string stays a string. To store dates, declare the property in the schema ("format": "date-time"): in open and closed mode a string written to it is converted on write. Or convert in the query: property("at", __.constant(text).as_date()), or write a date value (property("on", date("2023-08-02"))).

now() and today()

now() is the current time as a datetime in UTC; today() is its date, and today(zone) the date in a zone (an IANA name or an offset).

type_of(now())   // "datetime"
now() == now()   // true
type_of(today("Europe/Berlin"))   // "date"
g.add_v("event").property("at", now()).values("at").count().next()   // 1

The start of the evaluation

Like PostgreSQL's now() (CURRENT_TIMESTAMP), now() is the time the script evaluation started, the same value for every call in it: a script that stamps a thousand elements stamps them all with one instant, and now() == now() holds. In the playground a whole script is one unit, so now() is the start of that unit. A saved query called from a script sees its caller's now().

now() and today() are script functions, evaluated before the traversal runs: the traversal gets the resulting value as a constant (inject(now()), property("at", now()), has("at", P.lt(now()))). The journal of a Store and a change set record that value, never the call, so a replay or a recovery writes the same instant, not the time of the replay.

today() is the date of now() in UTC, PostgreSQL's current_date in a UTC session. For the date in another zone pass the zone, or convert the instant yourself:

today("UTC") == today()   // true
g.inject(now()).as_local("America/Los_Angeles").as_date(GType.DATE).next() == today("America/Los_Angeles")   // true

Pinning the clock (hosts)

A host that needs a deterministic clock (tests, a replay of a recorded session) pins it on its engine with graphersal::script::pin_now; every evaluation on that engine then returns the pinned instant, until it is unpinned with None:

use graphersal::script::{engine_with_options, pin_now};
use graphersal::temporal::DateTime;

let mut engine = engine_with_options(&limits, authorizer, &presets);
pin_now(&mut engine, Some("2023-08-02T23:30:00-07:00".parse::<DateTime>()?));
// now() is 2023-08-02T23:30:00-07:00, today() is 2023-08-03 (the UTC date)
pin_now(&mut engine, None); // the system clock again

The system clock is read through web_time, so now() works the same in the WebAssembly playground.

Clock precision

now(), today(), the GQL clocks (datetime(), date(), CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, X.statement(), ...) and the time a schema's defaultFunction: "now" stores all come from the system clock, taken once (at the start of the evaluation, or of the outermost open unit). The time is kept in nanoseconds, with the digits the platform clock gives and never invented ones (the digits below are zero):

PlatformDigits of the system clock
Linuxnanoseconds
macOSmicroseconds (CLOCK_REALTIME)
Windows100 nanoseconds
WebAssembly (the browser playground, Node.js)milliseconds (Date.now())

A pinned clock (pin_now, GraphTraversalSource::with_now) keeps every digit of the pinned value. A Store keeps every digit of a stored now() (file format version 3, Storage and Exchange).

Dates in a Schema

A schema declares a date property as a JSON Schema string with a format, and bounds it with the format* keywords. The full reference (every keyword, the errors and why, inference and diffs) is on the Schemas page; this page is the overview.

formatTypeExample value
date-timedatetime2024-05-01T09:30:00+02:00
local-date-timelocaldatetime2024-05-01T09:30:00 (a Graphersal name: JSON Schema has none)
datedate2024-05-01
timetime09:30:00 (local; JSON Schema's own time requires an offset)
offset-timeoffsettime09:30:00+02:00 (a Graphersal name: JSON Schema's time is this form, but Graphersal's time is local)
durationdurationP1Y2M3DT4H

JSON Schema validators treat format as an annotation and ignore one they do not know, so a schema with these formats stays usable with other tools; Pydantic writes date-time, date, time and duration for datetime, date, time and timedelta fields.

Coercion on write

In open and closed mode a string written to a declared date property becomes the date: the declaration says the property is a date, so nothing is guessed. The text must be one the type reads (Text Formats); a date-time text needs its UTC offset or a zone (2024-05-01T09:30 is refused, never read as UTC). A date value is stored as it is; a value of another date type is refused (a date is not a datetime). Reads never convert: a string stored before the schema was set does not conform to the format, and set_schema reports it.

g.set_schema(#{vertices: #{event: #{schema: #{type: "object", properties: #{
    at: #{type: "string", format: "date-time"},
    on: #{type: "string", format: "date", formatMinimum: "2000-01-01"}
}}}}}, SchemaMode.open);
g.add_v("event").property("at", "2024-05-01T09:30:00+02:00").property("on", date("2024-05-01")).iterate();
g.v().has_label("event").values("at").next().offset   // 7200: a datetime, not a string

{
    g.set_schema(#{vertices: #{event: #{schema: #{type: "object", properties: #{
        at: #{type: "string", format: "date-time"}
    }}}}}, SchemaMode.open);
    g.add_v("event").property("at", "2024-05-01T09:30").iterate()
}   // refused: the text has no offset

Bounds

formatMinimum, formatMaximum, formatExclusiveMinimum and formatExclusiveMaximum (the keywords of JSON Schema's format-comparison proposal, which ajv-formats implements) bound a date property. Their value is the text of a value of the node's type, and a value is compared as the type compares: a datetime by its instant, a duration by its length. minimum and maximum stay number keywords.

{ "type": "string", "format": "date-time", "formatMinimum": "2020-01-01T00:00:00Z" }
{ "type": "string", "format": "duration", "formatExclusiveMaximum": "P1D" }

Inference

infer_schema() reports a stored date with its format ({"type": "string", "format": "date-time"}), and a position that holds strings and dates as an anyOf, so freezing the structure you have (g.set_schema(g.infer_schema(), SchemaMode.closed)) keeps the dates dates. The playground's schema editor offers the date formats as types and their bounds as constraints.

Storage and Exchange

A date keeps its type wherever it goes: in memory, in a snapshot or a Store, in a change set and in a GraphSON file. GraphML has no date type and needs the schema.

In memory

A date is stored inline in the property value, 20 bytes at most, without a heap allocation: a date is a day number, a time and a localdatetime nanoseconds, a datetime nanoseconds since the epoch plus its offset in seconds and, when it has one, a two-byte index of its zone name in the bundled time zone database, an offsettime nanoseconds of the day plus its offset, a duration its months, days and nanoseconds. Equality and ordering compare these numbers (Comparing and Sorting).

Snapshots, journals and the Store

The binary format (packed snapshots .gsnap, Store segments, the write-ahead log) has a value tag per type, defined in the format specification: the exact payload, the range of each type, and the rule that a datetime keeps its offset while equality uses the instant. Every value is stored exactly as it is in memory: nanoseconds over the whole range of years, an offsettime with its offset, a datetime with its zone name (as text, Europe/Berlin, never as a number of this build), a duration over its whole range (a 64-bit count of seconds plus the nanoseconds of one second). Nothing is refused and nothing is cut.

These nanosecond tags came with file format version 3 (Graphersal 0.3.0); version 2 (0.2.x) had microsecond tags only and could not store a value with digits below the microsecond, an offsettime or a zone name. A build that knows version 3 writes version 3 and reads versions 1 to 3, so a .gsnap or a Store written by 0.1.x or 0.2.x still loads; a Store written by 0.2.x is continued as it is, with no upgrade. Graphersal 0.2.x refuses a version 3 file as written by a newer version instead of misreading it. A zone name that this build's time zone database does not know (a file written by a newer Graphersal with a newer database) is refused as content of a newer version, never taken for damage. See Format Versions and Upgrade.

Change sets

A serialized ChangeSet (feature serde) writes a date as a per-value type tag in TinkerPop's GraphSON style, so a replay restores the type without a schema:

TypeTag
datetime{"@type": "gx:OffsetDateTime", "@value": "2024-05-01T09:30:00+02:00"}
datetime with a zone name{"@type": "gx:ZonedDateTime", "@value": "2024-05-01T09:30:00+02:00[Europe/Berlin]"}
date, localdatetime, time, offsettimegx:LocalDate, gx:LocalDateTime, gx:LocalTime, gx:OffsetTime
duration of a time part onlygx:Duration (PT26H)
duration of months and days onlygx:Period (P1Y2M3D)
any other durationgraphersal:Interval (P1MT2H)

Reading is strict: the text must be a value of the tag's type, and a gx:OffsetDateTime must carry its offset.

GraphSON

GraphSON 3.0 reads and writes the java.time types: g:Date/g:Timestamp (epoch milliseconds) become a datetime in UTC, gx:OffsetDateTime, gx:Instant and gx:ZonedDateTime a datetime with the offset of the text (a gx:ZonedDateTime keeps its zone id when the bundled database knows it and the text's offset is that zone's offset at that instant; otherwise the id is dropped and reported, and the offset of the text is kept: the instant is never recomputed from the name, as in the store), gx:LocalDate, gx:LocalDateTime, gx:LocalTime and gx:OffsetTime the types without a date or a zone and the offsettime, gx:Duration and gx:Period a duration. The export writes the tags of the change set table above, which TinkerGraph's g.io(file).read() loads, with one exception: a duration with both months or days and a time part has no java.time type, so it is written as graphersal:Interval, which only Graphersal reads (a deliberate deviation), and a negative gx:Duration is written as java.time writes it, each field signed (PT-1H-30M), because java.time cannot read -PT2562047788015215H30M8S, the canonical text of the shortest duration. Up to nine fraction digits are kept in both directions, and the java.time types Graphersal cannot hold (gx:Year, gx:YearMonth, gx:MonthDay, gx:ZoneOffset) are skipped and reported. The full mapping is on the GraphSON page.

A date-like string without a type tag (GraphSON 1.0, types=false) stays a string; declare the property in the schema to store it as a date.

GraphML

GraphML has no date type: a date is written as its canonical text under a string key. It is read back as a date only when the target graph's schema declares the property with a date format: set the schema on the empty graph first, then import (the playground's "Load from file" takes the schema file next to the graph file; the CLI's --schema). Without a schema the text stays a string. See UUID Values, which describes the same rule for UUIDs, and the Schemas page.

JSON, tables and the playground

Tables, JSON results, the CLI's visualizers, MCP and the dev server write the canonical text ("2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00"); a script value prints as its literal (datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00")). The playground's property editor keeps the type: it shows and edits a date property as one of the date types (Text Formats).

From Python

The Python binding converts the six types to and from the standard datetime module, both as results and as params=. Python's types count microseconds, the engine nanoseconds: a value with digits below the microsecond becomes a pandas type, which holds nanoseconds and subclasses the standard type, when the optional extra is installed (pip install graphersal[pandas]); without pandas it raises ImportError naming the extra. Nothing is ever rounded.

GraphersalPythonWith digits below the microsecond
datetimeaware datetime.datetime with tzinfo=datetime.timezone(timedelta(seconds=offset))aware pandas.Timestamp, the same tzinfo
datetime with a zone nameaware datetime.datetime with tzinfo=zoneinfo.ZoneInfo(name)aware pandas.Timestamp in the ZoneInfo
localdatetimenaive datetime.datetimenaive pandas.Timestamp
datedatetime.date-
timenaive datetime.timeValueError
offsettimedatetime.time with tzinfo=datetime.timezone(timedelta(seconds=offset))ValueError
duration without monthsdatetime.timedelta (an Interval beyond 999999999 days)pandas.Timedelta (an Interval beyond an int64 of nanoseconds, about 292 years)
duration with monthsgraphersal.Intervalgraphersal.Interval

Why pandas: pandas.Timestamp and pandas.Timedelta are subclasses of datetime.datetime and datetime.timedelta, so code written for the standard types keeps working; they hold nanoseconds, fixed offsets and ZoneInfo zones, and pandas is the most widely installed library that has them. whenever holds nanoseconds too (also a time of day) but its types are not the standard ones, and numpy.datetime64 has neither offsets, zones nor a time of day. Which type comes back depends on the value only, never on what is installed. Limits:

  • A time of day (time, offsettime) with digits below the microsecond raises ValueError: no common Python type holds one (pandas has no time of day; a pandas.Timedelta since midnight would come back as a duration). Truncate it with date_trunc(DT.microsecond) or read it with as_string().
  • A pandas.Timestamp holds nanoseconds only from 1677-09-21 to 2262-04-11: a datetime or localdatetime with digits below the microsecond outside these years raises.
import datetime as dt
import graphersal

graph = graphersal.Graph()
at = dt.datetime(2023, 8, 2, 9, 30, tzinfo=dt.timezone(dt.timedelta(hours=2)))
graph.query("g.inject(x).date_add(DT.day, 1).next()", params={"x": at})
# datetime.datetime(2023, 8, 3, 9, 30, tzinfo=datetime.timezone(datetime.timedelta(seconds=7200)))
graph.query('duration("P1Y2M")')
# Interval('P1Y2M')
  • An aware datetime is passed with the UTC offset it has at that instant; with a zoneinfo.ZoneInfo its zone name is kept too (a name the bundled database does not know is an error), and it comes back as a ZoneInfo datetime (with the right fold in a repeated hour). Any other tzinfo gives its offset only. An offset with a fraction of a second is refused. A Python installation without the zone (no tzdata on some systems) raises when such a value is returned, rather than dropping the name.
  • An aware datetime.time with a fixed offset (datetime.timezone) is an offsettime; one whose tzinfo has no fixed offset (a ZoneInfo) is refused: a zone's offset needs a date.
  • A timedelta becomes whole days and the rest, both with the sign of the whole (timedelta(hours=-1) is -PT1H).
  • graphersal.Interval is immutable, equal when its three fields are equal (Interval("P1M") != Interval(0, 30), as in the engine), has months, days, micros and nanos (Python ints, exact over the whole range of a duration; micros raises ValueError for a time part with digits below the microsecond) and to_iso(), and is built from the fields or from ISO 8601 text with up to nine fraction digits (Interval("P1Y2M3DT4.000000001H")).
  • A pandas.Timestamp or pandas.Timedelta parameter keeps its nanoseconds; a pandas.Timestamp in a pytz zone keeps the zone name as a ZoneInfo one does. pandas.NaT is refused (pass None).
  • Python's datetime holds the years 1 to 9999; a date before year 1 cannot be returned as one (read it with as_string()).

The binding's README has the details and more examples.

TinkerPop Compatibility

TinkerPop 3.8 has one date type, datetime (a Java OffsetDateTime), the literal datetime(..), the steps asDate(), dateAdd() and dateDiff(), the units DT.second, DT.minute, DT.hour and DT.day, and the tokens GType.DATETIME and GType.DURATION (a Java Duration, which no TinkerPop step produces). Graphersal implements all of it as TinkerPop specifies, with no deviation:

  • datetime("..") (also spelled DateTime("..")) reads ISO 8601 text, a text without an offset as UTC;
  • asDate() converts text and epoch milliseconds, and fails with "Can't parse" for the same inputs as TinkerPop;
  • dateAdd(DT.unit, n) keeps the offset and moves the instant, a day being 24 hours;
  • dateDiff(other) is the difference in milliseconds, null being the epoch;
  • asNumber() of a datetime is its epoch milliseconds;
  • equality and ordering use the instant ("Dates are evaluated based on the numerical comparison of Unix Epoch time"), and dates sort after numbers and before strings.

Every date scenario of the vendored TinkerPop 3.8.2 suite passes (DateTime, AsDate, DateAdd, DateDiff, the date cases of TypeOf and AsNumber), except two Orderability scenarios that also hold a set literal ({"x", "y", "z"}), for which Graphersal has no value type (TinkerPop Compliance).

Extensions

Everything else on the pages of this part is a Graphersal extension, modelled on PostgreSQL:

  • the types date, localdatetime, time and offsettime (GType.DATE, LOCALDATETIME, TIME, OFFSETTIME; typeOf names LocalDate, LocalDateTime, LocalTime, OffsetTime), and duration as a value with months, days and nanoseconds (PostgreSQL's interval, broader than Java's Duration), with their constructors;
  • a zone name kept in a datetime written with one (datetime("..[Europe/Berlin]"), Java's ZonedDateTime, which TinkerPop's datetime() does not produce): its calendar arithmetic follows the zone; a datetime without a name behaves as TinkerPop specifies;
  • the units DT.nanosecond, DT.microsecond, DT.millisecond, DT.week to DT.millennium and the parts DT.day_of_week, DT.iso_day_of_week, DT.day_of_year, DT.iso_year, DT.epoch, DT.offset;
  • date_add(duration), zone arguments, date_diff(other, DT.unit), age(), date_trunc(), date_part(), at_zone(), as_local(), as_duration(), as_date(GType.X);
  • now(), today(), the getters and operators of script values;
  • the schema formats and bounds, GraphSON's java.time types beyond g:Date, and the Python mapping.

The extensions add behaviour where TinkerPop defines none; none of them changes what a TinkerPop step returns. The one deliberate difference in the exchange formats is GraphSON's graphersal:Interval for a duration that no java.time type can hold (Storage and Exchange); all deviations are listed on TinkerPop Deviations.

Dates in GQL

gql() has openCypher's temporal functions (date(), datetime(), duration(), x.year, date.truncate(), duration.between(), ...) with Neo4j's meaning. They build and read the same six values as the Gremlin steps of this part (Cypher's time is the offsettime, its localtime the time): a date a GQL query returns is a date value, and a date a Gremlin step stored reads as a date in GQL. The full list of forms is on The Supported Subset, the differences from Neo4j on Semantics.

The Gremlin steps keep their PostgreSQL-style rules; where a GQL function means something else, the GQL function changes, never the step. This page sets each GQL form beside the Gremlin step or Rhai literal that does the same, and names the differences.

g.gql("RETURN date('2024-03-15') AS d").select("d").next() == date("2024-03-15")   // true
g.gql("RETURN $d + duration('P1M') AS d", #{d: date("2024-01-31")}).to_list()   // #{"d": date("2024-02-29")}

g.add_v("event").property("at", date("2024-03-15")).iterate();
g.gql("MATCH (e:event) RETURN e.at.year AS y, e.at + duration('P1M') AS next").to_list()   // #{"next": date("2024-04-15"), "y": 2024}

Building values

GQLGremlin / RhaiDifference
