date('2015-07-21'), localtime('21:40'), time('21:40+01:00'), localdatetime('..'), datetime('..'), duration('P1D')the literals date("2015-07-21"), time("21:40"), offsettime("21:40+01:00"), localdatetime(".."), datetime(".."), duration("P1D")GQL also reads Neo4j's forms: week, ordinal and quarter dates (2015-W30-2, 2015-202, 2015-Q3-21), basic forms (20150721T2140, 2140-02), fractions on any duration unit (P1.5Y); GQL's time('21:40') without an offset is UTC, Rhai's offsettime() needs the offset; both keep a zone in brackets ([Europe/London]) and nine fraction digits
date({year: 2015, week: 30, dayOfWeek: 2}) and the other mapsnone: build the text, or date_add() from a start
date(x), localdatetime(x), datetime(x) of another temporal valueas_date(GType.DATE), as_date(GType.LOCALDATETIME), as_date(GType.DATETIME)the same projections (the date of a datetime at its own offset, a localdatetime read at UTC); GQL's localdatetime(date) and datetime(date) are errors as in Neo4j (localdatetime({date: d}) is midnight), as_date(GType.LOCALDATETIME) of a date is midnight
datetime({.., timezone: 'Europe/Berlin'}), datetime({datetime: x, timezone: z})at_zone(z)the same: both resolve a zone name to its offset at that instant and keep the name in the value (a fixed offset keeps no name)
time(x), time({time: x, timezone: z})as_date(GType.OFFSETTIME)the same projections (a localtime or localdatetime at UTC, a datetime with its offset)
datetime.fromepochmillis(ms), datetime({epochMillis: ms}), datetime({epochSeconds: s})as_date() of an int64 (epoch milliseconds)
the ISO literals DATE '2015-07-21', TIME '21:40+01:00', TIMESTAMP '..', DURATION 'P1D' (Literals)the literals date("2015-07-21"), offsettime("21:40+01:00"), localdatetime(".."), duration("P1D")TIME '..' / TIMESTAMP '..' are the zoned type when the text has an offset, the local one otherwise
date(), datetime(), CURRENT_DATE, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, LOCAL_TIMESTAMP, X.statement(), X.transaction()today(), now()both are one instant per run; a query run from a script reads the script's instant, so datetime() in g.gql(..) equals the script's now() (a host's pinned clock too); run alone, a query takes it when it starts
g.gql("RETURN date(datetime('2015-07-21T23:40:32+02:00')) AS d").to_list()   // #{"d": date("2015-07-21")}
g.inject(datetime("2015-07-21T23:40:32+02:00")).as_date(GType.DATE).next()   // date("2015-07-21")

Reading components

GQLGremlin / RhaiDifference
x.year, x.month, x.day, x.hour, x.minute, x.seconddate_part(DT.year), ..., or the getters d.year of a script valuethe same
x.quarter, x.week, x.weekYear, x.ordinalDaydate_part(DT.quarter), DT.week, DT.iso_year, DT.day_of_yearthe same (ISO 8601 weeks)
x.dayOfWeek (1 = Monday)date_part(DT.iso_day_of_week)DT.day_of_week is PostgreSQL's 0 = Sunday
x.millisecond, x.microsecond, x.nanoseconddate_part(DT.millisecond), DT.microsecond, DT.nanosecondthe same: the fraction of the second
x.epochSeconds, x.epochMillisdate_part(DT.epoch) (seconds with the fraction), the getter epoch_millis
x.offset ('+01:00'), x.timezone (the zone name, else the offset), x.offsetSecondsdate_part(DT.offset) (seconds), the getter timezoneGQL writes the offset as text
dur.months, dur.years, dur.days, dur.hours, ... (totals)date_part(DT.month) of a duration is the remainder field (PostgreSQL: P1Y has month 0); the getters months, days, microsGQL's names are Neo4j's totals (duration('P1Y').months is 12); its remainders are monthsOfYear, minutesOfHour, ...
g.gql("RETURN date('2015-07-21').dayOfWeek AS a, duration('P1Y').months AS b").to_list()   // #{"a": 2, "b": 12}
g.inject(date("2015-07-21")).date_part(DT.iso_day_of_week).next()   // 2
g.inject(duration("P1Y")).date_part(DT.month).next()   // 0

Truncation

GQLGremlinDifference
date.truncate('month', d), localdatetime.truncate(..), datetime.truncate(..), localtime.truncate(..), time.truncate(..)date_trunc(DT.month)the same for year down to nanosecond and week
X.truncate('millennium' | 'century', d)date_trunc(DT.millennium), DT.centuryGQL follows Neo4j (2017 gives 2000, 1984 gives 1900), Gremlin PostgreSQL (2001, 1901)
X.truncate('weekYear', d), a map of overrides ({dayOfWeek: 2})none
datetime.truncate(unit, d, {timezone: z})date_trunc(unit, z)GQL keeps the wall clock and reads it in z; Gremlin truncates on the wall clock of z
g.gql("RETURN date.truncate('millennium', date('2017-10-11')) AS d").to_list()   // #{"d": date("2000-01-01")}
g.inject(date("2017-10-11")).date_trunc(DT.millennium).next()   // date("2001-01-01")

Arithmetic

GQLGremlin / RhaiDifference
x + dur, x - durdate_add(dur), the Rhai operators x + durthe same order (months clamped, days, time); but in GQL a date takes the whole days of a time part (date + PT33H adds a day) and a localtime ignores months and days, where date_add is an error
dur + dur, dur * n, dur / ndate_add(dur) on a duration (field by field)GQL scales with the fraction cascade (P1M * 0.5 is P15DT5H14M33S)
duration.between(a, b)age() (the operands swapped: age counts from the incoming value back to other)GQL counts whole months, then days, then time, each part signed (Neo4j); age borrows as PostgreSQL does; GQL takes two different types, age one type
duration.inMonths(a, b), duration.inDays(a, b)date_diff(other, DT.month), DT.day (a number, the incoming value minus other)GQL gives a duration (P30Y8M), date_diff an integer (368)
duration.inSeconds(a, b)date_diff(other) (the milliseconds, an integer)GQL gives a duration of seconds only (PT24H)
g.gql("RETURN date('1997-09-11') + duration('P29DT33H') AS d").to_list()   // #{"d": date("1997-10-11")}
g.inject(date("1997-09-11")).date_add(duration("P29DT33H")).next()   // error: adding a duration with a time part is not defined for a date
g.gql("RETURN duration.between(date('1984-10-11'), date('2015-06-24')) AS d").to_list()   // #{"d": duration("P30Y8M13D")}
g.inject(date("2015-06-24")).age(date("1984-10-11")).next()   // duration("P30Y8M13D")
g.inject(date("2015-06-24")).date_diff(date("1984-10-11"), DT.month).next()   // 368

Comparing and text

GQLGremlinDifference
a = b, a < b on one typeis(P.eq(..)), is(P.lt(..)) (Comparing and Sorting)the same; two datetimes by their instant
a < b on two durationsis(P.lt(..)) orders by lengthGQL gives NULL; ORDER BY and order() sort by length
a = b, a < b on two different temporal typesGQL: = is FALSE, < is NULL, as for any two kinds
toString(x)as_string()GQL writes Neo4j's text ('12:00'), as_string() the canonical ISO text ("12:00:00"), as GQL's CAST(x AS STRING) does
g.gql("RETURN toString(localtime('12:00')) AS a, CAST(localtime('12:00') AS STRING) AS b").to_list()   // #{"a": "12:00", "b": "12:00:00"}
g.inject(time("12:00")).as_string().next()   // "12:00:00"

Zone names and the zoned time

A zone name in a value (datetime('2017-08-08T12:31[Europe/Stockholm]'), datetime({.., timezone: 'Europe/Stockholm'})) is kept, printed (toString writes ..+02:00[Europe/Stockholm]), read as x.timezone, and later arithmetic, truncation and duration.between follow the zone's daylight saving rules, as Neo4j does; the Gremlin steps with a zone argument keep the name in the same way. Cypher's time() (ISO zoned_time(), the literal TIME '12:00+01:00', the clock CURRENT_TIME) is the offsettime; a named zone gives a time the zone's offset at the query's instant (Semantics).

g.gql("RETURN datetime('2024-03-30T12:00[Europe/Berlin]') + duration('P1D') AS d").to_list()   // #{"d": datetime("2024-03-31T12:00:00+02:00[Europe/Berlin]")}
g.gql("RETURN time({hour: 12, timezone: '+01:00'}) AS t").to_list()   // #{"t": offsettime("12:00:00+01:00")}

X.realtime() stays refused: Semantics.

Schemas

A graph can store a schema: which vertex and edge labels exist, which properties they carry, of which types and within which constraints, and how edges may connect labels. The schema is plain data in one format, the same in Rust, the script DSL, Python and the playground: our envelope outside, standard JSON Schema 2020-12 inside (a strict subset), so a model_json_schema() from Pydantic can be pasted as a label's schema.

The rule behind enforcement: the storage owns consistency. Every operation that changes the graph passes the schema inside one storage call, never in a step, and every traversal is one unit of work: it is applied completely or not at all.

A first schema

g.set_schema(`{
  "mode": "closed",
  "vertices": {
    "person": {"schema": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "name": {"type": "string", "minLength": 1},
        "age":  {"type": ["integer", "null"], "minimum": 0}
      },
      "required": ["name"]
    }}
  },
  "edges": {
    "knows": {"connections": [{"from": "person", "to": "person"}],
              "schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"weight": {"type": "number"}}}}
  }
}`)
g.add_v("person").property("name", "Ann").next()     // ok
g.add_v("person").property("age", -1).next()         // error: age >= 0 (and name is required)

g.get_schema() returns the stored schema as a map (() without one), g.infer_schema() the schema the data satisfies. Rendered as the final value of a session (the CLI, the playground) a schema shows as a table; --format mermaid|plantuml|json|jsonschema|markdown|tree picks another view.

Freeze the structure you have

A common way to start: build the graph without a schema, experiment until the shape is right, then freeze that shape so every later write has to follow it:

g.set_schema(g.infer_schema(), SchemaMode.closed)   // or SchemaMode.open / SchemaMode.none

set_schema(schema, mode) stores schema with its mode replaced by mode (an inferred schema has mode none, which enforces nothing). The mode is a SchemaMode token (SchemaMode.closed, SchemaMode::closed) or one of the strings "none", "open", "closed"; validate_schema(schema, mode) is the dry run. SchemaMode is a reserved name in the script scope.

BindingFreeze
DSLg.set_schema(g.infer_schema(), SchemaMode.closed) (the mode also as a string: "closed")
Rustlet s = g.infer_schema()?.with_mode(SchemaMode::Closed); g_mut.set_schema(s)?
Pythongraph.set_schema(graph.infer_schema(), mode="closed")
PlaygroundSchema panel: Freeze as open / Freeze as closed (shown while the graph stores no enforcing schema)

What each mode freezes:

  • open: the labels and properties that exist get their types and required lists; new labels and new properties stay allowed (unchecked).
  • closed: additionally, no other label, no other property (at any depth) and no edge between other labels than the ones that exist.

It always succeeds on the data the schema was inferred from, in both modes: inference declares every kind seen at every position and requires only the keys every element has (see Inference). The one exception is closed with elements without a label: an unlabeled vertex or edge has no label to declare, and a closed schema admits only declared labels. Then the call fails, changes nothing, and the report names them:

Cannot apply the Closed schema: the existing data violates it (2 kinds of violations on 2 elements of 6 checked)
  1) 1 edge without a label (Closed admits only declared labels) [ids: "7"]
  2) 1 vertex without a label (Closed admits only declared labels) [ids: "3"]

Freeze such a graph in open mode (it admits unlabeled elements unchecked), or give those elements a label first with the label steps (add_label, drop_label, set_label) and freeze again:

g.v("3").add_label("thing").to_list();                                  // a vertex from the report
g.e().not(__.has_label()).set_label("link").to_list();   // every unlabeled edge
g.set_schema(g.infer_schema(), SchemaMode.closed)

(g.v().not(__.has_label()).add_label("thing") labels every unlabeled vertex; Rust: the same steps, or GraphStorage::add_vertex_label/set_edge_label.) (The generated large sample graph has unlabeled edges: it freezes open, not closed.)

Later changes go through patch_schema (add a property, relax a rule) like any other schema.

The format

Envelope

KeyTypeMeaning
$schemastring, optionalThe format: https://graphersal.dev/schema/v1 (any other value is an error).
metaobject, optionalFree-form data the library stores, round-trips and never interprets (a version, a status, server data). Changing it is a schema change.
mode"none" | "open" | "closed", default "none"What is enforced, see Modes.
verticesobjectVertex label → {"schema": <label schema>}.
edgesobjectEdge label → {"connections": [{"from": .., "to": ..}], "schema": <label schema>}.

A label schema is a JSON Schema object node describing the element's property map: {"type": "object", "properties": {..}, "required": [..], "additionalProperties": ..} plus annotations. It may carry $defs (for $ref), $schema and $id (accepted and not stored). A label without schema declares no properties. A connection's from/to is a vertex label or * (any label).

Unknown keys are errors everywhere, the envelope included: {"mdoe": "closed"} is rejected with its location (Invalid schema at /mdoe: unknown key 'mdoe'), never silently ignored.

The canonical form (what get_schema, to_json and every binding return) always writes $schema, mode, vertices and edges, keywords in a fixed order, integers as integers. The empty schema (mode none, no meta, no labels) is no schema: set_schema({}) removes the stored schema. The format is described by the meta-schema graphersal-schema-v1.json (graphersal::schema::META_SCHEMA_JSON).

Types

JSON SchemaEngine typeNote
"integer"int64A value outside i64 cannot be stored at all; 3.0 is not an integer.
"number"float64An int64 written to it is coerced when exactly representable; a stored int64 does not conform.
"string"string
"string" + "format": "uuid"uuidA canonical UUID string is coerced on write; a stored string does not conform.
"string" + "format": "date-time"datetimeAn instant with its UTC offset (2024-05-01T09:30:00+02:00).
"string" + "format": "date"dateA calendar day (2024-05-01).
"string" + "format": "local-date-time"localdatetimeA date and time without a zone (2024-05-01T09:30:00). A Graphersal format name: JSON Schema has none.
"string" + "format": "time"timeA time of day without an offset (09:30:00). JSON Schema's own time requires an offset; Graphersal's is local.
"string" + "format": "offset-time"offsettimeA time of day with its UTC offset (09:30:00+02:00). A Graphersal format name (JSON Schema's time is this form, but Graphersal's time is local).
"string" + "format": "duration"durationISO 8601 (P1Y2M3DT4H): months, days and nanoseconds.
"boolean", "null"boolean, null
"array" + itemsarray<T>items is a full schema (constraints and nullability apply to the items); without items any item.
"array" + "format": "vector" (+ element, dimension, metric)vector<f32, 768>A vector of the declared element (f32 default, f16, i8, bit) and dimension (optional). A list of numbers is coerced on write, a vector of another element quantized; a stored list does not conform. items is not allowed next to it; metric is an annotation; embedder (a label's top-level property only) records the model identity of the embedder that produced the vectors ("hash-ngram/1"), which embed_property() fills in and checks and the text queries of nearest()/similarity() read; a plain write does not check it. Book page Vectors.
"object" + propertiesobjectWith required and additionalProperties.
["integer", "null"]union<int64|null>A type array: any of the listed types.
anyOf: [..]union<..>At least one member accepts the value (Pydantic's Optional[X] is anyOf: [X, {"type": "null"}]).
{} (no type)anyAdmits every value.

Diagnostics, Display and GType keep the engine's names (int64, float64, uuid, datetime, localdatetime, ...).

Dates and times. In open and closed mode a property declared with a temporal format coerces a string on write: any text the type's parser accepts (ISO 8601 / RFC 3339; the canonical form and the usual variants such as 2024-05-01 09:30Z or 09:30) becomes the temporal value, and text it refuses is a coercion failure that names the expected form. A date-time text must carry its UTC offset or a time zone (2024-05-01T09:30:00Z, 2024-05-01T09:30[Europe/Berlin]): 2024-05-01T09:30 is refused, never read as UTC, and the same holds for a formatMinimum/formatMaximum bound and a typed gx:OffsetDateTime (only the explicit conversion step as_date() keeps TinkerPop's "no offset is UTC"). This is the explicit declaration at work, like the uuid coercion, never a guess from content: an undeclared date-like string stays a string. A stored string does not conform to a temporal format (reads never coerce), and one temporal type never conforms to another (a date is not a datetime). A front end that compares user text with stored values (the playground's Graph panel filter) coerces the text first with GraphSchema::coerce_value(kind, labels, key, value) in Rust: the same coercion a write applies, without writing. JSON Schema's format is an annotation for other validators, which ignore a format they do not know, so a schema with local-date-time stays usable with them. The part Dates and Times describes the types themselves; its page Dates in a Schema has examples.

Keywords

KindKeywords
Structuretype, format (uuid, date-time, date, local-date-time, time, offset-time, duration on a string; vector on an array), element, dimension, metric, embedder (with format: "vector"; embedder on a top-level property only), items, properties, required, additionalProperties (true/false), anyOf
Constraintsminimum, maximum, exclusiveMinimum, exclusiveMaximum (numbers), formatMinimum, formatMaximum, formatExclusiveMinimum, formatExclusiveMaximum (dates and times), minLength, maxLength, pattern (strings), minItems, maxItems (arrays), enum, const (any value)
Annotations (no effect on validation)title, description, $comment, examples, deprecated
Create-time defaults (Defaults on create)default (also an annotation below the top level), defaultFunction (uuidv4, uuidv7, now, today)
References$ref: "#/$defs/Name" with $defs at the label schema's root; inlined when the schema is loaded

A constraint applies to the values of its own kind and ignores the others (JSON Schema semantics): in {"type": ["integer", "string"], "minimum": 10, "minLength": 3} the bound checks the integers and the length the strings. Next to a declared type, a keyword of another kind is an error (minLength on an integer is a mistake, not a no-op). enum/const compare JSON values (1 equals 1.0, a uuid and a date or time compare as their canonical text, so a datetime matches only the text with its own offset).

formatMinimum, formatMaximum, formatExclusiveMinimum and formatExclusiveMaximum bound a date or time: the keywords of JSON Schema's format-comparison proposal (ajv-formats implements them; other validators ignore unknown keywords). Their value is the text of a value of the node's temporal format, and they are valid only next to one (minimum stays a number keyword):

{ "type": "string", "format": "date-time", "formatMinimum": "2020-01-01T00:00:00Z" }
{ "type": "string", "format": "duration", "formatExclusiveMaximum": "P1D" }

A value is compared with its type's ordering: a datetime by its instant (2020-01-01T01:00:00+01:00 equals the minimum above), a duration by its length (a month counts 30 days, a day 24 hours, as PostgreSQL orders intervals), the others by their calendar or clock value.

Local references are inlined: a loaded schema has no $ref/$defs, and a reference cycle is an error (recursive schemas are not supported). Only annotations, default and defaultFunction may sit next to a $ref; they override the definition's.

What is an error, and why

InputWhy it is rejected
An unknown key or keyword, anywhereA typo must never weaken a schema silently.
format other than uuid, date-time, date, local-date-time, time, offset-time, duration (email, uri, ...)Accepting an unknown format as a plain string now would let a later version silently change what an existing schema accepts. Remove the format (the value is a string).
formatMinimum (and the other format bounds) without a temporal format, or with text that is not of the format's typeA bound needs the type it compares in; the hint shows an example of the type's text.
additionalProperties: {schema} (a map of T, Pydantic dict[str, T])No map type yet. Use {"type": "object", "additionalProperties": true}.
oneOf, allOf, not, if/then/elseNot implemented; anyOf covers oneOf when the members cannot both match.
prefixItems, contains, tuples (items: [..])An array has one item schema.
uniqueItems, multipleOfNot yet (additive later).
patternProperties, propertyNames, minProperties, dependent*, unevaluated*Keys are declared with properties, required, additionalProperties.
readOnly, writeOnly, content*Not among the accepted annotations.
A remote or non-$defs $ref, a reference cycleReferences are inlined at load.
nullable, variants, min, min_length, int64, ... (spellings of other schema dialects, such as OpenAPI's nullable)The hint names the JSON Schema spelling.

Every error is SchemaError::InvalidSchema { path, reason, hint }, path a JSON Pointer into the input (/vertices/person/schema/properties/age/minimum), and its help names the fix.

Defaults on create

default has SQL DEFAULT semantics: when a vertex or edge is created without a property whose schema declares a default, the default is stored, as if the query had written it.

g.set_schema(#{mode: "open", vertices: #{person: #{schema: #{type: "object", properties: #{
    name: #{type: "string"},
    active: #{type: "boolean", default: true},
    uid: #{type: "string", format: "uuid", defaultFunction: "uuidv7"}}}}}});
g.addV("person").property("name", "alice").iterate();
g.V().valueMap("name", "active").toList()   // [#{"active": [true], "name": ["alice"]}]
  • Only on create: addV()/addE() (also with their folded property() steps), mergeV()/mergeE() when they create (never on a match), GQL's INSERT (Cypher CREATE), the playground's create dialog, and GraphStorage::add_vertex/add_edge in Rust (and their _with forms). The default is filled in before the new element is coerced and validated, so a required property with a default is satisfied, and a canonical string default of a uuid property is stored as a uuid.
  • Only what is missing: a value the create writes wins, also an explicit null (property("k", ()) stores null). A property() that is not folded into the creation (a traversal value, say) overwrites the default afterwards.
  • default: null is never stored. Pydantic writes "default": null on every optional field; storing it would fill the data with nulls nobody wrote. Write the null explicitly when you want one.
  • Never on read: values("k"), valueMap(), the display and every export show what is stored, nothing is substituted for an absent property.
  • No backfill: setting or changing a schema never fills existing elements, and a changed default is never re-applied. To fill existing elements, use the backfill recipe.
  • Stored data is reproduced, not re-created: GraphML/GraphSON imports, apply_change_set, replay, recovery and snapshot loads store exactly what they carry: they go through the storage primitive GraphStorage::insert_vertex/insert_edge, which applies no default (call it yourself to store an element exactly as given, like a load).
  • Modes open and closed only: mode none stores the schema without enforcing anything, and applies no default either.
  • Top-level properties only: a default inside an object value's schema (address.city) stays an annotation; nothing fills in keys of a value the create supplies.
  • Multi-label vertices: the first label, in label order, that declares a key decides, as for coercion: its default is stored, or nothing when that label declares the key without one.

A default must be a valid value of its property (after the write coercion): set_schema, patch_schema and validate_schema reject {"type": "integer", "default": "x"} or a default below the property's minimum with an InvalidSchema error. Only the defaults that are applied are checked: a default: null and a nested default are not.

defaultFunction computes the value instead (like PostgreSQL's gen_random_uuid()/uuidv7()/now()/current_date):

defaultFunctionValueThe property must admit
uuidv4a random version-4 UUID, new for every element{"type": "string", "format": "uuid"}
uuidv7a time-ordered version-7 UUID (RFC 9562: 48 bits of Unix milliseconds, then random bits; increasing within a process), new for every element{"type": "string", "format": "uuid"}
nowthe datetime of the unit's start: ONE value for every element created in the same unit{"type": "string", "format": "date-time"}
todaythe UTC date of that same time{"type": "string", "format": "date"}

set_schema, patch_schema and validate_schema reject a function on a property that does not admit its value (now on a string or a date, uuidv4 on an integer) with an InvalidSchema error whose hint names the declaration it needs. A property has either default or defaultFunction, never both, and defaultFunction sits only on a label's top-level property (a saved query's parameter schema rejects it). The generated value is stored as a plain value: the change set and the journal record it, so replay and recovery reproduce the same UUID or time.

Which time now stores (PostgreSQL's now(): the start of the transaction):

  • In a script it is the time the DSL's now() returns in the same evaluation: one clock per evaluation, so let t = now(); g.addV("event").iterate(); stores exactly t, and every element the script creates gets the same time. A host pins that clock with script::pin_now (the playground and the CLI use the system clock).
  • In Rust it is the start of the storage's outermost open unit (GraphStorage::unit_started_at): the traversal's own unit, or the explicit transaction(|g| ..) around several traversals. GraphTraversalSource::with_now(t) pins it for one traversal (deterministic tests). GraphStorage::add_vertex/add_edge take the unit's start (CreateContext::for_storage); add_vertex_with/add_edge_with take a CreateContext (CreateContext::at(t) pins).
  • A later unit never gets an earlier time than a previous one of the same graph (the system clock is raised to the previous unit's start and the last commit time).
  • The time is kept in nanoseconds, with the digits the platform clock gives (Clock precision).
g.set_schema(#{mode: "open", vertices: #{event: #{schema: #{type: "object", properties: #{
    at: #{type: "string", format: "date-time", defaultFunction: "now"},
    day: #{type: "string", format: "date", defaultFunction: "today"}}}}}});
let t = now();
g.inject(1, 2, 3).addV("event").iterate();
g.V().values("at").dedup().toList() == [t]   // true: three events, one time

A change of a default or defaultFunction is listed by diff_schema as default_changed, and it is always backward compatible: it changes only what future creates store.

Required and nullable

required (on the object) and nullability (the type) are independent, as in JSON Schema:

null not admitted ("type": "string")null admitted ("type": ["string", "null"])
in requiredmust be present, non-nullmust be present, may be null
not in requiredmay be absent, never nullmay be absent or null

A missing required key is MissingRequiredProperty; a null where the type does not admit it is a TypeMismatch (expected string, got null). null stays a real stored value (property("k", ()) stores it, it never removes a property: use remove_property, see Removing Properties). Inside a JSON value {"a": null} differs from {}.

Required properties must be supplied when an element is created. The optimizer rule add_property_fold folds addV(..)/addE(..) and the property(k, v) steps that follow into one creation, so g.addV("Person").property("name", "Ann").property("age", 30) creates a valid element in one call. With the rule disabled, or for a property() that cannot be folded, the empty creation is rejected before anything is written. Removing a required property is rejected in open and closed mode.

Modes and additionalProperties

noneopenclosed
Coercion on write (canonical string to uuid, date and time text to its declared type, int64 to float64)nodeclared propertiesdeclared properties
Types, constraints, required of declared labels (any depth)noyesyes
Undeclared labelsallowedallowed, uncheckedrejected (also unlabeled elements)
Default additionalProperties of an object node-truefalse
Defaults on create (default, defaultFunction)noyesyes
Edge topology (connections)nonoyes

mode governs undeclared labels and topology, and it is the default additionalProperties of every node typed object that does not state its own. An explicit value wins, both ways: a free-form object in a closed graph is {"type": "object", "additionalProperties": true}, a strict object in an open graph says false. A node without type: "object" (an anyOf wrapper) puts no constraint on keys; its members do.

Multi-label vertices (see Multi-Label Vertices): every label checks the properties it declares and its own required list; a top-level property that no label declares is allowed when ANY label admits additional properties (the same "any label" rule as topology). Coercion uses the first label, in label order, that declares the key. closed rejects a vertex without a label or with an undeclared label. Adding or removing a label re-validates the vertex under the new label set and commits only on success.

Edge labels are single, but can be changed (set_label(..), GraphStorage::set_edge_label). The change checks the edge as stored under the new label (closed: a declared label and a declared connection; open and closed: the new label's required keys and declared types) and changes nothing on a violation. Stored values are not coerced by a label change (reads never coerce); later writes coerce by the new label's declarations.

none describes without enforcing; the GraphML import still restores the declared logical types from it (uuid, the date and time types, array, object; see UUID Values). A date or time is written to GraphML as its canonical text under a string key (up to nine fraction digits, a zone name in brackets, an offsettime with its offset) and read back exactly as a temporal value where the target schema declares its format (date-time, date, local-date-time, time, offset-time, duration; text that is not of the type, such as an offset-time without its offset, fails the import with InvalidAttributeValue); without a declaration it stays a string.

Edge topology (closed)

An edge label declares its allowed connections ({"from": "Person", "to": "Company"}, * matches every label). Because labels are a set, an edge is accepted if ANY label of the source and ANY label of the target matches a declared connection. An edge label without connections allows every pair. A label change that would make an incident edge violate the connections is rejected as a whole.

Nested values

The content of an object, array or anyOf value is validated at any depth: declared nested keys are type- and constraint-checked, required nested keys must be present, undeclared nested keys follow the object's additionalProperties. Errors name the canonical path ($.address.zip, $.items[1].n). A nested write (property(jpath("address.zip"), v)) coerces the leaf to the type declared at that location. See Path Keys (jpath).

Constraints

pattern is a regular expression with JSON Schema semantics: it is not anchored, so a value matches when the expression matches anywhere in it. Write ^...$ to match the whole value:

{ "type": "string", "pattern": "^[A-Z][a-z]+$" }
{ "type": "string", "pattern": "@" }
{ "type": "string", "pattern": "^\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}$" }

The syntax is the ECMA-262-like subset of the Rust regex crate: literals, ., classes ([a-z], [^0-9], \d, \w, \s), anchors, groups, alternation | and the quantifiers *, +, ?, {n}, {n,}, {n,m}. Two differences to ECMA-262: look-around and back-references are not supported (matching stays linear in the input), and \d, \w, \s, \b are Unicode-aware (write [0-9] for ASCII digits). A JSON text doubles every backslash. The expression is compiled once, when the schema is loaded, and an invalid one rejects the schema.

minLength/maxLength count characters (code points). An empty array satisfies every items (it has no item of a wrong type); use minItems: 1 to require one.

The schema methods

Seven methods, the same everywhere. They are plain calls on the graph source, not traversal steps (like g.statistics()); each runs in the current unit (a transaction, a whole-script unit) or as a unit of its own.

MethodReturnsAuthorization
get_schema()the stored schema, or none (never inferred)Read on Schema
set_schema(schema), set_schema(schema, mode)- (replaces the stored schema; mode replaces the schema's mode)Update on Schema
patch_schema(patch)the new schema (JSON Merge Patch, RFC 7396, onto the stored one)Update on Schema
validate_schema(schema), validate_schema(schema, mode){violations, diff, compatible}: a dry run against the dataRead on Schema
validate_schema_patch(patch)the same for a patchRead on Schema
infer_schema()the schema the data satisfiesRead on Schema
diff_schema(schema){changes, compatible} from the stored schemaRead on Schema
InputOutput
Rust (GraphTraversalSource)GraphSchema (GraphSchema::from_json(text), from_value, or the builders), SchemaPatch (graphersal::schema)GraphSchema, SchemaValidation, SchemaDiff (to_value() gives the data shape)
DSL (get_schema, set_schema, ...)a map or JSON texta map
Python (Graph.get_schema(), ...)a dict or JSON str (keyword policy=)a dict
Playground engine (wasm getSchema, ...)JSON textJSON

A map built in the DSL keeps its keys in alphabetical order (Rhai maps are sorted), so the property order of a schema that went through a map is alphabetical; JSON text and Python dicts keep it. The traversal step g.v()...infer_schema() infers over a stream, with the same inference.

In a DSL map literal, quote the keys that are not plain identifiers: $ref, $defs, $schema and $id start with $. default (a word Rhai reserves) is accepted as a plain key in the Graphersal DSL, quoted or not:

g.patch_schema(#{vertices: #{person: #{schema: #{type: "object", properties: #{
    age: #{type: ["integer", "null"], default: 7}
}}}}})

JSON text needs no quoting rules of its own: g.set_schema(text) takes the schema as written.

A schema change is a database change: it advances the commit sequence number, makes the run mutated, is recorded as Mutation::SetSchema { before, after } (the canonical JSON) in the same change set as the data, rolls back with its unit, and is reported in the result's changes: {data, schema} (Execution::changes(), the DSL's r.changes, the playground's response). Validation is immediate: the existing data is checked when the schema is set, not at commit.

Applying a schema to existing data

set_schema and patch_schema validate all existing data first, in one pass over the vertices and edges, when the mode is open or closed. If anything violates the schema, the graph and its current schema stay unchanged and the call fails with one aggregated error that lists every kind of violation, grouped by rule with a count and a few sample ids:

Cannot apply the Closed schema: the existing data violates it (5 kinds of violations on 22 elements of 22 checked)
  1) Person.age is declared mandatory but is missing on 12 vertices [ids: "p0", "p1", "p2", "p3", "p4" and 7 more]
  2) vertex label Alien is not declared (Closed): 5 vertices [ids: "x0", "x1", "x2", "x3", "x4"]
  3) Company.name is declared mandatory but is missing on 3 vertices [ids: "c0", "c1", "c2"]
  4) Person.age has the wrong type on 1 vertex (declared int64, found string) [ids: "t"]
  5) Robot.model is not declared (Closed) on 1 vertex [ids: "r"]
  • A group is (kind, label, field or path): missing required keys, undeclared labels or properties, type mismatches, constraint violations, edge topology violations (closed) and nested path violations (Person $.address.zip is declared mandatory but is missing on 1 vertex).
  • Every violation inside a value is listed, not only the first: all keys, all array items, at any depth, each under its own path ($.address.zip wrong type, $.address.street missing and $.address.city undeclared are three groups). Array indices are collapsed into [*]: a rule broken by any item of an array is ONE group ($.addresses[0].zip and $.addresses[2].zip missing are the group $.addresses[*].zip), which shows the first concrete path it met (Person $.addresses[*].zip is declared mandatory but is missing on 5 vertices (first at $.addresses[1].zip) [ids: ...]). Per node only the first failing constraint is named. An element counts once per group, however many of its items break the rule. A single write still fails on the first violation it meets.
  • Groups are ordered by count (largest first), then kind, element, label and field, so the same data gives the same report.
  • Each group shows its count and up to 5 sample ids (cut to 40 characters, escaped); at most 20 groups are printed, the structured report keeps up to 1000, further violations are only counted.
  • Stored data is checked exactly as it is: nothing is coerced and nothing is written.
  • validate_schema returns the same report as data: violations: {mode, elements_checked, violating_elements, total_violations, omitted_violations, groups: [{kind, element, label, field, example_field, detail, count, sample_ids, omitted_ids}]} (example_field is the first concrete path of a [*] field, null otherwise), with kind one of unknown_label, missing_required, type_mismatch, constraint_violation, undeclared_property, invalid_topology.

How to proceed: fix or migrate the offending data, relax the schema (make a key optional, admit null, declare the label or property), apply it with mode none, or start from infer_schema(), which is valid for the data it came from.

Making a key required: backfill first, in one transaction

A schema that requires a key the existing elements lack is rejected. Backfill first and tighten last, all in one transaction, so no reader ever sees the intermediate state:

let declare = SchemaPatch::from_json(
    r#"{"vertices": {"person": {"schema": {"properties": {"email": {"type": "string"}}}}}}"#)?;
let require = SchemaPatch::from_json(
    r#"{"vertices": {"person": {"schema": {"required": ["name", "age", "email"]}}}}"#)?;
graph.transaction(|g| -> TraverserResult<()> {
    // 1. In a closed schema, declare the key (optional) so it may be written.
    g.traversal_mut().patch_schema(&declare)?;
    // 2. Backfill.
    g.traversal_mut().v(None).has_label("person").property("email", "unknown").to_list()?;
    // 3. Make it required.
    g.traversal_mut().patch_schema(&require)?;
    Ok(())
})?;

(schema_api_tests::backfill_then_require_in_one_transaction runs this recipe.)

The same in a script run as one unit (atomic=True in Python, every playground run): patch to optional, backfill, patch to required. A schema default does not backfill anything: it is stored only for elements created after it is set (Defaults on create).

Changing a schema: patch and diff

patch_schema applies a JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396) to the canonical form of the stored schema ({} without one): an object merges member by member (property order is kept), null removes a member, any other value (an array too) replaces it. RFC 7396 cannot set a member to null; use set_schema for a "default": null. validate_schema_patch previews the result against the data.

diff_schema lists the changes (kind, element, label, path such as $.address.zip or $.tags[*], before, after) and whether each is backward compatible: data and clients written against the old schema keep working: the old data stays valid and every write that followed the old schema still succeeds. In short, a compatible change only adds (an optional key, a label, an allowed value) or relaxes (a wider type, a looser bound, a less strict mode); tightening a rule or removing a declaration something could depend on (a label, a key of a closed object) is incompatible. This is the usual schema-registry convention: adding an optional property is compatible, also to an open object, and so is removing a property declaration from an open object (the key becomes an undeclared one, which the object admits; the change is still listed as property_removed). A server's "compatible changes only" policy can veto the rest in a before_commit hook.

ChangeCompatible when
modeit gets less strict (closed → open → none); open → closed is incompatible
meta, annotations (title, description, ...)always
default, defaultFunction (added, changed, removed; kind default_changed)always: it changes only what future creates store
embedder of a vector (kind embedder_changed)when it is declared where there was none; changing or removing it is incompatible: the stored vectors and a text query embedded by another model are not comparable, and a text query needs the model
label addedthe old mode was closed (no client could write it), or its schema requires no key and admits undeclared keys (an open graph)
label removednever
connection added/removedthe label's connections still allow every old pair (an empty list allows all), or the new mode is not closed (topology binds only there)
property addedit is optional (not in required), also in an open object
property removedthe object admits undeclared keys (open: mode open/none or additionalProperties: true), whether the key was optional or required; from a closed object never
key made required / optionalnever / always
additionalPropertiesfalse → true
typethe new type admits every kind the old one did ("integer" → ["integer", "null"])
minimum, maxLength, minItems, formatMinimum, ...removed or relaxed (a later formatMaximum, an earlier formatMinimum)
formatnever (date → date-time is another type, so are adding and removing a format)
pattern, constremoved
enumremoved, or a superset

A key the old schema listed in required without declaring it was written by every old client, with any value: declaring it later is compatible only if the declaration accepts everything. With a new mode none every change is compatible (nothing is enforced any more).

The diff is static: it compares the two schemas, never the data. Existing data that conflicts with a compatible change (an element that already holds a newly declared optional key with another type, say) is found by validate_schema / validate_schema_patch, and set_schema refuses to apply the schema until it is fixed.

Inference

infer_schema() (and the step) report what the data holds, at every position: the kinds seen (a type array, or anyOf when a string, a uuid and the date and time types share a position: a datetime is {"type": "string", "format": "date-time"}), items of arrays, properties of objects, and required only for keys every object at that position has, at any depth (also inside arrays and next to other kinds). Every label of a vertex is declared; connections use the endpoints' first labels. The result has mode none and is valid for the data it came from in open and in closed mode (an unlabeled element has no label to declare, so closed rejects it; see Freeze the structure you have). It never guesses from string content: a UUID-shaped string is a string. Inference statistics (counts) are not part of the format.

Renderers

FormatShows
table, markdownone row per property path (address.zip, roles[].name), type, required, nullable, constraints (0..150, length 1..80, pattern ^x$), notes (description, default, marked (annotation) where it is not applied: null or below the top level, defaultFunction)
treethe labels and their properties as a tree
jsonthe canonical format
jsonschemaone standalone JSON Schema per label ($defs: vertex:person, edge:knows), the mode's default additionalProperties written out
mermaidan erDiagram; nested objects are entities of their own (`person
plantumlthe label topology as entity diagrams, then a @startjson view of the condensed schema

The meta-graph (schema.to_graph() in the DSL, GraphSchema::to_graph in Rust) has one vertex per vertex label and one edge per connection, each with its schema node as the schema property.

The playground's Schema panel shows the same schema as editable tables, as JSON, as a graph of its labels (node size and count from the data) and as the Mermaid diagram, here for a small cloud inventory:

Pasting a Pydantic model

Model.model_json_schema() loads as a label schema as it is ($defs/$ref, anyOf with null, title, description, default, enum, const, exclusive*, additionalProperties: false, and the date and time fields: datetime ("format": "date-time"), date, time and timedelta ("format": "duration")), except for one thing to remove first:

  • dict[str, T] fields ("additionalProperties": {..}): no map type; write {"type": "object", "additionalProperties": true}.

A Pydantic time field is a time of day: Graphersal's time has no offset, so a text with one (10:00:00+02:00) is refused by the coercion (declare a date-time for an instant).

Tuples (prefixItems) and Decimal (anyOf with a string pattern for some versions) are not supported either. The top level of the model must be an object ("type": "object").

A field's non-null default (active: bool = True) becomes a default on create in mode open/closed; the "default": null Pydantic writes on every optional field stores nothing.

GQL writes

A GQL INSERT creates each element in one storage call with every property of its map, so defaults, required, coercion and the mode apply to the whole element, as for a folded addV(..).property(..). A NULL value is not stored, so it does not satisfy required. A violation fails the query, and its help line is written for GQL (toInteger() for a type mismatch, the INSERT map and coalesce() for a missing property):

g.set_schema(#{mode: "closed", vertices: #{person: #{schema: #{type: "object", properties: #{
    name: #{type: "string"}, active: #{type: "boolean", default: true}}, required: ["name"]}}}});
g.gql("INSERT (:person {name: 'alice'})").iterate();
let refused = g.gql("INSERT (:robot {name: 'r2'})").execute();   // fails: the closed schema has no label robot
g.gql("MATCH (n) RETURN labels(n) AS labels, n.active AS active").to_list()   // #{"active": true, "labels": ["person"]}

GQL's SET and REMOVE change an existing element property by property and label by label, as property(), remove_property(), add_label() and drop_label() do, and each change is checked like theirs: a value of the wrong type, an undeclared property or label in a closed schema, and removing a required property (with REMOVE n.k, SET n.k = NULL, or a SET n = {..} whose map lacks it) fail the query, which then changes nothing:

g.set_schema(#{mode: "closed", vertices: #{person: #{schema: #{type: "object", properties: #{
    name: #{type: "string"}, age: #{type: "integer"}}, required: ["name"]}}}});
g.gql("INSERT (:person {name: 'alice'})").iterate();
let refused = g.gql("MATCH (p:person) SET p.age = 3, p.name = NULL").execute();   // fails: 'name' is required
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN properties(p) AS props").to_list()   // #{"props": #{"name": "alice"}}

A failing query changes nothing

The schema is validated per storage call (one add_v with its folded properties, one single property(key, value), one drop, ...), and every traversal is one unit of work: when a call fails, the whole traversal is rolled back, including what its earlier steps wrote (see Transactions).

In the playground a refused write shows the failing step and how to fix it (here a closed schema that declares cpus as int64):

CaseTest
property(map) with several entriesschema_gap_tests::gap4_property_map_is_atomic
property_json (Rust API)schema_gap_tests::gap4_property_json_is_atomic
mergeV/mergeE option(Merge.onMatch, map) with several entriesschema_gap_tests::gap4_merge_v_on_match_is_atomic
addE over several start verticesschema_gap_tests::gap4_add_e_over_several_endpoints_is_atomic
any traversal with several stepstransaction_tests::a_schema_violation_rolls_back_the_whole_traversal

A GraphML import into an existing graph is one unit too: an invalid element rolls back the elements imported before it. GraphML carries no schema: set the schema first, then import. The CLI does both in that order with graphersal --graph g.graphml --schema schema.json [--schema-mode closed] (also for GraphSON, and with --server); a violation stops the start with exit code 1.

Saved Queries

A saved query is a named, parameterized piece of DSL stored IN the database, next to the schema: written once, called by name from any front end (the CLI, Python, the playground).

g.query("older_than", #{age: 30}).values("name").toList()
// ["josh", "peter"]
  • The body is the text of ONE Rhai function, or ONE GQL query; its parameters are named and typed.
  • A call returns what the function returns: a traversal can be continued by the caller (like a SQL view), a value (a number, a list, a map) is a value (like a stored procedure).
  • A query reads, unless its body writes data: then it is saved as a query that writes, and a call may write exactly what the engine infers from the body (its effects), as one transaction. Nobody declares effects, and a query never writes the schema, the saved queries or files.
  • Queries live in folders (an attribute, not part of the name) and carry an optional description.

Every example on this page was run with graphersal on the default modern graph; the line after // is its real output. Each block starts from a fresh graph.

Defining a query

g.define_query(#{
    name: "older_than",
    folder: "reports/people",
    description: "Persons older than the given age.",
    params: #{
        age: #{schema: #{type: "integer", minimum: 0, maximum: 150,
                         description: "Age in years"},
               default: 30}
    },
    body: `fn older_than(age) {
        g.v().has_label("person").has("age", P.gt(age)).order().by("age")
    }`
})
g.query("older_than").values("name").toList()
// ["josh", "peter"]

g.define_query(#{..}) stores a new query or replaces the one of that name. The keys:

KeyRequiredMeaning
nameyesthe query's name, also its Rhai function name: [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*, 1 to 128 bytes, not a Rhai keyword; case-sensitive, unique per database
bodyyesthe text of ONE Rhai function named like the query (with language: "gql": one GQL query)
languageno"rhai" (the default) or "gql" (see Saved queries in GQL)
paramswhen the function has parametersparameter name -> its declaration (see Parameters)
foldernoa /-separated path such as "reports/sales"; "" or () is the root
descriptionnofree text (at most 4 KiB); defaults to the function's doc comment
metanofree text, stored and never interpreted

The definition is checked before anything is stored, and refused with an error naming the problem:

  • the body compiles and is exactly one function named like the query, with nothing beside it (closures inside it, such as .filter(|n| n.len() > 3), are part of that function);
  • every parameter of the function is declared in params, and params declares nothing else;
  • the catalog rules: name, folder (at most 8 segments, 255 bytes), sizes (source at most 64 KiB), parameter names (not a DSL global such as g, P or T), every parameter schema, and every default against its schema.

Saved queries called by the body are not checked at definition: a missing one fails when it is called.

Several queries at once

g.define_queries(folder, source[, params]) stores every function of a source as a query of its own, named like the function, described by its doc comment (/// lines or a /** .. */ block). params maps each function name to its parameter map. All of them are stored in one unit: either every query is stored or none. It returns the names.

g.define_queries("reports/sales", `
    /// Persons, oldest first.
    fn oldest(n) { g.v().has_label("person").order().by("age", Order.desc).limit(n) }

    /// Software names.
    fn software() { g.v().has_label("software").values("name") }
`, #{oldest: #{n: #{schema: #{type: "integer", minimum: 1}, default: 2}}})
// ["oldest", "software"]
g.query("oldest").values("name").toList()
// ["peter", "josh"]
g.get_query("oldest")["body"]
// fn oldest(n) { g.v().has_label("person").order().by("age", Order.desc).limit(n) }

Each query stores the text of its own function only.

Parameters

A parameter is declared as #{schema: <schema node>, default: <value>}, or as a bare type name (the short form): "integer", "number", "string", "boolean", "array", "object", "null" or "uuid".

  • The schema uses the node format of the graph schema: type, enum, minimum, maximum, pattern, minLength, items, ..., and the annotations title, description, examples.
  • The default sits beside the schema, not inside it: a default keyword inside the parameter's schema is an annotation (a data schema's default applies only when a vertex or edge is created), while a parameter default IS substituted when the argument is left out. A parameter without a default is required. A defaultFunction (uuidv4, now, ...) anywhere in a parameter's schema is an error: it fills a property of a created element and means nothing for an argument.

params may also be the list g.get_query(name)["params"] returns, one #{name, schema, default?, required?} per parameter (required must match the default: a parameter is required exactly when it has none), so a stored definition can be read, changed and given back:

let q = g.get_query("older_than");
let body = q["body"];
body.replace("P.gt", "P.gte");
g.define_query(#{name: "older_than", params: q["params"], body: body})

Arguments are named: g.query("x", #{limit: 5}), or g.query("x") when every parameter has a default. An argument is a data value (a string, a number, a boolean, a UUID, a date or time, a list, a map; never a traversal or a closure), bound to the function's parameter like a prepared-statement parameter, never spliced into text. It is checked against its schema before the body runs; the only conversion is the schema's write coercion (an int64 where a float64 is declared, a canonical UUID string where a uuid is declared, the ISO 8601 text of a declared date or time format such as date-time). () is a value (null), not an omitted argument.

g.query("older_than", #{age: 200})
// Error: Invalid argument 'age' for saved query 'older_than': Constraint violation on 'older_than.age': value <= 150 (actual: 200)
g.query("older_than", #{years: 30})
// Error: Saved query 'older_than' has no parameter 'years'

Calling a query

g.query(name) / g.query(name, #{..}) calls the query at the start of a traversal, on g; it works anywhere a script can use g (loops, functions, the body of another saved query). It is not a step: g.v().query(..) and __.query(..) fail with an error that says so (calling a query on incoming traversers is a later feature).

A traversal result is continued like any other traversal, and the optimizer sees the whole plan: the caller's filters are pushed into the body's steps.

g.define_query(#{name: "everything", body: "fn everything() { g.v() }"})
g.query("everything").has_label("person").count().profile()
// Step                                    Call      In     Out  ...
// v(labels: ["person"]).count()              1       0       4  ...
// Optimizer rules applied: source_filter_pushdown, count_pushdown

A value result is returned as it is:

g.define_query(#{name: "stats", body: `fn stats() {
    #{people: g.v().has_label("person").count().next(), software: g.v().has_label("software").count().next()}
}`})
g.query("stats")
// #{"people": 4, "software": 2}

A call does not recompile an unchanged body: a compiled body is cached per thread, keyed by the stored text, so a redefined query (or one restored by a rollback) always runs its current body, and the plan is made anew on every call (new optimizations apply to old queries).

Saved queries may call each other up to 16 levels deep; a deeper call (usually a query that calls itself without an end) fails with Saved query calls nested deeper than 16 levels.

Queries that read and queries that write

Whether a query may write is decided when it is SAVED, from its body: the engine walks the body's Rhai syntax tree and infers its effects, the data writes its steps can make. A query with no effects is saved in the dialect graphersal-rhai/1 and only reads; a query with effects is saved in graphersal-rhai/2 and may write exactly those. Every save (define_query, define_queries, a replacement, the playground's editor) sets the dialect again, also back to /1 when the body no longer writes; moving or describing a query does not.

g.define_query(#{name: "add_person", params: #{name: "string", age: "integer"},
                 body: "fn add_person(name, age) { g.add_v(\"person\").property(\"name\", name).property(\"age\", age).next() }"})
g.get_query("add_person")["dialect"]
// graphersal-rhai/2
g.get_query("add_person")["effects"].map(|e| e.text)
// "Create Data(vertex \"person\")"
// "Update Data(vertex \"person\")"
g.query("add_person", #{name: "ann", age: 41})
// v[7]

An effect is a request as an authorizer sees it: an action (Create, Update, Delete) on Data, with the element kind and label the chain states before the writing step. The inference follows the same rules as the authorization check of a plan, so the run-time check can hold every write against it:

BodyInferred
add_v("person"), add_e("knows")Create on that label
add_v(label) (a variable)Create on any vertex
g.e().has_label("knows").drop(), out_e("knows").property(..)Delete / Update on knows edges
g.v().has_label("person").property(..)Update on any vertex: a vertex has a label SET, so has_label("person") says nothing about its other labels
a chain from a variable or __ (t.drop(), side_effect(__.property(..)))Delete / Update on any data
merge_v(..) / merge_e(..)Create and Update on the kind
g.query("other")the effects of other, when it writes
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) INSERT (p)-[:owns]->(:pet)")the writes of the lowered GQL query: Create on pet vertices and owns edges
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) SET p.age = 1")Update on any vertex, as for property()
g.gql(text) with a computed text (a variable, a concatenation)Create, Update and Delete on any data: pass values as $parameters to keep a GQL read read-only
a method of the same name on something else (m.drop() on a map)counted as a write

The inference may claim more than a body writes, never less. What it cannot see, it refuses:

  • a body that writes the schema, the catalog or files (set_schema, define_query, create_index, export_graphml, import_graphson, mark, ...) is refused when it is saved: a saved query writes data only;
  • a body that writes and hides what it calls (Fn(..), call, curry, eval, import, or g.query(name) with a computed name) is refused when it is saved. A closure passed to a method (names.for_each(|n| g.add_v(label).property("name", n).iterate())) hides nothing: its writes are inferred like the function's, also when it uses the function's parameters. Without writes such a body is saved as a read-only query, and whatever it reaches stays read-only.
g.define_query(#{name: "q", params: #{n: "string"}, body: "fn q(n) { g.query(n); g.add_v(\"x\").next() }"})
// Error: Invalid body of saved query 'q': it writes data (Create Data(vertex "x")) and uses g.query(name) with a computed name, which hides what it calls, so its effects cannot be inferred; ...

Effects are never stored. They are inferred again when a query is saved, listed or called, so a newer version of Graphersal may infer more or less for the same text; a call always uses the effects inferred now.

A call of a query that writes

  • Invoker rights. The whole effect set is asked of the caller's authorizer before the body runs (Permission denied for 'query("name")' (Delete Data(edge "knows"))), so a denial comes before the first write. The body then runs under the caller's rights restricted to the effects: a write the effects do not cover is denied (it would be a bug of the inference, and the message says so).
  • One unit. The body runs as one transaction: a failing body rolls back everything it wrote, and the commit's ChangeSet carries the query's name and arguments as metadata (saved_query, saved_query_args). Inside a running unit (the playground runs a whole script as one) the call is a savepoint: a later failure of the script rolls it back too. A dry run (eval_value_dry_run) of a call previews its changes; nothing stays.
  • Nesting. A query that writes may call queries that read and queries that write; their effects are part of its own. A read-only query that calls one that writes stays read-only: that call's writes are denied.
  • The result is read-only. What the query returns is used after the call, outside its unit, so it can be continued only by reading; a returned traversal that writes runs INSIDE the call (next section).
g.define_query(#{name: "unfriend", params: #{name: "string"},
                 body: "fn unfriend(name) { g.v().has(\"name\", name).out_e(\"knows\").drop().iterate(); g.v().has(\"name\", name).out(\"knows\").count().next() }"})
g.get_query("unfriend")["effects"].map(|e| e.text)
// "Delete Data(edge \"knows\")"
g.query("unfriend", #{name: "marko"})
// 0

What a query that writes returns

A query that writes may end with the writing traversal itself, without a terminal. The call runs that traversal inside its unit, as if it ended in toList(), and returns a read-only traversal over what it wrote (inject(results) on the caller's graph). The caller continues it like the result of a read-only query:

g.define_query(#{name: "add_person", params: #{p_name: "string"},
                 body: "fn add_person(p_name) { g.add_v(\"person\").property(\"name\", p_name) }"})
g.query("add_person", #{p_name: "Bill"}).count().next()
// 1

Each call writes once, whatever the caller does with the result; the result only reads what was written:

g.query("add_person", #{p_name: "Bill"}).values("name").toList()
// ["Bill"]
g.query("add_person", #{p_name: "Bill"}).id().toList()
// ["7"]
g.v().has("name", "Bill").count().next()
// 1

Without a step after it, the result is shown like any traversal (in the playground and the CLI: the written elements as a table). The written elements are the stored ones, so the continuation walks the graph from them:

g.define_query(#{name: "befriend", params: #{a: "string", b: "string"},
                 body: "fn befriend(a, b) { g.v().has(\"name\", a).add_e(\"knows\").to(__.v().has(\"name\", b)) }"})
g.query("befriend", #{a: "vadas", b: "peter"}).in_v().values("name").toList()
// ["peter"]

The continuation itself may not write: the call's effects end with the call.

g.query("add_person", #{p_name: "Bill"}).property("age", 30).iterate()
// Error: ... Permission denied for 'property' (Update Data): a saved query is read-only: ...

Write the change into the query, or write in a traversal of your own after the call. The rules in detail:

  • Only the returned traversal is run. A traversal the body ends with a terminal (next(), toList(), iterate()) has already run; its value is returned as a value (fn add(n) { g.add_v("person").property("name", n).next() } returns the vertex v[7], which is no traversal: g.query("add", ..).count() fails with Function not found: count). Return the traversal, or g.v(written) after let written = ...toList();, to let callers continue.
  • Also inside a list or a map: fn pair() { [g.add_v("a"), g.add_v("b")] } writes both and returns two read-only traversals.
  • In the call's unit: a returned traversal that fails rolls back everything the body wrote, and a dry run of the call previews its writes too.
  • The results are kept in memory until the caller reads them, like a toList(): a query that writes millions of elements should end the writing traversal with iterate() and return a count or nothing instead.
  • An anonymous writing traversal (__.add_v("x")) is no query of the graph: returning one fails the call (returned a traversal with a writing step).

Read-only queries

A query of the dialect graphersal-rhai/1 never writes. The call runs under a read-only restriction on top of the host's authorizer: creating, changing or deleting data, the schema, saved queries or files is denied with PermissionDenied (a saved query is read-only) before anything runs, and nested queries inherit it. A traversal ANY query returns carries the restriction too:

g.define_query(#{name: "people", body: "fn people() { g.v().has_label(\"person\") }"})
g.query("people").property("seen", true).toList()
// Error: ... Permission denied for 'property' (Update Data(vertex)): a saved query is read-only: ...

Write in a traversal of your own after the call:

let ids = g.query("people").id().toList();
g.v(ids).property("seen", true).toList();
g.v().has("seen").count().next()
// 4
  • A graph the query builds itself (GraphSource::empty(), __) stays writable; it is not the database.
  • Terminals inside the body (next(), toList()) are allowed: a value-returning query needs them.
  • Nothing built from a query result is mutating (is_mutating() is false); whether a script that calls a query that writes changed the graph is what its run reports (mutated).
  • Stored before queries could write. Opening a database never changes a dialect: a graphersal-rhai/1 query whose body has writing steps (saved by 0.2.0, or through the Rust API or a catalog file, which keep the dialect as given) stays read-only and its writes are denied; g.queries() lists them as denied_writes. Saving the query again makes it one that writes.

Unavailable queries and older versions

A query that cannot run is listed with status: "error" and the reason, and a call fails with Invalid body of saved query: its body does not compile (after an upgrade of the language, or stored through the Rust API), it is a graphersal-rhai/2 query whose effects cannot be inferred, or its dialect is one this version does not know. Such a query never blocks opening a database.

A database written by this version keeps every read-only query in graphersal-rhai/1, so Graphersal 0.2.0 runs them; 0.2.0 lists a query that writes (graphersal-rhai/2) as not runnable ("its dialect is 'graphersal-rhai/2', this version runs 'graphersal-rhai/1'"). A version without saved queries in GQL (0.2.2 and older, or a build without the feature gql) lists a GQL query (graphersal-gql/1, graphersal-gql/2) the same way, keeps it unchanged and writes it back byte for byte; so does this version with a dialect of a newer one (graphersal-gql/3).

Saved queries in GQL

With language: "gql" the body is one GQL query, written as it is, with no g.gql(..) around it and no quotes to escape; $name reads the parameter name:

g.define_query(#{
    name: "older",
    language: "gql",
    params: #{min: #{schema: #{type: "integer"}, default: 30}},
    body: "MATCH (p:person) WHERE p.age > $min RETURN p.name AS name, p.age AS age ORDER BY age"
})
g.query("older").toList()
// [#{"age": 32, "name": "josh"}, #{"age": 35, "name": "peter"}]
g.query("older", #{min: 26}).select("name").toList()
// ["vadas", "marko", "josh", "peter"]
  • Defining checks the query before anything is stored: it parses, binds and plans like a g.gql() call (a GQL error keeps its GQLSTATUS, the caret under the offending text and its Help:, with the line in saved query: "name"), every $name it reads is declared in params and every declared parameter is read. The parameters are stored in the order the query first reads them. The other keys (folder, description, meta) are those of a Rhai query; a GQL body has no doc comment, so description has no default.
  • Calling is the same g.query(name, #{..}) with the same argument checks; the call runs the query like g.gql(body, args) (no Rhai is evaluated) and returns its rows, one map per row, a traversal Gremlin steps may continue (select("name") above).
  • Reads and writes: the dialect comes from the query's plan, graphersal-gql/1 when it writes nothing and graphersal-gql/2 when it writes (INSERT / CREATE, SET, REMOVE, DELETE, MERGE); its effects are the writes of the plan, exact per label (a SET on a node is Update Data(vertex), as for property()). A call is authorized and limited exactly like a Rhai query of the same kind: a read-only query (and any query called from one) cannot write, also not through its result; a query that writes asks its whole effect set of the caller's authorizer first and runs as ONE transaction whose commit names the query and its arguments, then returns a read-only traversal over the rows it produced:
g.define_query(#{
    name: "hire",
    language: "gql",
    params: #{name: "string", company: "string"},
    body: "MATCH (c:software {name: $company}) INSERT (p:person {name: $name})-[:created]->(c) RETURN p.name AS name"
})
g.get_query("hire")["effects"].map(|e| e.text)
// ["Create Data(vertex \"person\")", "Create Data(edge \"created\")"]
g.query("hire", #{name: "ann", company: "lop"}).toList()
// [#{"name": "ann"}]
g.define_query(#{
    name: "birthday",
    language: "gql",
    params: #{name: "string"},
    body: "MATCH (p:person {name: $name}) SET p.age = p.age + 1 RETURN p.age AS age"
})
g.get_query("birthday")["effects"].map(|e| e.text)
// ["Update Data(vertex)"]
  • A Rhai query may call a GQL query (g.query("hire", #{..}) in its body); its effects then include those of the GQL query, as with any called query. A GQL query calls one with CALL folder.name(args) (Calling saved queries from GQL).
  • get_query and queries() show language: "gql" and the dialect; the body is the query text.
  • g.define_queries(folder, source) stays Rhai only: define GQL queries one by one.
  • Every front end below works with GQL queries: the playground's editor has a Rhai / GQL switch, MCP and Python list them with their language and call them like any other.

Calling saved queries from GQL

A GQL query calls a saved query written in GQL with CALL folder.name(args), the procedure call of GQL and Cypher: the segments before the name are the query's folder (joined by /, so CALL people.older() calls older of the folder people, and CALL older() one of the root folder), the arguments are its parameters in order, and YIELD names the columns of its RETURN that the query reads after the call:

g.define_query(#{
    name: "older",
    folder: "people",
    language: "gql",
    params: #{min: #{schema: #{type: "integer"}, default: 30}},
    body: "MATCH (p:person) WHERE p.age > $min RETURN p.name AS name, p.age AS age"
});
g.gql("CALL people.older(26) YIELD name RETURN name ORDER BY name").to_list();
// [#{"name": "josh"}, #{"name": "marko"}, #{"name": "peter"}, #{"name": "vadas"}]
g.gql("CALL people.older(26) YIELD name AS who, age WHERE age < 35 RETURN who ORDER BY who").to_list();
// [#{"who": "josh"}, #{"who": "marko"}, #{"who": "vadas"}]
g.gql("CALL people.older(26) YIELD age RETURN count(age) AS n, max(age) AS oldest").to_list();
// [#{"n": 4, "oldest": 35}]
g.gql("MATCH (s:software) CALL people.older($min) YIELD name RETURN s.name AS sw, name ORDER BY sw, name", #{min: 33}).to_list();
// [#{"name": "peter", "sw": "lop"}, #{"name": "peter", "sw": "ripple"}]: the call runs once per row
  • Arguments are constants or the caller's $parameters (also lists, maps and arithmetic of them), evaluated once when the query is compiled; an argument that reads the row (CALL people.older(s.age)) is not supported yet. They bind the saved query's parameters in the order its query first reads them (g.get_query(name)["params"] lists that order): a query RETURN $a AS a, $b AS b takes a first. Trailing parameters left out take their defaults (CALL people.older() is min: 30). Each argument is checked against its parameter's schema like an argument of g.query(..), with its write coercion (an integer for a number parameter arrives as a float: 42 becomes 42.0); a value that does not fit is an error before the run.
  • YIELD names columns of the saved query's RETURN: YIELD a AS x renames one, every yielded name must be new in the query, and YIELD .. WHERE <condition> filters the rows. Inside a query a call of a saved query that returns columns needs YIELD.
  • Standalone: a call that is the whole query returns every column of the saved query, in its order, with no YIELD or with YIELD *; without parentheses it reads its arguments from the query's parameters of the same names (a missing one takes its default):
g.define_query(#{
    name: "older",
    folder: "people",
    language: "gql",
    params: #{min: #{schema: #{type: "integer"}, default: 30}},
    body: "MATCH (p:person) WHERE p.age > $min RETURN p.name AS name, p.age AS age"
});
g.gql("CALL people.older()").to_list();
// [#{"age": 32, "name": "josh"}, #{"age": 35, "name": "peter"}]
g.gql("CALL people.older YIELD *", #{min: 33}).to_list();
// [#{"age": 35, "name": "peter"}]
  • VOID: a saved query without RETURN (one that ends in a write or in FINISH) returns no columns. Called alone it returns no rows; inside a query it runs once per row and keeps each row once, so the query goes on after it. A saved query that writes is called like any other; its writes are part of the calling query, which is ONE unit (a failure anywhere leaves nothing):
g.define_query(#{
    name: "hire",
    folder: "staff",
    language: "gql",
    params: #{name: "string"},
    body: "MATCH (c:software {name: 'lop'}) INSERT (:person {name: $name})-[:created]->(c)"
});
g.gql("CALL staff.hire('ann')").to_list();   // [] (VOID), and ann is created
g.gql("FOR n IN ['bob', 'cy'] CALL staff.hire('temp') RETURN n").to_list();
// [#{"n": "bob"}, #{"n": "cy"}]: two persons named temp, one per row
g.gql("FOR n IN ['bob', 'cy'] CALL staff.hire('tmp')").to_list();
// []: like a last clause that writes, a VOID call may end the query (zero rows)

  • Yielded nodes and edges keep their properties and labels, and a later pattern may start at one (CALL sw() YIELD s MATCH (s)-->(x) ..); the kind is checked when a row reaches the pattern: NULL gives no row, any other value that is not a node (or edge) is 22G03.

  • A body that is only a call without parentheses (body: "CALL people.older") reads the called query's parameters by name: declare them in the calling query's params.

  • Effects are transitive: a saved GQL query that calls another is checked against the catalog when it is saved (the called query must exist, its arguments fit), and its dialect and effects include those of the queries it calls. A query that only reads but calls one that writes is saved as a query that writes (graphersal-gql/2):

g.define_query(#{
    name: "hire",
    folder: "staff",
    language: "gql",
    params: #{name: "string"},
    body: "MATCH (c:software {name: 'lop'}) INSERT (:person {name: $name})-[:created]->(c)"
});
g.define_query(#{
    name: "onboard",
    folder: "staff",
    language: "gql",
    body: "CALL staff.hire('dan') RETURN 'dan' AS hired"
});
g.get_query("onboard")["dialect"];   // "graphersal-gql/2"
g.get_query("onboard")["effects"].map(|e| e.text);
// ["Create Data(vertex \"person\")", "Create Data(edge \"created\")"]
g.gql("CALL staff.onboard()").to_list();   // [#{"hired": "dan"}]

A call is checked again when the calling query runs: a read-only saved query (graphersal-gql/1) whose plan would write through a call (the called query was changed since) is refused, so no read-only query ever writes.

  • Permissions: a call asks Execute on Definition(query "name"), like g.query(..), and every read and write of the called query is asked of the caller's authorizer, as part of the calling query; under AccessPolicy::read_only() a call of a saved query that writes is denied before anything runs (Permissions).
  • One unit, no commit attribute: unlike g.query(..) of a query that writes, which commits as a unit of its own that names the query and its arguments, a GQL call is part of the calling query's unit, and its commit names no saved query.
  • Only GQL bodies: a saved query written in Rhai cannot be called from GQL in this version (0A000, the help names g.query(name, #{..})); call it with g.query(..) from the DSL, or save it again in GQL. Calls nest at most 16 levels deep (and one query resolves at most 1024 calls in all, 54001); a saved query that calls itself, directly or through others, is an error (42002), since its arguments are constants and the recursion would never end.
  • Names: saved-query names are unique across all folders, so a name found in another folder than the call names gets a "did you mean": CALL older() answers did you mean: CALL people.older. Names are case-sensitive; a folder segment with other characters is back-quoted (CALL `my reports`.top()). The vendor namespaces db, dbms, apoc and gds stay refused (CALL db.labels()).

The errors point at the call:

g.gql("CALL people.older()")   // error: there is no saved query `older` in the folder `people` (42002)
g.gql("CALL db.labels()")   // refused: the vendor procedures of db, dbms, apoc and gds (0A000)

Error: GQL semantic error at line 1, column 22: too many arguments: people.older(min :: integer) takes 1 argument, 2 given ...
Error: GQL data exception at line 1, column 19: the argument for `min` of CALL people.older must be integer: Type mismatch on query 'older.min': expected int64, got string ...
Error: GQL semantic error at line 1, column 25: CALL people.older inside a query names the columns it reads with YIELD: the saved query returns `name`, `age` ...
Help: add YIELD, as in CALL people.older(..) YIELD name, age. CALL folder.name(args) runs the saved query `name` of the catalog folder `folder` ...
Error: GQL construct not supported yet at line 1, column 38: an argument of CALL people.older that reads the row is not yet supported (the variable s is not defined) ...
Help: pass a constant or a $parameter, or write the saved query's pattern in the query itself. CALL folder.name(args) runs ...
Error: GQL construct not supported yet at line 1, column 6: the saved query `rh` is written in Rhai; CALL runs saved queries written in GQL in this version ...
Help: run it from the DSL with g.query("rh", #{..}), or save it again in GQL (language: "gql"). CALL folder.name(args) runs ...

The GQL error reference lists every error of a call.

Errors name the query

An error inside a body keeps its diagnostic and gains one line per call, innermost first:

g.define_query(#{name: "broken", body: "fn broken() { g.v().values(\"name\").as_number(GType.LONG).toList() }"})
g.query("broken")
// Error: Step #2 'as_number(GType.LONG)' execution failed
//   at #2: v().values("name").as_number(GType.LONG)
// ...
// Caused by: Cast exception: expected type [int64], got type 'string'
//   value:  "marko"
//   origin: vertex id="1" label="person" property="name"
//   in saved query: "broken" (line 1, position 58 of its body)
// Help: ...

A missing query, a body that no longer compiles and a call at the wrong position fail with errors naming the query and a Help: line with the fix.

Managing queries

CallResult
g.queries()every saved query as a list of maps, by name
g.queries("reports")the queries in reports and the folders below it (reports/sales, not reportsx)
g.get_query(name) / getQueryone query as a map, () when there is none
g.drop_query(name) / dropQueryremoves it; false when there was none
g.move_query(name, folder) / moveQuerymoves it ("" or (): the root)
g.describe_query(name, text) / describeQuerysets the description ("" or () removes it)
